DE.label: Direct empirical
DE.desc: A finding from observed or measured facial behavior in a primary study, coded from the full text of the report (design and numbers available to the coder). Whether a record was later re-checked against its source is shown separately.

SA.label: Secondary analysis
SA.desc: A new analysis run here on available data (open datasets or tables published with a study). Exploratory unless stated otherwise.

AR.label: Author-reported
AR.desc: A result or interpretation as stated by the original authors, coded from the abstract, a summary or a secondary source; the underlying numbers were not inspected.

RL.label: Review-level
RL.desc: A conclusion of a systematic review, meta-analysis or narrative review.

TH.label: Theoretical
TH.desc: A proposal or prediction from a theory or coding system (for example, a hypothesized configuration) that is not itself a test.

IN.label: Indirect or contextual
IN.desc: Evidence that informs an interpretation without establishing the AU-emotion relation: non-human species, studies of detectors or datasets, display-rule surveys, and similar.

streams.posed: Production, posed: people asked to show an emotion (by label, scenario, muscle instruction or imitation).
streams.spontaneous: Production, spontaneous: faces recorded during an elicited or naturally occurring state, without instructions to show it.
streams.posed vs spontaneous: Direct comparisons of posed and spontaneous expressions, usually within the same people.
streams.perception: Perception: which actions lead observers to attribute a state; says nothing about what the expresser felt.
streams.function: Functions beyond emotion: what actions do for the producer (sensory, effort), in conversation and language, and for perceivers (decisions, approach).
streams.comparative: Comparative: non-human primates (for example, chimpanzees coded with ChimpFACS). Kept out of the readings for human faces; bears on evolutionary questions only.
streams.automated: Studies of automated detectors and classifiers.

meta.physicalSource: Names and muscular basis: FACS manual (Ekman, Friesen, & Hager, 2002), cross-checked with a public FACS summary table (accessed 2026-10-21). Appearance: plain-language paraphrase of FACS appearance criteria; not a substitute for FACS training.
meta.intensity: FACS scores intensity on five levels, A (trace) to E (maximum). Automated detectors report either a probability that the action is present or an intensity estimate on their own scale; neither is a FACS intensity score.

1.name: Inner brow raiser
1.movement: Raises the inner (nose-side) ends of the eyebrows.
appearance: Inner corners of the brows move up; the brows can take an oblique shape, higher at the inner ends.
Short horizontal wrinkles may appear in the centre of the forehead.
Skin above the inner brow is pulled up; the upper eyelid fold can look stretched near the nose.
1.coordination: Often occurs with AU2 (together they raise the whole brow) or with AU4 (brows raised at the inner ends and drawn together, the AU1+4 pattern).
1.confusions: AU1+2 versus AU2 alone; AU1+4 versus AU4 alone. Forehead lines that are permanent can be mistaken for AU1 at low intensity.
1.detector: Usually detected well when the forehead is visible; fringes, glasses and head pitch reduce accuracy.

assoc.state: power appraisal (low vs. high control over outcome)

interp.summary: Inner-brow raising is reported with surprise in spontaneous data and is part of posed surprise and fear. With AU4 it forms the oblique brow; perceivers link it to sadness in naturalistic clips. Brow raises also mark news and responses in conversation.

context.t: Reported surprise predicted AU1 in covert viewing, but the full surprise display was rare; in one small sample spontaneous surprise began with upper-lid raising, an order a later study did not find.
Brow raises were slightly more frequent in responses than in questions and can mark news.
Requested brow raises had faster onsets than spontaneous ones; brow and eyelid movements were less tightly coupled in spontaneous surprise.

alternatives.s: news marking and responses in conversation

distinguish: Whether AU2 and AU5 co-occur (surprise configuration) or AU4 (oblique brow).
Speech and turn-taking context.
Onset speed (V06).

examples.setting: Participant reading an unexpected message
examples.observed: AU1 alone, brief
examples.readings: Consistent with surprise as a single action (S02); conversation-like news marking is another reading (F07).
examples.caution: Most surprised people show no full display (S15); its absence does not mean no surprise.

interp4.summary: Inner-brow raising (AU1) accompanies surprise: reported surprise predicted it when 29 Japanese students watched films alone (odds ratio 3.40), and posers use it for surprise, fear and sadness. Yet only 4–25% of adults meeting surprising events showed brow raising, eye widening or jaw drop in eight experiments, and brow raises are common in conversation.

best.why: Reported surprise predicted AU1 when 29 students watched films alone (odds ratio 3.40).

readings.t: Reported surprise predicted AU1 in 29 Japanese students filmed covertly (odds ratio 3.40); students showed AU1 in 23% of spontaneous surprise.
Japanese posers raised both brows for surprise; in 604 actors' photographs, a cluster of AU1 + AU2 + AU25 poses resembled fear.
Sadness ratings of 39 hidden-camera airport clips rose with AU1 duration; observers unmasking posed faces only tended to use the brows.
In 34 Dutch conversations, brow raises accompanied 25% of responses and 20% of questions; analysts separate raises marking news from mere receipt.
Frontalis (brow-raising muscle) activity rose with mental load in a demanding reaction-time task (EMG; abstract only).

context.t: Across eight experiments, only 4–25% of adults meeting surprising events showed brow raising, eye widening or jaw drop, mostly a brow raise alone.
Students raised inner brows in 57% of posed but 23% of spontaneous surprise; requested brow raises had faster onsets.
On avatars, AU1 alone drew almost no sadness rating (0.8, scale −100 to 100); lip-corner depression (AU15) drew 28.7.

distinguish.t: Co-occurring actions: AU2 and AU5 fit posed surprise; AU4 with AU1 (oblique brows) fits perceived sadness.
Speech: raises while listening or replying often mark news or receipt of information.
Onset speed: in 42 adults, requested brow raises rose faster than spontaneous ones.

examples.setting: Participant reading an unexpected message
examples.observed: Brief AU1 + AU2, no AU5 or jaw drop
examples.readings: Surprise is plausible: rare displays after surprising events were mostly brow raises (S15); marking news is another reading (F07).
examples.caution: Most people meeting surprising events show no brow raise; absence does not rule out surprise.

examples.setting: Video interview, person describing a loss
examples.observed: AU1 with AU4 (oblique brows) and AU15
examples.readings: Observers would likely read sadness, which theory proposes for AU1 + AU4 + AU15; naturalistic sadness ratings rose with AU1 (Q11).
examples.caution: A sad film produced no facial movement in Japanese students (V13).

2.name: Outer brow raiser
2.movement: Raises the outer (temple-side) ends of the eyebrows.
appearance: The lateral part of the brow lifts and arches.
Horizontal wrinkles may appear in the lateral forehead.
Can occur on one side only.
2.coordination: Usually occurs with AU1; AU2 without AU1 is less common.
2.confusions: Unilateral brow raising is often coded as asymmetric AU2.
2.detector: Often detected together with AU1; the two are hard for detectors to separate.

assoc.state: power appraisal (low vs. high control over outcome)

interp.summary: Outer-brow raising usually occurs with AU1. It is part of posed surprise and fear and of perceivers' models, but is rare in spontaneous surprise.

context.t: Brow raising was far more frequent when posing surprise than when surprised.

distinguish: Co-occurrence with AU1 and AU5.
Conversation context.

examples.setting: Video call, the first seconds of the conversation
examples.observed: A brief AU1+AU2 brow flash with a smile as the other person appears
examples.readings: A greeting reading has some support: brow flashes were longer at conversation openings than later in conversations in three populations (S20-030; secondary source), and their meaning varies with culture and relationship (S12-054; review). Brow raises also mark news (F07; abstract only) and were slightly more frequent in responses than in questions in Dutch conversation (F06). Surprise is a weaker reading, since brow raising was rare in spontaneous surprise (S15).
examples.caution: Brow raises follow talk; separate frames by speaker and turn before counting them.

examples.setting: Consumer test, the moment a new product is revealed
examples.observed: AU1+AU2 with AU5 for about half a second
examples.readings: These actions make up posed surprise (P04), but in eight experiments with surprised participants, display components were rare and the full display did not appear (S15). Requested brow raises had faster onsets than spontaneous ones (V06), and frontalis activity also rises with mental load (F03; abstract only).
examples.caution: Absent brow raises do not rule out surprise, and present ones do not confirm it. In a review, more than half of consumer-research studies using FACS did not validate inferred emotions against another measure (M01).

interp4.summary: Outer-brow raising (AU2) occurs mostly with AU1 and accompanies posed surprise and fear: 28 students raised it in 57% of posed surprise, and observers' models use brow raising to mark surprise. Felt surprise seldom shows it (23% of the same students' spontaneous surprise), and brow raises accompany 20–25% of utterances in Dutch conversation.

best.why: Posers raised both brows for surprise; observers' models used brow raising to separate surprise from fear.

readings.t: Sixty-five Japanese posers raised both brows with AU5 and an open mouth for surprise; students raised AU2 in 57% of posed surprise.
In 604 actor photographs, one of 80 data-driven clusters, brow raising with parted lips (AU1 + AU2 + AU25), resembled fear.
In 60 Western observers' dynamic models, AU5 came early in fear and surprise; brow raising (AU1 + AU2) later marked surprise.
In 34 Dutch conversations, brow raises accompanied 25% of responses and 20% of questions; some raises mark news.
Field films in three small-scale societies showed longer brow flashes at conversation openings; their meaning varies by culture (descriptive reports).
Frontalis (brow-raising muscle) activity rose with mental load in a demanding reaction-time task (EMG; abstract only).

context.t: In eight experiments, only 4–25% of adults meeting surprising events showed brow raising, eye widening or jaw drop, mostly brow raising alone.
Students raised outer brows in 57% of posed but 23% of spontaneous surprise; requested raises were faster, larger and shorter.
AU2 usually occurs with AU1, detectors struggle to separate the two, and one-sided raises are often coded as AU2.
In Sign Language of the Netherlands, grammatical brow raises in questions combine with affective brow actions.

distinguish.t: Speech and turn position: raises while talking or replying often mark responses or news.
Openings: a brief raise as someone appears suggests a greeting flash.
Onset: in 42 adults, requested raises were faster, larger and shorter than spontaneous ones.

examples.setting: Video call, first seconds of the conversation
examples.observed: Brief AU1 + AU2 with a smile as the other person appears
examples.readings: A greeting brow flash fits (S20-030); raises also mark news and responses (F06, F07); surprise is a weaker reading (S15).
examples.caution: Brow raises follow talk; align frames with speaker turns before counting.

examples.setting: Consumer test, the moment a new product appears
examples.observed: AU1 + AU2 with AU5 for about half a second
examples.readings: These actions make up posed surprise (P04), but people meeting surprising events rarely show them (S15); requested raises rise faster (V06).
examples.caution: Validate with another measure; over half of 55 consumer FACS studies did not.

4.name: Brow lowerer
4.movement: Lowers the eyebrows and/or draws them together.
appearance: Vertical (sometimes oblique) wrinkles appear between the brows.
The brows move down and toward each other; skin bulges above the inner brow.
The upper eye opening can narrow from above.
4.coordination: Common with AU7 (lid tightening), with AU1 (oblique brows) and with lower-face actions such as AU17, AU23 or AU24.
4.confusions: Different muscle groups produce lowering versus drawing together; shadows and head tilt can imitate low-intensity AU4.
4.detector: One of the more reliably detected actions; low intensities are frequently missed or confused with resting brow shape.

assoc.state: expectation violation (schema-discrepant information; authors frame as a negative-affect account of surprise)

interp.summary: Brow lowering is produced in posed anger, accompanies effort, pain and concentration, marks questions in conversation and sign language, and leads perceivers to infer unpleasantness or anger. It is linked to many states and functions in the evidence base.

context.t: Corrugator activity rose with mental load and physical effort; upper-face anger actions were excluded from one stress study because they also mark concentration.
Most brow frowns in Dutch conversation accompanied questions; furrowed brows mark wh-questions in ASL.
Brow lowering is part of the pain configuration and appears with disgust as well.
Posers lowered their brows in nearly all anger portrayals.
AU4 alone led observers to infer unpleasantness and anger.

alternatives.s: questions in conversation and sign language
confusion and worry in everyday settings

distinguish: Whether the person is working on a task, speaking, or asking a question (F06).
Co-occurring actions: AU7 and AU23/24 versus AU1 versus AU9/10 (P02, S22).
Duration: brief frowns during speech versus sustained lowering.
Task difficulty, physiological effort measures and self-report.

examples.setting: Student solving arithmetic problems on screen
examples.observed: Sustained AU4 with AU7
examples.readings: Effort and concentration are well-supported readings (F03, S25); anger is one possibility but has weak spontaneous evidence.
examples.caution: Compare with task difficulty and errors before inferring an emotion.

examples.setting: Interviewer asking a question
examples.observed: Brief AU4 at the end of the question
examples.readings: Questions are a documented context for brow frowns (F06).
examples.caution: Speech context matters; separate frames by talk turns.

interp4.summary: Brow lowering (AU4) accompanies unpleasant or effortful states: it was pain-related in about 80% of 37 FACS pain studies, rose with disgust pictures, negative imagery and mental or physical effort, and alone it led observers to infer anger. It is not specific: in Dutch conversation, 71% of 1,269 brow frowns accompanied questions.

best.why: AU4 alone led observers to infer unpleasantness; corrugator (AU4 muscle) activity rose with unpleasant imagery.

readings.t: On avatars, AU4 alone led observers to infer unpleasantness; corrugator (AU4 muscle) activity rose with angry, disgusting and sad imagery (abstracts).
Pain-related in about 80% of 37 FACS studies (pain versus rest); it rose across four experimental pain types in 41 adults.
Corrugator activity rose with mental load and physical effort (EMG; abstracts); a stress study set aside upper-face codes that also mark concentration.
Pooled across 60 Quebec and Gabon posers, 90% showed AU4 when posing anger; on avatars, AU4 alone drew observers' highest single-action anger rating.
In 34 Dutch conversations, 71% of 1,269 brow frowns accompanied questions; in American Sign Language, furrowed brows obligatorily mark wh-questions.

context.t: AU4 appeared in 28% of disgust-picture and 24% of heat-pain segments (60 adults); pain added orbit tightening (AU6/AU7) more often.
When 95 young adults relived anger, brow lowering or one-sided lip actions appeared in 25% versus 18% at rest (p = .27).
Quebecois posers lowered brows for sadness and contempt, whereas Gabonese posers mostly moved the head for sadness.
In sign languages the same brow lowering serves grammar in questions and affect, and the two combine.

distinguish.t: With AU4, orbit tightening (AU6/AU7) marked heat pain; AU9/AU10 with AU4 marked disgust pictures.
Task demands: AU4 rising with difficulty or exertion favours effort over an emotional reading.
Speech: a brief frown during a question marks the question.

examples.setting: Student solving arithmetic problems on screen
examples.observed: Sustained AU4 with AU7, no other actions
examples.readings: Effort or concentration fits (F03, S25); unpleasantness is possible (Q09); relived anger barely raised anger-related actions (S23).
examples.caution: Compare with task difficulty and errors before inferring an emotion.

examples.setting: Interviewer asking a question
examples.observed: Brief AU4 at the end of the question
examples.readings: Question marking: 71% of 1,269 brow frowns in Dutch conversation came with questions (F06).
examples.caution: Separate frames by speaker turn before counting frowns.

5.name: Upper lid raiser
5.muscles: Levator palpebrae superioris (with the superior tarsal muscle)
5.movement: Raises the upper eyelid, widening the eye opening.
appearance: More of the eyeball is exposed above the iris; the upper lid fold may disappear.
The eyes look wider; at high intensity white may show above the iris.
5.coordination: Often occurs with AU1+2; can co-occur with AU4 or AU7.
5.confusions: Head pitch and eye shape change how much white shows; looking up widens the eye without AU5.
5.detector: Low base rate in most recordings; small changes are hard to detect at typical video resolution.

interp.summary: Upper-lid raising is central in perceivers' models of fear and surprise and appears early in them. In spontaneous data it predicted reported fear and tension during films that did not target fear, and it led spontaneous surprise in one small sample, an order not replicated. Posed eye widening also widened the expresser's visual field.

context.t: Observers relied on the eye region and AU5 for fear; AU5 appears early in fear and surprise models.
AU5 predicted reported fear and tension in films that did not target fear; it led spontaneous surprise in six displays, an order a later study did not find.
Posed eye widening enlarged the visual field and improved peripheral detection.

alternatives.s: fear and tension (spontaneous; films not targeting fear)
surprise (posed; spontaneous onset in one small sample)

distinguish: Head pitch and gaze direction (looking up widens the eyes).
Co-occurring AU1+2 and mouth opening.
Duration and timing.

examples.setting: Driver monitoring camera
examples.observed: Brief AU5 with head up
examples.readings: Looking toward something above eye level or a startle are both possible; fear is one of several readings.
examples.caution: Detectors are sensitive to head pose for AU5.

interp4.summary: Upper-lid raising (AU5) accompanies fear and surprise: it predicted reported fear and tension when 29 Japanese students watched films alone, appeared in 36% of spontaneous and 75% of posed surprise, and observers rely on it for both. Only a minority of adults meeting surprising events widen their eyes, and looking up or head pitch can mimic it.

best.why: AU5 predicted reported fear and tension in covert film viewing; observers rely on AU5 for fear.

readings.t: In 29 Japanese students filmed covertly, AU5 predicted reported fear and tension, although none of the four films targeted fear.
Students widened their eyes in 36% of spontaneous and 75% of posed surprise; Japanese posers raised upper lids for surprise.
On avatars, AU5 alone led observers to infer unexpectedness and surprise; fear judgments needed several actions together.
Fear ratings of 39 hidden-camera airport clips rose with AU5 duration; with posed faces, observers relied most on the AU5 region.
Eye widening enlarged the subjective visual field and improved peripheral discrimination by 9.4% (posed, laboratory; abstracts).

context.t: Only a minority of adults widened their eyes after surprising events: 21–33% after an engulfing surprise, fewer in eight milder experiments.
Looking up and head pitch change how much white shows, and small AU5 changes are hard to detect in video.
Gabonese posers most often combined AU4 with AU5 for anger, so AU5 also marks some posed anger.
Trobriand adolescents matched a wide-eyed gasping face (AU1 + AU2 + AU5 + AU26) to anger and threat, not fear; a commentary agreed, citing local art.

distinguish.t: In observers' models AU5 comes early in fear and surprise alike; later brow actions separate the two.
AU4 with AU5 occurred in posed anger; AU1 + AU2 with AU5 in posed surprise.
Gaze and head pitch: the eyes look wider when looking up, without AU5.

examples.setting: Driver monitoring camera
examples.observed: Brief AU5 while the head tilts up
examples.readings: Looking up can mimic AU5; observers infer surprise from AU5 alone (Q07), fear only from more actions (Q10).
examples.caution: Head pose changes apparent eye opening; detectors are sensitive to it.

6.name: Cheek raiser
6.movement: Raises the cheeks and gathers skin toward the eye from below and from the sides.
appearance: Wrinkles may fan out from the outer eye corners (crow's feet).
The lower eyelid area is pushed up and the eye opening narrows from below.
The outer end of the brow may be pulled down slightly.
6.coordination: Very often occurs with AU12. Together, AU6+AU12 is the configuration called the Duchenne smile.
6.confusions: A strong AU12 alone also raises the cheeks, which is the main reason AU6 is hard to code; AU7 also narrows the eye.
6.detector: Detectors partly track smile intensity when estimating AU6, so AU6 and AU12 outputs are strongly correlated.

assoc.state: power appraisal (low vs. high control over outcome)

interp.summary: Cheek raising is the marker that, with AU12, defines the Duchenne smile. It is read by perceivers as a sign of genuineness in smiles, but it also occurs in deliberate smiles, tracks smile intensity, and accompanies stronger cry-faces as well as stronger smiles in infants.

context.t: Its association with rated amusement (one item asking about happiness, joy and amusement) largely reflected the intensity of lip-corner pulling.
Cheek raising occurred in deliberate smiles as often as in amused smiles, but in a smaller share of requested than spontaneous smiles in another study.
In infants it accompanied stronger cry-faces as well as stronger smiles; observers read it as intensity in sad faces.
Smiles with cheek raising are judged more positively; removing it lowered perceived happiness only slightly; models placed it in the dominance smile.
Duchenne smiles occurred more when sharing resources with a friend, without a change in reported emotion, and among judo winners almost only during interaction.

distinguish: The intensity of AU12 at the same moment (S07).
Whether AU7 or AU4 co-occur, as in pain (S34).
The timing of onset relative to AU12 (V06).
The situation and self-report.

examples.setting: Customer reacting to a product sample
examples.observed: AU6 + AU12 at high intensity
examples.readings: A strong smile. The presence of AU6 adds little beyond intensity in some data (S07) and occurs in deliberate smiles (V10).
examples.caution: Do not label it as a felt or genuine smile on the basis of AU6 alone.

interp4.summary: Cheek raising (AU6) mostly accompanies smiling: in 34 women watching films alone, time in AU6 + AU12 smiles correlated with rated amusement (r = .70) and happiness (r = .59), and it appears in posed happiness. It also tracks intensity: controlling smile strength cut its link with amusement by 64%, and it accompanies pain, infant cry-faces and deliberate smiles.

best.why: Smiles with AU6 accompanied amusement and happiness, though AU6 largely tracks smile intensity.

readings.t: In 34 women watching films alone, AU6 + AU12 smile duration correlated with amusement (r = .70) and happiness (r = .59).
In 136 people's spontaneous smiles, AU6's link with a happy-joyful-amused rating fell 64% once AU12 intensity was controlled.
Among 174 judo winners, AU6 + AU12 smiles came almost only during interaction (8 of 8; 23 of 25).
Orbit tightening (AU6 and AU7 pooled) was pain-related in about 80% of 37 FACS studies; observers' pain models include AU6.
In 12 infants, AU6 accompanied 70% of cry-faces while the parent stayed unresponsive (still-face); authors read it as affective intensity.
Smiles with AU6 are rated more positively (meta-analysis); botulinum toxin removing AU6 cut perceived happiness by 0.11 (0–8 scale).

context.t: One study found AU6 as often in deliberate as in amused smiles; another, in 56% of requested and 97% of spontaneous smiles.
Korean adults showed more intense AU6 in film-elicited smiles and more intense AU12 in posed smiles (automated estimates).
Observers read AU6 as genuineness in smiles but only as intensity in sad faces (abstract only).
A strong AU12 alone raises the cheeks, and detectors partly track smile intensity when scoring AU6.
Sixty people smiled with AU6 + AU12 more while sharing resources with a friend; reported emotion did not differ (abstract).

distinguish.t: AU12 strength at the same moment: once smile intensity is known, AU6 adds little about amusement.
AU4, AU7 or AU9/AU10 with AU6 and no AU12 point to pain or disgust rather than a smile.
Social setting: interaction predicted AU6 + AU12 smiles better than winning a medal.
Onset speed: requested smiles had faster onsets than spontaneous ones in 57 adults.

examples.setting: Customer tasting a product sample
examples.observed: AU6 + AU12 at high intensity
examples.readings: A strong smile; enjoyment is plausible, but AU6 adds little beyond smile intensity (S07) and appears in deliberate smiles (V10).
examples.caution: Do not label a smile felt or genuine on AU6 alone.

examples.setting: Patient moving a painful shoulder in a clinic
examples.observed: AU6 with AU4 and AU9, no AU12
examples.readings: Pain fits: orbit tightening alone or with brow lowering made up nearly two-thirds of heat-pain responses (S22).
examples.caution: Pain studies pool AU6 with AU7, so coders may not separate them.

7.name: Lid tightener
7.movement: Tightens the eyelids, narrowing the eye opening.
appearance: The lower lid rises and straightens; the lid margin can bulge.
The eye opening narrows without the cheek raising of AU6.
7.coordination: Common with AU4 and in squinting; often present during effortful looking.
7.confusions: Confused with AU6 and with squinting in bright light (AU44).
7.detector: Some detectors report AU7 at high rates in neutral faces; check its base rate in your own data.

interp.summary: Lid tightening is part of pain responses and of posed anger; perceivers relied on it for anger in one masking study.

context.t: Orbit tightening is a core pain action.
Posed anger combined AU4 with AU5 or AU7.

distinguish: Bright light and squinting.
Co-occurring AU4 and AU9/10.

examples.setting: Physiotherapy assessment of an older adult moving a painful joint
examples.observed: AU7 with AU4, AU6 and AU9 during the movement, absent at rest
examples.readings: Pain is well supported. Orbit tightening (AU6 and AU7 pooled) was pain-related in more than 70% of 37 FACS studies (S35; review), and lid tightening belongs to a pain index that rose from baseline during a movement-based exam in 102 older adults (S10-033). The same review notes that AU6/7 also occurs in disgust and anger (S10-011).
examples.caution: Pain faces vary: responses to heat pain fell into four patterns plus a group with no facial response (S36; abstract only). A missing AU7 does not rule out pain.

examples.setting: Customer-service video call, agent listening to a complaint
examples.observed: AU4+AU7 held for several seconds
examples.readings: Viewers may read anger: posed anger often combined AU4 with AU5 or AU7 (P02), and perceivers relied on lid tightening for anger (Q01). Production evidence is weaker: actors' anger portrayals matched the hypothesized configuration only weakly (P10), and in one recall study anger-related actions were not more frequent than at rest (S23). Brow lowering also accompanies effort and concentration (F03, abstract only; S25).
examples.caution: Treat anger as one reading among several; consider the task and what the agent says next.

interp4.summary: Lid tightening (AU7) accompanies pain: pooled with AU6, it was pain-related in about 80% of 37 FACS studies and appeared in 52% of heat-pain segments in 60 adults. It also occurs with disgust pictures (31%) and in posed anger, and observers rely on it for anger.

best.why: Lid tightening, pooled with AU6, was pain-related in about 80% of 37 FACS studies.

readings.t: Pain-related (with AU6) in about 80% of 37 FACS studies; lid tightening rose across four experimental pain types in 41 adults.
In 60 adults, orbit tightening (AU6/AU7) appeared in 31% of disgust-picture segments versus 52% of heat-pain segments.
Posers in Quebec and Gabon combined brow lowering (AU4) with AU5 or AU7 for anger.
Ninety-four observers unmasking two posed faces relied most on the AU7 region to recognise anger.
In 29 students filmed covertly, reported contempt predicted AU7, but contempt and disgust ratings correlated at r = .83.

context.t: Squinting in bright light (AU44) and cheek raising (AU6) narrow the eyes; some detectors report AU7 at high rates in neutral faces.
Observers' pain models in two cultures lacked lid tightening, although published pain productions include it.
Heat-pain faces of 240 adults fell into four patterns plus a group with no facial response (abstract).
Eye-region movements tracked pain's sensory side, brow lowering and upper-lip raising its unpleasantness (22 adults; abstract).

distinguish.t: AU9/AU10 with AU7 points to pain or disgust; AU4 + AU7 alone fits both heat pain and posed anger.
Lighting and gaze: squinting at bright light or a screen narrows the eyes without pain or anger.
Timing: AU7 during a painful movement but absent at rest favours pain.

examples.setting: Physiotherapy assessment, older adult moving a painful joint
examples.observed: AU7 with AU4, AU6 and AU9 during movement, absent at rest
examples.readings: Pain is well supported: in 102 older adults, a pain score built on these actions rose during a movement exam (S10-033).
examples.caution: Pain faces vary (S36); a missing AU7 does not rule out pain.

examples.setting: Customer-service call, agent listening to a complaint
examples.observed: AU4 + AU7 held for several seconds
examples.readings: Viewers may read anger (Q01), but relived anger barely raised anger-related actions (S23); concentration is another reading (S25).
examples.caution: Treat anger as one reading; consider what the agent says next.

8.name: Lips toward each other
8.movement: Pulls the lips toward each other when the mouth is open.
appearance: The lips move toward each other with the jaw lowered.
8.confusions: Rarely coded outside detailed FACS coding.

9.name: Nose wrinkler
9.movement: Wrinkles the skin along the sides and bridge of the nose.
appearance: Wrinkles appear along the sides and top of the nose; the nostril wings lift.
The upper lip is pulled up; the inner brow can be pulled down.
9.coordination: Often occurs with AU10, and AU4 can accompany it.
9.confusions: AU9 versus AU10: both raise the upper lip; nose wrinkling is the distinguishing sign.
9.detector: Moderate base rate in disgust tasks, low elsewhere; detectors often confuse AU9 and AU10.

interp.summary: Nose wrinkling accompanied reported disgust in one horror-film study, whereas upper-lip raising did in a covert film study; it appears early in perceivers' models of disgust and anger, and it is part of pain responses.

context.t: Disgusted viewers of a horror film wrinkled the nose and did not raise the upper lip, whereas in a covert film study AU10 was common and AU9 rare.
Much production evidence comes from EMG over the levator region, which covers AU9 and AU10.
Pain and disgust recruited the same actions.

distinguish: Upper-lip raising (AU10) without nose wrinkling.
Eye closure and orbit tightening (pain).
Chemosensory context (tastes, smells).

examples.setting: Sensory lab, participant tasting a bitter drink sample
examples.observed: Brief AU9 just after the sip, without AU10
examples.readings: Distaste is a supported reading: EMG over the levator region rose to unpleasant tastes (S19), and perceivers matched nose wrinkling mainly to bad smells and less to bad tastes (S05-004; abstract only). A review reports nose wrinkling to sweet, salty, sour and bitter tastes, so it may not mark dislike specifically (S12-056; review).
examples.caution: Social presence changed levator responses in two studies (S38, S39; abstract only). In a review, more than half of consumer-research studies using FACS did not validate inferred emotions (M01); ask for liking ratings.

examples.setting: Wound-care clinic, patient during a dressing change
examples.observed: AU9 with AU4 and AU6/7
examples.readings: Both pain and disgust are supported readings: the two recruited brow lowering, orbit tightening and nose wrinkling or upper-lip raising alike, differing mainly in intensity and combination (S22). Nose wrinkling or upper-lip raising (pooled) was pain-related in more than 70% of studies in one review (S35), which notes that it also occurs in disgust (S10-012).
examples.caution: The face alone may not separate pain from disgust here; ask the patient and note smells and sights in the room.

interp4.summary: Nose wrinkling accompanied reported disgust in 8 of 22 horror-film viewers, and, pooled with AU10, rose with pain in over 70% of 37 reviewed FACS studies. In 60 adults exposed to both, AU9/AU10 appeared in 8 per 100 five-second segments of pain and 11 of disgust, so AU9 alone may not separate them.

best.why: Observers read AU9 alone as disgust; production links to disgust and pain are thin or pooled.

readings.t: 8 of 22 horror-film viewers reporting disgust wrinkled the nose; levator EMG (AU9/AU10) rose to bad tastes and contamination photos.
Pooled with AU10, rose above baseline in over 70% of 37 FACS pain studies and across four pain types in 41 people.
On avatars, AU9 alone drew a disgust rating of 32 (-100 to 100) from 29 Geneva students (Scherer et al., 2018).
AU9 came early in both disgust and anger in 60 Western observers' dynamic face models, and alone drew anger ratings of 26.4.
Observers matched nose wrinkling mainly to bad smells (Rozin et al., 1994; abstract); newborns also showed it to sweet tastes (review).

context.t: Pain studies and levator EMG count AU9 and AU10 together, so their figures do not isolate nose wrinkling.
An observing experimenter amplified disgust-related EMG to odours (20 people); an unfamiliar observer reduced levator activity to food images (70 people).
Five-country posers included AU9 in disgust, but 65 Japanese posers showed less of it for scenarios than when copying photos.
In 720 social drinkers' three-person conversations, AU9 occurred less often after alcohol than after placebo or control drinks (automated coding).

distinguish.t: Orbit tightening (AU6/AU7), alone or with AU4, marked pain; AU4 with AU9/AU10 marked disgust.
Timing: observers separated disgust from anger only after AU9, by later upper-lip and brow actions.
The situation: tastes, smells or contamination suggest disgust; a painful stimulus to the person suggests pain.

examples.setting: Wound-care clinic, patient during a dressing change
examples.observed: AU9 with AU4 and AU6/AU7, held for several seconds
examples.readings: Pain or disgust: both recruited these; AU6/AU7 dominated pain, AU4 with AU9/AU10 disgust (Kunz et al., 2013).
examples.caution: Smells and sights can add disgust; ask the patient.

examples.setting: Taste test, participant sipping a bitter drink
examples.observed: Brief AU9 just after the sip, without AU10
examples.readings: Distaste fits: levator EMG rose more to bitter, salty and sour than sweet drinks in 27 people (Chapman et al., 2009).
examples.caution: Newborns in some studies wrinkled the nose to sweet tastes; collect liking ratings.

10.name: Upper lip raiser
10.movement: Raises the upper lip, the centre more than the corners.
appearance: The upper lip lifts; the upper part of the nasolabial furrow deepens.
The upper teeth may show; at high intensity the lips part.
10.coordination: Often occurs with AU9; AU10 with AU25 is common.
10.confusions: Confused with AU9 and with AU12 when the lip corners also rise.
10.detector: Frequently reported by detectors during speech and smiling; check rates against a neutral baseline.

interp.summary: Upper-lip raising predicted reported disgust in one covert film-viewing sample and was much more frequent there in spontaneous than posed disgust; in a horror-film study disgusted viewers wrinkled the nose instead. It also accompanies pain and can occur in speech.

context.t: AU10 appeared in half of spontaneous but almost no posed disgust expressions in one sample.
In a horror-film study, none of 22 disgusted viewers raised the upper lip, and 8 wrinkled the nose.
An unfamiliar observer reduced levator activity to food; an audience amplified disgust-related EMG to odors.

distinguish: Nose wrinkling (AU9), eye closure (pain), speech.
What the person is tasting, smelling or seeing.

examples.setting: Economic-game experiment with facial EMG, participant receiving an unfair offer
examples.observed: Activity over the levator labii rises after the offer appears
examples.readings: Disgust is a supported reading in this setting: levator activity rose to unfair offers, unpleasant tastes and contamination photographs (S19) and to purity and fairness violations (S20). It did not rise to heretical thoughts that participants called disgusting (S21; abstract only).
examples.caution: A single EMG site over the levator region covers both AU9 and AU10 (S19).

examples.setting: Video interview, speaker answering "no, that is not what happened"
examples.observed: AU10 with AU4 and AU17 during the negation
examples.readings: A "not face" built from a subset of AU4, 7, 9, 10, 14, 17 and 24 accompanied negation in English, Spanish and Mandarin (S20-027; abstract only), so the speech act is a documented context. Disgust (S03) and anger as read by perceivers (Q11) remain possible.
examples.caution: Align the actions with the transcript; the negation evidence is abstract-level.

interp4.summary: Upper-lip raising accompanied reported disgust in one covert film study of 29 Japanese students (odds ratio 2.65), appearing in 14 of 28 spontaneous but 1 of 28 posed disgust expressions. Yet none of 22 horror-film viewers reporting disgust raised the upper lip, and, pooled with AU9, it also rises with pain.

best.why: Reported disgust predicted it in covert film viewing; observers read AU10 alone as disgust.

readings.t: Reported disgust predicted AU10 at film apexes of 29 covertly filmed Japanese students (odds ratio 2.65; Namba, Kabir, et al., 2017).
Pooled with AU9, rose with pain in over 70% of 37 studies; tracked unpleasantness while orbit tightening tracked intensity (22 adults).
Quebec and Gabon posers used AU10 for contempt; in Japanese students AU10 predicted higher contempt ratings (not the reverse), and contempt and disgust ratings correlated .83.
AU10 alone on avatars drew a disgust rating of 32.4 (-100 to 100); in observers' models it later separated disgust from anger.
Its duration predicted observers' anger ratings of 39 hidden-camera clips of airline passengers, in an exploratory analysis (Hyniewska et al., 2019).
Raising the infraorbital region, an AU10 sign, on a neutral computer face made it look physically stronger to 86% of 141 students.

context.t: Horror-film viewers reporting disgust wrinkled the nose (8 of 22) but never raised the upper lip; Japanese film viewers showed the reverse.
Japanese students raised the upper lip in 14 of 28 spontaneous but 1 of 28 posed disgust expressions.
Spontaneous disgust included lip-corner pulling (AU12) in 6 of 28 Japanese students, so a smile does not rule disgust out.
An unfamiliar observer reduced levator activity to food images in 70 adults; an observing experimenter amplified disgust-related EMG to odours.
Levator EMG rose to unfair offers and to purity and fairness violations (39 adults), but not to heretical thoughts rated disgusting.

distinguish.t: Nose wrinkles mark AU9; surface EMG over the levator region cannot separate AU9 from AU10.
Orbit tightening (AU6/AU7), alone or with AU4, marked pain; AU4 with AU9/AU10 marked disgust.
Timing: in observers' models AU10 came after AU9 and helped separate disgust from anger.
Ask about the situation: contempt and disgust ratings overlapped (r = .83) in the film study.

examples.setting: Economic game with facial EMG, responder sees unfair offers
examples.observed: Levator-region activity rises as offers become less fair
examples.readings: Disgust-like rejection is supported: in 16 responders, levator activity rose with unfairness and disgust was endorsed more than anger.
examples.caution: One EMG site covers AU9 and AU10; anger was endorsed too.

11.name: Nasolabial deepener
11.movement: Pulls the upper lip up and out a little, deepening the middle of the nasolabial furrow.
appearance: The middle of the furrow between nose and mouth deepens.
11.coordination: Can occur with AU12 or AU10.
11.confusions: Hard to separate from AU10 and AU12 even for trained coders.
11.detector: Treat automated AU11 outputs with caution; some detectors return values near 0 or 1 for it.

interp.summary: Nasolabial furrow deepening has little evidence in this base. One pain study summarized earlier work as linking it to pain only occasionally and less reliably than the core pain actions, and observers' mental models of pain included it although the published pain productions they were compared with did not. A critical review lists it in the "common view" sadness configuration.

context.t: The introduction of one pain study summarized earlier spontaneous studies as finding nasolabial deepening only occasionally and less reliably with pain, possibly as part of a reaction separate from the core pain actions (S10-034). In neonatal surgical patients, deepened nasolabial folds were one sign in a combination that separated painful from non-painful stimuli (S18-022; abstract only, coded interpretively as AU11).

Western observers' mental models of pain included AU11, but the published Western pain productions they were compared with did not (Q12). On synthetic avatars, AU11 alone drew a low disgust rating (7.9 on a -100 to 100 scale) against about 32 for AU9 or AU10 alone (Q09, from the study's key numbers).
A critical review lists AU11 in the "common view" configuration for sadness (AU1+4+11+15+17) (review).

alternatives.s: pain (spontaneous; less reliable than the core pain actions; neonatal evidence abstract only)
pain (perceivers' mental models; absent from the productions compared)

distinguish: AU10 and AU12: AU11 is hard to separate from them even for trained coders (physical layer), and one naturalistic perception study reported "upper lip raiser/nasolabial deepener" as a single predictor (S14-058).
Whether the core pain actions co-occur: brow lowering, orbit tightening, and nose wrinkling or upper-lip raising (S35; review).

Detector output: AU11 was one of 19 actions in an evaluation of three detectors on conversation data, where accuracy varied by action and system (S16-043); some detectors return values near 0 or 1 for AU11 (physical layer).

examples.setting: Pain observation in a long-term care facility, video of a resident during a care routine
examples.observed: AU11 flagged together with AU4, AU6/7 and AU9/10
examples.readings: The pain evidence rests on the other actions: brow lowering, orbit tightening and nose wrinkling or upper-lip raising were pain-related in more than 70% of 37 FACS studies in one review (S35). AU11 adds little; it was described as less reliably linked to pain (S10-034) and was absent from the published pain productions compared in Q12.
examples.caution: Check AU11 against AU10 and AU12 by eye before using it; automated AU11 values can be unreliable.

interp4.summary: Nasolabial furrow deepening has almost no direct evidence: earlier pain studies found it only occasionally, less reliably than the core pain actions (AU4, AU6/AU7, AU9/AU10, AU43), and observers' pain models included it though published pain productions did not. It is hard to separate from AU10 and AU12, even for trained coders.

best.why: Occasionally linked to pain, less reliably than AU4 or AU6/AU7; observers' pain models include it.

readings.t: Earlier pain studies found it occasionally and less reliably than AU4, AU6/AU7, AU9/AU10 or AU43 (Browne et al., 2019).
Deepened nasolabial folds were one sign in a combination that flagged pain in 93 neonatal surgical patients (abstract only).
40 Western observers' pain models included AU11, but 11 published pain-production studies did not (Chen et al., 2018).
Barrett et al. (2019) give two 'common view' sadness configurations; one includes AU11 (AU1 + AU4 + AU11 + AU15), the other AU17 instead.

context.t: Hard to separate from AU10 and AU12 even for trained coders; some detectors return values near 0 or 1 for it.
On synthetic avatars, AU11 alone drew a disgust rating of 7.9 (-100 to 100), against 32.0 and 32.4 for AU9 and AU10.
Coders marked AU11 in 41% of BP4D+ frames, with the lowest agreement of any action, .59 on a 0 to 1 index.

distinguish.t: Co-occurring AU4, AU6/AU7 and AU9/AU10 carry the pain evidence; AU11 adds little on its own.
Inner-brow raising (AU1) with AU4, AU15 and AU17 would match the sadness configuration of theory.
Check by eye: AU10 lifts the centre of the upper lip, AU12 pulls the corners up and back.

12.name: Lip corner puller
12.movement: Pulls the lip corners up and back at an angle.
appearance: The lip corners rise obliquely; the nasolabial furrow deepens.
At higher intensity the cheeks rise and the eye opening narrows, which can mimic AU6.
Can occur on one side only (unilateral AU12).
12.coordination: Often with AU6; frequently with AU25 or AU26 when the mouth opens.
12.confusions: AU12 versus AU13 and AU14; asymmetric smiles may be coded as unilateral AU12 or AU14.
12.detector: Among the most reliably detected actions; speech can produce brief lip-corner movements.

assoc.state: power appraisal (low vs. high control over outcome)

interp.summary: Lip-corner pulling accompanied amusement and reported happiness in spontaneous production, though not every positive state, and perceivers rely on it for happiness. In field studies it depended heavily on social engagement; it also accompanies distress and embarrassment, and requested and spontaneous smiles unfold differently over time.

context.t: Smiling rose sharply when people interacted with others and was rare when they were happy but alone or facing away; judo winners smiled with cheek raising almost only during interaction. Hockey fans, however, also smiled after favorable events.
Smiles occurred during distressing films (most in social conditions) and as part of embarrassment displays.
Requested smiles had faster onsets and were more irregular; lip-corner pulling was more intense in posed smiles.
How often posers combined AU12 with AU6 differed between Quebec and Gabon.
Perceivers rely on AU12 for happiness; smiles with an open mouth that are larger, longer and faster are read as amused rather than polite.
Smiling photographs increased acceptance of ultimatum offers; effects of smiles on trust were mixed.

alternatives.s: happiness inferred from winning (spontaneous; findings conflict)
pride, with head tilted back (read by authors)
pain (part of some pain responses; observers' pain models)

distinguish: Whether cheek raising (AU6) accompanies it, keeping in mind that a strong AU12 raises the cheeks too (S07, V10).
Onset speed, duration and regularity of the smile (V06, V07, V08, Q14).
Co-occurring actions such as AU24 or AU14 (controlled or asymmetric smiles) and gaze or head down (S33).
Whether the person is talking with or looking at someone (S09, S10).
Self-report, the situation and other modalities such as voice and words.

examples.setting: Video call, participant listening to a colleague
examples.observed: AU12 at moderate intensity with AU25, short and repeated, timed with the speaker's pauses
examples.readings: Consistent with listener feedback or politeness in conversation; also with amusement. Evidence for the conversational reading is indirect (smiling depends on interaction: S09, S10).
examples.caution: Detector output alone cannot separate these; check timing against the partner's speech.

examples.setting: Participant watching a distressing film in the lab, with an experimenter present
examples.observed: Brief AU12 during the most distressing scenes
examples.readings: Smiling during distress has been reported, more in social conditions (S46); amusement is not the only candidate.
examples.caution: Ask for ratings of distress and amusement before interpreting.

interp4.summary: Lip-corner pulling accompanies amusement most reliably: in a meta-analysis, 60% of amused people smiled or laughed, the highest rate of any emotion tested, and observers read it as happiness. It also accompanied embarrassment, frustration and pain, and happy bowlers and fans smiled mainly while interacting (probability .70 to .78, against .07 to .09 otherwise).

best.why: Smiling or laughter accompanied amusement in 60% of people, the highest rate in a meta-analysis.

readings.t: 60% of amused people smiled or laughed across lab studies (meta-analysis); AU12 predicted reported amusement in 29 covertly filmed Japanese students.
Happy bowlers and soccer fans rarely smiled outside interaction; 8 of 55 and 25 of 119 judo winners showed AU6 + AU12.
AU12 alone drew happiness ratings of 38.4 (-100 to 100) on avatars, and 94 observers relied on the mouth for happiness.
70% of embarrassed versus 32% of amused smiles came with lower-face controls (AU14, AU15, AU17 or AU24; 35 and 28 people).
About 90% of participants smiled during frustrating interactions; their smiles were shorter and weaker than delighted ones (Hoque et al., 2012).
AU12 was the commonest action in a shoulder-pain video archive, yet rose with pain in only a minority of 37 FACS studies.

context.t: 22 gold medalists smiled with AU6 during 48% of the medal presentation, about 3% of the waiting and never during the anthem.
In 64 students, zygomatic EMG rose when a friend was believed to be watching elsewhere; reported happiness did not change.
Judo gold medalists smiled within 15 s (13 of 14); in 5 to 7 s windows few winners showed AU6 + AU12.
Requested smiles had faster onsets and included AU6 in 56% versus 97% of spontaneous smiles (57 adults; Schmidt et al., 2009).
In 136 people, AU6's link to self-rated amusement fell by 64% once AU12 intensity was controlled (Girard et al., 2019).

distinguish.t: Smiles judged amused rather than polite more often had AU6 and an open mouth (AU25/AU26).
Dynamics: amused-looking smiles were larger, faster and longer (about 4 s versus 2 s for polite ones).
Gaze down, then smile controls (AU14, AU15, AU17, AU24), then head down marked embarrassment.
Frustrated smiles lasted 7.45 s versus 13.84 s for delighted ones, at lower intensity (47.38% vs 76.26%).

examples.setting: Video call, participant listening to a colleague
examples.observed: Short, repeated AU12 with AU25, timed to the speaker's pauses
examples.readings: Listener feedback or politeness are candidates besides amusement: in field studies, smiling tracked interaction more than reported happiness.
examples.caution: Align smiles with the partner's speech before inferring a feeling.

examples.setting: Usability test, a form keeps rejecting the user's input
examples.observed: Several brief, weak AU12 smiles while the user retries
examples.readings: Frustration fits: about 90% of participants smiled when frustrated, with shorter, weaker smiles than in delight (Hoque et al., 2012).
examples.caution: Read smiles with task logs and self-report, not alone.

13.name: Sharp lip puller
13.movement: Pulls the lip corners up sharply, narrowing the lips near the corners.
appearance: The corners rise steeply and the cheeks below the corners puff out.

14.name: Dimpler
14.movement: Tightens the lip corners and pulls them inward, creating dimple-like wrinkles beyond the corners.
appearance: The corners tighten and may angle slightly upward; dimples or wrinkles form beside them.
Can occur on one side only.
14.coordination: Common with AU12 and AU24, and during speech.

interp.summary: Dimpling, especially on one side, is part of the contempt expression matched above chance in forced-choice studies but not with other response formats.

context.t: Matching held in forced-choice studies, was replicated in four non-American cultures, and failed with other formats; Matsumoto and Ekman (2004) attributed such failures to the word "contempt".

distinguish: Asymmetry and AU12 co-occurrence.
Speech.

examples.setting: Repeated clinical interviews during treatment for depression
examples.observed: More AU14, including during smiles, in high-severity than in low-severity sessions
examples.readings: This matches two reports on one clinical interview sample (18 and 19 patients analysed), in which AU14 rose with symptom severity, also during smiles (S07-007, S07-013). The authors read less AU12 and AU15 with more AU14 as nonverbal social withdrawal (S07-011, S07-017). Contempt is a perceivers' reading under forced choice (Q24; abstract only) that failed with other response formats (Q25; abstract only).
examples.caution: Within-patient comparisons in small samples; AU14 is not a diagnostic marker.

examples.setting: Rating study, judges label photographs of a one-sided lip curl
examples.observed: Most judges choose "contempt" from a list of emotion words
examples.readings: Forced-choice matching to contempt replicated across cultures (Q24, Q37), but contempt was not the main label with free labeling or rating scales (Q25, S05-027), and the same face was labeled disgust or sadness in other judgment contexts (S05-024, S05-025). All these sources were checked at abstract level only.
examples.caution: The result reflects the response format as much as the face; it says nothing about what the expresser felt.

interp4.summary: Dimpling is tied to contempt mostly by judgment studies: observers in 10 cultures picked 'contempt' for a one-sided lip curl (unilateral AU12 + AU14) from fixed word lists, and posers in five countries used AU14 for contempt. With free labels the match failed, and spontaneous AU14 rose with depression severity and accompanied controlled smiles.

best.why: Five-country posers used it for contempt; observers chose 'contempt' mainly from fixed word lists.

readings.t: Observers in 10 cultures matched a one-sided lip curl to 'contempt' from fixed lists; four more cultures replicated it (abstracts).
With free labels or rating scales, observers did not choose contempt; in other judgment contexts they called the face disgust or sadness.
Posers from five countries portrayed contempt with AU4 + AU14 + AU25 (Cordaro et al., 2018).
Judo silver medalists facing officials after losing combined smiles with AU14, AU17 or AU24, which the authors read as regulation.
In repeated clinical interviews (two reports, 18 and 19 patients), AU14 was more frequent at high severity, also during smiles.
Over 70% of 158 people posing negation used AU4 + AU17 with AU14 or AU24; spoken negation rarely showed it.

context.t: Contempt judgments concern a one-sided lip curl; two-sided AU14 alone on avatars drew happiness ratings of 30.0 (-100 to 100).
In 720 social drinkers' three-person conversations, AU14/AU15 occurred less often after alcohol than after other drinks (automated coding).
FaceReader matched manual FACS poorly on AU14 in posed portrayals (F1 score .11 of a possible 1; Skiendziel et al., 2019).
Reliving anger did not raise AU4 or one-sided AU10, AU12 or AU14 above rest (25% vs 18% of 95 students).

distinguish.t: Asymmetry: the contempt reading concerns one-sided AU14 (with AU12); two-sided AU14 during a smile suggests control.
AU4 with AU17 and AU14 or AU24 while saying 'no' matches the posed negation face.
Gaze down, smile controls and head down point to embarrassment rather than contempt.

examples.setting: Repeated clinical interviews during depression treatment
examples.observed: More AU14, including during smiles, in high-severity sessions
examples.readings: Social withdrawal, the authors' reading: two reports on 18 and 19 patients found less AU12 and AU15 and more AU14.
examples.caution: Within-patient change in small samples; not a diagnostic marker.

15.name: Lip corner depressor
appearance: The corners angle down; the lower lip may stretch horizontally.
Wrinkles or bulges can appear below the corners.
15.coordination: Often with AU17; with AU1 and AU4 in some configurations.
15.confusions: Resting mouth shape can look like slight AU15.
15.detector: Moderately reliable; low intensities are hard to separate from resting shape.

interp.summary: Lip-corner depression is part of hypothesized sadness and contempt configurations; posed sadness in one sample used chin raising and brow lowering more than AU15.

context.t: Gabonese posers combined upper-lip raising with lip-corner depression for contempt.
In one sample AU15 appeared in 4% of posed sadness expressions.

distinguish: Resting mouth shape.
AU17 co-occurrence.

examples.setting: Repeated clinical interviews during treatment for depression
examples.observed: AU15 becomes less frequent as symptoms worsen
examples.readings: In one clinical interview sample (19 patients analysed), AU15 was less frequent at high than at low symptom severity (S07-008), with a non-significant trend in the same direction in another report on the same sample (S07-014). This runs against the hypothesized role of AU15 in sadness; the authors read reduced AU12 and AU15 with more AU14 as social withdrawal (S07-011).
examples.caution: Neither the presence nor the absence of AU15 indicates sadness on its own.

examples.setting: Designing a sad expression for a virtual character
examples.observed: AU15 alone on the character's otherwise neutral face
examples.readings: Perceivers gave AU15 alone the highest sadness ratings among single actions on synthetic avatars (Q36), so viewers may read the character as sad. Production evidence is weaker: in one sample, AU15 appeared in 4% of posed sadness expressions (V13).
examples.caution: Perception evidence describes viewers' inferences, not how sad people move their faces.

interp4.summary: Observers read lip-corner depression as sadness more than any other single action (28.7 on -100 to 100, synthetic avatars), and it belongs to the configuration proposed for sadness (AU1 + AU4 + AU15). Production data are thin: 1 of 28 Japanese students' posed sadness expressions included it, and patients showed less as depression worsened.

best.why: Observers rate AU15 alone as sad; production evidence is mostly posed and mixed.

readings.t: Of single actions on synthetic avatars, AU15 drew the highest sadness rating, 28.7 on -100 to 100, from 29 Geneva students.
Korean and US posers added AU15 to sadness (Cordaro et al., 2018); 1 of 28 Japanese students did in another study.
In 5 studies, 28% of people in sadness conditions showed AU1 + AU4 + AU15 whole or in part (meta-analysis).
Gabonese posers combined AU10 with AU15 or AU17 for contempt; Quebec posers used AU4 with AU10 (Elfenbein et al., 2007).
Lower-face controls (AU14, AU15, AU17 or AU24) accompanied 70% of embarrassed and 32% of amused smiles (35 and 28 people).
AU1 and AU15 were the strongest predictors of a classifier's correct sadness labels across 14 databases (model R² = .48).

context.t: In repeated interviews of 19 patients, AU15 was less frequent at high than at low severity, against its proposed role in sadness.
Coders marked AU15 in 1.7% of 397,800 frames of YouTube videos (Aff-Wild2), so detections are rare events.
A resting mouth shape can look like slight AU15, and low intensities are hard to tell from rest.
AU14/AU15 occurred less often after alcohol in 720 social drinkers' three-person conversations (automated coding; Sayette et al., 2012).

distinguish.t: Inner-brow raising (AU1) and brow lowering (AU4) complete the configuration proposed for sadness (AU1 + AU4 + AU15).
A smile (AU12) with AU15 points to a controlled smile, as in embarrassment, rather than sadness.
With AU10 rather than brow actions, AU15 matched Gabonese posers' contempt.

examples.setting: Designing a sad expression for a virtual character
examples.observed: AU15 alone on an otherwise neutral face
examples.readings: Viewers will probably read sadness: AU15 alone drew the highest sadness rating of single actions on avatars (Scherer et al., 2018).
examples.caution: This shows viewers' inferences, not how sad people move their faces.

16.name: Lower lip depressor
appearance: The lower lip lowers and may stretch sideways; lower teeth may show.
16.confusions: Confused with AU25 and AU26 during speech.

interp.summary: Lower-lip depression is documented mainly in posed portrayals. In one five-culture study it was part of the open-mouthed smile in posed amusement and in posed happiness, and in one actor study it was among the actions coded across portrayals of five emotions. It appears in theoretical disgust configurations, but an animated disgust prototype that included it was rarely judged as disgust; no spontaneous production record links it to a state.

context.t: In one five-culture study of free-response portrayals, "lower lip and jaw dropped" was a core action, with a Duchenne smile and parted lips, in posed amusement and in posed happiness (S11-032, S11-045). The study was re-checked only against its abstract (P12).

In one actor study of hot anger, panic fear, elation, sadness and pride portrayals (10 actors per emotion), AU16 was among the coded actions, and the authors' controllability framework classed it as "reliable" rather than "versatile". Most actions in that study were associated with several emotions rather than one.

Darwin's description of disgust (coded interpretively) and a FACS-based guide (secondary source) include lower-lip depression (theory). On synthetic avatars, the full AU9+15+16 disgust prototype drew a near-floor disgust rating (5.3 on a -100 to 100 scale), well below AU9 or AU10 alone (S14-063, S14-064).
In an exploratory perception study of hidden-camera clips, the authors linked lower-lip depression to observers' ratings of fear and of goal obstruction (authors' conclusion).

alternatives.s: amusement and happiness, with an open-mouthed Duchenne smile (posed; one five-culture study)
portrayals of several emotions, without specificity (posed; one actor study)
disgust (theory; an animated prototype was not read as disgust)
fear and goal obstruction (perceivers; naturalistic clips; exploratory)

distinguish: Speech: AU16 is confused with AU25 and AU26 during speech (physical layer); separate talk from non-talk frames.
Co-occurring actions: AU6+AU12 with jaw drop, as in posed amusement and happiness (S11-032, S11-045), versus nose wrinkling and lip-corner depression, as in theoretical disgust (S01-012).
Few detectors output AU16 (physical layer); manual coding may be needed.

examples.setting: Lab study of people watching comedy clips
examples.observed: AU16 with AU6, AU12, AU25 and AU26 during the funniest scenes
examples.readings: The configuration matches the open-mouthed smile of posed amusement and posed happiness in one five-culture study (S11-032, S11-045). Spontaneous evidence on amusement in this base concerns AU12 and AU6 (S01, S06), not AU16, so AU16 adds little beyond an open-mouthed smile.
examples.caution: AU16 is easily confused with AU25 and AU26; ask viewers how amused and how happy they felt rather than reading either state from the mouth.

interp4.summary: Lower-lip depression has no spontaneous evidence in this evidence base; five-country posers used it in the open-mouthed smile (AU6 + AU12 with AU16 and AU25) portraying amusement and happiness. Theory places it in disgust; an avatar showing the authors' full disgust prototype, whose actions appear only in the paper's supplement, drew a disgust rating of 5.3 (-100 to 100).

best.why: Posed only: part of the open-mouthed smile portraying amusement and happiness in five countries.

readings.t: Above chance in amusement and happiness portrayals in each of five countries, with AU6 + AU12 and parted lips.
Analysed in 50 actor portrayals of five emotions, where most actions went with several emotions rather than one.
Its duration predicted observers' fear and goal-obstruction ratings of 39 hidden-camera clips, a link the authors had not predicted (exploratory).
Darwin and a FACS guide include it in disgust; an avatar showing the authors' full disgust prototype (actions unverified) drew a disgust rating of 5.3.

context.t: Easily confused with lips parting and jaw drop (AU25, AU26) during speech; separate talking frames first.
Few automated detectors output AU16, so it may need manual coding.
It usually comes with lips parting (AU25); in posed amusement it came with jaw drop and head tilted up.

distinguish.t: With AU6 + AU12 and an open mouth, it matches the posed amusement and happiness smile.
The FACS Investigator's Guide puts it in disgust with AU9 or AU10 and parted lips or jaw drop (AU25/26); the avatar prototype's actions are unverified.
During speech, check whether the lower lip moves only with articulation before coding AU16.

examples.setting: Lab study, people watching comedy clips
examples.observed: AU16 with AU6, AU12, AU25 and AU26 at the punchlines
examples.readings: Matches the open-mouthed smile of posed amusement; spontaneous amusement evidence concerns smiling and laughter (60% of amused people), not AU16.
examples.caution: AU16 adds little beyond the smile and is confused with AU25/AU26.

17.name: Chin raiser
17.movement: Pushes the chin boss and the lower lip up.
appearance: The chin skin wrinkles or dimples; the lower lip pushes up and may protrude.
17.coordination: Common with AU15, AU24 and AU23.
17.confusions: Confused with AU24 (lip pressing) and with chin shape.
17.detector: Moderately reliable; frequently active during speech pauses.

interp.summary: In one sample chin raising was the most frequent action in posed sadness and appeared in posed but not spontaneous disgust. It can also occur in speech.

context.t: In one Japanese sample, posed disgust included AU17 in a quarter of cases and spontaneous disgust in none.
AU17 appeared in 36% of posed sadness expressions in the same sample.

distinguish: Speech context.
AU15 and AU24 co-occurrence.

examples.setting: Training an emotion classifier on a database of requested expressions
examples.observed: AU17 is frequent in clips labeled sad and disgusted
examples.readings: This matches posed data: in one Japanese sample, AU17 was the most frequent action in posed sadness (36%) and appeared in a quarter of posed but in no spontaneous disgust expressions (V13, V02).
examples.caution: Cues learned from posed data may not transfer: classifiers and observers were less accurate on spontaneous than on posed expressions (Q26, Q27).

examples.setting: Televised debate, candidate listening to an opponent
examples.observed: AU17 with AU24 for several seconds, without speech
examples.readings: Perceivers judged synthetic faces with a raised chin as physically stronger (S04-013), and in an exploratory study of hidden-camera clips, chin raising was associated with observers' ratings of goal obstruction (S14-062, Q11). These results concern impressions. In one five-culture study, AU17 was a culture-specific addition to posed anger in China, India and Japan (S11-055, S11-056, S11-057).
examples.caution: Perception evidence is not evidence about the candidate's state; check for speech and negation (S20-027; abstract only).

interp4.summary: Chin raising appears mostly in posed negative portrayals: Japanese students used it in 36% of 28 posed sadness and 25% of 28 posed disgust expressions, but in none of their spontaneous disgust. Observers barely read AU17 alone as sad (1.9 on -100 to 100), and it also appears in posed negation and in smile control.

best.state: not specific to any state; posed sadness and negation are candidates
best.why: The commonest action in 28 students' posed sadness (36%) and in posed negation; absent from spontaneous disgust.

readings.t: The commonest action in 28 Japanese students' posed sadness (36%), and a sadness addition for posers in four of five countries.
7 of 28 posed but none of 28 spontaneous disgust expressions included it; the authors suggest it marks posed negative expressions.
Over 70% of 158 people posing negation combined AU4 + AU17 with AU14 or AU24; spoken negation rarely showed it.
Its duration predicted observers' ratings that a goal was blocked, in 39 hidden-camera clips of airline passengers (exploratory).
A raised chin on a neutral computer face looked physically stronger to 78% of 141 students (Sell et al., 2014).
Published pain productions included AU17, but 40 Western observers' pain models did not (Chen et al., 2018).

context.t: 65 Japanese posers showed less AU17 in scenario-based anger and disgust than when imitating photographs (automated coding).
Chinese, Indian and Japanese posers added AU17 to anger; Gabonese posers used it, with AU10, for contempt.
Lower-face controls (AU14, AU15, AU17 or AU24) accompanied 70% of embarrassed and 32% of amused smiles (Keltner, 1995).
On avatars AU17 alone drew a sadness rating of 1.9 (-100 to 100) and lowered rated pleasantness.

distinguish.t: AU4 with AU24 or AU14 while saying 'no' matches the posed negation face.
With a smile (AU12), AU17 acts as a smile control; adding gaze and head down suggests embarrassment.
How it was elicited: frequent in requested displays, absent in the same students' spontaneous disgust.
Speech pauses: detectors often report AU17 then, so check it against the audio.

examples.setting: Training a classifier on a database of requested expressions
examples.observed: AU17 is frequent in clips labelled sad and disgusted
examples.readings: Consistent with posed data: 36% of posed sadness and 25% of posed disgust included it, but no spontaneous disgust did.
examples.caution: Humans and a classifier did worse on spontaneous clips (Krumhuber et al., 2021).

examples.setting: Televised debate, candidate listening to an opponent
examples.observed: AU17 with AU24 for several seconds, without speech
examples.readings: Viewers may infer strength or a blocked goal: raised chins looked stronger on synthetic faces and predicted goal-obstruction ratings in passenger clips.
examples.caution: These are viewers' impressions, not evidence of the candidate's feelings.

18.name: Lip pucker
18.movement: Pulls the lips toward the centre, puckering them.
appearance: The lips push forward and narrow, as in a kiss.

interp.summary: Lip puckering has very little evidence in this base: one posed record (relief, in a five-culture study), one theoretical pain configuration in a review, and a detector evaluation. On synthetic faces, perceivers rated it alone as moderately pleasant.

context.t: In one five-culture study, the core sequence for posed relief combined a smile, lips puckered and apart, jaw drop, drooping eyelids and the head moving up or down (S11-049). The study was re-checked only against its abstract (P12).
On synthetic avatars, AU18 alone received a mean pleasantness rating of 27.0 on a -100 to 100 scale, below AU13 and AU12 (Q08, from the study's key numbers).
A review from a basic emotion theory perspective lists AU18 in a configuration for pain.

alternatives.s: relief, with a smile and jaw drop (posed; one study)

distinguish: AU18 versus AU22, funneling (physical layer).
The rest of the face: a smile with jaw drop and drooping lids, as in posed relief (S11-049), versus tight eye closure and nose wrinkling, as in the theoretical pain configuration (S01-035; review).
Few detectors output AU18 (physical layer); it was one of 19 actions in one detector evaluation (S16-043).

examples.setting: Usability test, participant learns that a long upload has finally succeeded
examples.observed: AU18 with AU12 and AU25, and drooping eyelids
examples.readings: This resembles the posed relief sequence of one five-culture study (S11-049), and perceivers rated AU18 alone as moderately pleasant on synthetic faces (Q08). Both sources are thin: one posed study and one perception study.
examples.caution: No spontaneous study in this base links AU18 to relief; ask the participant before using that label.

interp4.summary: In relief portrayals by 120 people, lip puckering exceeded chance in all five countries studied, and a review of 37 pain studies noted it more in clinical than experimental pain. That is one posing study and one passing note in a review, and few detectors output the action.

best.state: not specific to any state; relief (posed) and pain are candidates
best.why: One posing study and one review note link it to relief and clinical pain.

readings.t: Relief portrayals by 120 people in five countries shared smiling (AU12), puckered parted lips (AU18 + AU25) and drooping lids (AU43).
A review of 37 pain studies saw lip puckering more in clinical than experimental pain; a basic-emotion review lists it for pain.
Geneva students rated an avatar showing AU18 alone 27.0 for pleasantness (−100 to 100), below AU13 (47.9) and AU12 (43.7).

context.t: Few detectors output lip puckering, so its absence from detector output says little.
The pleasantness rating comes from avatars and describes what observers infer, not what people who pucker feel.

distinguish.t: Lips pushed forward and narrowed, as in a kiss (AU18), versus lips turned outward in a funnel (AU22).
Smile and drooping lids (AU12, AU43) point to posed relief; brow lowering and nose wrinkling (AU4, AU9), to theorized pain.

examples.setting: Usability test, a long upload finally succeeds
examples.observed: AU18 with AU12, AU25 and drooping lids (AU43)
examples.readings: Resembles the posed relief core of one five-country study (S11-049); observers rated AU18 alone 27.0 for pleasantness on avatars (−100 to 100).
examples.caution: No spontaneous study links AU18 to relief; ask the participant.

19.name: Tongue show
appearance: The tongue is visible between the lips.

20.name: Lip stretcher
appearance: The lip corners pull straight out to the sides; the mouth elongates and flattens.
Neck tendons can tense.
20.coordination: Can occur with AU25 or AU26.
20.confusions: Confused with AU12 at low intensity and with mouth shapes in speech.
20.detector: Low base rate in most data; some detectors return values near 0 or 1 for it.

interp.summary: Lip stretching is part of hypothesized fear configurations and of perceivers' pain models; in infants, stronger lip stretching in cry-faces accompanied cheek raising.
distinguish: Mouth shapes in speech.

examples.setting: Pediatric clinic, infant during a routine vaccination
examples.observed: Cry-face with AU20 and an open mouth, together with AU6
examples.readings: In an archival sample of 24 infants, cry-faces with eye constriction were common in the first 10 seconds after vaccination, as they were during a still-face episode in a sample of 12 infants (S02-032, S02-031). The authors call this distress and read eye constriction as a sign of intensity in both smiles and cry-faces (S47).
examples.caution: Small samples; these studies do not separate pain from distress.

examples.setting: Archive of everyday online video coded automatically
examples.observed: Occasional AU20 detections across many hours of video
examples.readings: AU20 was rare in manually annotated in-the-wild video (2.9% of frames; S16-033) and in a study of group conversation, where it was the only negative-affect action that alcohol did not reduce, which the authors attributed to its rarity (S02-036). Perceivers' pain models include lip stretching (Q12).
examples.caution: Manual coders agreed only weakly on AU20 in one naturalistic corpus (Q11, study notes); validate detections before interpreting them.

interp4.summary: Lip stretching marks infant cry-faces (32% of time with an unresponsive parent versus 11% in play, 12 infants) and appears in pain portrayals and observers' pain models; theory proposes it for fear. It is rare in YouTube video (2.9% of annotated frames) and hard to code (coder agreement kappa .21 to .40).

best.state: not specific to any state; distress, pain or fear
best.why: Infant cry-faces, pain portrayals and pain models include it; fear rests mainly on theory.

readings.t: Cry-faces (AU20) filled 32% of time with an unresponsive parent versus 11% in play (12 infants), and 50% after vaccination (24 infants).
Pain portrayals in five countries shared furrowed brows (AU4), tightly closed eyes (AU6, AU7, AU43) and stretched, parted lips (AU20, AU25).
Western and Chinese observers' models of pain faces (80 observers) shared AU4, AU6, AU9, AU10 and lip stretching (AU20).
In several fear combinations of the FACS Investigator's Guide, such as AU1 + AU2 + AU4 + AU5 + AU20 with mouth opening, or AU5 + AU20.
Lip stretching helped predict observers' shame ratings of airport videos, and joined AU4 and AU43 in a low-valence pattern in observers' animated-face models.

context.t: Coded in 2.9% of annotated YouTube frames; in group conversation, alcohol did not change it, which the authors attributed to rarity.
Certified coders agreed on AU20 at only kappa .21 to .40 (1 is perfect) in hidden-camera videos (Hyniewska et al., 2019).
Browne et al. (2019) call lip stretching occasionally but less reliably pain-related; a 37-study review saw it more in clinical pain.
Across 14 video databases, AU5 and AU20 best predicted automated fear recognition, the weakest of six emotion models (R2 = .38).
Japanese posers (n = 65) stretched the lips less for a fear scenario than when imitating a fear photograph.

distinguish.t: Eye constriction (AU6) and open mouth fit infant cry-faces; raised brows and lids (AU1 + AU2 + AU5) fit the fear proposal.
Brow lowering with narrowed or closed eyes (AU4, AU6, AU7, AU43) fits pain portrayals and observers' pain models.
Lips stretched sideways and flattened (AU20) versus corners rising obliquely (AU12); check the audio for speech.

examples.setting: Pediatric clinic, infant during a routine vaccination
examples.observed: Cry-face with AU20 and an open mouth, plus AU6
examples.readings: Matches the cry-faces that filled half of the first 10 s after vaccination in 24 infants (S02-032); the authors call this distress and read AU6 as intensity (S47).
examples.caution: Small samples; these studies do not separate pain from distress.

examples.setting: Automated coding of everyday online video
examples.observed: Occasional AU20 detections
examples.readings: Expect few true events, since AU20 was in 2.9% of annotated YouTube frames (S16-033) and hand coders agree on it poorly (kappa .21 to .40).
examples.caution: Hand-check detections before reading pain, distress or fear.

21.name: Neck tightener
