appearance: Neck cords and skin tense.

22.name: Lip funneler
appearance: The lips turn outward into a funnel shape, as in saying "sh".

interp.summary: Lip funneling has no posed or spontaneous production record linking it to a state in this base. It appears in theoretical anger configurations; with synthetic faces, it was among the early actions in observers' dynamic expression models, and observers judged a face with lips pushed forward as physically stronger. FACS also describes it in speech sounds such as "sh".

context.t: Lip funneling is part of hypothesized anger configurations (theory), and Darwin's descriptions of contempt and disgust were coded interpretively as including it.
On computer-generated faces, 80% of participants judged the face with lips pushed forward as physically stronger when the faces were young (n = 141), and 70% when they were older (n = 132).
In Western observers' dynamic models built from synthetic faces, AU22 peaked early, with AU5, AU9 and AU27, carrying coarse information shared across emotions.
ChimpFACS prototypes of the chimpanzee pant-hoot and pout include AU22; this bears on cross-species structure, not on human states (non-human primates).

alternatives.s: coarse early signal in dynamic expression models (perceivers; synthetic faces)

distinguish: Speech: FACS describes funneled lips in sounds such as "sh" (physical layer); check the audio.
AU22 versus AU18, puckering (physical layer).
Co-occurring brow lowering, lid tightening and lip pressing, as in theoretical anger (S01-016, S04-008).
Few detectors output AU22 (physical layer); it was one of 19 actions in one detector evaluation (S16-043).

examples.setting: Recorded negotiation between two business teams
examples.observed: AU22 with AU4 and AU24 while one negotiator listens to an offer
examples.readings: Theoretical anger configurations include this combination (S01-016, S04-008), but no human production study in this base tested it. Perceivers judged synthetic faces with lips pushed forward as physically stronger (S04-014); that concerns how the face may be seen, not what the negotiator feels.
examples.caution: Rule out speech first; treat any emotion reading as a hypothesis.

interp4.summary: Lip funneling shapes speech sounds such as "sh" (FACS); theory lists it with AU4, AU5, AU23 and AU24 for anger, and 80% of 141 observers judged avatars with lips pushed forward as physically stronger. No production study in the evidence base links it to any state.

best.state: speech articulation, as in "sh"; no state tested
best.why: FACS describes it in "sh"; only theory and avatar studies tie it to anger or strength.

readings.t: FACS describes the funnel shape in speech sounds such as "sh"; in talking video, check the audio first.
Two theoretical anger faces include it with AU4, AU5, AU23 and AU24 (Matsumoto & Ekman, 2008; Sell et al., 2014); untested in production.
Lips pushed forward on avatars looked physically stronger to 80% of 141 viewers (young faces) and 70% of 132 (older faces).
In Western observers' dynamic avatar models, AU22 peaked early with AU5, AU9 and AU27, carrying information shared across emotions.

context.t: On avatars, a combination with lip funneling (AU4 + AU10 + AU22 + AU27), predicted to signal confrontation, was read as "not wanted" instead.
Few detectors output lip funneling; one test of three detectors in group conversation included it among 19 actions.

distinguish.t: Lips turned outward in a funnel (AU22) versus pushed forward and narrowed, as in a kiss (AU18).
An "sh"-type sound at the same moment points to articulation.
Brow lowering and lid tightening with lip tightening (AU4, AU7, AU23) would match the theoretical anger faces.

examples.setting: Recorded negotiation, one negotiator listening to an offer
examples.observed: AU22 with AU4 and AU24
examples.readings: Only theory links this combination to anger (S01-016, S04-008); avatars with lips pushed forward looked stronger to observers (S04-014), which concerns impressions, not feelings.
examples.caution: Rule out speech first; treat any emotion reading as a hypothesis.

23.name: Lip tightener
appearance: The red parts of the lips narrow and the lip edges become firmer.
23.coordination: Common with AU4, AU17 and AU24.

interp.summary: Lip tightening predicted reported sadness in one spontaneous sample and is part of hypothesized anger configurations.
distinguish: AU24 versus AU23.
Speech context.

examples.setting: Automated analysis of recorded team meetings
examples.observed: Frequent AU23 detections during discussion
examples.readings: In one evaluation of three detectors on conversation data, AU23 was the worst-detected action (AUC about .56 for all systems) (S16-043), so many detections may be errors. Sadness (S05) and anger (P10) become readings to consider only after detections are confirmed.
examples.caution: Hand-code a sample of frames before using AU23 output.

examples.setting: Lab study, participants watching films alone under covert recording
examples.observed: AU23 during several films, more often in participants who later report sadness
examples.readings: This matches one covert-viewing sample in which reported sadness predicted lip tightening across films (S05, S12-009), although the sad film itself produced no facial movement in that sample (S05).
examples.caution: Single sample; the finding was not predicted by the hypothesized sadness configurations (S12-009).

interp4.summary: Lip tightening is part of the configuration proposed for anger (AU4 + AU5 + AU7 + AU23) and of some anger portrayals, but the only spontaneous study of it alone linked it to sadness (29 students filmed covertly). In conversation, three detectors found it the hardest of 19 actions (AUC about .56; .5 is chance).

best.state: not specific to any state; anger is most often proposed
best.why: Anger theories and portrayals use it; the only spontaneous study of it alone found sadness.

readings.t: In the configuration proposed for anger (AU4 + AU5 + AU7 + AU23); 30 Quebec posers' anger variants included lip tightening or pressing.
In 29 Japanese students watching four films alone, covertly recorded and FACS-coded, lip tightening (AU23) in the peak frame predicted higher sadness ratings.
Geneva students rated the authors' full anger prototype on an avatar 65.2 for anger (−100 to 100); whether it included AU23 is unverified (supplement only).

context.t: All or part of AU4 + AU5 + AU7 + AU23 appeared in 35% of people in anger conditions (meta-analysis of 5 studies).
Japanese posers (n = 65) tightened and pressed the lips less for an anger scenario than when imitating an anger photograph.
Across 14 video databases, AU4, AU7 and AU23 best predicted automated anger recognition (R2 = .65).
Thinned lips (AU23 + AU24) made young avatars look stronger to 71% of 141 viewers in a two-way choice; for older avatars 52% was chance.

distinguish.t: Red lips narrowed with firm edges (AU23) versus lips pressed together (AU24); detectors confuse the two.
With brow lowering, upper-lid raising and lid tightening (AU4 + AU5 + AU7) it forms the set proposed for anger.

examples.setting: Automated analysis of recorded team meetings
examples.observed: Frequent AU23 detections during discussion
examples.readings: Many may be errors, since three detectors scored AU23 the hardest of 19 actions in conversation (AUC about .56; S16-043).
examples.caution: Hand-code a sample of frames before using AU23 output.

examples.setting: Lab study, participants watch films alone, recorded covertly
examples.observed: AU23 more often in participants who later report sadness
examples.readings: This matches one sample of 29 students in which lip tightening predicted higher sadness ratings (S12-009), although the sad film itself produced no facial movement there (S05).
examples.caution: Single small sample; the configuration proposed for sadness (AU1 + AU4 + AU15) does not include AU23.

24.name: Lip pressor
appearance: The lips press together and narrow; skin may bulge above and below the lips.
24.detector: Moderately reliable; common in pauses between words.

interp.summary: Lip pressing occurred in spontaneous embarrassment as part of a smile controlled by lower-face actions (one study), and it appears in posed anger in some cultures and in theoretical anger configurations. Perceivers' models placed it in the affiliative smile, and in clinical interviews it did not change with depressive symptom severity. A negation display in speech and sign language includes it (abstract only).

context.t: In one spontaneous study, embarrassment produced downward gaze, a smile controlled by lower-face actions and head movement down, differing from amusement in frequency and timing (S33). A review describes the sequence gaze down, lip press, non-Duchenne smile and face touch (S08-035; review).

In one perception study of unrequested smiles, lower-face smile controls, lip pressing among them, were more frequent in smiles judged amused than in smiles judged polite, and did not separate amused from embarrassed or nervous smiles (S03-003). Data-driven models of U.S. perceivers placed AU24, with AU12 and AU14, in the affiliative smile (Q18, from the study's key numbers).

Quebecois posers' anger variants included lip pressing or tightening (S15-025), and lip pressing was a culture-specific addition to posed anger in China, India and Japan in one five-culture study (S11-055, S11-056, S11-057). Japanese posers showed less AU24 when portraying anger from a scenario than when imitating photographs, and more AU24 in scenario-based fear (S11-116, S11-118).

Alone on an avatar, AU24 drew a low anger rating (8.9 on a -100 to 100 scale) against 47.8 for AU4 (Q09, from the study's key numbers). Thinned lips (AU23+24) made young, but not older, computer-generated faces look physically stronger (S04-015).
In two reports on one clinical interview sample (18 and 19 patients analysed), AU24 did not change between sessions of high and low depressive symptom severity.

A "not face" built from a subset of AU4, 7, 9, 10, 14, 17 and 24 accompanied negation in English, Spanish and Mandarin, and serves as a grammatical marker of negation in American Sign Language (abstract only).

alternatives.s: embarrassment, within a controlled smile (spontaneous; one study; review)
negation in speech and sign language (abstract only)
perceived strength, with lip tightening (perceivers; young synthetic faces only)

distinguish: AU24 versus AU23 and AU28 (physical layer).
Whether a smile accompanies it, and whether gaze and head go down (S33).
Speech: negation (S20-027; abstract only) and pauses between words (physical layer).
Co-occurring AU4 and AU7, as in posed anger variants (S15-025).

examples.setting: Online job interview, candidate receives a compliment
examples.observed: Gaze down, then AU12 with AU24, then head down
examples.readings: This order matches spontaneous embarrassment in one study (S33). In one perception study, smile controls were more frequent in smiles judged amused than in smiles judged polite, and they did not separate amused from embarrassed or nervous smiles (S03-003).
examples.caution: The perception result describes observers' judgments; the smilers' experience was not measured.

examples.setting: Video of a Deaf signer using American Sign Language
examples.observed: AU4 with AU14, AU17 and AU24 during a signed sentence that contains negation
examples.readings: In ASL this "not face" is described as a grammatical marker of negation, and in some constructions as its only marker (S20-028; abstract only). Brow actions also carry grammar in ASL questions (F08; abstract only). An anger, disgust or contempt reading would ignore this documented use.
examples.caution: The evidence is abstract-level; consult a fluent signer before interpreting.

interp4.summary: Lip pressing is common in pauses between words and in controlled smiles: lower-face "smile controls" appeared in 83% of 35 spontaneous embarrassment displays versus 48% of 28 amusement displays. Those counts pool it with AU14, AU15 and AU17, and its anger links rest on theory and portrayals in some cultures.

best.state: not specific to any state; often a speech pause or a smile control
best.why: Common between words; spontaneous data tie it to embarrassment only within controlled smiles.

readings.t: Lip pressing is common in pauses between words (physical description); compare its timing with the audio.
Gaze down, a smile control, then head movement appeared in 46% of 35 embarrassment and 7% of 28 amusement displays (Keltner, 1995).
U.S. perceivers' data-driven model of the affiliative smile combined lip-corner pulling with dimpling and lip pressing (AU12 + AU14 + AU24).
Theory lists it for anger; posers in China, India and Japan, but not all five countries, added it to anger portrayals.
Over 70% of 158 people posing negation combined AU4 + AU17 with AU14 or AU24 (a 'not face'); spoken negation rarely showed it.

context.t: On avatars, lip pressing alone drew an anger rating of 8.9, against 47.8 for brow lowering (AU4) (−100 to 100).
In 53 spontaneous smiles judged by observers, smile controls (lip pressing among them) did not separate amused from embarrassed or nervous.
In two reports (18 and 19 patients in clinical interviews), lip pressing did not change with depression severity.
Thinned lips (AU23 + AU24) made young avatars look stronger to 71% of 141 viewers in a two-way choice; for older avatars 52% was chance.

distinguish.t: Whether pressing falls in pauses between words, where it is common, or during listening and smiling.
A smile with gaze down and head movement fits embarrassment; without the smile that link does not apply.
Lips pressed together (AU24) versus red lips narrowed (AU23) or lips sucked between the teeth (AU28).

examples.setting: Online job interview, candidate receives a compliment
examples.observed: Gaze down, then AU12 with AU24, then head down
examples.readings: This order matches spontaneous embarrassment in one study (S33); smiles that observers judged amused or embarrassed did not differ in smile controls (S03-003).
examples.caution: The perception result reflects observers' judgments, not the smilers' experience.

examples.setting: Video of a Deaf signer using American Sign Language
examples.observed: AU4 with AU14, AU17 and AU24 during a signed negation
examples.readings: In ASL this "not face" is a grammatical marker of negation, in some constructions the only one (S20-028); an anger reading would ignore that use.
examples.caution: Abstract-level evidence; consult a fluent signer.

25.name: Lips part
25.muscles: Depressor labii inferioris, or relaxation of mentalis or orbicularis oris
appearance: The lips part by any amount; the teeth may or may not be visible.
25.coordination: Very frequent during speech and breathing; accompanies many other mouth actions.
25.confusions: AU25 versus AU26 (jaw drop) and AU27 (mouth stretch).
25.detector: Detected often during speech; treat as speech-related unless speech is controlled.

interp.summary: Lips parting accompanies many expressions and nearly all speech. It contributed to perceivers' reliance on the mouth for happiness and to posed surprise.

context.t: Treat AU25 as speech-related unless speech is controlled.

distinguish: Whether the person is speaking.

examples.setting: Webinar recording, presenter speaking most of the time
examples.observed: AU25 in most frames
examples.readings: The entry treats AU25 as speech-related unless speech is controlled. Perceivers' use of lips parting for happiness comes from posed happy faces in which it accompanied lip-corner pulling (Q01, S14-013).
examples.caution: Mask talk segments before interpreting AU25.

examples.setting: Lab session, unrequested smiles between tasks with an experimenter present
examples.observed: AU12 with AU25 in some smiles, larger and longer than the others
examples.readings: Observers more often judged such smiles amused than polite: mouth opening, larger amplitude and longer duration marked smiles judged amused (Q14, S03-002). Mouth opening did not separate smiles judged amused from those judged embarrassed or nervous (S03-002).
examples.caution: These are observers' judgments; the smilers' own experience was not measured.

interp4.summary: Parted lips accompany speech, breathing and portrayals of most emotions (above chance in all five countries for 15 of 22 emotions posed), and mouth opening (AU25 to AU27 pooled) increased during pain in about 60% of 37 studies. It is not specific to any state, and talking must be ruled out first.

best.state: not specific to any state; check speech or breathing first
best.why: Very frequent in speech and breathing; posed portrayals of 15 of 22 emotions included it.

readings.t: Parted lips are very frequent in speech and breathing (physical description); treat detections as speech-related unless speech is controlled.
In a review of 37 FACS studies of adults, mouth opening (AU25 to AU27 pooled) increased during pain in about 60%.
Judo bronze medallists smiled with AU6 + AU12 + AU25 on receiving medals (spontaneous); 90% of 30 Gabonese posers smiled open-mouthed for happiness.
Of 53 spontaneous smiles classified by observers, those judged polite had mouth opening less often than those judged amused or embarrassed/nervous.
Observers (n = 94) uncovering two posed, open-mouthed faces tile by tile relied most on lip-corner and parted-lip tiles for happiness.

context.t: Of 60 adults entering an unexpectedly changed room, 0% to 16% per condition opened the mouth without smiling, laughing or speaking (Schützwohl & Reisenzein, 2012).
Parted lips exceeded chance in all five countries for 15 of 22 portrayed emotions, so posing cannot single out a state.
Nations valuing excitement more had legislators with more open smiles (AU6 + AU12 with AU25 or AU26) in official photos (10 nations).
OpenFace and AFAR detected parted lips well on posed video (AUC .89, .85; .5 is chance); FaceReader 7 scored .55.

distinguish.t: Whether the lips part during talk or silence; during talk, treat them as speech-related.
Cheek raising with lip-corner pulling (AU6 + AU12) makes it an open smile; brow lowering (AU4) with narrowed eyes fits pain.
Lips apart only (AU25) versus a lowered jaw (AU26) or a mouth stretched wide (AU27).

examples.setting: Webinar recording, presenter talking most of the time
examples.observed: AU25 in most frames
examples.readings: Speech is the likeliest source, since parted lips are very frequent in speech (physical description).
examples.caution: Mask talk segments before interpreting AU25.

examples.setting: Lab session, unrequested smiles between tasks, experimenter present
examples.observed: AU12 with AU25 in some smiles, larger and longer than the others
examples.readings: Smiles like these were more often judged amused than polite (Q14), but mouth opening did not separate amused from embarrassed or nervous smiles (S03-002).
examples.caution: These are observers' judgments; the smilers' feelings were not measured.

26.name: Jaw drop
26.muscles: Relaxation of masseter, temporalis and internal pterygoid
26.movement: The jaw lowers so the mouth opens.
appearance: The jaw drops in a relaxed way and the teeth separate.
26.coordination: Usually with AU25; frequent during speech.

interp.summary: Jaw drop is part of posed surprise and is frequent during speech.
distinguish: Speech context.

examples.setting: Lab study, a magic trick with an unexpected outcome
examples.observed: AU26 with AU1+AU2 and AU5 for about a second
examples.readings: These are the actions of posed surprise (P04, V01). In eight experiments with surprised participants, display components were rare and the full display did not appear (S15), so this display is uncommon in surprise and its absence would not argue against it. In pooled models from British and Chinese observers, upper-lid raising with jaw drop formed a pattern labeled surprise, excited or ecstatic (S14-045).
examples.caution: Jaw drop is frequent during speech; check whether the participant is talking.

examples.setting: Archive of official portrait photographs of national legislators
examples.observed: Smiles with AU6+AU12 and an open mouth (AU25 or AU26) more frequent in some countries
examples.readings: In one archival study of ten nations, national ideal-affect scores collected years earlier predicted the rate of these open, excited smiles (S02-042). The study speaks to display norms, not to how the legislators felt.
examples.caution: Nation-level correlations across ten nations, from posed photographs.

interp4.summary: Jaw drop is frequent in speech and posed surprise, and mouth opening (AU25 to AU27 pooled) increased during pain in about 60% of 37 studies. In surprise, bare mouth opening is rare: 0% to 16% of 60 adults per condition opened the mouth without smiling, laughing or speaking.

best.state: not specific to any state; speech, posed surprise or pain
best.why: Frequent in speech; posers use it for surprise, but people meeting surprising events rarely show it.

readings.t: Jaw drop is frequent during speech and usually comes with parted lips (AU25) (physical description).
Actors' surprise portrayals matched the configuration proposed for surprise (AU1 + AU2 + AU5 + AU26) at a median .44 (overlap, 0 to 1).
In eight experiments, brow raising, eye widening or jaw drop appeared in 4% to 25% of adults meeting surprising events; all three together never.
In a review of 37 FACS studies of adults, mouth opening (AU25 to AU27 pooled) increased during pain in about 60%.
In British and Chinese observers' models, upper-lid raising with jaw drop (AU5 + AU26) was one of four shared patterns, conveying high arousal.

context.t: Of 60 adults entering an unexpectedly changed room, 10% to 24% per condition opened the mouth just before smiling or speaking (Schützwohl & Reisenzein, 2012).
The same students opened the mouth far more often posing surprise than when surprised by films (Namba, Makihara, et al., 2017).
Across 14 video databases (9 posed), outer-brow raising and jaw drop (AU2, AU26) best predicted automated surprise recognition (R2 = .50).
Western, but not East Asian, observers' models of orgasm faces included jaw drop and mouth stretch (AU26, AU27).

distinguish.t: Speech, laughter or an "Oh" with the jaw drop points to talking or vocalizing, not a bare facial movement.
Raised brows and lids (AU1 + AU2 + AU5) fit posed surprise; lowered brows and narrowed eyes (AU4, AU6, AU7) fit pain.
Relaxed jaw drop (AU26) versus a wide, stretched opening (AU27); the pain review pooled both with AU25.

examples.setting: Lab study, a magic trick with an unexpected outcome
examples.observed: AU26 with AU1 + AU2 and AU5 for about a second
examples.readings: Posers use these actions for surprise (P04, P08), but people meeting surprising events rarely show them (S15), so their absence would not argue against surprise.
examples.caution: Check the audio, since the opening may come with an "Oh", laughter or speech.

examples.setting: Archive of official portrait photos of national legislators
examples.observed: Open smiles (AU6 + AU12 with AU25 or AU26), more frequent in some countries
examples.readings: In ten nations, how much people valued excitement predicted the rate of these smiles (S02-042); this concerns display norms, not the legislators' feelings.
examples.caution: Nation-level correlations across ten nations, from posed photos.

27.name: Mouth stretch
27.movement: The mouth is stretched open widely by pulling the jaw down.
appearance: The mouth opens very wide, beyond a relaxed jaw drop.

interp.summary: Mouth stretching has been studied mostly within pooled mouth opening: in one review of 37 pain studies, opening the mouth (AU25, AU26 or AU27) was pain-related in about 60%. Perceivers inferred surprise and unexpectedness from AU27 alone on synthetic faces. Posed "jaw dropped" actions in many emotions were coded interpretively as AU26 or AU27, so posed evidence does not isolate AU27.

context.t: In a systematic review of 37 FACS studies, mouth opening (AU25, AU26 and AU27 pooled) was pain-related in about 60% of studies, and the authors suggest it may prepare pain vocalizations (review). The introduction of another pain study summarized earlier work as finding mouth or jaw opening less reliably than the core pain actions (S10-034).

On synthetic avatars, AU27 alone was enough for observers to infer unexpectedness and surprise (Q07); its mean surprise rating was 67.1, against 79.5 for the full surprise prototype (S14-066). It peaked early in Western observers' dynamic models (S14-042). Western, but not East Asian, observers' mental models of orgasm faces included it (S10-008).

In one five-culture study, "jaw dropped" was a core action in posed surprise, fear, happiness, amusement and awe, among others; the dictionary's coders mapped it to AU26 or AU27, so these records do not isolate AU27.

alternatives.s: pain (spontaneous; mouth opening pooled with AU25 and AU26; review)
surprise and unexpectedness (perceivers; synthetic single action)
"jaw dropped" in posed portrayals of many emotions (posed; coded as AU26 or AU27)

distinguish: Degree of opening: AU27 versus AU26 (physical layer); several sources pool them, including a review (S35) and a posed study (S11-052).
Whether the person vocalizes or speaks (S10-013; review).
Co-occurring actions: brow lowering and orbit tightening, as in pain (S35; review), versus brow and upper-lid raising, as in surprise (Q07, S14-066).
Few detectors output AU27 (physical layer).

examples.setting: Hospital ward, patient being repositioned after surgery
examples.observed: Brief AU27 with AU4 and AU6/7, and a vocalization
examples.readings: Pain is the best-supported reading. In one review, brow lowering and orbit tightening were pain-related in more than 70% of studies and mouth opening in about 60% (S35); the review authors suggest that mouth opening may prepare vocalization (S10-013).
examples.caution: The review pooled AU25, AU26 and AU27, so it does not single out mouth stretching; pain faces vary between people (S36; abstract only).

examples.setting: Spectator camera at a football match, crowd just after an unexpected goal
examples.observed: AU27 with AU1+AU2 and AU5 in several spectators
examples.readings: Observers shown synthetic faces inferred surprise and unexpectedness from AU27 alone (Q07, S14-066), so viewers of the footage may read surprise. Production evidence is weaker: in eight experiments with surprised participants, display components were rare (S15).
examples.caution: Perception evidence describes what observers infer. Speech and other vocalizing also open the mouth (see AU25 and AU26), so check the audio.

interp4.summary: Mouth stretching is studied mostly within pooled mouth opening (AU25 to AU27), which increased during pain in about 60% of 37 studies; on avatars, observers read it alone as surprise (67.1 on a −100 to 100 scale). No production study in the evidence base isolates it, and few detectors output it.

best.state: not specific to any state; pain (pooled) or perceived surprise
best.why: Pain studies pool it with AU25 and AU26; observers of avatars read it as surprise.

readings.t: In a review of 37 FACS studies of adults, mouth opening (AU25 to AU27 pooled) increased during pain in about 60%.
The review authors suggest pain-related mouth opening may prepare vocalization; check the audio for cries.
AU27 alone on an avatar scored 67.1 for surprise (−100 to 100), against 79.5 for the authors' full surprise prototype (actions in a supplement).
Western, but not East Asian, observers' models of orgasm faces included jaw drop and mouth stretch (AU26, AU27).

context.t: The pain review, like most of its 37 studies, pooled AU25 to AU27, so mouth stretching alone has no rate.
"Jaw dropped" exceeded chance in all five countries for 10 of 22 portrayed emotions, mapped here to AU26 or AU27.
In eight experiments, brow raising, eye widening or jaw drop appeared in 4% to 25% of adults meeting surprising events; all three together never.
On avatars, a combination with mouth stretching (AU4 + AU10 + AU22 + AU27), predicted to signal confrontation, was read as "not wanted".

distinguish.t: A cry or exclamation with the opening points to vocalizing, which pain-related opening may prepare.
Lowered brows and narrowed eyes (AU4, AU6, AU7) fit pain; raised brows and lids (AU1 + AU2 + AU5) fit perceived surprise.
A wide, stretched opening (AU27) versus a relaxed jaw drop (AU26); several sources do not separate them.

examples.setting: Hospital ward, patient repositioned after surgery
examples.observed: Brief AU27 with AU4, AU6 or AU7, and a vocalization
examples.readings: Pain is the best-supported reading, since brow lowering and orbit tightening were pain-related in over 70% of 37 studies and mouth opening in about 60% (S35).
examples.caution: The review pooled AU25 to AU27, and pain faces vary between people (S36).

examples.setting: Spectator camera at a football match, just after an unexpected goal
examples.observed: AU27 with AU1 + AU2 and AU5 in several spectators
examples.readings: Viewers may read surprise, as observers did from AU27 alone on avatars (Q07, S14-066), though people meeting surprising events rarely show surprise actions (S15).
examples.caution: Vocalizing also opens the mouth; check the audio.

appearance: The cheeks puff and air escapes.

appearance: The cheeks swell outward.

appearance: A bulge appears in the cheek or lip.

41.name: Lid droop
appearance: The upper lids lower partly, without squeezing.
41.detector: Rarely output; may appear as low AU5 or high AU43.

42.name: Slit
42.movement: The eyes narrow to a slit.
appearance: The lids nearly close.

43.name: Eyes closed
43.muscles: Relaxation of levator palpebrae superioris; orbicularis oculi, pars palpebralis
appearance: The eyelids close and stay closed longer than a blink.
43.coordination: Can accompany pain and strong laughter.
43.confusions: Eyes closed versus a blink (AU45) and downward gaze (AU64).
43.detector: Downward gaze and blinks are often reported as AU43; use duration to separate closure from blinking.

interp.summary: Eye closure was one of four pain actions in an early study but was pain-related in only about a fifth of the experimental-pain studies in a later review; detectors can confuse it with blinks and downward gaze.
distinguish: Duration (blink versus closure).
Gaze direction.

examples.setting: Shoulder-pain clinic, patient during range-of-motion tests
examples.observed: AU43 with AU4, AU6/7 and AU9/10 during the most difficult movements
examples.readings: Eye closure is part of a pain composite that, with brow lowering, orbital tightening and levator contraction, carried most of the pain information in one shoulder-pain sample (S10-031). In a review, eye closure met the pain criterion in half of clinical but about a fifth of experimental pain studies (S10-014, S35).
examples.caution: Detectors can confuse closure with blinks and downward gaze; check how long each closure lasts.

examples.setting: Annotating a database of acted expressions
examples.observed: AU43 in many clips labeled pain, sadness, relief and boredom
examples.readings: In one five-culture posed study, tightly closed eyes were a core action of posed pain, and drooping eyelids (coded as AU43) of posed sadness, relief and boredom (S11-047, S11-050, S11-049, S11-035). Eye closure is therefore not specific to one posed category.
examples.caution: Posed evidence describes portrayals on request; tight closure and drooping lids look different and may need separate labels.

interp4.summary: Eye closure (AU43) is evidenced mainly in pain: it rose across four experimental pain types in 41 adults, yet was pain-related in half of 10 clinical and about a fifth of 27 experimental pain studies. Posers in five countries also drooped their eyelids for sadness, relief, boredom and contentment.

best.why: Pain-related in half of 10 clinical pain studies, but about a fifth of 27 experimental ones.

readings.t: Eye closing rose across four experimental pain types in 41 adults and was pain-related in half of 10 clinical studies.
Posers in five countries drooped their eyelids, coded AU43, for sadness, relief, boredom and contentment.
The same posers closed their eyes tightly, with brow lowering (AU4), AU6, AU7 and lip stretching (AU20), to portray pain.
Western and East Asian observers' mental models of orgasm faces shared eye closure with brow raising (AU1 + AU2).
Pooling observers' models of 60-plus emotion words gave four data-driven patterns; one, conveying low valence, combined AU4, AU20 and AU43.

context.t: Detectors often report blinks and downward gaze as AU43; closure duration separates eye closure from blinking.
In shoulder-pain patients, a frame-by-frame pain score adds AU43 to AU4, AU6 or AU7, and AU9 or AU10.
Eye closure rose above rest in about a fifth of 27 experimental pain studies; heat-pain faces fell into four patterns.

distinguish.t: Duration: a blink reopens quickly, while eye closure lasts longer.
Tight closure with AU4, AU6 and AU7 (posed pain) differs from drooping lids (posed sadness, relief, boredom).
Clinical setting: closure during painful movements but not at rest favours pain.

examples.setting: Shoulder-pain clinic, range-of-motion tests
examples.observed: AU43 with AU4, AU6/AU7 and AU9/AU10 during the hardest movements
examples.readings: Pain fits: these actions form a clinical pain score (S10-031), and eye closure is pain-related more often in clinical pain (S10-014).
examples.caution: Check closure duration; detectors confuse closure with blinks and downward gaze.

examples.setting: Annotating a database of acted expressions
examples.observed: AU43 in clips labeled pain, sadness, relief and boredom
examples.readings: Expected: posers closed their eyes tightly for pain and drooped their lids for sadness, relief and boredom (S11-047, S11-050).
examples.caution: Tight closure and drooping lids look different; consider separate labels.

44.name: Squint
44.muscles: Orbicularis oculi, pars palpebralis (some summaries also list corrugator supercilii)
appearance: The eye opening narrows with tightened lids.

45.name: Blink
45.muscles: Relaxation of levator palpebrae superioris; orbicularis oculi, pars palpebralis
45.movement: The eyes close and reopen quickly.
appearance: A brief closure of both eyes.
45.coordination: Occurs continually; rate varies with attention, speech and dryness.
45.detector: Frame-level detectors can register blinks as momentary AU43 or as dips in AU5.

interp.summary: Blinking has mainly non-emotional and conversational evidence. In Dutch conversation, listeners' blinks clustered at the ends of speakers' turn units and long blinks worked as feedback; in one small sample, blink rate fell during an engaging narrative video and blink timing was synchronized across viewers. Blinking increased under instructions to suppress expression (abstract only) and during electrical pain, which a review attributed to startle.

context.t: In a corpus of Dutch face-to-face conversation (20 participants), addressees' blinks clustered just after the ends of speakers' turn-constructional units. Long blinks (410 ms or more) co-occurred with nods or vocal continuers about twice as often as short blinks (18% vs 8-9%) and concentrated in particular sequential contexts (S20-011, S20-012). With a virtual listener, long blinks led speakers to give shorter answers, while short blinks had no effect (S20-013).

In one sample of 14 adults, blink rate fell below rest only while watching a narrative video, not background video or audio alone (S23-010), and blink timing was synchronized within and across viewers of a silent video story (S23-011).
Instructions to conceal emotion while watching a disgust film reduced expressive behavior and increased blinking (abstract only).

In a systematic review, blinking increased during electrical pain stimulation, which the authors attributed to startle rather than to pain itself (S10-038; review). Two older studies with separate samples listed blinking among responses to cold-pressor and electric-shock pain (S10-003, S10-029; abstract only), and a later study described it as less reliably linked to pain (S10-034). Blinking appeared in published pain productions but not in observers' mental models of pain (Q12).

alternatives.s: listener feedback in conversation (function; one Dutch corpus and one avatar experiment)
visual attentional engagement, as a lower blink rate (spontaneous; one small sample)
suppression of emotional expression (function; abstract only)
pain (spontaneous; older abstract-level studies; absent from perceivers' models)

distinguish: Duration: short and long (410 ms or more) blinks had different conversational effects (S20-012, S20-013); longer closures are coded AU43 (physical layer).
Timing: relative to the partner's turn ends (S20-011) or to events in a story (S23-011).
Rate against the same person's resting baseline (S23-010).
A sudden stimulus (startle) versus sustained pain (S10-038; review).
Frame-level detectors can register blinks as momentary AU43 or as dips in AU5 (physical layer).

examples.setting: Recorded face-to-face conversation for a communication study, participant listening
examples.observed: Long blinks, around half a second, near the ends of the speaker's sentences, some with small nods
examples.readings: Listener feedback is the best-supported reading: in one Dutch corpus, addressees' blinks clustered at turn ends and long blinks co-occurred with nods (S20-011, S20-012), and in an avatar experiment long blinks shortened speakers' answers (S20-013).
examples.caution: The evidence comes from one research group and Dutch speakers; check blink timing against the speaker's turns before counting blinks.

examples.setting: Emotion-regulation experiment, participants told to hide their reactions to an unpleasant film
examples.observed: Blink rate rises while other facial activity falls
examples.readings: This matches one study in which suppression instructions reduced expressive behavior and increased blinking (S05-019; abstract only). Because blink rate also falls with engagement in a narrative video (S23-010), compare each person with their own resting baseline.
examples.caution: The suppression result is known only from the abstract; blink rate alone does not show that someone is suppressing.

interp4.summary: Blink evidence concerns mainly conversation and attention: in Dutch conversation (20 participants), listeners' blinks clustered at the ends of speakers' utterances, and long blinks (410 ms or more) came with nods twice as often as short ones. Links to emotion are thin: blinking rose during electrical pain, which a review attributed to startle.

best.why: Listeners' blinks clustered at utterance ends; a virtual listener's long blinks shortened speakers' answers.

readings.t: Long listener blinks (410 ms or more) came with nods or 'mm-hm' twice as often as short ones in Dutch conversation.
With a nodding virtual listener, long blinks led 35 Dutch speakers to give shorter answers; short blinks had no effect.
In 14 adults, blink rate fell below rest only during a narrative video, and blink timing synchronized across viewers.
Told to conceal their reactions to a disgust film, 85 adults showed less facial expression but more blinking (abstract only).
Blinking rose during electrical pain, which a 37-study review attributed to startle; observers' pain models lacked blinking, though productions include it.

context.t: Long (410 ms or more) and short blinks had different conversational effects; longer closures are coded AU43.
Blink rate varies with attention, speech and eye dryness, so compare each person with their own resting rate.
Frame-level detectors can register blinks as momentary AU43 or as dips in AU5.

distinguish.t: Timing against the partner's speech: blinks near the ends of utterances suggest listener feedback.
Duration: long blinks (410 ms or more) acted as feedback; short ones did not.
A sudden stimulus suggests startle; blinking during sustained pain or a task needs other evidence.
Rate against the person's resting baseline: engagement with a story lowered it.

examples.setting: Recorded conversation, participant listening
examples.observed: Long blinks near the ends of the speaker's sentences, some with nods
examples.readings: Listener feedback is the best-supported reading (S20-011, S20-013).
examples.caution: Evidence comes from one Dutch research group; align blinks with speaker turns.

examples.setting: Participants told to hide reactions to an unpleasant film
examples.observed: Blink rate rises while other facial activity falls
examples.readings: Matches one suppression study (S05-019, abstract only); engagement lowers blink rate (S23-010), so compare with each person's baseline.
examples.caution: Blink rate alone does not show that someone is suppressing.

46.name: Wink
appearance: A brief closure of one eye.

51.name: Head turn left
51.muscles: Not a facial muscle action; a head movement code in FACS
appearance: Head turn left (position or movement of the head).
51.coordination: Head and gaze codes are recorded alongside facial actions; several displays studied in the literature (for example embarrassment, pride and shame) include them.
51.confusions: Head rotation changes how facial actions look in two-dimensional video.
51.detector: Detectors estimate head pose (pitch, yaw, roll) and gaze as continuous angles, not as FACS codes.

interp.summary: Head turn left is a head movement, not a facial muscle action. Its only direct record is a hypothesized embarrassment configuration tested on professional actors' photographs, in which head and eye positions could not be coded from stills and the match was weak. A review describes embarrassment and coyness with the head turned, coded there as a turn to the right (AU52).

context.t: Le Mau et al. tested a hypothesized embarrassment configuration with AU51, AU54 and AU64 against actors' photographs; head and eye positions could not be coded from the stills and were estimated by simulation, and the match was weak.
A review from a basic emotion theory perspective describes embarrassment and coyness with the head turned and down, coded as AU52 with AU54 (review).
In one perception study of unrequested smiles, head yaw (turning) did not differ between smiles judged amused, polite or embarrassed/nervous, whereas downward head pitch did.

alternatives.s: embarrassment (hypothesized configuration; not codable from posed photographs)
embarrassment and coyness with the head turned (theory; review; coded as AU52)

distinguish: Whether gaze and head also move down and a controlled smile follows, as in spontaneous embarrassment (S33).
In one perception study, head yaw did not change how smiles were read, whereas downward pitch did (S03-007).
Head rotation changes how facial actions look in two-dimensional video (physical layer); re-check facial AUs during turns.

examples.setting: Online job interview, candidate notices a mistake on a shared slide
examples.observed: Head turns left, with gaze down and a brief smile
examples.readings: The gaze-down and controlled-smile parts match spontaneous embarrassment in one study (S33). The head turn itself is supported only by hypothesized and theoretical configurations (S11-006; S01-031, review).
examples.caution: Nothing in this base shows that the side of the turn matters; turning also changes the camera's view of the face.

interp4.summary: In one spontaneous study, embarrassed people made their first head movements and gaze shifts to the left, while amused people looked right (Keltner, 1995: 35 vs 28 people). The side difference comes from one situation with no reported count, and head turning did not differ among 53 smiles judged amused, polite or embarrassed.

best.why: Only spontaneous evidence: embarrassed people's first head movements went left (Keltner, 1995).

readings.t: After an awkward face-posing task, embarrassed people (35) turned head and gaze left first; amused people (28) looked right.
Keltner et al. (2019) list embarrassment and coyness with head turned and down, coded as a right turn (AU52) plus AU54.
One embarrassment variant tested by Le Mau et al. (2021), AU51 + AU54 + AU64, could not be coded in 604 actor photographs.
Infant coyness was described as a smile with gaze and head turned away, with adults or a mirror (publisher summary only).

context.t: In 53 spontaneous smiles judged by 101 students, head turning did not differ between amused, polite and embarrassed or nervous ones.
Head and eye actions cannot be coded from stills; Le Mau et al. (2021) simulated them at a base rate of 0.104.
Detectors report head yaw as a continuous angle, and turning changes how facial actions look in two-dimensional video.

distinguish.t: Gaze and pitch: in spontaneous embarrassment, gaze went down first and the head moved down later.
Side: Keltner (1995) reported left turns in embarrassment, but a review codes its embarrassment turn as right (AU52).
During a turn, re-check facial detections: rotation changes how actions look on camera.

52.name: Head turn right
52.muscles: Not a facial muscle action; a head movement code in FACS
appearance: Head turn right (position or movement of the head).
52.coordination: Head and gaze codes are recorded alongside facial actions; several displays studied in the literature (for example embarrassment, pride and shame) include them.
52.confusions: Head rotation changes how facial actions look in two-dimensional video.
52.detector: Detectors estimate head pose (pitch, yaw, roll) and gaze as continuous angles, not as FACS codes.

53.name: Head up
53.muscles: Not a facial muscle action; a head movement code in FACS
appearance: Head up (position or movement of the head).
53.coordination: Head and gaze codes are recorded alongside facial actions; several displays studied in the literature (for example embarrassment, pride and shame) include them.
53.confusions: Head rotation changes how facial actions look in two-dimensional video.
53.detector: Detectors estimate head pose (pitch, yaw, roll) and gaze as continuous angles, not as FACS codes.

interp.summary: Head up is a head movement, not a facial muscle action. After winning, sighted and blind judo athletes tilted the head back more than after losing; the authors read this as pride, which was not measured. Head up is part of posed amusement and awe in one five-culture study, and on avatars an upward tilt alone was not rated more prestigious than a level head.

context.t: At the 2004 Olympic and Paralympic Games, sighted, blind and congenitally blind judo athletes tilted the head back more after winning than after losing (sighted athletes: d = 0.84) (S32, S08-023). The authors read this as pride; the study took no self-report, and winning may also evoke joy, relief or happiness (study caveats).

In one five-culture study, head up was a core action in posed amusement, with a Duchenne smile and dropped jaw, and in posed awe, with raised brows and upper lids (S11-032, S11-034). The head and eye positions of a hypothesized pride configuration could not be coded from actors' photographs (S11-010, P16).
A review from a basic emotion theory perspective lists head back with a Duchenne smile for amusement and head up with eyes down for pride (review).

On avatars, a 10-degree upward tilt alone was rated about as prestigious as a level head, both above a downward tilt; a prestige display that combined the upward tilt with a smile and expansive posture was chosen 53% of the time against 25% chance.

alternatives.s: pride, as read by the authors from winning (spontaneous; pride not measured)
amusement and awe (posed; one five-culture study)
prestige, only together with a smile and expansive posture (perceivers; avatars)

distinguish: Co-occurring smile, raised arms and expanded chest after success (S08-023).
Gaze: the theoretical pride configuration pairs head up with eyes down (S01-036; review).
The event: success in competition (S32) versus amusing or awe-inspiring material (S11-032, S11-034).
Head pitch changes how facial actions look in two-dimensional video, for example how open the eyes appear (physical layer; see AU5).

examples.setting: Sports broadcast, athlete just after winning a match
examples.observed: Head tilted back, a smile and raised arms
examples.readings: This matches the winners' display in one Olympic and Paralympic judo sample, including blind athletes (S32, S08-023). The authors read it as pride; because pride was not measured, joy, relief or happiness remain possible (S32, study caveats).
examples.caution: The head movement changes the camera's view of the face; re-check facial AUs at that moment.

examples.setting: Comedy club audience filmed for a study of laughter
examples.observed: Head back with AU6+AU12 and an open mouth at a punchline
examples.readings: Head up with a Duchenne smile and dropped jaw formed the core of posed amusement in one five-culture study (S11-032), and a review lists head back for amusement (S01-023). No spontaneous record in this base codes head up during amusement.
examples.caution: The head-up evidence is posed and theoretical; for amusement, rely on the smile evidence (see AU12) and on self-report.

interp4.summary: Head up most often follows winning: judo athletes at the 2004 Olympics (87 sighted) and Paralympics (53 blind) tilted the head back more after wins than losses (d = 0.84, 1.11), which the authors read as pride without measuring it. A posing study of 120 students in five countries also found it in amusement and awe.

best.why: Winners tilted the head back more than losers (d = 0.84); pride itself was not measured.

readings.t: Judo winners tilted the head back more than losers: sighted d = 0.84 (111 matches), blind d = 1.11 (60 matches); no self-report.
In five-country portrayals by 120 students, head up was core to amusement (with AU6 + AU12) and awe (with AU1 + AU2 + AU5).
US, Italian and Burkinabe observers recognized pride from a small smile, head tilted back and expanded posture (abstracts only).

readings.s: prestige, only with smile and posture
readings.t: On avatars, a 10-degree upward tilt alone was rated no more prestigious than a level head by US raters (d = .05).

context.t: Three coders rated head tilt back in post-match photographs on a 0 to 5 intensity scale; it was not FACS-coded as AU53.
Among 12 congenitally blind athletes, winners raised arms, clenched fists and expanded the chest more; no head-tilt difference was reported.
Upward tilt plus smile and expansive posture: chosen as prestigious in 53% (chance 25%), yet rated no higher than smile alone.
Le Mau et al. (2021) could not code head or eye actions in 604 stills, so pride (AU53 + AU64) was only simulated.

distinguish.t: Posture and smile: winners combined head tilt back with raised arms, expanded chest and smiling.
Gaze: a review pairs head up with eyes down for pride (AU53 + AU64).
Situation: success, or amusing and awe-inspiring material; posers also lifted or lowered the head for pain, boredom and relief.
Head pitch changes how open the eyes look on camera; check AU5 and AU43 detections against pitch.

54.name: Head down
54.muscles: Not a facial muscle action; a head movement code in FACS
appearance: Head down (position or movement of the head).
54.coordination: Head and gaze codes are recorded alongside facial actions; several displays studied in the literature (for example embarrassment, pride and shame) include them.
54.confusions: Head rotation changes how facial actions look in two-dimensional video.
54.detector: Detectors estimate head pose (pitch, yaw, roll) and gaze as continuous angles, not as FACS codes.

interp.summary: Head down is a head movement, not a facial muscle action. In one spontaneous study it followed downward gaze and a controlled smile in embarrassment, and in one five-culture posed study it was a core action in shame, sadness, coyness and embarrassment. Perceivers rated a downward tilt with the eyes looking forward as more dominant, and in one perception study smiles judged embarrassed or nervous had more downward head pitch.

context.t: In one spontaneous study, embarrassment produced a sequence of downward gaze, a controlled smile and head movement down that differed from amusement in frequency and timing (S33). In one perception study of unrequested smiles, those judged embarrassed or nervous had more downward head pitch than those judged amused or polite (S03-007).

In one five-culture study, head down was a core action in posed shame, sadness, coyness and embarrassment, and a culture-specific addition to anger among Korean participants (S11-051, S11-050, S11-039, S11-043, S11-058). Gabonese posers showed head and gaze down for shame more often than Quebecois posers (S15-022). The head and eye positions of hypothesized shame and embarrassment configurations could not be coded from actors' photographs (S11-012, S11-006, P16).

In an Olympic and Paralympic judo sample, the shame behaviors coded in losers included head tilt down, but the reported differences between losers and winners concerned slumped shoulders and a narrowed chest.

In five studies, a downward head tilt on a neutral face with the eyes looking forward raised perceivers' dominance ratings (d about 0.8 in Studies 1 and 2). The effect disappeared when the upper face was hidden, and the authors attribute it to an apparent brow lowering without AU4 (S22-029). A display with a downward tilt, no smile and expansive posture was chosen as dominant 69% of the time against 25% chance (S22-031).

Reviews list head down with eyes down for shame (S01-038, S08-036) and head turned and down for embarrassment and coyness (S01-031, S01-028). Infant coyness was described as smiling with gaze and head aversion (S08-030; publisher summary only).

alternatives.s: embarrassment, after gaze down and with a controlled smile (spontaneous; one study)
sadness and coyness (posed; one five-culture study)
dominance, when the eyes look forward (perceivers; avatars and photographs)

distinguish: Gaze: head down with eyes down, as in shame descriptions and in embarrassment (S01-038, review; S33), versus head down with the eyes looking forward, as in the dominance studies (S22-029).
Sequence and smile: in spontaneous embarrassment, gaze went down first, then a controlled smile, then the head (S33).
A downward tilt can make the brows look lowered without AU4 (S22-029); check AU4 detections against head pitch.
Posture: slumped shoulders and a narrowed chest after losing (S08-024) versus expansive posture in the dominance display (S22-031).

examples.setting: Recorded wedding speech, speaker forgets a name
examples.observed: Gaze down, a smile with pressed lips, then head down
examples.readings: This sequence matches spontaneous embarrassment in one study (S33), and observers judged smiles with more downward head pitch as embarrassed or nervous (S03-007).
examples.caution: The perception result describes how smiles are read, not what the speaker feels.

examples.setting: Leadership assessment based on recorded talks
examples.observed: Head tilted down with the eyes on the camera, no smile
examples.readings: Viewers may rate this pose as more dominant: a downward tilt with forward gaze raised dominance ratings in five studies (S22-029), and a display with a downward tilt, no smile and expansive posture was chosen as dominant (S22-031). Shame descriptions combine head and eyes down (S01-038; review), which is not the case here.
examples.caution: These are perceivers' impressions of avatars and photographs, not evidence about the speaker's state. AU4 detections in this pose may reflect head pitch (S22-029).

interp4.summary: Head down most often accompanies embarrassment: it appeared in 51% of 35 embarrassed versus 17% of 28 amused people, often after gaze down and a controlled smile (Keltner, 1995), and smiles judged embarrassed or nervous tilted further down. Posing studies tie it to shame and sadness, yet losing a judo match did not predict it.

best.why: Head movement down in 51% of 35 embarrassed vs 17% of 28 amused people.

readings.t: After an awkward face-posing task, 51% of 35 embarrassed vs 17% of 28 amused people moved the head down.
Of 53 spontaneous smiles judged by 101 students, those judged embarrassed or nervous had more downward head pitch than amused or polite.
Core to posed shame with brow lowering and chin raising (AU4 + AU17) in five countries; Gabonese posers also lowered the gaze.
Also core to posed sadness, with brow lowering and drooping lids (AU4 + AU43), and to coyness, with a smile (AU6 + AU12).
With eyes forward, tilting a neutral face down raised dominance ratings in five studies (d = .79 and .82 in two).

context.t: Among 87 sighted Olympic judo athletes, losing did not predict head tilt down; losers slumped the shoulders instead (d = 0.82).
In the same five-country posing study, head up or down was also core to pain, boredom and relief.
Le Mau et al. (2021) could not code head or eye actions in 604 stills, so shame (AU54 + AU64) was simulated.
Reviews describe shame as head and eyes down (AU54 + AU64), and embarrassment and coyness as head turned and down.

distinguish.t: Gaze: eyes down with the head in embarrassment and shame descriptions; eyes forward in the dominance studies.
Order: embarrassment ran gaze down, controlled smile, head down (46% of embarrassed vs 7% of amused).
A downward tilt can make the brows look lowered without AU4; check AU4 detections against head pitch.
Posture: slumped shoulders after losing versus expansive posture in the dominance display.

55.muscles: Not a facial muscle action; a head movement code in FACS
appearance: Head tilt left (position or movement of the head).

55.detector: Detectors estimate head pose (pitch, yaw, roll) and gaze as continuous angles, not as FACS codes.

56.detector: Detectors estimate head pose (pitch, yaw, roll) and gaze as continuous angles, not as FACS codes.

appearance: Head forward (position or movement of the head).
57.coordination: Head and gaze codes are recorded alongside facial actions; several displays studied in the literature (for example embarrassment, pride and shame) include them.
57.confusions: Head rotation changes how facial actions look in two-dimensional video.
57.detector: Detectors estimate head pose (pitch, yaw, roll) and gaze as continuous angles, not as FACS codes.

interp.summary: Head forward is a head movement, not a facial muscle action. Its coded evidence concerns sympathy: it was a core action in posed sympathy in one five-culture study and is part of a theoretical sympathy configuration. A review of compassion research describes "concerned attention", with head and body oriented forward, which related to reported sympathy or compassion and to helping.

context.t: In one five-culture study, the core sequence for posed sympathy was lips parted, jaw dropped and head forward (S11-053). The study was re-checked only against its abstract (P12).
A review from a basic emotion theory perspective lists inner-brow raising, lower-lip raising, lip pressing and head forward for sympathy (review).

A review describes "concerned attention" (brows pulled down flat with central furrowing, head and body oriented forward) in observational studies of people facing someone in need; it related to reported sympathy or compassion and to later helping (S08-001; review). In forced-choice tasks, a posed compassion display with oblique brows and forward head movement was recognized as sympathy above chance but with low accuracy, and was often confused with sadness (S08-002; review).

alternatives.s: concerned attention, related to reported sympathy or compassion and helping (review of observational studies)

distinguish: Brow actions: oblique brows in posed compassion, which perceivers confused with sadness (S08-002; review), versus brows pulled down in concerned attention (S08-001; review).
The situation: someone in need or distress (S08-001; review).

interp.summary: Eyes down is an eye movement, not a facial muscle action. In one spontaneous study, downward gaze began the embarrassment sequence, and reviews and theories place it in shame, embarrassment, pride and sadness configurations. In one five-culture posed study it was a culture-specific addition to sadness in four of the five cultures, not part of the shared core.

context.t: Downward gaze opened the spontaneous embarrassment sequence in one study (S33). A review describes gaze down, then lip press, a non-Duchenne smile and face touch, reported in American and Indian participants (S08-035; review).

In one five-culture study, eyes down exceeded chance in posed sadness within China, Japan, Korea and the United States but was not part of the core shared by all five cultures (S11-060, S11-062, S11-063, S11-064). Gabonese posers showed head and gaze down for shame (S15-022). The eye positions of hypothesized shame, pride and embarrassment configurations could not be coded from actors' photographs (S11-012, S11-010, S11-006, P16).
Reviews list eyes down with head down for shame and with head up for pride (S01-038, S08-036, S01-036), and an appraisal-theory prediction for sadness includes eyes down (S14-001; theory).
An ethnographic report from Bengkulu, Indonesia, describes malu with gaze averted to the ground and a lowered posture.
In Dutch conversation, gaze shifts away from the addressee were frequent with self-directed (thinking or word-search) questions; the record does not give the direction of the shift.

alternatives.s: embarrassment, at the start of the sequence (spontaneous; one study; review)

distinguish: Head position: eyes down with head down, as in shame descriptions (S01-038; review), or with head up, as in the theoretical pride configuration (S01-036; review).
Order: in spontaneous embarrassment, gaze went down before the controlled smile and the head movement (S33).
What the person is looking at: notes, a keyboard or a phone below the camera also put the eyes down.
Detectors estimate gaze as continuous angles (physical layer), and blinks or eye closure can be mistaken for downward gaze (see the AU43 and AU45 entries).

examples.setting: Online tutoring session, student gives a wrong answer
examples.observed: Eyes down, then a smile with pressed lips, then a hand to the face
examples.readings: This order matches the embarrassment sequence in one spontaneous study (S33) and the sequence described in a review (S08-035).
examples.caution: Looking down at notes or a keyboard also puts the eyes down; check what the student is looking at before reading the gaze.

examples.readings: In one five-culture study, eyes down was a culture-specific addition to posed sadness, not part of the shared core (S11-060, S11-062, S11-063, S11-064).
examples.caution: Posed clips show how people portray sadness on request; classifiers and observers were less accurate on spontaneous than on posed expressions (Q26, Q27).

interp4.summary: Eyes down most often accompanies embarrassment: in Keltner's (1995) spontaneous study it was the first action in 81% of 35 embarrassment displays, and longer gazes down went with stronger reported embarrassment (r = .51). Yet 72% of 28 amused people also looked down (94% of embarrassed), and posers add it to shame and sadness.

best.why: Gaze down began 81% of 35 embarrassment displays; its duration tracked reported embarrassment (r = .51).

readings.t: After an awkward face-posing task, gaze down opened 81% of 35 embarrassment displays; its duration tracked reported embarrassment (r = .51).
Singh and Bhushan (2025) describe gaze down, lip pressing (AU24), a smile without cheek raising (AU6), then face touch.
Gabonese posers lowered head and gaze more than Quebecois; reviews describe shame as head and eyes down (AU54 + AU64).
Posers in China, Japan, Korea and the US added eyes down to sadness; it was not shared by all five countries.
An account from Bengkulu, Sumatra, describes "malu", which Fessler (2004) compares with shame, as staring at the ground with a lowered posture.
A review pairs eyes down with head up for pride (AU53 + AU64).

context.t: Gaze down also occurred in 72% of 28 amused people (94% of embarrassed); it came first and lasted longer in embarrassment.
Le Mau et al. (2021) simulated eyes down for shame, pride and embarrassment because it cannot be coded from 604 stills.
In Dutch conversation, gaze shifts away from the addressee were frequent with questions asked while thinking; their direction was not reported.
An appraisal prediction for sadness includes inner-brow raising, lip-corner depression, lid droop and eyes down (AU1 + AU15 + AU41 + AU64).

distinguish.t: Head position: eyes down with head down in shame descriptions, with head up for pride.
Order: in embarrassment, gaze went down first, before the controlled smile and the head movement.
Target: notes, a keyboard or a phone below the camera also put the eyes down.
Detectors often report downward gaze as eye closure (AU43); check AU43 against gaze angle and duration.

interp.summary: Head nodding is a head movement, not a facial muscle action. Its one directly coded record is posed: in one five-culture study, a head nod was the only core action for interest. Other records, not coded as AU85, link nods to listener feedback and, together with other cues, to reported love (abstract only).

context.t: In one five-culture study, a head nod was the only action in the core sequence for posed interest (S11-046). The study was re-checked only against its abstract (P12).

Speakers talking to a virtual listener produced more disfluencies and pause fillers when its nods, mirroring and gaze shifts were not timed to their speech (S20-009), and rapport with a responsive agent was rated close to that with a human listener (S20-010). The design does not separate nods from the other behaviors. In Dutch conversation, addressees' long blinks co-occurred with nods about twice as often as short blinks did (S20-011).
During interactions designed to elicit love, head nods, Duchenne smiles, gesticulation and forward leans together correlated with reported love and with partners' estimates of it (abstract only).

alternatives.s: listener feedback (function; virtual-agent experiment, nods combined with other behaviors)
affiliation cue linked with reported love (spontaneous; combined with other cues; abstract only)

distinguish: Whether the nods are timed to the other person's speech (S20-009) and co-occur with long blinks or vocal continuers (S20-011).
Co-occurring affiliation cues such as Duchenne smiles and forward leans (S08-011; abstract only).
Detectors report head pitch as a continuous angle, not nods (physical layer); define a nod from the pitch time series.

examples.setting: Online lecture with cameras on, student listening
examples.observed: Repeated small nods near the ends of the lecturer's sentences, some with long blinks
examples.readings: Listener feedback is the best-supported reading: timed nods and other listener behaviors reduced speakers' disfluencies with a virtual listener (S20-009), and long blinks co-occurred with nods in Dutch conversation (S20-011). Interest rests only on posed portrayals (S11-046).
examples.caution: Only one record codes AU85 directly, and the conversational studies did not isolate nods.

interp4.summary: Head nodding has one directly coded link: it was the only core action when 120 students in five countries portrayed interest (Cordaro et al., 2018). In Dutch conversation, addressees' long blinks came with nods twice as often as short ones (18% vs 9%), but no study here isolated the nod.

best.why: The sole core action of portrayed interest in five countries; conversation studies never isolated nods.

readings.t: A head nod was the only core action when 120 students in five countries portrayed interest to a short story.
Speakers facing a virtual listener whose nods, mirroring and gaze shifts ignored their speech timing made more disfluencies (22.17 vs 11.75).
In Dutch face-to-face conversation, addressees' long blinks came with nods twice as often as short blinks did (18% vs 9%).
Nods, smiles with cheek raising (AU6 + AU12), gesticulation and forward leans together correlated with reported love (abstract only).

context.t: The five-country results come from the author's dissertation on the same data; the article was checked only against its abstract.
Rated rapport with a responsive virtual listener did not differ from a human listener's; its nods were bundled with mirroring and gaze.
In 19 patients interviewed at high and low symptom severity, vertical and horizontal head motion was smaller and slower when severe.
Detectors report head pitch as a continuous angle, not nods; define a nod from the pitch time series.

distinguish.t: Timing: listener nods time-locked to the speaker's speech, as in the virtual-listener study.
Co-occurring long blinks or vocal continuers, which marked addressee feedback in Dutch conversation.
Co-occurring smiles and forward leans, as in the love study (abstract only).

keltner_2019_emotional.cit: Keltner, D., Sauter, D., Tracy, J., & Cowen, A. (2019). Emotional expression: Advances in basic emotion theory. Journal of Nonverbal Behavior, 43(2), 133-160.
keltner_2019_emotional.design: Narrative review from a basic emotion theory (BET) perspective of multimodal expression, perception and social functions.
keltner_2019_emotional.numbers: No new coherence data; the 50% prototype / 25% dialect figures come from posed (free-response) portrayals.
keltner_2019_emotional.conclusion: Upwards of 20 emotions have distinct multimodal expressions; expressions vary within categories and across cultures; they coordinate social interaction.
