fridlund_1994_human.cit: Fridlund, A. J. (1994). Human facial expression: An evolutionary view. San Diego, CA: Academic Press.

scherer_2001_appraisal.cit: Scherer, K. R. (2001). Appraisal considered as a process of multilevel sequential checking. In K. R. Scherer, A. Schorr, & T. Johnstone (Eds.), Appraisal processes in emotion: Theory, methods, research (pp. 92-120). New York: Oxford University Press.

ekman_1982_felt.cit: Ekman, P., & Friesen, W. V. (1982). Felt, false, and miserable smiles. Journal of Nonverbal Behavior, 6(4), 238-252.
ekman_1982_felt.design: Theoretical paper proposing appearance-based distinctions among three smile types, with 'preliminary evidence' (details of the evidence could not be read in the primary source).
ekman_1982_felt.numbers: Not verifiable from the primary text. According to Frank et al. (1993), Ekman & Friesen (1982) predicted five markers of enjoyment smiles: (a) AU6 with AU12; (b) synchronized apex of AU12 and AU6; (c) symmetrical AU12; (d) smooth onset/apex/offset not as long or short as in other smiles; (e) AU12 duration of 0.5-4 s. Frank et al. state that by 1993 four of five markers had some confirmation and the synchrony marker 'has yet to be systematically explored'.
ekman_1982_felt.conclusion: Per the abstract: the paper proposes theory-based distinctions among felt, false and miserable smiles, and 'preliminary evidence supports some of the hypotheses'.
ekman_1982_felt.caveats: The 1982 text could not be read (image-only scan), so which hypotheses the 'preliminary evidence' addressed, and with what data, is unverified. The prediction details come from later descriptions by Frank, Ekman & Friesen (1993) (Ekman a co-author) and Krumhuber & Kappas (2005). Frank et al. put the range at '0.5 and 4 s'; the commonly repeated '2/3 s to 4 s' range was not found in any source that could be read.
terms: deliberate attempts to appear as if positive emotion is felt

friesen_1983_emfacs7.cit: Friesen, W. V., & Ekman, P. (1983). EMFACS-7: Emotional Facial Action Coding System. Unpublished manual, University of California, San Francisco.

duchenne_1862_mecanisme.cit: Duchenne de Boulogne, G.-B. (1862). Mecanisme de la physionomie humaine, ou analyse electro-physiologique de l'expression des passions. Paris: Ve Jules Renouard. [English translation: Duchenne de Boulogne, G.-B. (1990). The mechanism of human facial expression (R. A. Cuthbertson, Trans. & Ed.). Cambridge University Press.]

matsumoto_2006_thrill.cit: Matsumoto, D., & Willingham, B. (2006). The thrill of victory and the agony of defeat: Spontaneous expressions of medal winners of the 2004 Athens Olympic Games. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 91(3), 568-581.
matsumoto_2006_thrill.design: Naturalistic field study: still photographs (Nikon D2H, 8 frames/s) taken by one professional photographer of judo athletes at the 2004 Athens Olympic Games at three points: (1) immediately at match completion, until the referee awarded the match (generally within 15 s); (2) when receiving the medal from a dignitary; (3) when posing on the podium (after the gold medalist's anthem). N = 84 gold, silver, bronze and fifth-place athletes from 35 countries (six continents). Apex photographs were coded with FACS (inter-rater agreement .79) and AU combinations interpreted with the EMFACS dictionary. Countries grouped into three cultural groups: North America-Western Europe, East Asia, and 'all others'. No self-reports of emotion ('logistically impossible').
matsumoto_2006_thrill.numbers: Match completion: 13/14 gold and 18/26 bronze medalists smiled; of these 31 smiles 29 were Duchenne (24 open-mouth); 0/14 silver and 1/26 fifth placers smiled; silver/fifth showed sadness (43%/35%), nothing (29%/23%), contempt (14%/15%). Receiving medal: 54/56 smiled; all 14 gold showed Duchenne smiles (12 open-mouth); only 6/14 silver showed Duchenne smiles, 3 'controlled Duchenne smiles'. Podium posing: all gold smiled, 13/14 Duchenne; 9/14 silver smiled, only 5 uncontrolled. Culture: no cultural differences at match completion or when receiving the medal; on the podium gold/bronze medalists from North America-Western Europe and East Asia showed Duchenne smiles 96% of the time vs more non-Duchenne smiles (47%) among those from other countries, chi-square(4, N = 56) = 14.71, p = .01.
matsumoto_2006_thrill.conclusion: Spontaneous expressions at match completion corresponded to the universal emotion expressions, occurred in relation to emotionally evocative contexts across cultures and differentiated winning from losing; expressions in the staged, interactive ceremonies differed from these uninhibited first expressions. Silver medalists' controlled smiles and blank/uninterpretable expressions with AU 14 were interpreted as regulation, linked to a display rule to 'be a good loser'. Cultural differences appeared only on the podium; the authors attribute their emergence there to weaker contextual pressure […]
matsumoto_2006_thrill.caveats: No self-reports of emotion, so 'emotion' is inferred from match outcome and EMFACS predictions. Data are single apex photographs selected by the researchers from one photographer's shots, not continuous video; the 15-s window at match completion may already include interaction (with opponent, coaches, audience), which Crivelli et al. (2015) argue matters. Cultural cells are small (N = 56 in the ceremony analyses) and the 'all others' group is heterogeneous. […]
terms: controlled / uncontrolled Duchenne smiles (smiles co-occurring with buccinator, AU 14)
facial expressions of emotion considered to be universal
display rule for athletes to 'be a good loser'
FACS (printed in the abstract as 'Facial Affect Coding System')

fridlund_1991_sociality.cit: Fridlund, A. J. (1991). Sociality of solitary smiling: Potentiation by an implicit audience. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 60(2), 229-240.
fridlund_1991_sociality.design: Laboratory experiment, between-subjects, 4 sociality conditions: (a) alone (solitary); (b) alone but believing a friend nearby was completing psychological tests ('implicit irrelevant task'); (c) alone but believing the friend was viewing the same videotape in another room ('implicit coviewing'); (d) friend physically present ('explicit coviewing'). N = 64 undergraduate volunteers participating for course credit (author's affiliation: University of California, Santa Barbara, USA; 32 men, 32 women; 8 men and 8 women per condition; study advertised as measuring 'unconscious physiological activity while watching videotapes'); the 48 who arrived with same-sex friends were assigned to conditions b-d. Stimulus: pleasant videotape, 13 min 15 s, five segments (babies, a dog, sea otters, a comedy sketch). Facial measure: surface EMG over left and right zygomatic major ('cheek sites') and left corrugator supercilii ('brow' control site); dummy electrodes and a cover story ('brain wave activity'). Self-report: modified Differential Emotions Scale, 12 dimensions on unanchored 0-100 scales, before and at the conclusion of the videotape; the key rating was 'happiness'. Elicitation: spontaneous […]
fridlund_1991_sociality.numbers: N = 64 (16 per condition). Cheek-site (zygomatic) EMG: linear trend over the four conditions F(2, 59) = 5.72, p < .003; friend present > alone F(2, 59) = 4.65, p < .007; implicit coviewing > alone F(2, 59) = 4.32, p < .01; implicit coviewing did not differ from friend present; friend-doing-other-task vs alone F(1, 59) = 1.50, p < .13 (non-significant trend). (The df of 2 for the multivariate tests reflect the two cheek sites.) Happiness ratings: no difference among conditions, F(3, 56) = 0.65, p > .58 (error df imply ratings from 60 participants). Within-condition regressions of cheek EMG on post-video ratings all non-significant. Alone participants still showed cheek EMG consistent with 'weak but visible smiling' (p. 232).
fridlund_1991_sociality.conclusion: Smiling while alone is potentiated by an implicit audience; solitary faces may be 'implicitly social', consistent with a behavioural-ecology/ethological view of facial displays as social communications rather than read-outs of emotion, and with role and impression-management theories.
fridlund_1991_sociality.caveats: Small cells (n = 16). Emotion was a single retrospective rating after a 13-min tape, which may be insensitive to moment-to-moment feeling; null differences in self-report are not evidence of equal feeling. Only friends (same-sex) were used as audiences, so the generality to strangers is untested here (see Hess et al., 1995). EMG at the zygomatic site can reflect other lower-face activity. The implicit-irrelevant-task condition did not differ reliably from alone […]

fernandezdols_1995_smiles.cit: Fernandez-Dols, J. M., & Ruiz-Belda, M. A. (1995). Are smiles a sign of happiness? Gold medal winners at the Olympic Games. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 69(6), 1113-1119.
fernandezdols_1995_smiles.design: Naturalistic field study of televised award ceremonies (Televisión Española broadcasts, Barcelona 1992 Olympics). Study 1: all facial behaviour of 22 gold medalists (14 women, 8 men; from China, former Czechoslovakia, Germany, Greece, Russia, Spain, Switzerland, Tajikistan, Ukraine, UK, USA; individual sports such as running, gymnastics, weightlifting, fencing) coded with FACS, second by second, across three ceremony stages: Stage A, waiting behind the podium (non-interactive); Stage B, standing on the podium and interacting with authorities and the public (medal presentation; interactive); Stage C, turned toward the flagpoles during the flags and national anthem (non-interactive). Duchenne smile = AU 6 + AU 12 observed simultaneously; 'other smiles' coded separately. Recorded time: A 398 s, B 467 s, C 499 s. Happiness was not reported by the filmed athletes ('The actual recorded medalists were unavailable'): instead 10 Spanish gold medalists from team sports (7 women field hockey, 3 men soccer) rated their own emotional experience at moments of their final match and in the three ceremony stages on six 0-10 scales (happiness, sadness, anger, fear, disgust, surprise) […]
fernandezdols_1995_smiles.numbers: Percentage of total time (Table 2): Duchenne smile A 2.76%, B 47.75%, C 0.00%; other smiles A 7.29%, B 28.05%, C 2.80% (A: 11 s Duchenne, 29 s other of 398 s; B: 223 s and 131 s of 467 s; C: 0 s and 14 s of 499 s). A vs B paired t: Duchenne t(21) = 12.05, p < .001; other smiles t(21) = 4.42, p < .001; A vs C no significant differences. Duchenne smiles: 4 of 22 briefly in A, 22 of 22 in B, 0 of 22 in C. Table 1 ('Mean Judgments From Seven Gold Medalists'), happiness 0-10: A 9.85, B 9.42, C 9.28; surprise 1.42-1.85; other emotions ≤ 0.85. Study 2: all 10 medalist judges judged the two models as feeling the same emotion (8 'alegría', 1 'tranquilidad'); all 32 students judged both as happy, 20 judged the sad-looking one happiest, 6 the smiling one, 6 equal.
fernandezdols_1995_smiles.conclusion: Happiness was not sufficient for smiling (and smiles were not a necessary sign of happiness): although medalists were presumed/judged to be intensely happy throughout the ceremony, smiling (and Duchenne smiling) was concentrated in the interactive stage, consistent with the behavioural-ecology view that expressions mark social motives in interaction rather than the peak of emotion. The authors considered and argued against a display-rule explanation (inhibition during the anthem) by noting that the non-ceremonial, non-interactive Stage A also showed little smiling […]
fernandezdols_1995_smiles.caveats: Proxy emotion measure: the 22 filmed athletes did not report their feelings; the 7 Spanish raters were different people, from team sports, rating their own retrospective feelings, so the inference that each filmed medalist was happy in every stage is indirect. Only six basic-emotion scales were used, so states such as being moved, pride or solemnity during the anthem were not assessed. Stages differ in more than interaction […]
terms: behavioral ecology view / behavioral ecological theories of facial behavior

kraut_1979_social.cit: Kraut, R. E., & Johnston, R. E. (1979). Social and emotional messages of smiling: An ethological approach. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 37(9), 1539-1553.

ruizbelda_2003_spontaneous.cit: Ruiz-Belda, M. A., Fernandez-Dols, J. M., Carrera, P., & Barchard, K. (2003). Spontaneous facial expressions of happy bowlers and soccer fans. Cognition & Emotion, 17(2), 315-326.
ruizbelda_2003_spontaneous.design: Two naturalistic field studies (authors at Universidad Autónoma de Madrid and UNLV; field locations not verifiable from the abstract) in which bowlers and soccer fans reported their emotions; facial behaviour of those who reported happiness was analysed as a function of whether they were engaged in social interaction. Sample sizes, coding system (the group typically uses FACS) and the timing/method of emotion reports could not be verified from the abstract.
ruizbelda_2003_spontaneous.numbers: Among people who reported happiness: probability of smiling without social interaction .09 (bowlers) and .07 (soccer fans); during social interaction .78 (bowlers) and .70 (soccer fans). Ns not available from the abstract.
ruizbelda_2003_spontaneous.conclusion: Smiles are not an indicator of happiness per se; the relation between smiling and happiness is complex and indirect, with social interaction strongly increasing the probability of smiling among happy people.
ruizbelda_2003_spontaneous.caveats: Abstract-level verification only (no OA copy found); sample sizes, how/when happiness was reported (likely retrospectively, after the observed moments), and the coding method are unverified. Interaction episodes may coincide with the most intense moments of celebration, so sociality and emotional intensity are not independent; the study cannot show that smiles during interaction were not also emotion-driven.

crivelli_2015_smiles.cit: Crivelli, C., Carrera, P., & Fernandez-Dols, J. M. (2015). Are smiles a sign of happiness? Spontaneous expressions of judo winners. Evolution and Human Behavior, 36(1), 52-58.
crivelli_2015_smiles.design: Two naturalistic field studies of winning judo fighters (total N = 174), video-recorded, FACS-coded frame by frame by two independent FACS-certified judges (Duchenne smile = AU 6 + AU 12) in a fixed window after match completion (7 s in Study 1, 5 s in Study 2). Records were classified as interactive vs non-interactive: social interaction 'defined exclusively as explicit communicative gestures made with the arms and hands linked with verbal messages while the fighter was facing the audience'. There were no ceremony 'phases'; the comparison is interactive vs non-interactive episodes within the post-match window. Study 1: 55 winners at the 2010 Under-23 Spanish National Judo Championship (13 gold-medal, 13 bronze-medal and 29 preliminary-round matches); the author manuscript prints '43 males, 22 females', which does not sum to 55. Happiness: self-report only in Study 1, from a subsample of 20 gold/bronze winners (10 male, 10 female) who completed 16 0-7 Likert scales (including happy, euphoric, proud, pleasure) about 'the moment in which the match ended', 2-30 min after their final matches. […]
crivelli_2015_smiles.numbers: Study 1 (N = 55): 8 Duchenne smilers (.15), all 8 during social interaction (8 of 32 interactive records vs 0 of 23 non-interactive), chi-square(1, N = 55) = 6.73, p = .009, phi = .35. Self-report subsample (n = 20): 3 Duchenne smilers vs 17 non-smilers; happy ratings 6.33 (SE .67) vs 5.29 (SE .50), p = .082, r = -.39 (non-significant, in the direction of more happiness in smilers). Study 2 (N = 119): 25 Duchenne smilers (.21); 23 of 79 interactive vs 2 of 40 non-interactive records; logistic regression (interaction term dropped): social interaction OR = 5.95, 95% CI [1.29, 27.56], Wald = 5.21, p = .022; winning a medal OR = 2.58, 95% CI [0.97, 6.84], Wald = 3.60, p > .05.
crivelli_2015_smiles.conclusion: Social interaction, not happiness, was the strongest predictor of Duchenne smiles; Duchenne smiles were not a necessary sign of happiness; results support Behavioral Ecology Theory (facial displays as tools for social interaction) over the Facial Expression Program.
crivelli_2015_smiles.caveats: Very small self-report subsample (only 3 smilers), with the authors acknowledging Type II risk; the null for happiness is weak evidence of no relation, and the medal effect was marginal (CI 0.97-6.84). The 5-7 s windows are short. 'Social interaction' was defined by communicative arm/hand gestures with verbal messages while facing the audience, which may itself co-occur with peak positive emotion (celebration), so interaction and emotional expression are not independent. […]
terms: social interaction (communicative gestures with arms and hands while facing the audience)

mattson_2013_darwins.cit: Mattson, W. I., Cohn, J. F., Mahoor, M. H., Gangi, D. N., & Messinger, D. S. (2013). Darwin's Duchenne: Eye constriction during infant joy and distress. PLOS ONE, 8(11), e80161.
mattson_2013_darwins.design: Study 1: 12 six-month-olds (66.7% male; 16.7% African American, 16.7% Asian American, 33.3% Hispanic American, 33.3% European American) with a parent (11 mothers, 1 father) in the Face-to-Face/Still-Face (3 min play, 2 min still-face); spontaneous naturalistic lab interaction. Automated FACS intensity measurement (active appearance models plus SVMs trained on manual FACS) of AU12 (smile), AU20 (cry-face) and AU6 (eye constriction), dichotomized at FACS B for presence; agreement with manual coding kappa .78 (AU6), .77 (AU12), .76 (AU20). Study 2: 24 publicly posted vaccination videos (12 at 6 months, 12 at 12 months), first 10 s after injection; manual frame-by-frame FACS coding of AU20 and AU6 (kappa .86 AU6, .71 AU20). No self-report or observer emotion ratings.
mattson_2013_darwins.numbers: Study 1: proportion of smiles with AU6, Play .64 vs Still-Face .34, F(1, 11) = 6.70, p = .03; proportion of cry-faces with AU6, Still-Face .70 vs Play .36, F(1, 11) = 11.43, p < .01. Smiles with AU6 had higher AU12 intensity (3.07 vs 2.61), t(10) = 4.86, p = .001; cry-faces with AU6 had higher AU20 intensity (3.61 vs 3.16), t(9) = 3.77, p < .01. Study 2: AU6 accompanied cry-faces in .87 of cry-face time (6 months .82; 12 months .92; no age difference).
mattson_2013_darwins.conclusion: Eye constriction 'indexes the affective intensity' of both smiles and cry-faces; the authors propose a 'Duchenne distress expression' parallel to the Duchenne smile, and suggest eye constriction may regulate exposure to intense stimuli or focus on internal state. They note eye constriction is unlikely to play the same role in all adult negative expressions (fear and anger involve eye opening).
mattson_2013_darwins.caveats: 'Intensified' implies causation; the data show co-occurrence. 'Intensity' here is expression intensity (AU12/AU20 strength), not measured feeling; there were no self-report or observer ratings (those are in M9, the same infants). Very small samples (12 infants; 24 YouTube infants). Study 1 is the same 12-infant FFSF sample as Messinger et al. (2012), so M8 and M9 are not independent replications. Infants only; the authors themselves do not generalize to all adult negative expressions.

hoque_2012_exploring.cit: Hoque, M. E., McDuff, D. J., & Picard, R. W. (2012). Exploring temporal patterns in classifying frustrated and delighted smiles. IEEE Transactions on Affective Computing, 3(3), 323-334.

sayette_2012_alcohol.cit: Sayette, M. A., Creswell, K. G., Dimoff, J. D., Fairbairn, C. E., Cohn, J. F., Heckman, B. W., Kirchner, T. R., Levine, J. M., & Moreland, R. L. (2012). Alcohol and group formation: A multimodal investigation of the effects of alcohol on emotion and social bonding. Psychological Science, 23(8), 869-878.

tsai_2016_leaders.cit: Tsai, J. L., Ang, J. Y. Z., Blevins, E., Goernandt, J., Fung, H. H., Jiang, D., Elliott, J., Koelzer, A., Uchida, Y., Lee, Y. C., Lin, Y., Zhang, X., Govindama, Y., & Haddouk, L. (2016). Leaders' smiles reflect cultural differences in ideal affect. Emotion, 16(2), 183-195.
tsai_2016_leaders.design: Posed official photographs (naturalistic archival). Study 1: top-ranked US (N = 98) and Chinese (N = 91) government leaders, CEOs and university presidents. Study 2: winning vs losing political candidates (US vs Taiwan) and higher vs lower ranked CEOs/university presidents (US vs China); US N = 223, Taiwan/China N = 266. Study 3: ideal and actual affect (Affect Valuation Index) in college students from 10 nations (N = 1,267), and FACS coding of official photos of legislators from those nations about 8 years later (N = 3,372). FACS occurrence coding by two coders (one blind; kappa .61-.98, mean .77 on a separate set of 118 photos); replicated with Emotient Analytics and Noldus FaceReader.
tsai_2016_leaders.numbers: Study 1: any smile US .94 vs China .55 (OR = 5.00); excited smile US .40 vs China .07 (OR = 6.25, p = .046); calm smiles did not differ. Study 2: US leaders showed more excited smiles regardless of election outcome or rank. Study 3 (10 nations): ideal HAP with excited smiles r = .81; ideal LAP with calm smiles r = .75; actual HAP and LAP correlations smaller (.57, .41); ideal LAP predicted calm smiles controlling for actual LAP (beta = .87, p = .035); held after controlling democratization, human development and GDP per capita.
tsai_2016_leaders.conclusion: Leaders' smiles in official photos reflect the affective states their cultures value (ideal affect) more than the states people actually feel (actual affect).
tsai_2016_leaders.caveats: Evidence is about display (cultural products), not felt emotion; nation-level correlations with n = 10; static posed photos coded without neutral baseline (addressed with software). Both smile types contain the Duchenne marker, so the study speaks to open vs closed Duchenne smiles, not to Duchenne vs non-Duchenne.

lafrance_2003_contingent.cit: LaFrance, M., Hecht, M. A., & Paluck, E. L. (2003). The contingent smile: A meta-analysis of sex differences in smiling. Psychological Bulletin, 129(2), 305-334.

keltner_1997_study.cit: Keltner, D., & Bonanno, G. A. (1997). A study of laughter and dissociation: Distinct correlates of laughter and smiling during bereavement. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 73(4), 687-702.

ansfield_2007_smiling.cit: Ansfield, M. E. (2007). Smiling when distressed: When a smile is a frown turned upside down. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 33(6), 763-775.
ansfield_2007_smiling.design: Study 1: laboratory experiment; participants viewed moderately and intensely distressing, amusing and neutral videos in social or nonsocial conditions; smiling coded from video (coding system not verifiable from abstract); self-reported distress/affect during and after videos. Study 2: raters judged participants from Study 1 (social appropriateness, likability). A secondary summary (BPS Research Digest) reports '80 men and 80 women' who watched 'disgusting videos, either alone or in the company of someone else'; not verified in the primary text. Note: the DOI supplied with the claim was not checked; the correct DOI per PubMed is 10.1177/0146167206297398.
ansfield_2007_smiling.numbers: Not available from the abstract. Secondary summary (BPS Research Digest): 80 men and 80 women; participants smiled more when viewing with someone else than alone; more smiling during the video related to less reported distress afterwards (unverified).
ansfield_2007_smiling.conclusion: Smiling while distressed is most common when distress is greatest (and, for men, in social conditions and with intense stimuli), is associated with more negative affect during but more positive affect after distressing videos, suggesting a self-regulatory function; observers judge distressed smilers as less socially appropriate and less likable.
ansfield_2007_smiling.caveats: Full text not accessed; design details (N, nature of the social condition, smile coding, whether Duchenne markers were coded) unverified. Correlational links between smiling and later affect do not establish a regulatory effect. The sex difference was moderated by condition and stimulus intensity.

ekman_1988_smiles.cit: Ekman, P., Friesen, W. V., & O'Sullivan, M. (1988). Smiles when lying. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 54(3), 414-420.

ekman_1990_duchenne.cit: Ekman, P., Davidson, R. J., & Friesen, W. V. (1990). The Duchenne smile: Emotional expression and brain physiology II. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 58(2), 342-353.

frank_1993_behavioral.cit: Frank, M. G., Ekman, P., & Friesen, W. V. (1993). Behavioral markers and recognizability of the smile of enjoyment. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 64(1), 83-93.
frank_1993_behavioral.design: Study 1 (production): spontaneous lab-elicited smiles of 44 women from two earlier experiments in which faces were recorded without their knowledge while they watched positive emotion films (22 alone, 22 in a social interaction). FACS coding; enjoyment smile defined a priori as AU12 + AU6 (Duchenne marker), nonenjoyment smile as AU12 without AU6; one smile of each type randomly selected per subject (44 pairs). Durations of onset, apex, offset and overall AU12 action measured. Study 2 (perception): 80 Cornell undergraduates judged 20 enjoyment/nonenjoyment smile pairs matched on AU12 intensity (4 very slight, 9 slight, 7 moderate), 40 judging single smiles and 40 judging the two smiles of a pair, as 'a true, genuine expression of enjoyment' or 'a false or social expression'. Study 3 (perception): 30 undergraduates rated the smiling women on 15 bipolar adjective scales.
frank_1993_behavioral.numbers: Study 1: variance of overall duration smaller for Duchenne-marked than unmarked smiles, F(1, 31) = 8.11, p < .005; mean Duchenne smile duration 0.5-4 s in the social situation (as predicted) but 6.18 s alone (outside the predicted range). 'Smoothness' operationalized as correlations of overall duration with component durations: Duchenne-marked smiles r = .81 (onset), .52 (apex), .67 (offset), all p < .001; unmarked smiles only overall-apex correlated (r = .94). Study 2: accuracy 74% (SD = .12) when judging smile pairs and 56% (SD = .13) when judging single smiles, chance 50%; accuracy better for slight than moderate AU12 intensity smiles; observers reporting an eye-based ('oculi') strategy were more accurate, r = .22 (r = .26 for very slight smiles). Study 3: people were rated more positively when showing enjoyment smiles (M = 4.41) than nonenjoyment smiles (M = 3.96), F(1, 29) = 11.93 […]
frank_1993_behavioral.conclusion: Enjoyment smiles behave more like emotional, 'extrapyramidally driven' facial actions than other smiles; the enjoyment smile 'differs not only in morphology but also in dynamics and social signal value' from smiles in general. The authors caution that they showed enjoyment smiles can have, not that they typically do have, social signal value.
frank_1993_behavioral.caveats: Circularity: 'enjoyment smile' was defined by the Duchenne marker; no self-report of enjoyment was collected for the specific smiles in Study 1. 'Smoothness' was measured as correlations among phase durations, not by counting irregularities. The predicted 0.5-4 s duration held only in the social situation. Single-smile accuracy was modest. Observers' accuracy link to the eyes rests on their self-described strategy (r = .22) and on better accuracy for low-intensity AU12 […]

jakobs_1999_social.cit: Jakobs, E., Manstead, A. S. R., & Fischer, A. H. (1999). Social motives and emotional feelings as determinants of facial displays: The case of smiling. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 25(4), 424-435.
jakobs_1999_social.design: Laboratory experiment (authors at the University of Amsterdam). Social motives varied via two aspects of social context: pairs of friends performed either the same or a different task, in either the same or a different room (2 x 2), plus an alone control group. Emotional feelings varied within subjects via two film clips differing in the intensity of positive emotional feelings evoked. Dependent variables: facial activity coded with FACS, self-reported emotional feelings, and measures of social motives. N, which AUs were analysed, and statistics could not be verified (no OA full text).
jakobs_1999_social.conclusion: Smiling is determined both by emotional feelings and by social motives, but in different ways; both affected FACS-coded facial activity, contrary to a purely social (behavioural-ecology) or purely emotional (read-out) account.
jakobs_1999_social.caveats: Abstract-level only. The 'different room' conditions implement an implicit audience as in Fridlund (1991); results for each cell, AU definitions (e.g., AU 12 with/without AU 6) and sample size are unverified.

krumhuber_2009_duchenne.cit: Krumhuber, E. G., & Manstead, A. S. R. (2009). Can Duchenne smiles be feigned? New evidence on felt and false smiles. Emotion, 9(6), 807-820.
krumhuber_2009_duchenne.design: Exp. 1: participants smiled spontaneously to amusing material or posed a smile on instruction; smiles were FACS-classified as Duchenne (D) or non-Duchenne (ND). Exps. 2-4: observers rated subsets of smiles (full face, upper or lower face, static vs dynamic).
krumhuber_2009_duchenne.conclusion: Duchenne smiles can be produced deliberately. The D marker is a weak cue to felt enjoyment compared with dynamic and other features.

messinger_2001_smiles.cit: Messinger, D. S., Fogel, A., & Dickson, K. L. (2001). All smiles are positive, but some smiles are more positive than others. Developmental Psychology, 37(5), 642-653.
messinger_2001_smiles.design: Longitudinal naturalistic observation of mother-infant interaction: 13 infants observed weekly from 1 to 6 months of age. Smile types defined by cheek raising (AU6) and mouth opening; coding system and setting details not verified from the full text.
messinger_2001_smiles.numbers: N = 13 infants, weekly from 1 to 6 months. Effect sizes not verified (abstract only).
messinger_2001_smiles.conclusion: Smiling alone already indexes positive engagement; cheek raising amplifies the sharing of positive affect (linked to mother smiling) and mouth opening amplifies visual engagement (linked to gazing at mother's face); 'all smiles are positive, but some smiles are more positive than others'.
messinger_2001_smiles.caveats: Abstract only; 13 infants; the positive-affect interpretation is inferred from contexts (mother smiling, gaze at mother), not from an independent emotion measure. The title asserts all smiles are positive, which contrasts with the Ekman/Frank claim that only Duchenne smiles index enjoyment.
terms: smiling alone (without cheek raising or mouth opening)
smiling involving both cheek raising and mouth opening

papa_2008_smiling.cit: Papa, A., & Bonanno, G. A. (2008). Smiling in the face of adversity: The interpersonal and intrapersonal functions of smiling. Emotion, 8(1), 1-12.

schmidt_2006_movement.cit: Schmidt, K. L., Ambadar, Z., Cohn, J. F., & Reed, L. I. (2006). Movement differences between deliberate and spontaneous facial expressions: Zygomaticus major action in smiling. Journal of Nonverbal Behavior, 30(1), 37-52.
schmidt_2006_movement.design: Within-participant comparison of deliberately posed and spontaneously occurring smiles during a directed facial action task. Automated facial image analysis quantified lip-corner movement during periods of visible zygomaticus major activity (AU 12). N not stated in the abstract.
schmidt_2006_movement.numbers: Not available beyond the abstract (no N or statistics in the abstract).
schmidt_2006_movement.conclusion: Deliberate smiles were faster at onset and offset, larger and longer at offset than spontaneous smiles produced in the same session, but not more asymmetric. The differences may reflect the different context and purpose of the signals.
schmidt_2006_movement.caveats: Full text not reachable: the PMC author manuscript could not be accessed. Sample size and effect sizes not verified. Spontaneous smiles during a posing session may be social or embarrassed smiles, which limits generalisation to emotion-elicited smiles.
terms: deliberately posed and spontaneously occurring smiles
context and purpose of the facial signal

soussignan_2002_duchenne.cit: Soussignan, R. (2002). Duchenne smile, emotional experience, and autonomic reactivity: A test of the facial feedback hypothesis. Emotion, 2(1), 52-74.

girard_2021_reconsidering.cit: Girard, J. M., Cohn, J. F., Yin, L., & Morency, L.-P. (2021). Reconsidering the Duchenne smile: Formalizing and testing hypotheses about eye constriction and positive emotion. Affective Science, 2(1), 32-47.
girard_2021_reconsidering.design: Spontaneous lab-elicited expressions from the BP4D+ database: 751 smiles from 136 participants during tasks designed to elicit amusement, embarrassment, fear and physical pain. Study 1: smile characteristics vs participants' self-reported (experienced) positive emotion. Study 2: third-party observers' perceptions of videos of the same smiles. Manual FACS intensity coding of AU6 and AU12 (per the 2019 precursor: five certified coders, about 15 s per task, AU6 S = .70, AU12 S = .84; participants 60% female, 46% White, 34% Asian, 10% Latino/Hispanic, 7% Black, aged 18-30, US residents). Bayesian (multilevel) models.
girard_2021_reconsidering.numbers: 2021 paper: numerical results not verified (full text inaccessible). 2019 precursor (same BP4D+ smiles, full text read): AU6 and AU12 intensity correlated r = .64; self-reported amusement correlated r = .21 with AU6 and .28 with AU12; controlling for AU12 intensity reduced the AU6 effect on amusement by 64% (from 0.22 [0.15, 0.29]) and the amusement effect on AU6 by 79% (from 0.24 [0.16, 0.31]); AU6 + AU12 + sex explained R-squared = .30 of amusement; AU12 explained about half the variance in AU6 (R-squared = .51).
girard_2021_reconsidering.conclusion: Most proposed Duchenne-smile hypotheses were contradicted or only weakly supported. For experienced positive emotion, AU6 information was non-specific, redundant with other smile characteristics and context-dependent; for perceived positive emotion, AU6 carried some unique information but context also mattered. Inferring positive emotion requires more than the presence or intensity of eye constriction.
girard_2021_reconsidering.caveats: The hypotheses list and numerical results of the 2021 paper were not read. Terminology: in the 2019 precursor the 'amusement' rating was the single item 'How much did you feel happy, joyful, or amused?', so 'amusement'/'positive emotion' there merges happiness, joy and amusement; check whether the 2021 Study 1 'positive emotion' measure is the same item before citing it as amusement or happiness. The tasks include negative-emotion contexts […]

gunnery_2013_deliberate.cit: Gunnery, S. D., Hall, J. A., & Ruben, M. A. (2013). The deliberate Duchenne smile: Individual differences in expressive control. Journal of Nonverbal Behavior, 37(1), 29-41.
gunnery_2013_deliberate.design: Posed/deliberate production. Role-play task (smile while enacting scripted scenarios: three faked positive / masked negative affect, three genuine positive affect) and an imitation task (imitate photographs of Duchenne and non-Duchenne smiles). Per the BPS Research Digest (secondary): 96 students (49 men); smiles coded by two experienced coders.
gunnery_2013_deliberate.numbers: Primary: not verifiable (full text not accessible). Secondary (BPS Research Digest): N = 96; 28% of role-play smiles were Duchenne (31% in genuine-positive scenarios, 24% in fake-positive scenarios); 71% successfully imitated the Duchenne smile. It is unclear from the digest whether 71% refers to participants or imitation trials.
gunnery_2013_deliberate.conclusion: 'Substantial minorities' of people can deliberately produce a Duchenne smile, with individual differences in consistency across tasks related to self-reported ability to put on convincing false displays.
gunnery_2013_deliberate.caveats: Full text not read; the proportion requested could not be confirmed from the primary source. Note the apparent tension between 'substantial minorities' (role-play usage) and the secondary report that 71% could imitate a Duchenne smile (capability).

mehu_2007_smiles.cit: Mehu, M., Grammer, K., & Dunbar, R. I. M. (2007). Smiles when sharing. Evolution and Human Behavior, 28(6), 415-422.
mehu_2007_smiles.design: From the published abstract: 60 people were covertly filmed while interacting with a friend in two conditions, control and sharing (production in a naturalistic laboratory interaction; covert filming). Smiles were classified into Duchenne ('spontaneous') and non-Duchenne smiles. Participants completed questionnaires including the Altruism Scale and a self-report questionnaire of emotional state. Not reported in the abstract: sex and population of participants, country, what was shared, duration of interactions, the coding system (e.g., FACS AU6+AU12), inter-coder reliability, the smile metric, the statistics, and whether the friend's (perceiver's) behaviour or decisions were measured.
mehu_2007_smiles.numbers: Abstract: N = 60; two conditions (control, sharing). Direction only: Duchenne smiles at 'higher rates' in sharing; non-Duchenne smiles 'unaffected'; Duchenne smiles in sharing 'positively affected' by altruism; self-reported emotional states 'did not vary between conditions'. No rates, test statistics or effect sizes in the abstract.
mehu_2007_smiles.conclusion: The Duchenne smile 'is relevant to situations that involve the sharing of material resources because it would reliably advertise altruistic intentions' and 'could therefore be an important signal in the formation and maintenance of cooperative relationships' (Abstract). The authors frame smiles with an emotional component as honest signals of altruistic dispositions 'because they are not easy to produce voluntarily'.
mehu_2007_smiles.caveats: Abstract only; published full text not retrieved. The coding method behind the Duchenne/non-Duchenne classification (e.g., FACS AU6+AU12) and all numbers are unverified. The authors label Duchenne smiles 'spontaneous'; that is their term, not a measured property. Because self-reported emotion did not change between conditions and was poorly related to smiling, the result does not show that Duchenne smiles tracked felt positive emotion here. […]

harker_2001_expressions.cit: Harker, L., & Keltner, D. (2001). Expressions of positive emotion in women's college yearbook pictures and their relationship to personality and life outcomes across adulthood. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 80(1), 112-124.

ambadar_2009_smiles.cit: Ambadar, Z., Cohn, J. F., & Reed, L. I. (2009). All smiles are not created equal: Morphology and timing of smiles perceived as amused, polite, and embarrassed/nervous. Journal of Nonverbal Behavior, 33(1), 17–34.
ambadar_2009_smiles.design: Perception study of spontaneous smiles. Stimuli: 122 smiles from 66 people (91% female) that occurred, unrequested, between trials of the directed facial action task while recording the Cohn-Kanade database (experimenter present). Judges: 101 University of Pittsburgh undergraduates (61% female; 78% Caucasian) chose amused, embarrassed, nervous, polite or other. A smile was assigned a type if at least 50% endorsed it and no more than 25% endorsed another: 19 amused, 23 polite, 3 embarrassed, 8 nervous (pooled with embarrassed), 1 other, i.e., 53 classified smiles. Morphology by manual FACS (AU6 kappa .83; smile controls AU15/17/23/24 kappa .65; mouth opening AU25/26; AU12 duration); dynamics and head motion by automated facial image analysis (AFA v.3).
ambadar_2009_smiles.numbers: AU6 more frequent in perceived amused than perceived embarrassed/nervous (chi-square = 4.85, p < .05) and polite (10.71, p < .001); AU6 comparable in embarrassed/nervous and polite. Mouth opening less frequent in polite than amused or embarrassed/nervous. Amplitude: polite smaller than amused and embarrassed/nervous. Duration: amused about 4 s, polite 2 s, embarrassed/nervous 2.9 s; only amused vs polite significant. Velocity: amused had higher onset and offset velocity than polite, and higher maximum offset velocity than embarrassed/nervous (t(39) = 2.54). Downward head pitch greater for embarrassed/nervous than amused or polite. No asymmetry effects. Only about 40% of smiles met the classification criteria.
ambadar_2009_smiles.conclusion: Perceived smile meanings relate to multiple morphological and dynamic features; AU6 with a smile is not sufficient to communicate felt enjoyment; perceived meaning need not correspond to the smiler's experience, which was not measured.
ambadar_2009_smiles.caveats: Internal inconsistencies: the abstract says perceived amused had 'lower maximum offset velocity' than embarrassed/nervous, but the Results report larger offset velocity for amused (t(39) = 2.54); the abstract says embarrassed smiles more often included 'smile controls' than polite, but the Results report no significant difference (t(50) = -1.69, p > .05); the Discussion says embarrassed/nervous smiles had 'longer duration' than polite, but the Results report no difference (t(40) = -1.22). calvo_2018_visual.cit: Calvo, M. G., Krumhuber, E. G., & Fernández-Martín, A. (2018). Visual attention mechanisms in happiness versus trustworthiness processing of facial expressions. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 72(4), 729–741.

martin_2017_smiles.cit: Martin, J., Rychlowska, M., Wood, A., & Niedenthal, P. (2017). Smiles as multipurpose social signals. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 21(11), 864–877.
martin_2017_smiles.design: Theoretical review (social-functional account of smiles) drawing mainly on reverse-correlation modelling, human and Bayesian classifier validation, laughter studies and cross-cultural recognition work.
martin_2017_smiles.conclusion: The smile can be productively investigated according to how it helps the smiler meet the challenges and opportunities of social living, rather than only as a sign of happiness.
martin_2017_smiles.caveats: Full text not read; specific claims beyond the abstract (e.g., cross-cultural recognition evidence) unverified.

niedenthal_2010_simulation.cit: Niedenthal, P. M., Mermillod, M., Maringer, M., & Hess, U. (2010). The Simulation of Smiles (SIMS) model: Embodied simulation and the meaning of facial expression. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 33(6), 417–433.

johnston_2010_smiling.cit: Johnston, L., Miles, L., & Macrae, C. N. (2010). Why are you smiling at me? Social functions of enjoyment and non-enjoyment smiles. British Journal of Social Psychology, 49(Pt 1), 107–127.

rychlowska_2015_heterogeneity.cit: Rychlowska, M., Miyamoto, Y., Matsumoto, D., Hess, U., Gilboa-Schechtman, E., Kamble, S., Muluk, H., Masuda, T., & Niedenthal, P. M. (2015). Heterogeneity of long-history migration explains cultural differences in reports of emotional expressivity and the functions of smiles. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 112(19), E2429–E2436.
rychlowska_2015_heterogeneity.design: Survey/self-report, not facial measurement. (1) Reanalysis of display-rule data from 32 countries (n = 5,340; Matsumoto, Yoo & Fontaine, 2008) against historical heterogeneity (number of source countries contributing to the present population over 500 years). (2) Original questionnaire study in nine countries (Canada, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Israel, Japan, New Zealand, United States; n = 726) on beliefs about what states a smile signifies; cluster and factor analyses.
rychlowska_2015_heterogeneity.numbers: 32 countries, n = 5,340 (reanalysis); 9 countries, n = 726 (smile-belief study). Effect sizes not verified (full text not accessed).
rychlowska_2015_heterogeneity.conclusion: Historical heterogeneity predicts norms favouring open emotional expression and groups countries into 'cultures of smiling' in which beliefs about smile functions (affiliative vs dominance) differ.
rychlowska_2015_heterogeneity.caveats: Country-level ecological associations; sample composition of the smile-belief study not verified.

rychlowska_2017_functional.cit: Rychlowska, M., Jack, R. E., Garrod, O. G. B., Schyns, P. G., Martin, J. D., & Niedenthal, P. M. (2017). Functional smiles: Tools for love, sympathy, and war. Psychological Science, 28(9), 1259–1270.
rychlowska_2017_functional.design: Perception (mental representation) study using reverse correlation with a Generative Face Grammar. Study 1: 55 US students (32 female; 43 analysed after exclusions, including 2 African American participants excluded because faces were white) judged 2,400 random 1.25-s 3D facial animations, each with AU12 (bilateral or unilateral) plus 1-4 of 36 other AUs, on 8 white face identities, against definitions of reward ('reflecting a happy response'), affiliative ('reflecting positive social intentions') and dominance ('reflecting superiority') smiles. Models validated with a naive Bayesian classifier (10-fold cross-validation) and a detection task with 107 white US students (71 female); social judgments by 62 US students (41 female) on 'positive feeling', 'social connection' and 'superiority/dominance'. No production data.
rychlowska_2017_functional.numbers: Reward: symmetrical AU12 with AU13, AU14, AU1-2. Affiliative: symmetrical AU12 with AU14 and AU24 (lip pressor). Dominance: asymmetrical AU12 (AU12L or AU12R) with AU10, AU6, AU9, AU5. Classifier: reward and dominance above chance; affiliative lower and misclassified as reward in 21.4%. Detection d': reward .81, dominance .77, affiliative .38. Social judgments: reward and affiliative smiles rated high on positive feeling and social connection and low on superiority; dominance the reverse.
rychlowska_2017_functional.conclusion: Provides 'the first detailed description of the physical form and social messages' of three functional smile types and documents the versatility of smiles; acknowledges the categories lack easily accessible semantic labels and calls for tests with physiological and behavioural responses in social situations.
rychlowska_2017_functional.caveats: Synthetic white faces, US (mostly white) student perceivers; the reward-smile definition invoked a 'happy response', so 'reward' is partly tied to perceived happiness. Affiliative smiles were less distinct. Production validity untested in this paper.

maringer_2011_beyond.cit: Maringer, M., Krumhuber, E. G., Fischer, A. H., & Niedenthal, P. M. (2011). Beyond smile dynamics: Mimicry and beliefs in judgments of smiles. Emotion, 11(1), 181–187.

rychlowska_2014_blocking.cit: Rychlowska, M., Cañadas, E., Wood, A., Krumhuber, E. G., Fischer, A., & Niedenthal, P. M. (2014). Blocking mimicry makes true and false smiles look the same. PLoS ONE, 9(3), e90876.

gunnery_2016_perceptions.cit: Gunnery, S. D., & Ruben, M. A. (2016). Perceptions of Duchenne and non-Duchenne smiles: A meta-analysis. Cognition & Emotion, 30(3), 501–515.
gunnery_2016_perceptions.design: Meta-analysis of perception studies comparing ratings of Duchenne smiles (with cheek raiser activation) and non-Duchenne smiles; moderator analyses of methodological, stimulus-specific and perceiver-specific variables. Number of studies and effect sizes not verified.
gunnery_2016_perceptions.numbers: Not verified: k, overall effect size and confidence intervals could not be read (full text inaccessible). Moderators per abstract: larger differences for video than photographs, for naturally elicited than posed smiles, and when AU12 intensity was not matched; 'other perceiver and methodological moderators' also reported.
gunnery_2016_perceptions.conclusion: Duchenne smiles and the people showing them are perceived more positively overall, with the size of the difference depending on stimulus format, elicitation method and AU12 matching.
gunnery_2016_perceptions.caveats: This is perception evidence (what observers infer), not evidence that Duchenne smiles reflect felt enjoyment. The larger effect when AU12 intensity is not matched is consistent with part of the Duchenne effect being an intensity effect.

thibault_2008_childrens.cit: Thibault, P., Gosselin, P., Brunel, M.-L., & Hess, U. (2008). Children's and adolescents' perception of the authenticity of smiles. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 102(3), 360–367.

krys_2016_careful.cit: Krys, K., Vauclair, C.-M., Capaldi, C. A., Lun, V. M.-C., Bond, M. H., Domínguez-Espinosa, A., et al. (2016). Be careful where you smile: Culture shapes judgments of intelligence and honesty of smiling individuals. Journal of Nonverbal Behavior, 40(2), 101–116.

jancke_1996_facial.cit: Jäncke, L. (1996). Facial EMG in an anger-provoking situation: Individual differences in directing anger outwards or inwards. International Journal of Psychophysiology, 23(3), 207–214.

keltner_1995_facial.cit: Keltner, D., Moffitt, T. E., & Stouthamer-Loeber, M. (1995). Facial expressions of emotion and psychopathology in adolescent boys. Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 104(4), 644–652.

reed_2014_commitment.cit: Reed, L. I., DeScioli, P., & Pinker, S. A. (2014). The commitment function of angry facial expressions. Psychological Science, 25(8), 1511–1517.
reed_2014_commitment.design: Two online experiments on Amazon Mechanical Turk with a modified ultimatum game. Exp 1: 870 participants randomly assigned to Proposer or Responder (mean age 30.21, SD = 9.34; 571 male, 299 female) (p. 5). Exp 2: 588 participants (mean age 30.80, SD = 10.08; 345 male) (p. 7); here the actor was described as a 'typical' Responder rather than the Proposer's actual partner. Country not reported. Stimulus: a short video clip (6 s, 30 fps) of one female actor posing either a neutral or an angry expression; the angry face is described as 'frowning eyebrows, intensely staring eyes, and a closed mouth with lowered corners' (p. 5, citing Ekman & Friesen, 1975); no FACS/AU coding of the clips is reported. The clip accompanied a written demand of 50% or 70% of $1.00 ('If you offer me less than [50/70] cents, I will reject your offer', p. 6). Design: 2 (angry vs neutral expression) x 2 (50% vs 70% demand), between participants. Perceivers: Proposers. Behaviour: offer in cents out of $1.00, with real bonus payments of up to $1.00 (p. 5); Responders set minimum acceptable offers by the strategy method. Proposers also rated the Responder's anger and happiness on 7-point scales […]
reed_2014_commitment.numbers: Exp 1 (p. 6): 50% demand, angry M = 49.98 cents (SD = 10.95) vs neutral M = 50.55 (SD = 11.17), no effect; 70% demand, angry M = 60.92 (SD = 11.23) vs neutral M = 54.77 (SD = 20.73), t(215) = -2.71, p = .007; ANOVA expression F(1, 431) = 4.19, p = .041; demand F(1, 431) = 30.96, p < .001; expression x demand F(1, 431) = 6.08, p = .014; manipulation checks anger F = 17.87, p < .001, happiness F = 21.01, p < .001. Exp 2 (pp. 7–8): 50% demand, angry M = 46.07 (SD = 16.11) vs neutral M = 46.12 (SD = 11.64); 70% demand, angry M = 54.04 (SD = 15.41) vs neutral M = 46.13 (SD = 17.24), t(145) = 2.91, p = .004; expression F(1, 290) = 4.86, p = .028; demand F(1, 290) = 5.02, p = .026; expression x demand F(1, 290) = 4.99, p = .026. The authors report no standardized effect sizes; computed here from the reported Ms and SDs (equal cell sizes assumed) […]
reed_2014_commitment.conclusion: Angry expressions function as honest signals of commitment that make less credible threats more effective; because the expression mattered only for the less credible 70% demand, the authors read the results as supporting the commitment hypothesis over cheap-talk, vestige and spillover alternatives. They note the expressions were posed ('literally faked') yet were responded to as genuine, and call for work with spontaneous expressions face to face (p. 9).
reed_2014_commitment.caveats: The stimulus was a single posed female actor; the angry expression is described in prose, with no FACS/AU coding reported, so the specific facial actions are not verified. The perceivers were online MTurk participants with small real stakes ($1.00). The effect occurs only in interaction with demand credibility; there is no main effect at 50%. Full text was read in excerpts; the reported numbers should be checked against the typeset article before quoting […]

chapman_2009_taste.cit: Chapman, H. A., Kim, D. A., Susskind, J. M., & Anderson, A. K. (2009). In bad taste: Evidence for the oral origins of moral disgust. Science, 323(5918), 1222–1226.
chapman_2009_taste.design: Three laboratory experiments with facial EMG over the levator labii region only (no other facial muscle recorded). Exp 1 (N = 27): ingestion of bitter, salty and sour liquids vs sweet and water; plus a separate video-recorded group used to build a computerized facial appearance model of the distaste response. Exp 2 (N = 18): IAPS photographs of contamination-related disgust (faeces, injuries, insects) vs equally negative sad and neutral photographs, with disgust and sadness ratings. Exp 3 (N = 16): Ultimatum Game responders receiving offers from $5:$5 to $9:$1 from 10 human proposers (confederates) and 10 computer rounds; feelings rated by choosing how well seven photographs of canonical facial expressions (disgust, anger, contempt, fear, sadness, surprise, happiness) represented them. Participants' population/country not stated in the text read (University of Toronto lab).
chapman_2009_taste.numbers: Exp 1: levator labii greater for unpleasant than sweet solutions, t(26) = 2.89, P < .01; unpleasantness ratings vs EMG linear r = .77, quadratic r = .93. Exp 2: disgusting > sad photographs, t(17) = 3.71, P < .01; disgust ratings vs EMG r = .52, P < .001; sadness ratings vs EMG r = .19, P = .15. Exp 3: rejection rose with unfairness, F(1,15) = 46.7; levator activity increased linearly with unfairness, F(1,45) = 6.34, P < .05; $9:$1 (73% rejected) > $5:$5 and $7:$3 (10% rejected), F(1,45) = 9.32, P < .004; unfair offers endorsed as disgust more than anger, F(1,135) = 25.0; disgust endorsement vs levator r = .61, anger r = .14, sadness r = .052, contempt r = .26 (ns); disgust endorsement vs rejection r = .70, anger vs rejection r = .58 (P = .078); levator activity vs rejection r = .71, P < .05. Human and computer proposers were treated almost equivalently.
chapman_2009_taste.conclusion: Distaste, contamination disgust and responses to unfairness share an oral-nasal rejection motor response (levator labii region), suggesting that moral disgust has its origins in oral distaste and that 'immorality elicits the same disgust as disease vectors and bad tastes'.
chapman_2009_taste.caveats: Small samples; single EMG site whose signal can include neighbouring muscle activity; 'moral' elicitor was unfair monetary offers (also endorsed as anger and sadness), including computer partners; the face-photograph rating method may have channelled endorsement toward the disgust face; correlations between ratings and EMG appear to be computed over offer levels or trials (unit of analysis not checked). […]

rozin_1994_varieties.cit: Rozin, P., Lowery, L., & Ebert, R. (1994). Varieties of disgust faces and the structure of disgust. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 66(5), 870–881.
rozin_1994_varieties.design: Three facial-expression identification (perception) studies: college students matched a variety of disgust faces, depicting specific FACS-defined muscle actions, to verbally described eliciting situations. Whether faces were posed photographs of one or more posers, the number of faces, judges per study, and percentages could not be verified (full text not accessible).
rozin_1994_varieties.conclusion: Different disgust facial actions are associated (by observers) with different elicitor domains: nose wrinkle with smells (and somewhat tastes), gape/tongue extrusion with core/food-offence disgust and oral irritation, and the raised upper lip with the broader animal-reminder, interpersonal and moral elicitors; this supports an account of disgust evolving from distaste toward a moral emotion.
rozin_1994_varieties.caveats: Abstract-level only; stimulus construction (poser, photographs vs. other) unverified; American college students; forced matching of faces to situations.

widen_2010_disgust.cit: Widen, S. C., & Russell, J. A. (2010). The ‘disgust face’ conveys anger to children. Emotion, 10(4), 455–466.

cannon_2010_transgressions.cit: Cannon, P. R., Schnall, S., & White, M. (2011). Transgressions and expressions: Affective facial muscle activity predicts moral judgments. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 2(3), 325–331.
cannon_2010_transgressions.design: Within-subject EMG study. N = 39 University of Plymouth community-panel volunteers (23 female; M age 27.2; predominantly White British). Block 1: participants listened to 90 third-person statements of good and bad behaviours across five moral foundations (purity, fairness, harm, authority, ingroup; based on Ranganath & Graham, 2010) while EMG was recorded over levator labii, corrugator supercilii and zygomaticus major (medial frontalis lost to hardware fault); EMG = 4 s after statement offset minus 500 ms baseline. Block 2: moral judgments of the same behaviours on a -3 to +3 scale. Item-level correlations between Block 1 EMG and Block 2 judgments.
cannon_2010_transgressions.numbers: Levator: purity violations t(37) = 3.68, p = .001, d = 1.2; fairness violations t(37) = 3.13, p = .003, d = 1.0. Corrugator: harm violations t(37) = 2.40, p = .02, d = 0.79. Item-level correlations with judgments: levator-purity r = -.72 (p < .001), levator-fairness r = -.45 (p < .05), corrugator-harm r = -.59 (p < .01), zygomaticus-ingroup r = .42 (p < .05). Authority and ingroup violations did not evoke strong negative facial responses; 9.5% of trials excluded for movement.
cannon_2010_transgressions.conclusion: People spontaneously show domain-specific facial affect to moral violations (disgust for purity and fairness, anger for harm), and the intensity of this facial affect predicts the extremity of later moral judgments.
cannon_2010_transgressions.caveats: Single-site EMG per putative emotion; corrugator activity is also linked to general negativity and effort; item-level correlations with few items per foundation; the authors note participants may have found some purity items amusing. Cross-cultural follow-up (Buchtel et al., 2022) did not reproduce the harm/fairness muscle mapping.
terms: purity, fairness, harm, authority, and ingroup

vrana_1993_psychophysiology.cit: Vrana, S. R. (1993). The psychophysiology of disgust: Differentiating negative emotional contexts with facial EMG. Psychophysiology, 30(3), 279–286.
vrana_1993_psychophysiology.design: Laboratory-elicited (tone-cued imagery, 8-s trials). N = 50 participants (population and country not given in the abstract; author at Purdue University). Imagery contents: disgust, anger, pleasure, joy. Measures: facial EMG over corrugator, zygomatic and levator labii superioris/alaeque nasi regions; heart rate; skin conductance level. Emotion criterion: self-reports of emotion after imagery trials, which the abstract says matched the affective categories of the images.
vrana_1993_psychophysiology.numbers: N = 50; 8-s imagery trials; three EMG sites. Means, effect sizes and test statistics: not reported in the abstract. Whether corrugator differed between anger and disgust imagery: not reported in the abstract (corrugator is described only as distinguishing negative from positive contents).
vrana_1993_psychophysiology.conclusion: Facial EMG can discriminate disgust imagery from anger imagery (via levator labii), and the expressive physiology of disgust reflects an action set of actively avoiding or rejecting sensory stimulation.
vrana_1993_psychophysiology.caveats: Abstract only. Imagery trials of 8 s, not real provocation. Only three sites; no sites for anger-specific lower-face actions (e.g., lip pressor/tightener, AU 23/24) were recorded, so the absence of an anger-specific pattern reflects the measurement choice. Surface EMG over the levator labii region can include neighbouring muscles (AU 9/10).
terms: active avoidance or rejection of sensory stimulation

gross_1993_emotional.cit: Gross, J. J., & Levenson, R. W. (1993). Emotional suppression: Physiology, self-report, and expressive behavior. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 64(6), 970–986.

ekman_1986_pancultural.cit: Ekman, P., & Friesen, W. V. (1986). A new pan-cultural facial expression of emotion. Motivation and Emotion, 10(2), 159–168.
ekman_1986_pancultural.design: Cross-cultural judgment study of still photographs (posed expressions) with a fixed-choice emotion-label response format (per Russell, 1991, who describes the measure as 'subjects choosing one label from a small, preselected list'). Observers in 10 cultures. Number of photographs, observers per culture, and the facial actions composing the expression could not be verified from the abstract.
ekman_1986_pancultural.numbers: 10 cultures: Estonia, Germany, Greece, Hong Kong, Italy, Japan, Scotland, Turkey, USA, West Sumatra. Agreement percentages not verified (abstract gives only a qualitative comparison with other emotions).
ekman_1986_pancultural.conclusion: A facial expression specific to contempt exists and, contrary to the authors' own prediction, is recognised across cultures with agreement comparable to that for other emotions.
ekman_1986_pancultural.caveats: Abstract only. The paper reports recognition (judgment) data, not production data. The forced-choice format became the central point of dispute (Russell, 1991; Ekman, O'Sullivan & Matsumoto, 1991; Matsumoto & Ekman, 2004; Wagner, 2000).

ekman_1988_universality.cit: Ekman, P., & Heider, K. G. (1988). The universality of a contempt expression: A replication. Motivation and Emotion, 12(3), 303–308.

russell_1991_contempt.cit: Russell, J. A. (1991). The contempt expression and the relativity thesis. Motivation and Emotion, 15(2), 149–168.

matsumoto_1992_evidence.cit: Matsumoto, D. (1992). More evidence for the universality of a contempt expression. Motivation and Emotion, 16(4), 363–368.
matsumoto_1992_evidence.design: Judgment study: observers in four non-American cultures judged all 12 photographs of the contempt expression used in previous studies. Cultures, Ns and response format not verified (abstract only).
matsumoto_1992_evidence.numbers: 12 photographs; 4 non-American cultures. Agreement levels not verified.
matsumoto_1992_evidence.conclusion: Judgments of the full set of contempt photographs in four further cultures replicate the universality of the contempt expression.
matsumoto_1992_evidence.caveats: Abstract only; cultures, Ns, response format and percentages unverified. Same stimulus set as the original studies.
terms: universal facial expression unique to contempt

russell_1991_negative.cit: Russell, J. A. (1991). Negative results on a reported facial expression of contempt. Motivation and Emotion, 15(4), 281–291.
russell_1991_negative.design: Two judgment studies of the photographed unilateral lip curl: Study 1 free (open-ended) emotion labelling; Study 2 quantitative ratings on six emotion scales. Published as a 'Letter'. Sample sizes and populations not verified.
russell_1991_negative.conclusion: Ekman and Friesen's contempt finding depends on the forced-choice response format; with free labels or rating scales, observers did not interpret the unilateral lip curl as contempt.
russell_1991_negative.caveats: Abstract only; numbers and samples unverified. Part of a 1991 exchange that also includes Russell's 'The contempt expression and the relativity thesis' (Motivation and Emotion, 15(2), 149-168; abstract not accessible) and replies.
terms: quantitative ratings on six emotion scales

rozin_1999_triad.cit: Rozin, P., Lowery, L., Imada, S., & Haidt, J. (1999). The CAD triad hypothesis: A mapping between three moral emotions (contempt, anger, disgust) and three moral codes (community, autonomy, divinity). Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 76(4), 574–586.

matsumoto_2004_relationship.cit: Matsumoto, D., & Ekman, P. (2004). The relationship among expressions, labels, and descriptions of contempt. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 87(4), 529–540.
matsumoto_2004_relationship.design: Four judgment studies: fixed-choice labelling (process-of-elimination test), matching expressions to situations, open-ended labelling of situations, and self-reported use/exposure to emotion words.
matsumoto_2004_relationship.conclusion: The contempt expression-emotion link is sound; labelling failures stem from the low accessibility of the term 'contempt'.

gottman_1999_stable.cit: Gottman, J. M., & Levenson, R. W. (1999). How stable is marital interaction over time? Family Process, 38(2), 159–165.

reisenzein_2006_evidence.cit: Reisenzein, R., Bördgen, S., Holtbernd, T., & Matz, D. (2006). Evidence for strong dissociation between emotion and facial displays: The case of surprise. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 91(2), 295–315.
reisenzein_2006_evidence.design: Eight laboratory experiments with adult (mostly student) participants in Germany. Surprise was induced by disconfirming an established schema or expectancy (e.g. unexpected display changes in reaction-time or memory tasks, a simulated computer malfunction, an unexpected tone sequence from a hidden loudspeaker, unexpected presentation of the participant's own photograph). Sociality (alone, mere presence, face-to-face interaction), intensity and duration/complexity of the event were varied. Faces were video-recorded and coded present/absent for brow raising (AU1–2), eye widening (AU5) and jaw drop/mouth opening (AU26–27) with reference to FACS by two independent trained observers (coders trained with written descriptions, pictures and videos; certification not stated). Frontalis EMG was added in later experiments. Self-reported surprise and behavioural measures (e.g. reaction times) indexed surprise.
reisenzein_2006_evidence.numbers: Any surprise component, by experiment (extracted from the full text; re-check against the paper's tables before quoting): Exp 1, 3/57 (5.3%), each one component only; Exp 2, 1/25 (4%; eye widening; no brow raises); Exp 3, 2/22 (9%; brow raises); Exp 4, 2/22 (9%); Exp 5, 5/20 (25%; brow raise 10%, eye widening 15%, mouth opening 5%); Exp 6, 2/23 (8.7%; one brow raise, one brow raise plus mouth opening); Exp 7, 5/28 (18%; four brow raises, two eye widenings); Exp 8, about 8% (brow raises). Full three-component display: 0 in all eight experiments. Self-report: almost all participants reported surprise (e.g. Exp 3: 19 of 22 strongly surprised). Beliefs: e.g. Exp 4, 77% believed they had shown at least one component; Exp 5, 80%; Exp 7, 93%, with near-zero correlation between observed and believed components.
reisenzein_2006_evidence.conclusion: Surprise and its facial display are strongly dissociated: most participants felt surprised, few showed any component, none showed the full display, and the original affect program account of surprise expressions is 'untenable'. Intensity, sociality and event duration/complexity did not change this; participants' beliefs that they had shown surprise appear to rest on generalised beliefs rather than facial feedback.
reisenzein_2006_evidence.caveats: Surprise was induced with fairly mild, task-embedded expectancy violations in the lab; the General Discussion could not be read (document truncated), so the authors' final theoretical conclusions are taken from the abstract and the interim discussions. Coding was a present/absent scheme for selected AUs, not full FACS. Per-experiment percentages were taken from a summary of the text and should be checked against the PDF.
terms: strong dissociation between emotion and facial displays

reisenzein_2007_expression.cit: Reisenzein, R., & Studtmann, M. (2007). On the expression and experience of surprise: No evidence for facial feedback, but evidence for a reverse self-inference effect. Emotion, 7(3), 612–627.

scherer_2004_beyond.cit: Scherer, K. R., Zentner, M. R., & Stern, D. (2004). Beyond surprise: The puzzle of infants' expressive reactions to expectancy violation. Emotion, 4(4), 389–402.
scherer_2004_beyond.design: Cross-sectional study of 58 infants aged 5, 7, 9, 11–12 and 14 months. Expectancy was violated by digitally filtering the experimenter's voice, and behavioural, facial and vocal reactions were measured.
scherer_2004_beyond.numbers: N = 58 infants across five age groups (5–14 months). Per Reisenzein et al. (2006, secondary): complete surprise displays were 3.5%.
scherer_2004_beyond.conclusion: Freezing and gaze changes, not facial or vocal expressions, reliably mark expectancy violation. A transition in cognitive evaluation of discrepant events may occur around 9 months, and componential (appraisal) theories may explain age-related changes in expression.
scherer_2004_beyond.caveats: Abstract only. The voice-filter manipulation differs from object-based violations. Small cells per age group.

susskind_2008_expressing.cit: Susskind, J. M., Lee, D. H., Cusi, A., Feiman, R., Grabski, W., & Anderson, A. K. (2008). Expressing fear enhances sensory acquisition. Nature Neuroscience, 11(7), 843–850.
susskind_2008_expressing.design: Multi-part laboratory study. (1) Statistical appearance model of expression photographs showing fear and disgust have opposite shape and surface-reflectance features. (2) Participants POSED fear, disgust and neutral expressions while their subjective visual field was estimated, (3) saccadic eye movements were measured during target localisation, and (4) nasal inspiratory volume and air velocity were measured; figure titles indicate an additional analysis of internal nasal anatomy (MeSH terms list magnetic resonance imaging). Sample sizes, training procedure and effect sizes could not be verified because the full text was not accessible.
susskind_2008_expressing.numbers: Not verifiable from accessible primary sources (full text and supplementary methods paywalled). Abstract reports direction only: fear > neutral > disgust for subjective visual field, saccade speed during target localisation, and nasal inspiratory volume/air velocity. Secondary only (Ed Yong, ScienceBlogs, 2008, unverified): about 20 students posed fearful or disgusted faces while looking at a large grid; MRI indicated that fear widened the nasal passages.
susskind_2008_expressing.conclusion: Fear and disgust expressions are biomechanically opposed configurations that respectively augment and diminish sensory exposure; this supports the Darwinian view that expressions originated in sensory regulation for the expresser rather than as arbitrary social signals.
susskind_2008_expressing.caveats: Full text not reached; numbers, Ns and training protocol unverified. Posed expressions may differ in intensity and morphology from spontaneous ones, and spontaneous fear rarely shows the full configuration in naturalistic studies. The sensory benefit to the expresser is an origin hypothesis; it does not show that people widen their eyes when afraid.
terms: nasal volume and air velocity during inspiration

lee_2013_social.cit: Lee, D. H., Susskind, J. M., & Anderson, A. K. (2013). Social transmission of the sensory benefits of eye widening in fear expressions. Psychological Science, 24(6), 957–965.
lee_2013_social.design: Laboratory experiments (details beyond abstract not verified): (a) expresser experiment testing target discrimination in the visual periphery with fear-based eye widening vs other eye configurations; (b) observer experiments testing discrimination of the expresser's gaze direction and speed of locating eccentric targets cued by the expresser's eyes, with tests to separate perceived emotion and attention from the physical signal of exposed iris and sclera. Expressions were posed/manipulated eye configurations; Ns not verified.
lee_2013_social.numbers: Expresser: 9.4% improvement in peripheral target discrimination with fear-based eye widening (abstract). Other numbers and Ns not verified.
lee_2013_social.conclusion: Eye widening benefits both the expresser (peripheral vision) and the observer (more legible gaze direction, faster localisation of eccentric targets), supporting a coevolution of sensory and social functions; the observer benefit is attributed to the physical eye-white/iris signal rather than to perceived fear.
lee_2013_social.caveats: Abstract-level verification only. Posed eye configurations in laboratory tasks; the 9.4% figure is a relative discrimination gain in the periphery. That the benefit is independent of perceived emotion supports a function-of-the-action claim rather than an emotion-expression claim.
terms: exposure of the iris and sclera

tracy_2004_show.conclusion: Pride has a distinct, recognizable expression distinguishable from happiness, challenging the assumption that all positive emotions share one expression; pride may be a basic emotion.

tracy_2007_prototypical.cit: Tracy, J. L., & Robins, R. W. (2007). The prototypical pride expression: Development of a nonverbal behavior coding system. Emotion, 7(4), 789-801.

tracy_2007_prototypical.conclusion: Pride can be reliably assessed from nonverbal behaviours; authentic and hubristic pride largely share one signal; a pride behavioural coding scheme is provided.

tracy_2008_nonverbal.cit: Tracy, J. L., & Robins, R. W. (2008). The nonverbal expression of pride: Evidence for cross-cultural recognition. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 94(3), 516-530.
tracy_2008_nonverbal.design: Perception of posed pride (facial-bodily) displays by Italian, US and Burkinabe participants; drawn figures varying ethnicity/gender.

tracy_2008_spontaneous.cit: Tracy, J. L., & Matsumoto, D. (2008). The spontaneous expression of pride and shame: Evidence for biologically innate nonverbal displays. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 105(33), 11655-11660.
tracy_2008_spontaneous.design: Naturalistic field: photographs taken by an official International Judo Federation photographer during and immediately after matches (about 15 s, 8 frames per second) at the 2004 Olympic and Paralympic Games. Sighted: 87 competitors (42 winners, 45 losers; 46% female) from 36 nations, 111 match outcomes because some were photographed in more than one match. Blind: 53 competitors (30 winners, 23 losers; 23% female) from 20 nations, 60 match outcomes; of those with known status, 12 congenitally blind. Three coders rated intensity (0-5) of pride behaviours (head tilt back, smile, arms extended, arms raised, hands in fists, chest expanded, torso pushed out) and shame behaviours (shoulders slumped, chest narrowed, head tilt down, face hiding); certified FACS coding of at least one photo for 69% of sighted athletes. No self-report of pride or shame.
tracy_2008_spontaneous.numbers: Sighted winners vs losers: head tilt back t(109) = 4.13, d = 0.84; smile t(109) = 6.85, d = 1.45; arms, fists, chest and torso also greater after wins (ps < .05). Blind: head tilt back d = 1.11; smile t(50) = 3.13, d = 1.31. Congenitally blind (n = 12): arms raised t(10) = 2.01, d = 0.68 (one-tailed), hands in fists d = 1.46, chest expanded d = 1.88, torso pushed out d = 2.04 (ps < .05); smiling and arms extended not significant; head tilt back not reported for this subgroup; after losing, shoulders slumped d = 1.97 and chest narrowed d = 1.95; composite pride score higher for winners, t(10) = 2.05, d = 1.74. Shame response moderated by culture among sighted athletes (weaker in individualistic, self-expression-valuing cultures).
tracy_2008_spontaneous.conclusion: Pride and shame displays are likely 'biologically innate behavioral responses' to success and failure; the shame display may be inhibited by some sighted individuals according to cultural norms.
tracy_2008_spontaneous.caveats: Winning likely evokes several positive states (e.g., joy, relief, happiness) besides pride; the design cannot isolate pride. The FACS detail on which AUs made up the smile was minimal in the text read (AU12 mentioned; no AU6/Duchenne analysis found). Very small congenitally blind subsample.

rozin_2003_high.cit: Rozin, P., & Cohen, A. B. (2003). High frequency of facial expressions corresponding to confusion, concentration, and worry in an analysis of naturally occurring facial expressions of Americans. Emotion, 3(1), 68–75.

prkachin_1992_consistency.cit: Prkachin, K. M. (1992). The consistency of facial expressions of pain: A comparison across modalities. Pain, 51(3), 297–306.

AU numbers, sample demographics and effect sizes were not available, because the full text could not be reached.
prkachin_1992_consistency.numbers: N = 41; 4 modalities (electric shock, cold, pressure, ischemia); 4 actions. AU codes per secondary sources (Lucey et al. 2011 TSMCB; Kunz et al. 2019): AU4, AU6/7, AU9/10, AU43. No effect sizes or factor loadings could be verified.

prkachin_1992_consistency.caveats: Verified at abstract level only: the full text was paywalled with no OA copy. AU-level statistics, inclusion of other actions (for example mouth opening or AU12) and demographics are unverified. Experimental, brief pain in a single sample. 'Universal' is an extrapolation: Williams (2002, §5.4) notes that 'Cross-cultural studies of facial expression of pain have not been published.'

prkachin_2008_structure.design: Clinical psychometric study. 129 people with shoulder pain did a battery of active and passive range-of-motion tests on affected and unaffected limbs, repeated on a second occasion (test–retest). After each test they rated maximum pain on three self-report scales. Faces were FACS-coded. Per the secondary sources, the index sums frame-level AU intensities.
prkachin_2008_structure.numbers: N = 129 shoulder-pain patients; 2 occasions; 3 self-report scales. Per secondary sources: PSPI = AU4 + max(AU6, AU7) + max(AU9, AU10) + AU43. AUs are scored 0–5 and AU43 0/1, giving a 0–16 range. In automated work, frames with PSPI ≥ 1 are labelled 'pain'. The PSPI–self-report correlations and test–retest coefficients could not be extracted.
prkachin_2008_structure.conclusion: Of the actions that discriminated painful from non-painful movements, brow lowering, orbit tightening, levator contraction and eye closing formed a 'distinct, unitary action'. An index built from them was reliable over time and showed concurrent validity with self-report, supporting a 'core pain expression'. Individual differences in pain expressiveness may explain why previous studies reported varying face–self-report relations.
prkachin_2008_structure.caveats: The full text was not accessible, so the size of the self-report correlations, which self-report scales were used, and whether the 2008 paper specified frame-level scoring could not be verified. Concurrent validity in this design is mostly within-person and across tests (painful vs non-painful movements), which differs from between-person agreement. The index is a measure of facial activity. […]

craig_1985_facial.cit: Craig, K. D., & Patrick, C. J. (1985). Facial expression during induced pain. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 48(4), 1080–1091.

chen_2018_distinct.cit: Chen, C., Crivelli, C., Garrod, O. G. B., Schyns, P. G., Fernández-Dols, J.-M., & Jack, R. E. (2018). Distinct facial expressions represent pain and pleasure across cultures. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 115(43), E10013–E10021.
