chen_2018_distinct.design: Data-driven reverse correlation of perceivers' mental representations, not of produced expressions. 80 heterosexual, sexually active observers with minimal cross-cultural exposure: 40 Western (white European) and 40 East Asian (Chinese), 20 women each. Each categorized 3,600 random dynamic facial animations as 'pain', 'orgasm' or 'other' and rated intensity. Each animation combined 1–4 AUs (median 3) from 42, with random temporal parameters, on same-race, opposite-sex faces. Per-observer models came from correlating AU presence with the pain = 0 / orgasm = 1 response. Validation used a Bayesian classifier, mutual information, and a perceptual discrimination task with 104 new observers (52 per culture). Models were compared with 11 pain and 3 orgasm production studies, Western data only.
chen_2018_distinct.numbers: 160 models (40 observers × 2 cultures × 2 states). Bayesian split-half classification of pain vs orgasm models: Western pain .97, orgasm .98; East Asian pain .99, orgasm .96. Mutual information: no AUs common to the pain and orgasm models in either culture. Pain models were culture-common (AU4, 6, 9, 10, 20) with no culture-specific AUs. Orgasm models shared AU1-2 and AU43; Western added AU5, 26, 27 and East Asian added AU12. Classifying the 80 Western models (40 pain + 40 orgasm) by Hamming distance to 14 production patterns (11 pain, 3 orgasm): χ²(1, N = 80) = 34.58. Pain models and productions converged on AUs 4, 6, 9, 10, 12, 20. AU11 appeared in models only; AUs 7, 17, 45 in productions only.
chen_2018_distinct.conclusion: In both cultures, mental representations of pain and orgasm faces are physically and perceptually distinct. Pain is represented with similar movements across cultures, whereas orgasm has cultural accents. This questions the 'nondiagnosticity' of these expressions and suggests they could serve communication. Representations are more distinct than real-world productions.
chen_2018_distinct.caveats: Only two cultural groups, of young students. East Asian observers were newly arrived in the UK, and their models were compared with Western production data only, because East Asian production data were lacking. The production comparison used just 3 orgasm studies. The Methods, as understood here: each observer's model was fitted by correlating AU presence with a binary pain(0)/orgasm(1) response, a contrastive fit that may favour disjoint pain and orgasm AU sets. […]

kunz_2019_facial.cit: Kunz, M., Meixner, D., & Lautenbacher, S. (2019). Facial muscle movements encoding pain—a systematic review. Pain, 160(3), 535–549.
kunz_2019_facial.design: Systematic review with semi-quantitative synthesis of studies that used the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) to code facial activity during pain in adults and reported single action units; children/neonates and animals excluded by search terms. 37 articles: 27 experimental-pain and 10 clinical-pain studies; 2237 individuals in total; 9 studies included cognitively impaired people (dementia). AUs classified as pain-related by two criteria: 'frequency of occurrence' (usually >5%) and the stricter 'pain>baseline' criterion (5 studies used only frequency; 32 used pain>baseline, 23 of them combined with frequency). Most studies aggregated AU1_2, AU6_7, AU9_10 and AU25_26_27.
kunz_2019_facial.numbers: 37 studies (27 experimental, 10 clinical); N = 2237 individuals; 9 studies with cognitively impaired participants. Pain>baseline criterion met in >=50% of studies by only four AUs: AU4 and AU6_7 (~80% of studies), AU9_10 (>70%), AU25_26_27 (~60%). AU43: pain-related in half (50%) of clinical-pain studies vs about 20–22% of experimental-pain studies (the manuscript gives both 20% and 22% in different places). Frequency-of-occurrence criterion met in >=50% of studies by 10 AUs: 1_2, 4, 6_7, 9_10, 12, 14, 17, 25_26_27, 43, 45. No single AU pain-related in all studies. People with dementia showed the same AUs, more intensely.
kunz_2019_facial.conclusion: A small subset of FACS AUs (AU4, AU6_7, AU9_10, AU25_26_27; plus AU43 in clinical pain) is consistently associated with pain, independent of cognitive status and comparable across clinical and experimental pain; but these AUs are combined differently across people and episodes, so the subset carries 'the bulk of information about pain' without being a uniform pain expression, and assessment should be individualized.
kunz_2019_facial.caveats: Semi-quantitative vote-counting (proportion of studies), not a meta-analysis; studies differ in coding criteria, AU aggregation, pain type and stimulus intensity. Adults only (children and neonates excluded), FACS only (no NFCS, automated or EMG studies). The searched author manuscript contains no mention of 'PSPI' or 'Prkachin and Solomon Pain Intensity'; it cites Prkachin & Solomon (2008) only for the claim that the set applies to clinical pain. […]

kunz_2014_faces.cit: Kunz, M., & Lautenbacher, S. (2014). The faces of pain: A cluster analysis of individual differences in facial activity patterns of pain. European Journal of Pain, 18(6), 813–823.
kunz_2014_faces.design: Two samples of pain-free individuals (n = 128 and n = 112) received heat pain. Faces were coded with FACS. Hierarchical cluster analyses looked for combinations of facial actions in pain episodes. Stability and replicability were tested across the two samples and across 'different basic social situations'.
kunz_2014_faces.numbers: Samples: n = 128 and n = 112 (total 240) pain-free adults; heat pain. Four activity clusters plus a stoic (unresponsive) cluster. Patterns were stable within individuals for 'nearly two-thirds'. The size of the stoic group and the AU codes per cluster are not given in the abstract.
kunz_2014_faces.conclusion: There is no uniform set of facial actions in pain. At least four distinct facial activity patterns exist, plus a stoic non-responder group. Raising awareness of these 'faces of pain' may improve detection and communication of pain.
kunz_2014_faces.caveats: Abstract only. AU codes, cluster sizes and the proportion of stoics are unverified. Heat pain in healthy adults. Hierarchical clustering is exploratory, and its solutions depend on the distance and linkage chosen. Cluster III (raised eyebrows, AU1/2) lies outside the 'core' pain actions.

grunau_1987_pain.cit: Grunau, R. V. E., & Craig, K. D. (1987). Pain expression in neonates: Facial action and cry. Pain, 28(3), 395–410.
grunau_1987_pain.design: Observational study of healthy neonates during heel lance for blood sampling. Facial expression and cry were measured and compared across sleep/waking states and sex. The abstract gives neither the N nor the list of facial actions coded.
grunau_1987_pain.numbers: Neither the N nor the facial action list is in the abstract. Findings: most facial activity in awake-alert inactive infants; least facial reaction and longest cry latency in quiet sleep; cry fundamental frequency unrelated to state; boys had shorter latency to cry and to facial action.
grunau_1987_pain.conclusion: Neonatal pain expression varies with the infant's behavioural state (sleep/waking), not only with tissue insult. This indicates that biological and behavioural context shapes expression before learning could operate. Measurement should be independent of preconceived affective categories.
grunau_1987_pain.caveats: Abstract only. Whether this paper introduced the NFCS under that name, and which actions it coded, are unverified here. The N is unknown. Healthy term neonates, one procedure (heel lance).

grunau_1998_bedside.cit: Grunau, R. E., Oberlander, T., Holsti, L., & Whitfield, M. F. (1998). Bedside application of the Neonatal Facial Coding System in pain assessment of premature neonates. Pain, 76(3), 277–286.

williams_2002_facial.cit: Williams, A. C. de C. (2002). Facial expression of pain: An evolutionary account. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 25(4), 439–455.
williams_2002_facial.design: Theoretical target article with a narrative review. Sections: 1 function of pain; 2 pain behaviour; 3 evolutionary psychology; 4 facial expression; 5 facial expression of pain (5.1–5.9: distinctiveness and specificity, consistency across lifespan, stimuli and cultures, detection by onlookers, suppression, amplification, simulation); 6 observer judgments; 7 evolved propensities. Followed by open peer commentary (pp. 455–488).
williams_2002_facial.numbers: Not empirical. The review cites core adult AUs (AU4, AU6/7, AU9/10, AU43), consistency across shock, cold, pressure and ischaemic pain (Prkachin 1992b), and an infant pain face from 25 weeks' gestation.
williams_2002_facial.conclusion: Pain expression and its detection are shaped by evolved, context-contingent propensities. Expression is costly near antagonists and beneficial near allies or caregivers. Increased pain behaviour around solicitous others may reflect release of suppression rather than operant amplification. Clinicians' scepticism and underestimation of pain can be understood through evolved cheater-detection and gatekeeping logic. An evolutionary account can improve pain assessment.
williams_2002_facial.caveats: Mainly a theoretical review: its specific empirical claims rest on the cited primary studies. The text was read in excerpts from the UCL PDF, and key quotes were re-checked for exact wording. Commentaries in the same issue critique aspects of it (e.g., 'Pain behaviour is not unitary'; not read).

kappesser_2002_pain.cit: Kappesser, J., & Williams, A. C. de C. (2002). Pain and negative emotions in the face: Judgements by health care professionals. Pain, 99(1–2), 197–206.
kappesser_2002_pain.design: Health care professionals judged facial expressions of pain and of fear, anger, sadness, surprise, disgust and embarrassment. Categorical accuracy (unbiased hit rate) plus multidimensional scaling.
kappesser_2002_pain.conclusion: Pain faces are identifiable but less accurately than other negative emotions. In similarity space, pain clusters with sadness and anger.
kappesser_2002_pain.caveats: Abstract only. Stimulus type (posed or spontaneous) not stated in the abstract.

simon_2008_recognition.cit: Simon, D., Craig, K. D., Gosselin, F., Belin, P., & Rainville, P. (2008). Recognition and discrimination of prototypical dynamic expressions of pain and emotions. Pain, 135(1–2), 55–64.
simon_2008_recognition.design: Stimulus-validation and judgment study. Eight actors produced 1-s dynamic clips of neutral, pain, anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness and surprise expressions. The clips were FACS-coded to confirm prototypical configurations. Naive observers rated the clips on intensity, arousal and valence, plus additional rating data. The number of observers is not given in the abstract.
simon_2008_recognition.numbers: 8 actors; 8 expression categories; 1-s clips. Observer N and accuracy figures are not in the abstract.
simon_2008_recognition.conclusion: Posed dynamic pain expressions have a distinct FACS configuration and are judged with high sensitivity and specificity. At comparable intensity, pain is perceived as more arousing and unpleasant than basic emotions. This supports the distinctness of pain expression and provides a stimulus set.
simon_2008_recognition.caveats: Abstract only. The stimuli were selected or produced to be prototypical, so distinctness is partly built in. There were only 8 actors. The abstract reports 'evaluations ... on intensity, arousal and valence' and 'sensitivity and specificity' without figures.
terms: facial expressions of pain and emotions

kunz_2007_facial.cit: Kunz, M., Scharmann, S., Hemmeter, U., Schepelmann, K., & Lautenbacher, S. (2007). The facial expression of pain in patients with dementia. Pain, 133(1–3), 221–228.
kunz_2007_facial.design: Experimental case–control study. 42 patients with dementia and 54 age-matched healthy controls received mechanical (pressure) stimulation at various intensities. Faces were videotaped and FACS-coded. Self-report ratings were collected, and the capacity to provide them was assessed.
kunz_2007_facial.numbers: Dementia n = 42; controls n = 54; pressure pain at multiple intensities. Effect sizes and the specific AUs are not in the abstract.
kunz_2007_facial.conclusion: Facial responses to experimental pressure pain are increased, not reduced, in dementia, mainly through pain-indicative actions. They scale with stimulus intensity and keep their pain typicalness, so facial expression could serve as an alternative pain assessment tool in verbally compromised patients.
kunz_2007_facial.caveats: Abstract only. Dementia type and severity, and the specific AUs, are unverified. Increased facial responding could reflect reduced inhibitory control (disinhibition) rather than more pain; the review literature raises this point (Oosterman et al., 2016). Experimental pressure pain differs from clinical pain in dementia.

patrick_1986_observer.cit: Patrick, C. J., Craig, K. D., & Prkachin, K. M. (1986). Observer judgments of acute pain: Facial action determinants. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 50(6), 1291–1298.

lucey_2011_painful.cit: Lucey, P., Cohn, J. F., Prkachin, K. M., Solomon, P. E., & Matthews, I. (2011). Painful data: The UNBC-McMaster shoulder pain expression archive database. In Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Automatic Face & Gesture Recognition and Workshops (FG 2011) (pp. 57–64).

browne_2019_pain.cit: Browne, M. E., Hadjistavropoulos, T., Prkachin, K. M., Ashraf, A., & Taati, B. (2019). Pain expressions in dementia: Validity of observers' pain judgments as a function of angle of observation. Journal of Nonverbal Behavior, 43(3), 309–327.

kunz_2006_differences.cit: Kunz, M., Gruber, A., & Lautenbacher, S. (2006). Sex differences in facial encoding of pain. The Journal of Pain, 7(12), 915–928.
kunz_2006_differences.design: 40 young pain-free adults (20 men, 20 women). Tonic heat at painful and non-painful levels, tailored to the individual pain threshold. VAS and FACS. Correlation analyses between self-report and face.
kunz_2006_differences.numbers: N = 40 (20 M, 20 F). No mean sex differences. Face–self-report correlations significant in women only.
kunz_2006_differences.conclusion: Sex moderates the face–self-report relationship. Facial responses may estimate subjective pain better in women than in men.
kunz_2006_differences.caveats: Abstract only; small samples per sex; tonic heat only.

lemau_2021_professional.cit: Le Mau, T., Hoemann, K., Lyons, S. H., Fugate, J. M. B., Brown, E. N., Gendron, M., & Barrett, L. F. (2021). Professional actors demonstrate variability, not stereotypical expressions, when portraying emotional states in photographs. Nature Communications, 12(1), 5037.
lemau_2021_professional.design: Stimuli: 604 of 731 photographs from Howard Schatz's two published volumes of actors' portrayals, posed by 155 professional actors (English-speaking, North American) to detailed scenarios written by Schatz; 127 photos excluded (hands over face, extreme head tilt). Sample 1 (839 US MTurk workers) rated each scenario alone for 13 categories (anger, amusement, awe, contempt, disgust, embarrassment, fear, happiness, interest, pride, sadness, shame, surprise). Three FACS-certified coders coded AU1–AU27 with intensity (median inter-coder match .71). Unsupervised hierarchical clustering of scenario ratings, with clusters chosen to maximise facial-pose match scores; supervised test of each photo's match to the hypothesised configurations (median across variants); specificity via false-positive rates (9 categories); Bayesian model selection; multiverse checks. Sample 2 (1,687 MTurk workers) rated faces alone or face + scenario.
lemau_2021_professional.numbers: Clustering: best solution 80 clusters (median within-cluster match .40); 34 clusters with match >= .40; one resembled fear (AU1, AU2, AU25), one a fear/surprise mix; none of the rest resembled hypothesised configurations; 10 of the 12 most reliable clusters (>= .5) had only 2–4 poses. Supervised: median match scores mostly < .40 (weak); moderate for awe .63, happiness .50, fear .44, surprise .44; overall median about .32 (multiverse .37). Specificity moderate except awe, contempt, disgust; best was anger .52 (false-positive rate .48). High-intensity subset (444 scenarios): reliability not higher (.30 vs .32) and false positives rose (.77 vs .58). Perception: face + scenario ratings tracked scenario-alone ratings (median r = .84) more than face-alone ratings (median r = .66).
lemau_2021_professional.conclusion: Professional actors portrayed emotion categories with variable, context-sensitive facial configurations; the hypothesised configurations are not expressive prototypes and may reflect Western stereotypes; only fear, happiness and surprise (plus awe for reliability) reached moderate reliability, and specificity fell for high-intensity scenarios.
lemau_2021_professional.caveats: Static photographs of portrayals (not felt emotion); scenarios assigned to categories by online raters; dynamic AUs (head and eye movements above AU27) could not be coded, so pride and shame were not codable and amusement and embarrassment only partly (simulated); inter-coder match .71 'lower than ideal'; actors and raters from one cultural context […]
terms: basic emotion hypothesis / basic emotion view

du_2014_compound.cit: Du, S., Tao, Y., & Martinez, A. M. (2014). Compound facial expressions of emotion. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 111(15), E1454-E1462.

du_2015_compound.cit: Du, S., & Martinez, A. M. (2015). Compound facial expressions of emotion: from basic research to clinical applications. Dialogues in Clinical Neuroscience, 17(4), 443-455.

cordaro_2018_universals.cit: Cordaro, D. T., Sun, R., Keltner, D., Kamble, S., Huddar, N., & McNeil, G. (2018). Universals and cultural variations in 22 emotional expressions across five cultures. Emotion, 18(1), 75-93.
cordaro_2018_universals.design: Posed (free-response) portrayals: participants in China, India, Japan, Korea and the US heard brief emotion scenarios and expressed each of 22 emotions nonverbally; displays FACS-coded (expanded system including body).
cordaro_2018_universals.numbers: Over 2,600 displays; 22 emotions; 5 cultures. Secondary (Keltner et al., 2019): about 50% of an individual's expressive behaviour adhered to the universal prototype and about 25% was dialect.
cordaro_2018_universals.conclusion: Cross-cultural core patterns and systematic cultural variants exist for 22 emotions, with a gradient of universality.

kohler_2004_differences.cit: Kohler, C. G., Turner, T., Stolar, N. M., Bilker, W. B., Brensinger, C. M., Gur, R. E., & Gur, R. C. (2004). Differences in facial expressions of four universal emotions. Psychiatry Research, 128(3), 235-244.
kohler_2004_differences.design: Mainly a recognition study of a stimulus set: 105 healthy young adults viewed 128 colour photographs of posed and evoked happy, sad, angry and fearful expressions (balanced for poser gender and ethnicity). The photographs were FACS-coded; categorical analyses assessed which AUs characterised each emotion, and logistic regression related AUs to recognition rates. How the 'evoked' expressions were produced is not stated in the abstract.
kohler_2004_differences.numbers: 105 perceivers; 128 photographs; 4 emotions; posed and evoked. AU frequencies by posed vs evoked not given in the abstract.
kohler_2004_differences.conclusion: Each emotion in the stimulus set was characterised by a distinct group of AUs, and specific AUs predicted recognition (e.g. cheek raise, lid tightening and outer brow raise for happy; brow lower and chin raise for sad).
kohler_2004_differences.caveats: Full text not reachable (closed). How the posers produced the 'evoked' expressions, and whether felt emotion was measured, is not described in the abstract and is unverified.
terms: happy, sad, angry and fearful emotions

gosselin_2010_voluntary.cit: Gosselin, P., Perron, M., & Beaupré, M. (2010). The voluntary control of facial action units in adults. Emotion, 10(2), 266-271.

scherer_2007_facial.cit: Scherer, K. R., & Ellgring, H. (2007). Are facial expressions of emotion produced by categorical affect programs or dynamically driven by appraisal? Emotion, 7(1), 113-130.
scherer_2007_facial.design: Theoretical review plus data from a large-scale actor portrayal study: 12 professional actors (German, per Sato et al., 2019) portraying 14 major emotions; frequencies of major facial muscle actions, singly and in combination, FACS-coded. Stimulus details (number of portrayals, scenarios, coding) could not be verified.
scherer_2007_facial.numbers: 12 professional actors; 14 emotions. Frequencies of prototype matches not obtained.
scherer_2007_facial.conclusion: Actors' facial action frequencies show little evidence for emotion-specific prototypical affect programs; the data 'encourage empirical investigation' of componential, appraisal-driven predictions.
scherer_2007_facial.caveats: Central item, but the full text could not be obtained (closed APA article; repository copy login-only). Whether the paper reports specific appraisal–AU correspondences (e.g. AU17 in pride, mentioned by Mortillaro et al., 2011) could not be checked.

mehu_2012_reliable.cit: Mehu, M., Mortillaro, M., Bänziger, T., & Scherer, K. R. (2012). Reliable facial muscle activation enhances recognizability and credibility of emotional expression. Emotion, 12(4), 701-715.

sato_2019_facial.cit: Sato, W., Hyniewska, S., Minemoto, K., & Yoshikawa, S. (2019). Facial expressions of basic emotions in Japanese laypeople. Frontiers in Psychology, 10, Article 259. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.00259
sato_2019_facial.design: 65 Japanese laypeople (44 women; mean age 22.9). Within-participant design: scenario condition first (deliberately show the expression one would display in a short scenario for anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise; practice with live video feedback), then photograph condition (imitate prototypical photographs). Experimenter in the room (out of sight), explicit videotaping. Final (apex) frames coded automatically with FaceReader 7.0: six basic emotion intensities plus 20 AU intensities (East Asian template).
sato_2019_facial.numbers: Scenario condition, FaceReader emotion scores: happiness and surprise > all other emotions; anger > other emotions except neutral; disgust > fear/happiness/surprise but not sadness or neutral (and anger > disgust); fear only > happiness (neutral > fear); sadness > others except neutral. AU intensities lower in scenario than imitation: anger AU4, 14, 17, 23, 24; disgust AU4, 6, 9, 17 (AU25 higher); fear AU1, 5, 12, 20, 25 (AU7, 24 higher); happiness AU12, 25; surprise AU1, 2, 5, 25, 26; sadness no single AU differed although the profile did. Emotion-intensity profiles differed between all pairs of scenario expressions; AU profiles differed for all pairs except anger vs disgust (trend).
sato_2019_facial.conclusion: Japanese laypeople can produce the prototypical configurations when imitating them, but scenario-based expressions match the prototypes clearly only for happiness and surprise, differ from prototypes for all emotions, yet still differ between emotions; partial support for prototypical expression theory, which may need modification.
sato_2019_facial.caveats: Posed (scenario-cued) not spontaneous; single static apex frame; FaceReader emotion scores are themselves prototype-based classifiers; scenario order not counterbalanced; experimenter present and explicit recording.

langner_2010_presentation.cit: Langner, O., Dotsch, R., Bijlstra, G., Wigboldus, D. H. J., Hawk, S. T., & van Knippenberg, A. (2010). Presentation and validation of the Radboud Faces Database. Cognition and Emotion, 24(8), 1377-1388.

olszanowski_2015_warsaw.cit: Olszanowski, M., Pochwatko, G., Kuklinski, K., Scibor-Rylski, M., Lewinski, P., & Ohme, R. K. (2015). Warsaw set of emotional facial expression pictures: A validation study of facial display photographs. Frontiers in Psychology, 5, 1516.

vanderschalk_2011_moving.cit: van der Schalk, J., Hawk, S. T., Fischer, A. H., & Doosje, B. (2011). Moving faces, looking places: Validation of the Amsterdam Dynamic Facial Expression Set (ADFES). Emotion, 11(4), 907-920.

tracy_2009_development.cit: Tracy, J. L., Robins, R. W., & Schriber, R. A. (2009). Development of a FACS-verified set of basic and self-conscious emotion expressions. Emotion, 9(4), 554-559.

fernandezdols_1997_spontaneous.cit: Fernández-Dols, J.-M., Sánchez, F., Carrera, P., & Ruiz-Belda, M.-A. (1997). Are spontaneous expressions and emotions linked? An experimental test of coherence. Journal of Nonverbal Behavior, 21(3), 163–177.
fernandezdols_1997_spontaneous.design: Laboratory study: a film was used to elicit intense emotions; participants gave subjective reports of their emotions; faces were recorded by a concealed camera. According to Reisenzein et al. (2013, secondary), the analysis concerned a specific scene of a horror film and participants who reported disgust as the dominant emotion (n = 22). N, coding system and other emotions could not be checked.
fernandezdols_1997_spontaneous.numbers: From the abstract: none. Secondary (Reisenzein et al., 2013): among 22 participants reporting disgust as the dominant emotion to one horror-film scene, 8 (36%) showed nose wrinkling and none showed upper-lip raising.
fernandezdols_1997_spontaneous.conclusion: The coherence between displayed facial expressions and subjective emotion reported by Rosenberg and Ekman (1994) was not found; certain emotions are neither necessary nor sufficient for certain spontaneous expressions.
fernandezdols_1997_spontaneous.caveats: Full text not reachable (closed access; publisher page not accessible). The abstract was read from a bibliographic database copy, not the publisher page. Sample size, emotions analysed and coding system unverified.

namba_2017_spontaneous_b.cit: Namba, S., Kabir, R. S., Miyatani, M., & Nakao, T. (2017). Spontaneous facial actions map onto emotional experiences in a non-social context: Toward a component-based approach. Frontiers in Psychology, 8, Article 633. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.00633
namba_2017_spontaneous_b.design: Re-analysis of data from 31 Japanese undergraduates (29 analysed; 116 apex expressions) watching four films (surprise, amusement, disgust, sadness) alone, recorded secretly by a laptop camera (consent obtained afterwards). Apex frames FACS-coded by a certified coder (second coder kappa .84). Self-report on 16 emotion items after each film. Stepwise logistic and multiple regressions with Bonferroni correction.
namba_2017_spontaneous_b.numbers: AU frequencies across 116 apexes: AU25 31%, AU6 27%, AU7 22%, AU12 21%, AU4 15%, AU10 14%, AU1 10%, AU5 10%, AU26 10%, AU2 8%, AU14 8%, AU23 7%; AU9 and others below 5% were excluded. Surprise ratings predicted AU1 (OR 3.40); disgust predicted AU10 (OR 2.65); AU12 predicted amusement (beta 2.06); AU5 predicted fear and tension; AU23 predicted sadness; AU7 related to happiness and contempt.
namba_2017_spontaneous_b.conclusion: Individual spontaneous facial components map onto reported emotions in ways consistent with their proposed functions; a component-based approach is preferable to prototype matching.
namba_2017_spontaneous_b.caveats: Small sample; single apex frame per film; ratings taken after each film; many models and stepwise selection; Japanese students only.

namba_2017_spontaneous.cit: Namba, S., Makihara, S., Kabir, R. S., Miyatani, M., & Nakao, T. (2017). Spontaneous facial expressions are different from posed facial expressions: Morphological properties and dynamic sequences. Current Psychology, 36(3), 593-605.
namba_2017_spontaneous.design: 31 Japanese undergraduates (13 male; M age 20.19, SD 1.37, range 18–24), Hiroshima University. Within participants, fixed order: spontaneous first, then posed. Spontaneous: participants watched films alone and were filmed secretly (camera in the PC screen): The Champ (sadness), Capricorn (surprise), Pink Flamingos (disgust), When Harry Met Sally (amusement; replaced by Trololo Cat after 10 participants); debriefed and asked for consent; self-reports on a 16-item 0–8 emotion inventory and an affect grid. Posed: asked 'to express the target emotions' while looking at the screen until they felt they had given their best expression. Measure: manual FACS, frame by frame (30 fps), neutral to apex (apex from eight evaluators' ratings); AU45, head and gaze codes excluded; second coder κ = 0.83 for AU presence, FACS reliability .84. Analysis: per-AU χ² tests with odds ratios (posed vs spontaneous occurrence); AU order compared with an extended Fisher's exact test (exact binomial test for disgust). Analysed: spontaneous amusement 19, spontaneous surprise and disgust 29 in the text (28 in Table 1 and 3 captions), posed 28 for all four emotions; spontaneous sadness excluded […]
namba_2017_spontaneous.numbers: Table 1, surprise, spontaneous vs posed (n = 28): AU1 6 (23%) vs 16 (57%), χ² 7.69**; AU2 6 (23%) vs 16 (57%), 7.69**; AU5 10 (36%) vs 21 (75%), 5.88*; AU25 5 (19%) vs 16 (57%), 7.69**; AU26 2 (7%) vs 9 (32%), 4* (* p < .05, ** p < .01). Table 2, amusement (n = 19): AU6 15 (79%) vs 9 (47%), 2.5; AU12 15 (79%) vs 15 (79%), 0; AU25 12 (63%) vs 10 (53%), 0.1; AU26 3 (16%) vs 3 (16%), 0; no significant differences. Table 3, disgust (n = 28): AU4 12 (43%) vs 19 (69%), 3.27; AU9 1 (4%) vs 3 (11%), 0.25; AU10 14 (50%) vs 1 (4%), 9.60**; AU12 6 (21%) vs 0 (0%), 4.17*; AU17 0 (0%) vs 7 (25%), 5.14*; AU25 13 (46%) vs 8 (29%), 1.07. Table 4, posed sadness only (n = 28): AU17 10 (36%), AU4 6 (21%), AU7 3 (11%), AU1, AU6, AU14, AU15 1 (4%) each; no tests. Sequences (Results; extended Fisher's exact test): surprise, spontaneous AU5 before AU1+2 vs posed AU1+2 (or AU1+2+5) earlier, spontaneous n = 6 […]
namba_2017_spontaneous.conclusion: Spontaneous and posed expressions differ: surprise in both AU frequency (AUs 1, 2, 5, 25, 26 more frequent when posed) and AU order (AU5 before AU1+2 when spontaneous); amusement only in AU order, not frequency; disgust morphologically (AU10 and AU12 more frequent when spontaneous, AU17 when posed), with AU17 proposed as a marker of posed negative expressions. Listed limitations: small sample of young Japanese adults, nontarget emotions elicited by films, constant order of generation, no duration/onset measures.
namba_2017_spontaneous.caveats: Read from an author-uploaded copy, only as a summary with short quoted excerpts; table cells were read individually, not from viewing the PDF. Printed percentages do not always match counts/28 (6/28 = 21% printed as 23%; 5/28 = 18% printed as 19%), and the text gives 29 spontaneous surprise/disgust participants while Table 1 and 3 captions say n = 28. Fixed order (posing followed film viewing); only neutral-to-apex frames coded; the disgust film also elicited surprise (self-report). […]

mauss_2005_binds.cit: Mauss, I. B., Levenson, R. W., McCarter, L., Wilhelm, F. H., & Gross, J. J. (2005). The tie that binds? Coherence among emotion experience, behavior, and physiology. Emotion, 5(2), 175-190.
mauss_2005_binds.design: N = 59 analysed (60 recruited) female US undergraduates (mean age 19.1; ethnically mixed). One 5-min film (scenes from Steel Magnolias): amusing scene, sad scene (a woman crying at her daughter's death), amusing scene. Experience: continuous rating dial during a second viewing. Facial behaviour: two coders rated amusement and sadness behaviour continuously with the same dial using 'a global cultural informant approach' (not FACS). Physiology: SCL, cardiovascular, somatic activity. Within-individual cross-correlations computed per participant, Fisher-z averaged.
mauss_2005_binds.numbers: Mean within-individual experience–facial behaviour r = .73 (amusement) and .74 (sadness). Experience/behaviour with physiology: amusement rs .22 to .51; sadness rs -.52 to .00. Average coherence across all pairs: amusement .39, sadness .36. Interrater reliability of behaviour ratings: alpha .84 (amusement), .80 (sadness).
mauss_2005_binds.conclusion: Experience and facial behaviour were highly associated within individuals for both amusement and sadness; physiology was only modestly linked; emotion intensity moderated behaviour–physiology coherence for amusement but not sadness. The authors present this as support for the coherence hypothesis under these conditions.
mauss_2005_binds.caveats: Single film, within-person correlations over a 5-min time series in which amusing and sad scenes alternate, which inflates correlations because both experience and behaviour follow the film structure. Global observer ratings are not measures of specific predicted configurations, so this is not a test of prototypical expressions.

kring_1998_differences.cit: Kring, A. M., & Gordon, A. H. (1998). Sex differences in emotion: Expression, experience, and physiology. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 74(3), 686-703.

reisenzein_2013_coherence.cit: Reisenzein, R., Studtmann, M., & Horstmann, G. (2013). Coherence between emotion and facial expression: Evidence from laboratory experiments. Emotion Review, 5(1), 16-23.
reisenzein_2013_coherence.design: Narrative review (not a meta-analysis) of laboratory experiments with adults. For each emotion the authors report, when available, (a) between-subjects correlations between the target emotion and the facial expression predicted by affect program theory (APT), (b) the percentage of facially reactive participants, and (c) the average intraindividual correlation between emotion and expression. Sections: Happiness I: Amusement; Happiness II: Other Positive Emotions (primarily joy and sensory pleasure); Surprise; Disgust; Sadness; Anger; Fear; then explanations (insufficient intensity; inhibition/display rules). The reviewed primary studies used FACS, EMFACS, facial EMG and observer ratings; emotion was usually self-reported.
reisenzein_2013_coherence.numbers: Figures as reported in the review (read from the publisher PDF only as a summary with short quoted excerpts; re-check before quoting numbers). Amusement: between-subjects r = .32 to .57 across studies; mean intraindividual r about .56 to .73; to jokes, 57% of reactive participants showed AU12 but only 28% AU6 and 23% Duchenne smiles; tickling 61% AU12, 24% AU6, 15% Duchenne. Other positive emotions: between-subjects r from .12 (ns) to .60; intraindividual r roughly .04 to .36. Surprise: full three-component displays in 0% to 7.6% of participants; one- or two-component displays in at most 25% to 52%. Disgust: some between-subjects r .37 to .55, others below .20; e.g. 37% showed upper lip raise and/or nose wrinkle to an accident film. Sadness: Mauss et al. (2005) mean intraindividual r = .74 (continuous observer ratings vs continuous self-ratings); other studies about .10 to .45. […]
reisenzein_2013_coherence.conclusion: Except for amusement (which the authors note is not usually considered a prototypical emotion), there is no convincing evidence that people undergoing APT's basic emotions typically show the predicted patterned facial expressions; even for amusement mostly AU12 alone is shown. Low coherence is not explained by insufficient emotion intensity (more sensitive EMG does not raise coherence) or by inhibition/display rules (coherence is low even when participants are alone).
reisenzein_2013_coherence.caveats: Narrative review by authors who also produced several of the surprise studies reviewed (Reisenzein et al., 2006). The amusement evidence is mostly AU12 alone. Coverage of anger, fear and sadness rests on a handful of studies with heterogeneous measures (EMG, EMFACS, observer ratings). Page numbers were read from excerpts and agree across two copies.
terms: coherence between emotion and facial expression

duran_2017_coherence.cit: Durán, J. I., Reisenzein, R., & Fernández-Dols, J.-M. (2017). Coherence between emotions and facial expressions: A research synthesis. In J.-M. Fernández-Dols & J. A. Russell (Eds.), The Science of Facial Expression (pp. 107-129). Oxford University Press.

duran_2021_emotions.cit: Durán, J. I., & Fernández-Dols, J.-M. (2021). Do emotions result in their predicted facial expressions? A meta-analysis of studies on the co-occurrence of expression and emotion. Emotion, 21.
duran_2021_emotions.design: Three random-effects meta-analyses of studies that measured both an elicited emotion (mostly self-reported) and facial behaviour in the same participants, for six categories: happiness, sadness, anger, disgust, fear, surprise. MA1: proportion of participants showing the full (whole) predicted expression, FACS studies only. MA2: full or partial predicted expressions, FACS or another system. MA3: Pearson correlation between intensity of reported emotion and intensity of the predicted facial expression (often EMG). Two further meta-analyses on amusement alone (proportion and correlation). Exclusions: infants and young children (under 5), clinical samples without a neurotypical group, dependent variables conflating several nonverbal channels. Predicted expressions taken from Ekman and Friesen. Laboratory vs field was not coded as a separate moderator (vividness of the elicitor partly captures it); posed expressions were not the object of the analysis.
duran_2021_emotions.numbers: 55 articles, 69 studies, 110 effect sizes; 3,847 participants (mean 55, median 34.5 per study). MA1 (whole expressions, FACS): prp = .13, 95% CI [.06, .27]; k = 13 (happiness k = 4, .12 [.02, .51]; surprise k = 5, .06 [.02, .15]; disgust k = 4, .30 [.20, .41]); only these three emotions had data; Qw(12) = 45.82, p < .001, I² = 81%. MA2 (whole + partial): prp = .23 [.13, .36]; happiness .20 [.07, .45] (k = 7); surprise .13 [.08, .21] (k = 19); disgust .42 [.14, .75] (k = 9); sadness .28 [.18, .41] (k = 5); anger .35 [.14, .64] (k = 5); fear .25 [.02, .84] (k = 4); Qw(49) = 353.22, I² = 91%. MA3 (intensity correlation): r = .30 [.18, .41], 35 estimates from 28 studies; happiness .32 [.24, .39] (k = 7); surprise .06 [-.62, .69] (k = 2); disgust .45 [.31, .57] (k = 10); sadness .36 [about .28, .43] (k = 5); anger .18 [.07, .28] (k = 10); fear .27 [-.20, .64] (k = 1); Qw(34) = 71.77, I² = 55% […]
duran_2021_emotions.conclusion: The six classic basic emotions do not reliably co-occur with their predicted facial signals; the theory that inspired co-occurrence research has not provided conclusive evidence that specific facial expressions distinguish basic emotions; heterogeneity suggests a more complex account, and the authors call for alternative approaches to the role of facial behaviour in affective processes. Amusement (smile or laughter) is the clear exception.
duran_2021_emotions.caveats: Per-emotion values, k and moderator results come from the author manuscript ('not the copy of record') read only as a summary with short quoted excerpts, in two repository copies (UAM and UDIMA) that gave identical tables; the typeset version may differ slightly. Count inconsistencies: MA1 is described as 15 effect sizes from 13 studies but per-emotion k sum to 13 (Qw df = 12); MA2 as 50 effect sizes from 35 studies but per-emotion k sum to 49; one reading gave the sadness r CI as [.30, .42] instead of [.28, .43] […]
terms: happiness, sadness, anger, disgust, fear, and surprise
proportion of participants who displayed the predicted expression (prp)

fernandezdols_2013_emotion.cit: Fernández-Dols, J.-M., & Crivelli, C. (2013). Emotion and expression: Naturalistic studies. Emotion Review, 5(1), 24-29.
fernandezdols_2013_emotion.design: Narrative review of studies in naturalistic (non-laboratory) settings. Keywords: emotion, expression, field studies, naturalistic studies, smiles. Which emotions and studies are covered could not be checked because the full text was not reachable.
fernandezdols_2013_emotion.conclusion: Field evidence shows a surprisingly weak correlation between basic emotions and their predicted expressions and fits better with facial behaviour having many causes, functions and meanings than with fixed signals of basic emotion; the studies rarely test causation.
fernandezdols_2013_emotion.caveats: Full text unavailable (Sage paywall; no repository copy found through Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, Crossref or web search), so the emotions covered, the studies reviewed and any statements about smiles could not be checked. The review comes from the research group that produced several of the field studies it reviews.

barrett_2019_emotional.cit: Barrett, L. F., Adolphs, R., Marsella, S., Martinez, A. M., & Pollak, S. D. (2019). Emotional expressions reconsidered: Challenges to inferring emotion from human facial movements. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 20(1), 1-68.
barrett_2019_emotional.design: Systematic narrative review of production and perception evidence for anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness and surprise, evaluated for reliability, specificity and generalisability across adults (industrialised and small-scale societies), infants and children, and congenitally blind people.
barrett_2019_emotional.numbers: Cites the 2017 chapter (37 articles; above chance except fear; weak) and an 'expanded version' (89 effect sizes, 47 studies, 3,599 participants; r = .32; proportion = .19). Judo study description: 8 of 55 winners (Study 1) and 25 of 119 (Study 2) produced Duchenne smiles.
barrett_2019_emotional.conclusion: Spontaneous facial configurations occur with weak reliability and undocumented specificity; posed and spontaneous expressions should be treated as different phenomena; facial movements carry information but their emotional meaning is more variable and context-dependent than the common view holds.
barrett_2019_emotional.caveats: Authored largely by constructionist critics of basic emotion theory; 'common view' is their own term for the position they test.

gentsch_2015_appraisals.cit: Gentsch, K., Grandjean, D., & Scherer, K. R. (2015). Appraisals generate specific configurations of facial muscle movements in a gambling task: Evidence for the Component Process Model of emotion. PLOS ONE, 10(8), e0135837.
gentsch_2015_appraisals.design: Two within-subject lab experiments with a gambling task; feedback symbols conveyed goal conduciveness (win/loss/break-even in Exp 1; win/loss in Exp 2) and power (free choice to accept/reject outcome or not); Exp 2 added block-wise control (75% vs 25% high-power trials). Exp 1: N = 24 right-handed female undergraduates, Geneva (18-28 y), 384 trials. Exp 2: N = 28 right-handed female students, Geneva (18-30 y), 864 trials. Facial EMG over corrugator, frontalis and cheek (zygomaticus) regions, feedback-locked, 100-ms bins 600-1400 ms; EEG recorded simultaneously. Participants were not told facial expression was recorded.
gentsch_2015_appraisals.numbers: Exp 1 corrugator: goal-conduciveness main effect from 600 ms (F = 5.19, partial eta2 = .18) and at 800, 1000-1400 ms (losses > wins; break-even > wins; losses ≈ break-even); power main effect at 800 ms (F = 5.96, partial eta2 = .21) and 1300 ms, high > low power; GC x power interaction at 800-900 ms (loss-related frowning only under high power). Exp 1 frontalis and cheek: no GC main effects. Exp 2: no GC or power effects over corrugator; GC effect over frontalis at 700 ms (wins > losses); power effect over frontalis at 1000 ms (low > high) and cheek at 1400 ms (low > high); no control main effects; predicted control x power interaction not found.
gentsch_2015_appraisals.conclusion: Appraisal outcomes (goal conduciveness, then power) drive facial muscle activity sequentially and cumulatively within ~600-1400 ms, as the CPM predicts; corrugator and frontalis track motivational pertinence and the cheek region coping implications; facial responses are not organised by discrete emotions.
gentsch_2015_appraisals.caveats: Small all-female, right-handed student samples; many time-bin tests without correction for multiple comparisons beyond planned contrasts; EMG regions (e.g. 'cheek region') are approximate stand-ins for AUs; loss vs win frowning partly confounded with valence; region-specific patterns did not replicate across experiments.

cacioppo_1986_electromyographic.cit: Cacioppo, J. T., Petty, R. E., Losch, M. E., & Kim, H. S. (1986). Electromyographic activity over facial muscle regions can differentiate the valence and intensity of affective reactions. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 50(2), 260–268.
cacioppo_1986_electromyographic.design: Pilot study: 16 subjects briefly exposed to slides and tones mildly to moderately evocative of positive and negative affect. Full experiment: 28 subjects briefly viewed slides of scenes mildly to moderately evocative of positive and negative affect. Surface EMG over corrugator supercilii ('corrugator supercilia' in the abstract), orbicularis oculi and zygomatic major regions; independent judges viewed videotapes of the faces.
cacioppo_1986_electromyographic.numbers: Pilot N = 16 (slides and tones); main experiment N = 28 (slides only). Stimuli varied in valence (positive/negative) and intensity (mild/moderate). No effect sizes or muscle-by-muscle results are given in the abstract.
cacioppo_1986_electromyographic.conclusion: Facial EMG over brow, eye and cheek regions differentiates the valence ('pleasantness') and intensity of mild-to-moderate affective reactions even when judges cannot see any expression, so EMG gradients can serve as 'objective and continuous probes of affective processes'.
cacioppo_1986_electromyographic.caveats: Abstract only; full text not reachable. Results are condition-level differences in small samples, not person-level classification. Stimuli were mildly-to-moderately evocative slides, so the range did not include highly arousing material (contrast E2/E3). The construct is broad affect/valence, not discrete emotions. The abstract does not say which muscles carried the intensity effect.
terms: valence and intensity of affective reactions
expressions of emotion were not apparent
too subtle or fleeting to evoke expressions observable

dimberg_2000_unconscious.cit: Dimberg, U., Thunberg, M., & Elmehed, K. (2000). Unconscious facial reactions to emotional facial expressions. Psychological Science, 11(1), 86–89.
dimberg_2000_unconscious.design: Backward masking: 30-ms exposures of happy, neutral and angry target faces immediately followed and masked by neutral faces; facial EMG (zygomaticus major and corrugator supercilii implied by 'emotion-relevant facial muscles'; the abstract does not name them). The abstract gives no sample size.
dimberg_2000_unconscious.numbers: 30-ms masked exposures; happy, neutral and angry faces. N, effect sizes and the awareness-check procedure are not in the abstract.
dimberg_2000_unconscious.conclusion: Masked happy and angry faces evoke distinct, corresponding facial EMG reactions without conscious perception, so 'both positive and negative emotional reactions can be unconsciously evoked' and aspects of face-to-face emotional communication operate unconsciously.
dimberg_2000_unconscious.caveats: Abstract only. The 'unconscious' claim depends on masking efficacy; Milders et al. (2008) found above-chance discrimination of masked expressions from 20 ms. Only two emotions were tested, so the result cannot show emotion-specific (vs valence-based) mimicry.

hess_2001_facial.cit: Hess, U., & Blairy, S. (2001). Facial mimicry and emotional contagion to dynamic emotional facial expressions and their influence on decoding accuracy. International Journal of Psychophysiology, 40(2), 129–141.

lang_1993_looking.cit: Lang, P. J., Greenwald, M. K., Bradley, M. M., & Hamm, A. O. (1993). Looking at pictures: Affective, facial, visceral, and behavioral reactions. Psychophysiology, 30(3), 261–273.
lang_1993_looking.design: Participants viewed coloured photographs varying widely in valence (pleasant-unpleasant) and arousal (excited-calm), each for 6 s. Measures: facial EMG (zygomatic, corrugator), heart rate, skin conductance, judgments of pleasure, arousal, interest and emotional state, and choice viewing time; gender and cognitive-style/personality factors examined. The abstract gives no N.
lang_1993_looking.numbers: Not available from the abstract (no N, no correlations). Secondary sources (Fujimura et al., 2013; Penn State open textbook table: 'Zygomatic Activity: U-shaped relationship with self-reported valence') attribute a quadratic or U-shaped zygomatic-valence relation to this paper.
lang_1993_looking.conclusion: Facial EMG covaries with valence judgments and skin conductance with arousal ratings. Facial expressiveness suggests affect-specific reactivity, but the dimensional consistency means 'emotion is fundamentally organized by these motivational parameters'.
lang_1993_looking.caveats: Abstract only; full text not reachable. This summary rests on secondary descriptions. The authors interpret facial EMG as indexing 'facial expressiveness' of valence, within a dimensional-motivational framework rather than discrete emotions.
terms: affective dimensions of valence (pleasant-unpleasant) and arousal (excited-calm)
facial electromyographic (zygomatic and corrugator muscle activity)

larsen_2003_effects.cit: Larsen, J. T., Norris, C. J., & Cacioppo, J. T. (2003). Effects of positive and negative affect on electromyographic activity over zygomaticus major and corrugator supercilii. Psychophysiology, 40(5), 776–785.
larsen_2003_effects.design: Women (n = 68) were exposed to series of affective pictures, sounds and words; self-reported positive and negative affective reactions and facial EMG over zygomaticus major and corrugator supercilii were recorded; the form (linear vs other) and strength of valence effects at each site were compared.
larsen_2003_effects.numbers: n = 68 women; three stimulus modalities (pictures, sounds, words). No effect sizes in the abstract. The shape of the zygomaticus function at the negative end could not be checked: full text not reachable.
larsen_2003_effects.conclusion: Valence has a stronger linear effect on corrugator than on zygomaticus activity, consistent with properties of the facial musculature. Positive and negative affect act reciprocally on corrugator (positive affect lowers it, negative affect raises it) but not on zygomaticus.
larsen_2003_effects.caveats: Abstract only, despite repeated attempts (Wiley, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, Europe PMC, web search for author copies). Women only. EMG 'over' a muscle region includes crosstalk from neighbouring muscles; the authors' own wording is 'activity over'. Stimulus modality may change the zygomaticus pattern; the abstract does not say.
terms: self-reported positive and negative affective reactions
electromyographic (EMG) activity over zygomaticus major / corrugator supercilii

sato_2008_enhanced.cit: Sato, W., Fujimura, T., & Suzuki, N. (2008). Enhanced facial EMG activity in response to dynamic facial expressions. International Journal of Psychophysiology, 70(1), 70–74.

schwartz_1976_facial.cit: Schwartz, G. E., Fair, P. L., Salt, P., Mandel, M. R., & Klerman, G. L. (1976). Facial muscle patterning to affective imagery in depressed and nondepressed subjects. Science, 192(4238), 489–491.

smith_1989_dimensions.cit: Smith, C. A. (1989). Dimensions of appraisal and physiological response in emotion. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 56(3), 339–353.
smith_1989_dimensions.design: Review of evidence to generate hypotheses linking appraisals to physiological activity, plus an imagery-based experiment manipulating appraisals (other-agency, anticipated effort, perceived goal obstacles) while recording eyebrow-frown (corrugator) EMG and heart rate (MeSH: electromyography; pilot projects). N not verified.
smith_1989_dimensions.conclusion: Physiological activity in emotion is organised around appraisals; specifically, the eyebrow frown was influenced by perceived goal obstacles (not by other-agency), while anticipated effort influenced heart rate.
smith_1989_dimensions.caveats: Abstract-level only; imagery induction; sample and effect sizes unverified.

waterink_1994_facial.cit: Waterink, W., & van Boxtel, A. (1994). Facial and jaw-elevator EMG activity in relation to changes in performance level during a sustained information processing task. Biological Psychology, 37(3), 183–198.
waterink_1994_facial.design: Spontaneous (task-irrelevant) EMG of six facial and jaw-elevator muscles during a 20-min visual two-choice serial reaction task: externally paced version (n = 21) and self-paced version (n = 24, different participants). Post hoc split into participants with stable vs declining performance. Tilburg University (Netherlands) laboratory; participant characteristics beyond N not verified.
waterink_1994_facial.numbers: n = 21 (externally paced) and n = 24 (self-paced); 6 muscles; 20-min task. Statistics not verified.
waterink_1994_facial.conclusion: Rising EMG in frontalis, corrugator and orbicularis oris inferior during sustained performance reflects compensatory mental effort (mobilisation of non-specific energetic resources); when performance declines, this EMG rise reverses.
waterink_1994_facial.caveats: Abstract only. Effort is an interpretation of time-on-task EMG increases; no subjective effort ratings are mentioned in the abstract; the performance split was post hoc.
terms: frontalis, corrugator, and orbicularis oris inferior

tassinary_1992_unobservable.cit: Tassinary, L. G., & Cacioppo, J. T. (1992). Unobservable facial actions and emotion. Psychological Science, 3(1), 28–33.

brown_1980_relationships.cit: Brown, S. L., & Schwartz, G. E. (1980). Relationships between facial electromyography and subjective experience during affective imagery. Biological Psychology, 11(1), 49–62.
brown_1980_relationships.design: Laboratory-elicited (affective imagery). N = 60 participants (population and country not given in the abstract); each exposed for 40 s to each of 48 standardized imagery situations designed to reflect happy, sad, angry and fearful conditions, at different intensities. Measure: surface facial EMG over zygomatic, corrugator, masseter and lateral frontalis muscle regions. Emotion criterion: the imagery script plus self-rated experienced emotion on a scale covering the four emotions ('present' and 'future' ratings).
brown_1980_relationships.numbers: N = 60; 48 imagery situations of 40 s each; four EMG sites. Effect sizes, means and test statistics: not reported in the abstract.
brown_1980_relationships.conclusion: Using a standardized imagery scale, rather than self-generated personally relevant situations, allowed more sensitive measurement of the relation between facial muscle activity and subjective experience during affective imagery; specific imagery intensities evoked the expected differential self-report and EMG patterns.
brown_1980_relationships.caveats: Abstract only; whether corrugator also rose during angry and fearful imagery, and the size of each effect, are not reported in the abstract. Imagery of scripted situations, not emotion elicited by real events. Four EMG sites only; surface EMG over a region can pick up neighbouring muscles (e.g., lateral frontalis for AU 2). The anger and fear null results concern the specific muscles chosen, not facial activity in general.

bradley_2000_affective.cit: Bradley, M. M., & Lang, P. J. (2000). Affective reactions to acoustic stimuli. Psychophysiology, 37(2), 204–215.

weyers_2006_electromyographic.cit: Weyers, P., Mühlberger, A., Hefele, C., & Pauli, P. (2006). Electromyographic responses to static and dynamic avatar emotional facial expressions. Psychophysiology, 43(5), 450–453.

kunecke_2014_facial.cit: Künecke, J., Hildebrandt, A., Recio, G., Sommer, W., & Wilhelm, O. (2014). Facial EMG responses to emotional expressions are related to emotion perception ability. PLoS ONE, 9(1), e84053.

sato_2020_physiological.cit: Sato, W., Kochiyama, T., & Yoshikawa, S. (2020). Physiological correlates of subjective emotional valence and arousal dynamics while viewing films. Biological Psychology, 157, 107974.

tamura_2006_facial.cit: Tamura, R., & Kameda, T. (2006). [Are facial expressions contagious in the Japanese?]. Japanese Journal of Psychology (Shinrigaku Kenkyu), 77(4), 377–382.

achaibou_2008_simultaneous.cit: Achaibou, A., Pourtois, G., Schwartz, S., & Vuilleumier, P. (2008). Simultaneous recording of EEG and facial muscle reactions during spontaneous emotional mimicry. Neuropsychologia, 46(4), 1104–1113.

wehrle_2000_studying.cit: Wehrle, T., Kaiser, S., Schmidt, S., & Scherer, K. R. (2000). Studying the dynamics of emotional expression using synthesized facial muscle movements. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 78(1), 105–119.

wegrzyn_2017_mapping.cit: Wegrzyn, M., Vogt, M., Kireclioglu, B., Schneider, J., & Kissler, J. (2017). Mapping the emotional face. How individual face parts contribute to successful emotion recognition. PLOS ONE, 12(5), e0177239.
wegrzyn_2017_mapping.design: Perception study. N = 94 student participants (60 female; mean age 24, range 18-36), Bielefeld University ethics board (Germany per affiliations). Stimuli: photographs of two identities from the NimStim database (female model #01, male model #28), each showing happy, sad, angry, fearful, disgusted, surprised and neutral expressions, all with open mouths, cropped, rescaled to 300x400 pixels and aligned (the paper does not describe how NimStim expressions were produced). Task: each face was hidden behind a 6x8 grid of 48 white tiles; one random tile was revealed at the start and one more every second in random order; participants clicked a stop button as soon as they could decide and then made a seven-way forced choice among the expression labels, with accuracy feedback after each trial. 224 trials per participant (2 identities x 7 expressions x 16 repetitions), run in a browser. Measure: a weight per tile that is larger the more often the tile was visible in short, correct trials ('(1-length of trial)/maximal trial length'), summed per participant and expression, after excluding the longest 25% of trials (more than 16 tiles revealed) […]
wegrzyn_2017_mapping.numbers: N = 94 (60 female), mean age 24 years, range 18-36 (Methods, Participants). Stimuli: 2 NimStim identities x 7 expressions = 14 faces, 300x400 pixels (Methods, Face stimuli). 224 trials per participant = 2 x 7 x 16; two blocks of 112; mean duration 50 min (range 33-72) (Methods, Design). Mask: 6x8 grid = 48 tiles, one tile revealed per second; seven-way forced choice. Trials with more than 16 revealed tiles (the longest 25%) excluded from tile weighting (Methods, Analysis). AU assignment threshold: at least 25 pixels of a hand-drawn AU per tile. No numeric accuracies, tile weights or confidence intervals are given in the text; they appear only in Figs 3-8, which were not readable in the copy read.
wegrzyn_2017_mapping.conclusion: Eye and mouth regions are the most diagnostic areas for recognising emotions, and expressions can be grouped into 'upper-face' expressions (sad, fearful, angry) and 'lower-face' expressions (happiness, disgust); regions belonging to emotion-relevant action units carry the most diagnostic value; faces cluster by the emotion expressed rather than by low-level physical (pixel) features; the study 'provides a first approximation of a representational map of emotion expressions in the observer's mind'. […]
wegrzyn_2017_mapping.caveats: Two stimulus identities (one per gender) from a single database, all open-mouth versions; sadness and anger were poorly recognised, differed between the two models, and their AU labelling 'deviated somewhat from the reference guide'. The 48-tile grid is coarse and AU assignment was deliberately liberal. Significance was judged by non-overlapping 95% CIs. The diagnosticity measure reflects which randomly revealed tiles were visible on short, correct trials, not where observers looked. […]
terms: happy, sad, angry, fearful, disgusted, surprised, neutral
happiness, sadness, anger, fear, disgust, surprise

calder_2000_configural.cit: Calder, A. J., Young, A. W., Keane, J., & Dean, M. (2000). Configural information in facial expression perception. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 26(2), 527–551.

hess_1997_intensity.cit: Hess, U., Blairy, S., & Kleck, R. E. (1997). The intensity of emotional facial expressions and decoding accuracy. Journal of Nonverbal Behavior, 21(4), 241–257.

aviezer_2008_angry.cit: Aviezer, H., Hassin, R. R., Ryan, J., Grady, C., Susskind, J., Anderson, A., Moscovitch, M., & Bentin, S. (2008). Angry, disgusted, or afraid? Studies on the malleability of emotion perception. Psychological Science, 19(7), 724–732.
aviezer_2008_angry.design: Perception; three studies in which identical (posed, prototypical) facial expressions were embedded in affective contexts (face-body/context compounds); categorization and dimensional ratings; eye-movement monitoring. Sample sizes and stimulus sets not verified (abstract only).
aviezer_2008_angry.conclusion: Perception of basic facial expressions is not context invariant; context can categorically change the emotion read from the same face, especially when the context's typical expression is perceptually similar to the face (e.g., disgust vs anger).
aviezer_2008_angry.caveats: Abstract-level only. Compound stimuli are artificial; effect size depends on similarity structure.
terms: similarity between the target facial expression and the facial expression typically associated with the context

aviezer_2012_body.cit: Aviezer, H., Trope, Y., & Todorov, A. (2012). Body cues, not facial expressions, discriminate between intense positive and negative emotions. Science, 338(6111), 1225–1229.
aviezer_2012_body.design: Perception of real-life peak-intensity expressions (photographs). Per abstract: positive and negative situations judged from isolated faces, isolated bodies, and face+body; then face-body compounds (intense negative faces on positive bodies and vice versa); perceived affect and facial mimicry of the faces measured. Secondary (Wenzler et al., 2016, abstract): stimuli included 'winning and losing professional tennis players'. Exact Ns, stimulus counts and the mimicry measure (EMG or coding) not verified.
aviezer_2012_body.numbers: Not verified (primary full text and supplement inaccessible).
aviezer_2012_body.conclusion: At peak intensity, faces alone do not reveal whether a situation is positive or negative, whereas bodies do; observers nonetheless perceive valence in the face that is borrowed from the body.
aviezer_2012_body.caveats: Primary text not read. Athletes' public displays may be strategically controlled (as Wenzler et al. 2016 note). The main follow-ups are from the same laboratory.

carroll_1996_facial.cit: Carroll, J. M., & Russell, J. A. (1996). Do facial expressions signal specific emotions? Judging emotion from the face in context. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 70(2), 205–218.
carroll_1996_facial.design: Perception; 3 studies pairing situational stories with posed 'facial expressions' of a different emotion, chosen under 'specified circumstances' (22 face-situation cases); judges attributed an emotion. Ns not verified.
carroll_1996_facial.numbers: 22 of 22 face-situation cases in 3 studies favoured the situation (per abstract).
carroll_1996_facial.conclusion: Faces carry emotion-relevant information (e.g., quasi-physical/affective) but do not signal specific emotions; in specified circumstances the situation determines the judged emotion.
carroll_1996_facial.caveats: Abstract-level only; posed faces (from standard sets) and verbal vignettes.
terms: easily recognizable signals of specific emotions
the face provides information relevant to emotion but does not signal a specific emotion

wenzler_2016_beyond.cit: Wenzler, S., Levine, S., van Dick, R., Oertel-Knöchel, V., & Aviezer, H. (2016). Beyond pleasure and pain: Facial expression ambiguity in adults and children during intense situations. Emotion, 16(6), 807–814.

smith_2005_transmitting.cit: Smith, M. L., Cottrell, G. W., Gosselin, F., & Schyns, P. G. (2005). Transmitting and decoding facial expressions. Psychological Science, 16(3), 184–189.
smith_2005_transmitting.design: Not reported in the abstract. The abstract does not state the number or population of observers, the stimulus set, the masking method (Bubbles is not named), the number of trials, or the analysis. It states only that the authors 'characterize the information underlying the recognition of the six basic facial expression signals and evaluate how efficiently each expression is decoded by the underlying brain structures.'
smith_2005_transmitting.conclusion: The abstract states two hypotheses (if the face evolved to optimise transmission, the basic expressions 'should have minimal overlap in their information'; if the brain evolved to optimise categorisation, it 'should be efficient with the information available from the transmitter') and the aims (characterise the information underlying recognition of the six basic expression signals; evaluate how efficiently each is decoded). It does not state results or conclusions.
smith_2005_transmitting.caveats: Abstract only; the full text (SAGE) is paywalled and no open copy was found. Every specific element of the claim (Bubbles, which posed set, which regions were diagnostic for which emotion, observer N, and whether the information used matched the information available) is not reported in the abstract. PubMed MeSH indexing includes 'Perceptual Masking', which is consistent with a masking method but is indexer metadata, not an author statement. Bibliographic details follow PubMed (16(3), 184-189) […]

jack_2012_facial.cit: Jack, R. E., Garrod, O. G. B., Yu, H., Caldara, R., & Schyns, P. G. (2012). Facial expressions of emotion are not culturally universal. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 109(19), 7241–7244.
jack_2012_facial.design: Perception (perceivers' internal representations), not production. Per abstract: 30 individuals from Western and Eastern cultures; a computer-graphics platform combining 'generative grammars' with visual perception reconstructed their 'mental representations' of the six basic expressions. Per the group's 2016 description of the same approach: random combinations of FACS action units animated on 3D faces, categorized by observers (reverse correlation). Exact 2012 parameters (number of AUs, trials, task options, residence of East Asian observers) could not be checked in the primary.
jack_2012_facial.numbers: N = 30 (Western and East Asian; split per group not verifiable from abstract). Secondary (Sauter & Eisner, 2013): Jack et al. reported 'correlations from 0.32 to 0.91 between the results of reverse-correlation analysis and established facial actions'.
jack_2012_facial.conclusion: The six basic facial expressions are not universal: East Asian mental representations of the six emotions are less distinct (overlapping) and use the eyes to convey intensity; culture shapes these representations.
jack_2012_facial.caveats: Primary full text not reachable. Sauter & Eisner (2013) argued that the paper's own Fig. 2 shows distinct constellations for each emotion in both groups except fear in the East Asian group, so the data do not refute universalist accounts; Jack et al. replied (2013, 'Differences outweigh commonalities'; text not accessed). The title's claim is stronger than the abstract's specific findings.
terms: six basic facial expressions of emotion

jack_2014_dynamic.cit: Jack, R. E., Garrod, O. G. B., & Schyns, P. G. (2014). Dynamic facial expressions of emotion transmit an evolving hierarchy of signals over time. Current Biology, 24(2), 187–192.
jack_2014_dynamic.design: Perception study using a Generative Face Grammar: random 3D facial animations built from subsets of 41 AUs with random temporal parameters were categorised by 60 Western white Caucasian observers into six emotion labels or 'don't know'; reverse correlation produced 720 dynamic models (60 observers x 6 emotions x male/female faces) of observers' perceptual expectations, analysed with information theory and Bayesian classifiers over time.
jack_2014_dynamic.numbers: 60 Western white Caucasian observers; 41 AUs sampled; 720 dynamic models. Early signals confuse fear with surprise (Upper Lid Raiser) and disgust with anger (Nose Wrinkler); these pairs are discriminated only later (e.g., by Brow Raiser/Brow Lowerer and Upper Lip Raiser).
jack_2014_dynamic.conclusion: Dynamic facial expressions transmit an evolving hierarchy: early, biologically rooted signals (e.g., eye widening, nose wrinkling) support four broad categories (happy, sad, fear/surprise, disgust/anger), and later signals support the six classic categories; emotion communication may rest on four rather than six basic categories.
jack_2014_dynamic.caveats: Perception-only and culture-specific (Western Caucasian observers); faces were synthetic animations; categories were constrained to six labels plus 'don't know'; the evolutionary interpretation of early AUs is inferred, not tested.

jack_2016_four.cit: Jack, R. E., Sun, W., Delis, I., Garrod, O. G. B., & Schyns, P. G. (2016). Four not six: Revealing culturally common facial expressions of emotion. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 145(6), 708–730.
jack_2016_four.design: Perception-based modelling (perceivers' representations), two cultures, all tested in the UK. Stage 1: emotion-word familiarity/typicality and pairwise semantic similarity (50 + 49 English; 50 + 50 Chinese speakers) to build semantic networks. Stage 2: Generative Face Grammar: random, biologically plausible combinations from 'a core set of 42 AUs' animated on faces; 36 Western (native English) and 32 Chinese observers each categorized 2,400-2,800 animations by emotion word and rated intensity on a 5-point scale (reverse correlation). Stage 3: validation of models by 29 Western and 28 Chinese new observers (yes/no word-face match). Stage 4: non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) over pooled validated models. East Asian observers were Chinese nationals with a maximum UK residence of 2.5 months.
jack_2016_four.numbers: Models: 30 Western and 52 East Asian dynamic facial expression models; validated (d' > 1): 25/30 (83.33%) Western and 37/52 (71.15%) East Asian, i.e., 62 'culturally valid' models. Semantic networks: English 28 words in 6 non-singleton clusters; Chinese 48 words in 7 non-singleton clusters (plus singletons). NMF: four factors best represented the pooled models. Pattern meanings (as read): pattern 1 high valence, high arousal, high dominance; pattern 2 low valence; pattern 3 high arousal; pattern 4 low valence, high arousal.
jack_2016_four.conclusion: Rather than six universal expression patterns, four latent, culturally common AU patterns (each conveying combinations of valence, arousal and dominance) form the basis on which culture-specific face movements build more complex expressions; the classic 'surprise'/'fear' and 'disgust'/'anger' confusions reflect shared patterns.
jack_2016_four.caveats: Accepted-manuscript page numbers; quotes were read in excerpts. The authors note commonalities alone are insufficient to conclude innateness. The four patterns are statistical factors over models, i.e., coarse signals; the two-culture design cannot establish universality.

liu_2022_facial.cit: Liu, M., Duan, Y., Ince, R. A. A., Chen, C., Garrod, O. G. B., Schyns, P. G., & Jack, R. E. (2021). Facial expressions elicit multiplexed perceptions of emotion categories and dimensions. Current Biology, 32(1), 200–209.e6.

snoek_2023_testing.cit: Snoek, L., Jack, R. E., Schyns, P. G., Garrod, O. G. B., Mittenbühler, M., Chen, C., Oosterwijk, S., & Scholte, H. S. (2023). Testing, explaining, and exploring models of facial expressions of emotions. Science Advances, 9(6), eabq8421.
snoek_2023_testing.design: Perception. 60 Western European (WE) and 60 East Asian (EA) participants each categorized 2,400 random dynamic AU-combination animations as one of six emotions or 'do not know'; seven published AU models (e.g., Darwin, Cordaro et al. 2018 reference and international core patterns, Keltner et al. 2019, Jack et al.) converted to predictive models; AUROC with noise ceilings; ablation and culture-accented optimization (cross-validated).
snoek_2023_testing.numbers: AUROC fear 0.57 vs surprise 0.76 (averaged across models); model range e.g. Keltner 2019 0.66 vs Jack 2014 0.74; mean 0.68 vs noise ceiling 0.88; optimized culture-accented models removed the WE-EA difference.
snoek_2023_testing.conclusion: Existing AU-based models capture much but not all of categorization behaviour, carry a Western bias, and fixed AU models cannot capture perceiver individual differences.

hyniewska_2019_naturalistic.cit: Hyniewska, S., Sato, W., Kaiser, S., & Pelachaud, C. (2019). Naturalistic emotion decoding from facial action sets. Frontiers in Psychology, 9, 2678.
hyniewska_2019_naturalistic.design: Perception study with naturalistic stimuli. Stimuli: unobtrusive hidden-camera recordings of airport passengers claiming lost luggage (Lost Luggage corpus, Scherer and Ceschi); clips were segmented into single mental states by expert judges (three per clip, a fourth in two ambiguous cases), giving 64 clips, of which 39 were used (4-56 s, mostly 20-28 s; 19 male and 20 female passengers from varied cultural backgrounds). All facial actions were FACS-coded in ANVIL (61 face tracks) by a certified coder and checked by a second certified coder on 12% of videos (mean frame-by-frame Cohen's kappa 0.66, SD 0.18; AU20 only weak/fair, 0.21-0.40). Observers: 122 students from a French technical university; only the 98 men were analysed (age 17-25, mean 19.0, SD 1.5) because the women were judged a non-homogeneous group; University of Geneva ethics approval. Task (web-based): each participant watched 6-39 clips and rated six appraisals (suddenness, goal obstruction, important and incongruent event, coping potential, respect of internal standards, violation of external standards; 0 = totally disagree to 6 = totally agree) and seven non-exclusive emotions […]
hyniewska_2019_naturalistic.numbers: Participants: 122 recruited, 98 men analysed, age 17-25, mean 19.0, SD 1.5 (Methods). Stimuli: 64 clips after segmentation, 39 retained, 4-56 s, 19 male and 20 female passengers (Methods). FACS reliability: mean Cohen's kappa 0.66 (SD 0.18), AU20 0.21-0.40; second coder on 12% of videos. Table 3 (final models; F, df as rendered, p, R2, power): joy 6.54, '6.34', .000, R2 0.54; anger 4.83, '14.26', .000, 0.72; sadness 5.00, '10.30', .000, 0.63; contempt 4.44, '14.26', .001, 0.71; fear 11.74, '8.32', .000, 0.75; shame 3.73, '22.18', .003, 0.82; suddenness 4.43, '11.29', .001, 0.63; goal obstruction 5.88, '6.34', .000, 0.51; relevance and discrepancy 3.57, '10.30', .003, 0.54; coping potential 4.39, '16.24', .001, 0.75; external standards violation 3.56, '8.32', .005, 0.47; internal standards violation 4.74, '18.22', .000, 0.80; 1 - beta = 1.00 for all. […]
hyniewska_2019_naturalistic.conclusion: Decoding of emotions and appraisals in spontaneous, naturalistic expressions 'is implemented by the perception of set of AUs', and 'the profiles of such AU sets could be different from previous theories' (Abstract). Some AU-label links match prior theories (AU1-sadness, AU12-joy, AU4-coping potential, AU17-goal obstruction) and are proposed as possible 'core facial movements', while others do not (outer brow raiser not linked to suddenness; lower lip depressor linked to fear and goal obstruction); absent movements (e.g. no smile) can also carry meaning. […]
hyniewska_2019_naturalistic.caveats: The unit of analysis is the video (N = 39), and the final models retained many AU predictors (6 for joy up to 22 for shame per Table 3/4), with p < .10 retention in stepwise selection; this carries a high risk of overfitting, which the authors acknowledge only as small sample size. The Table 3 df as rendered (e.g. '6.34', '22.18') imply 41 observations rather than 39 videos (arithmetic done here; possible rendering issue). The Introduction lists six rated emotions without fear […]
terms: spontaneous and dynamic facial expressions in naturalistic settings
joy, anger, relief, sadness, contempt, fear, shame
suddenness, goal obstruction, important and relevant (relevance and discrepancy), coping potential, external norm/standards violation, internal norm violation (respect of internal standards)

scherer_2018_appraisaldriven.cit: Scherer, K. R., Mortillaro, M., Rotondi, I., Sergi, I., & Trznadel, S. (2018). Appraisal-driven facial actions as building blocks for emotion inference. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 114(3), 358–379.
scherer_2018_appraisaldriven.design: Three perception experiments with synthetic dynamic avatar videos made with FACSGen 2.0 animation software. Study 1 (pp. 362-366): 57 French-speaking University of Geneva students (reported as 50.8% female, 18-33 years, M = 26.0); 128 videos combining 25 single AUs, the AU1+2 combination and six emotion prototype configurations (anger, disgust, fear, surprise, sadness, happiness), two avatars (male, female), two intensities (50% and 75% of maximum), 2-s clips; Part A (n = 29) rated six emotion scales, Part B (n = 28, one excluded) rated six appraisal scales (unexpectedness, pleasantness, unpleasantness, power, agency, norm compatibility) on sliders from -100 to 100; repeated-measures ANOVAs and k-means clustering of AU means. Study 2 (pp. 366-369): 156 Qualtrics-panel participants (native English speakers of Caucasian origin; reported 50.6% female, 18-65 years, M = 45.4, SD = 12.2), 145 after cleaning; 56 FACSGen videos with four avatars showing nine single AUs (1, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10, 12, 17, 24) and five pairs (1+4, 4+7, 6+12, 9+10, 17+24) plus neutral, at 60% intensity with timing based on the GEMEP corpus; four between-subject groups each rated one appraisal dimension […]
scherer_2018_appraisaldriven.numbers: Study 1 (p. 364), mean emotion ratings for single AUs on the -100 to 100 scale: anger AU4 47.8, AU9 26.4, AU24 8.9, AU10 5.4; happiness AU13 50.8, AU12 38.4, bilateral AU14 30.0; disgust AU10 32.4, AU9 32.0, AU11 7.9; sadness AU15 28.7, AU1 0.8, AU17 1.9; surprise AU27 67.1, AU5 37.8, AU26 23.2 (second cluster reported as AU1+2 31.4, AU2 28.7); fear: only the prototype configuration. Prototype recognition means (Table 2, as extracted): anger 65.2, sadness 52.9, fear 52.0, surprise 79.5 (happiness and disgust rows garbled in the text read). Study 1 appraisal ratings (p. 365): unexpectedness AU27 40.3, AU5 28.5; pleasantness AU13 47.9, AU12 43.7, AU14 30.4, AU18 27.0; unpleasantness AU9 48.5, AU4 37.3 (AU10 34.9, AU15 28.3 as extracted); power AU14 27.0, AU13 25.1, AU12 24.5; low power AU27 15.9; Cronbach's alphas .78 (power) to .96 (pleasantness), as extracted. […]
scherer_2018_appraisaldriven.conclusion: Observers 'first detect specific appraisals from different facial muscle actions and then use implicit inference rules to categorize and name specific emotions'; the results 'confirm that participants can infer targeted appraisals and emotions from synthesized facial actions based on appraisal predictions', and the ability to interpret the synthetic stimuli 'is highly correlated with emotion recognition ability as part of emotional competence'. Observers 'strongly agree on the meaning of these facial action configurations and accurately infer the nature of the respective appraisal'. […]
scherer_2018_appraisaldriven.caveats: The stimuli were synthetic avatar animations, not human faces, and judgments were rating or forced-choice tasks.
