Study 1 used Geneva students; Studies 2-3 used online panels restricted to native English speakers of Caucasian origin. Study 3 hit rates were 'relatively low' except for anger and surprise, and AU combinations in Study 2 added little beyond single AUs. The PDF was read only in excerpts: quotes are short fragments […]
terms: facial action units / facial muscle actions
unexpectedness, pleasantness, unpleasantness, power, agency, norm compatibility (Normative Significance) (Study 1)
anger, disgust, fear, surprise, sadness, happiness
enjoyment, interest, disappointment, relief (Study 3 response options)

ekman_1969_pancultural.cit: Ekman, P., Sorenson, E. R., & Friesen, W. V. (1969). Pan-cultural elements in facial displays of emotion. Science, 164(3875), 86-88.

ekman_1971_constants.cit: Ekman, P., & Friesen, W. V. (1971). Constants across cultures in the face and emotion. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 17(2), 124-129.

ekman_1987_universals.cit: Ekman, P., Friesen, W. V., O'Sullivan, M., Chan, A., Diacoyanni-Tarlatzis, I., Heider, K., ... Tzavaras, A. (1987). Universals and cultural differences in the judgments of facial expressions of emotion. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 53(4), 712-717.

russell_1994_universal.cit: Russell, J. A. (1994). Is there universal recognition of emotion from facial expression? A review of the cross-cultural studies. Psychological Bulletin, 115(1), 102-141.
russell_1994_universal.design: Narrative/methodological review of cross-cultural judgment (recognition) studies of posed facial expressions in modern cultures and in cultures 'relatively isolated from Western influence'. Perception only; no facial measurement.
russell_1994_universal.numbers: Not verified: the recognition percentages for Western literate, non-Western literate and isolated/illiterate samples are in the body tables, which could not be accessed (closed access; no repository copy found). Secondary descriptions only: Gendron et al. (2014, Introduction): 'Only six published experiments test universality of emotion perception using a two-culture approach (two in peer review outlets) and all but one were conducted nearly 40 years ago'; Gendron et al. (2020, Introduction) state that the pre-2008 small-scale-society studies were published 1969-1971, sampled four societies in Melanesia and Southeast Asia, and 'All used choice-from-array methods.' Do not cite specific isolated-culture percentages from Russell (1994) without checking the PDF.
russell_1994_universal.conclusion: Evidence for universal recognition is weakened by method artefacts; faces and emotion labels are 'probably associated' but the association may vary with culture and fits several alternative accounts (e.g., later 'Minimal Universality', Russell 1995).
russell_1994_universal.caveats: Russell's critiques were vigorously disputed at the time (Ekman 1994; Izard 1994); Russell (1995) records points of agreement, notably 'at least Minimal Universality'.
terms: preselected photographs of posed facial expressions

elfenbein_2002_universality.cit: Elfenbein, H. A., & Ambady, N. (2002). On the universality and cultural specificity of emotion recognition: A meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 128(2), 203-235.
elfenbein_2002_universality.design: Meta-analysis of cross-cultural emotion recognition (judgment) studies; perception only. The abstract speaks of 'emotion recognition' and 'emotional expressions' without restricting to the face; the channel composition (face vs voice vs body) and the study/sample counts could not be checked in the primary text (closed access; PsycNET and publisher pages not reachable). No facial measurement of expressers (judgment accuracy is the outcome).
elfenbein_2002_universality.numbers: Not verifiable in the primary text. Secondary (Matsumoto, 2002, pp. 236-239, as extracted from his PDF): the meta-analysis comprised 97 studies, of which 66 used one stimulus set judged by several cultural groups, 7 used several stimulus sets judged by one group, and 21 used balanced designs; the in-group advantage reported by Elfenbein and Ambady was 9.3% (Matsumoto, p. 239). Frequently cited further counts (articles, independent samples, total participants, mean accuracy) were NOT verified and should be checked in the PDF before citing.
elfenbein_2002_universality.conclusion: Recognition is both universal (better-than-chance cross-culturally) and culturally specific (in-group advantage that shrinks with intercultural exposure; asymmetry between majority and minority groups); design features moderate cross-cultural accuracy but not the in-group advantage.
elfenbein_2002_universality.caveats: Better-than-chance accuracy is a weak criterion: most included studies used forced choice with posed/prototypical stimuli and experimenter-defined 'correct' labels, which Russell (1994) and Nelson & Russell (2013) argue inflate scores. 'Universal' here means across the (largely literate, industrialised) samples available up to 2002, not small-scale societies. The in-group advantage was contested methodologically […]
terms: imitation rather than posed or spontaneous emotional expressions

marsh_2003_nonverbal.cit: Marsh, A. A., Elfenbein, H. A., & Ambady, N. (2003). Nonverbal "accents": Cultural differences in facial expressions of emotion. Psychological Science, 14(4), 373-376.

elfenbein_2007_toward.cit: Elfenbein, H. A., Beaupre, M., Levesque, M., & Hess, U. (2007). Toward a dialect theory: Cultural differences in the expression and recognition of posed facial expressions. Emotion, 7(1), 131-146.
elfenbein_2007_toward.design: Production + perception. Study 1 (production, posed): 60 French-speaking participants aged 20-30 (15 men and 15 women in Quebec, Canada; same in Gabon) posed 10 emotions 'so that their friends would be able to understand easily what they feel' (labels with dictionary definitions; mirrors allowed): anger, contempt, disgust, embarrassment, fear, happiness, sadness, serenity, shame, surprise. Apex expressions FACS-coded by a certified coder (10% double-coded, 82.2% agreement). Study 2 (perception): 40 Quebecois and 40 Gabonese students judged the 600 nonstandardized Study 1 expressions and standardized MSFDE expressions (posed via directed facial action), choosing 1 of 10 emotion labels.
elfenbein_2007_toward.numbers: Study 1 (as read): happiness, 53% of Quebecois vs 27% of Gabonese showed AU6+AU12, with 90% of Gabonese showing an open-mouthed smile; sadness, Gabonese head-movement element in 69% vs Quebecois eyebrow frown (AU4); contempt, Gabonese AU10 with AU15 and/or AU17 vs Quebecois AU4 and AU10; anger, AU4 in 90%, Gabonese most commonly AU4+AU5, Quebecois AU4 with AU5 or AU7; shame, idiosyncratic element in 60% Quebecois vs 20% Gabonese, Gabonese more head/gaze down. Study 2: culture-by-culture interaction (in-group advantage) for nonstandardized anger r = .45, contempt .57, disgust .56, serenity .34, sadness .24 (Table 4, as read); no in-group advantage for standardized MSFDE stimuli.
elfenbein_2007_toward.conclusion: Posed expressions show culture-specific 'dialects' in which muscles are used, and these dialects account for the in-group advantage in recognition (stronger for emotions with greater dialect differences; absent for standardized stimuli).
elfenbein_2007_toward.caveats: Posed (communicative) expressions only; single certified coder for most stimuli; AU-specific percentages and r values come from the text as read and should be checked against the Tables. The authors themselves call for spontaneously elicited emotion and other channels.

matsumoto_2009_sequential.cit: Matsumoto, D., Willingham, B., & Olide, A. (2009). Sequential dynamics of culturally moderated facial expressions of emotion. Psychological Science, 20(10), 1269-1275.
matsumoto_2009_sequential.design: Production, spontaneous, naturalistic: emotional displays of Olympic athletes (judo, 2004 Athens; the review by Gallant et al. 2026 lists 84 medal and fifth-place winners from 35 countries, the same set as Matsumoto & Willingham 2006) coded over time with FACS (coding per the 2006 study and the 2026 review; not verified for this paper); expressive styles classified and related to country-level characteristics (urbanism, individualism-collectivism).
matsumoto_2009_sequential.numbers: Not verified in primary (closed access). Source sample per Matsumoto & Willingham (2006) abstract: 84 athletes from 35 countries.
matsumoto_2009_sequential.conclusion: Universal and culture-specific displays unfold sequentially within an individual in a single context: an initial universal display followed within seconds by culturally moderated regulation (masking vs expressing).
matsumoto_2009_sequential.caveats: Abstract-level only for the 2009 paper. Small number of athletes per country; public, highly social setting; 'universal' initial displays defined by the investigators' FACS/EMFACS predictions.

cowen_2021_sixteen.cit: Cowen, A. S., Keltner, D., Schroff, F., Jou, B., Adam, H., & Prasad, G. (2021). Sixteen facial expressions occur in similar contexts worldwide. Nature, 589(7841), 251-257.
cowen_2021_sixteen.design: Two experiments using deep neural networks on 6 million videos from 144 countries: expression types (16) and contexts (thousands, e.g. weddings, sporting competitions) were annotated automatically and their co-occurrence compared across 12 world regions. No measure of the expressers' felt emotion.
cowen_2021_sixteen.numbers: 6 million videos; 144 countries; 16 expression types; context associations 70% preserved across 12 regions.
cowen_2021_sixteen.conclusion: Fine-grained patterns linking facial expressions to social contexts are preserved across the modern world.
cowen_2021_sixteen.caveats: Full text not read; online video is a selected, often public and performed sample.

crivelli_2016_fear.cit: Crivelli, C., Russell, J. A., Jarillo, S., & Fernandez-Dols, J.-M. (2016). The fear gasping face as a threat display in a Melanesian society. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 113(44), 12403-12407.
crivelli_2016_fear.design: Perception; Trobriand adolescents attributed emotions and/or social motives to facial displays (Study 1); chose the 'threatening' face (Study 2), with Spanish comparison.
crivelli_2016_fear.conclusion: The gasping face can function as a threat display; the Western reading (fear/submission) is not pancultural.

crivelli_2016_reading.cit: Crivelli, C., Jarillo, S., Russell, J. A., & Fernandez-Dols, J.-M. (2016). Reading emotions from faces in two indigenous societies. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 145(7), 830-843.
crivelli_2016_reading.design: Perception, choice-from-array. Study 1: Trobriand Islanders (Papua New Guinea), children and adolescents N = 68, aged 6-16 (most spoke no English), plus Spanish control group N = 113 of similar ages. Study 2: Matemo Island (Mozambique) children and adolescents N = 36. Stimuli: arrays of six still photographs (five prototypical posed expressions plus neutral) from ADFES and RaFD (Study 2 also dynamic ADFES clips; between- and within-subject versions). Task: 'point to the person' who felt a named emotion (happiness, fear, anger, disgust, sadness), terms given in Kilivila or Kimwani.
crivelli_2016_reading.numbers: Matching (% of trials), as read in the full text: Trobrianders happiness 58, sadness 46, anger 7, fear 31, disgust 25; Spaniards happiness 100, sadness 98, anger 91, fear 93, disgust 83; Matemo happiness 56, sadness 22, anger 22, fear 53, disgust 39. With a six-face array, chance is 1/6 (about 17%).
crivelli_2016_reading.conclusion: Indigenous children and adolescents did not associate their own emotion labels with the prototypical faces to the degree Spanish children did; results challenge the claim of a universal emotion-signalling system, though they do not support any one alternative theory. The authors note they tested only canonical Western displays and not possible indigenous signals.
crivelli_2016_reading.caveats: Child/adolescent samples; translation of emotion terms into Kilivila and Kimwani; small Matemo sample. Some values exceed chance (e.g., Matemo fear 53%), so 'no recognition' would overstate.
terms: point to the person feeling a specific emotion

gendron_2014_perceptions.cit: Gendron, M., Roberson, D., van der Vyver, J. M., & Barrett, L. F. (2014). Perceptions of emotion from facial expressions are not culturally universal: Evidence from a remote culture. Emotion, 14(2), 251-262.
gendron_2014_perceptions.design: Perception. Between-subjects sorting task. Himba (Otji-Herero speakers, two remote villages, Kunene region, Namibia; 65 recruited, 54 analysed) vs US community sample (Boston Museum of Science; 68 recruited). Stimuli: 36 photographs of posed facial expressions (anger, fear, sadness, disgust, happiness, neutral) by 6 African American posers from Gur, IASLab and NimStim sets. Random assignment to 'free sorting' or 'word-anchored' sorting (six emotion words given orally, repeated every 6 cards). Pile labels collected by open-ended question. Analyses: hierarchical cluster analysis, MDS with dimensions identified by US-normed behaviour vs emotion ratings, and a 'consistency' score. No facial measurement (FACS) of stimuli reported in the main text.
gendron_2014_perceptions.numbers: Discrete emotion words used to label piles: US M = 4.45 vs Himba M = .81; action descriptions: Himba M = 2.38 vs US M = .84. 'Consistency' (percentage of a category's items grouped together forming the majority of a pile): Himba 49.615% (SD 33.559) vs US 67.101% (SD 22.350), main effect of culture; words vs no words 58.576 vs 54.223, p = .067 (marginal); three-way interaction n.s. MDS: 3 dimensions (Himba) vs 4 (US); Himba dimensions identified by behaviour ratings, US by emotion ratings.
gendron_2014_perceptions.conclusion: Perceptions of emotion from posed faces are not universal but depend on cultural and conceptual (language) context; Himba perceivers construed faces as situated actions; emotion words pushed US sorts toward the Western model and Himba sorts only subtly.
gendron_2014_perceptions.caveats: Stimuli were Western-category posed portrayals; MDS dimension norms came only from US MTurk raters; 54 Himba analysed after exclusions; the authors note the Otji-Herero emotion words may be borrowed. The PMC author manuscript has some dropped symbols (e.g., t and p values) in the text.

gendron_2020_emotion.cit: Gendron, M., Hoemann, K., Crittenden, A. N., Mangola, S. M., Ruark, G. A., & Barrett, L. F. (2020). Emotion perception in Hadza hunter-gatherers. Scientific Reports, 10, 3867.
gendron_2020_emotion.design: Perception. Hadza hunter-gatherers (Lake Eyasi basin, northern Tanzania; data 2016; two bush camps; fewer than about 150 adults available). Study 1 free labeling: 43 Hadza (ages 18-70) vs 45 US adults; six posed facial configurations (anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise) by African American posers; responses in Hadzane or Swahili, translated live and audio-recorded. Study 2 choice-from-array: 54 Hadza (48 analysed) vs 48 US MTurk adults with high-school education or less; 24 trials, a vignette containing an emotion word then two faces (target vs foil matched/unmatched in valence and arousal: affect-controlled, valence-controlled, arousal-controlled, affect-uncontrolled).
gendron_2020_emotion.numbers: Study 1: mental-state language US 0.97 vs Hadza 0.70; expected emotion words US 0.73 vs Hadza 0.24 (also 0.25 among 17 Hadza with minimal Swahili and no schooling); action labels Hadza 0.49 vs US 0.06; smiling labeled happiness by 44% (19/43) of Hadza; scowl as 'ofa-' 65% but 'ofa-' also most characteristic for nose-wrinkle, gasping and pouting faces. Study 2: affect-controlled probabilities US 0.86-0.89 (anger, fear, disgust) vs Hadza fear 0.72, anger 0.61, disgust 0.59 (fear and anger above chance), falling to 0.65, 0.58, 0.60 controlling for other-culture exposure; 90% of Hadza above chance on arousal-controlled trials (valence available) vs 58% on affect-controlled trials.
gendron_2020_emotion.conclusion: Little evidence of universal emotion perception among the Hadza; valence perception appears universal; schooling/second-language exposure increased conformity to the 'universal' pattern; results support a constructionist account of culturally learned emotion concepts.
gendron_2020_emotion.caveats: Static posed faces by African American posers from Western sets; US Study 2 sample online; Hadza participants not testing-naive (active fieldwork sites); small samples; two-culture design.

masuda_2008_placing.cit: Masuda, T., Ellsworth, P. C., Mesquita, B., Leu, J., Tanida, S., & Van de Veerdonk, E. (2008). Placing the face in context: Cultural differences in the perception of facial emotion. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 94(3), 365-381.
masuda_2008_placing.design: Perception; cartoon central figure surrounded by others with same/different expressions; Study 2 eye tracking.
masuda_2008_placing.conclusion: Westerners treat emotions as individual feelings; Japanese see them as inseparable from the group's feelings.

cordaro_2020_recognition.cit: Cordaro, D. T., Sun, R., Kamble, S., Hodder, N., Monroy, M., Cowen, A., Bai, Y., & Keltner, D. (2020). The recognition of 18 facial-bodily expressions across nine cultures. Emotion, 20(7), 1292-1300.
cordaro_2020_recognition.design: Perception. College students aged 18-30 with at most 1 month of travel abroad, from China (54), Germany (54), India (44), Japan (55), Pakistan (46), Poland (64), South Korea (50), Turkey (61), United States (55) (N = 483), online, 2012. Stimuli: still photographs of facial-bodily expressions of 18 states posed by 8 paid U.S. posers (Asian American, African American, European American; both genders) following muscle-by-muscle instructions from two FACS-certified researchers based on prior encoding studies. Task: hear/read a translated causal-antecedent story and choose the matching photo among four same-valence photos (one the most anatomically similar 'Basic 6' alternative) or 'none of the above'; chance 25%.
cordaro_2020_recognition.numbers: 18 states: anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise, amusement, contentment, desire, embarrassment, interest, pain, pride, shame, sympathy, boredom, confusion, coyness. 15 of 18 at or above 58%; 16 of 18 reliably recognized in all nine cultures (interest and sympathy failed in at least one). Overall accuracy by perceiver gender: female 74%, male 71%; female posers 73% vs male 71%.
cordaro_2020_recognition.conclusion: Upward of 18 (and, with other evidence, about 20) states have facial-bodily expressions recognized across diverse cultures, but the authors flag serious methodological limitations (8 U.S. posers, prototypical poses, college students, stereotypical stories, background differences for boredom/confusion).
cordaro_2020_recognition.caveats: Story-to-photo matching among four same-valence options remains a forced-choice paradigm (with a 'none' option). Data were collected in 2012.

boecker_2015_face.cit: Boecker, L., Likowski, K. U., Pauli, P., & Weyers, P. (2015). The face of schadenfreude: Differentiation of joy and schadenfreude by electromyography. Cognition and Emotion, 29(6), 1117-1125.

menon_1994_kalis.cit: Menon, U., & Shweder, R. A. (1994). Kali's tongue: Cultural psychology and the power of shame in Orissa, India. In S. Kitayama & H. R. Markus (Eds.), Emotion and culture: Empirical studies of mutual influence (pp. 241-284). American Psychological Association.

haidt_1999_culture.cit: Haidt, J., & Keltner, D. (1999). Culture and facial expression: Open-ended methods find more expressions and a gradient of recognition. Cognition and Emotion, 13(3), 225-266.
haidt_1999_culture.design: Perception. 40 US participants (University of Wisconsin-Madison undergraduates, ages 18-21) and 40 participants in the Old Town of Bhubaneswar, Orissa, India (ages 15-60; mixed schooling, 14 Brahmin). 14 still photographs of posed expressions specified by FACS action units: the seven 'Ekman expressions' (anger, contempt, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise), four 'recently studied' expressions (embarrassment, shame, compassion, amusement) and three 'exploratory' expressions (tongue-bite, face-cover, gape). One female poser set (half of participants) and an equivalent Caucasian male poser set (other half). Interview: free response first ('what has happened to make the person feel this way?'), then forced choice from a 'Bicultural List of Emotions' with the option to name an unlisted emotion. Free responses coded for affect words and situation codes.
haidt_1999_culture.numbers: Tongue-bite, forced choice (Table 2): Wisconsin amusement 37.5%, happiness 12.5%, disgust 10%, shame 10%; Orissa guilt 27.5%, lajya 20%, happiness 12.5%, enthusiasm 12.5%. Free-response affect-word clusters (Table 3): Wisconsin happiness 33.1%, funny 28.6%; Orissa happiness 35.0%, lajya 25.0%. Situation codes (Table 6): Orissa 'Self-wrong' 47.1%; Wisconsin thinking 17.6%, success 17.6%, joke 11.8%. The authors treat 70-90% agreement as the range typical of strong universality claims and 20-40% as weak (p. 237, as read). Gradient (Results): the seven Ekman expressions highest; embarrassment and amusement elicited the predicted modal responses in both samples; shame and compassion mixed; among exploratory expressions only the face-cover showed cross-cultural similarity.
haidt_1999_culture.conclusion: Open-ended (free-response, situational) methods reveal more expressions with cross-cultural meaning than the classic six/seven, and recognition is graded rather than a binary universal/non-universal split; some expressions (tongue-bite) carry culture-specific meaning.
haidt_1999_culture.caveats: Two posers only (one female, one Caucasian male); stimuli are posed AU configurations, not spontaneous behaviour; the Wisconsin sample was students while the Orissa sample was a community sample. Page numbers are approximate.

fessler_2004_shame.cit: Fessler, D. M. T. (2004). Shame in two cultures: Implications for evolutionary approaches. Journal of Cognition and Culture, 4(2), 207-262.

zickfeld_2019_kama.cit: Zickfeld, J. H., Schubert, T. W., Seibt, B., Blomster, J. K., Arriaga, P., Basabe, N., ... Fiske, A. P. (2019). Kama muta: Conceptualizing and measuring the experience often labelled being moved across 19 nations and 15 languages. Emotion, 19(3), 402-424.

kulke_2020_comparison.cit: Kulke, L., Feyerabend, D., & Schacht, A. (2020). A comparison of the Affectiva iMotions facial expression analysis software with EMG for identifying facial expressions of emotion. Frontiers in Psychology, 11, 329.

hofling_2020_read.cit: Höfling, T. T. A., Gerdes, A. B. M., Föhl, U., & Alpers, G. W. (2020). Read my face: Automatic facial coding versus psychophysiological indicators of emotional valence and arousal. Frontiers in Psychology, 11, 1388.
hofling_2020_read.design: 43 healthy participants viewed pleasant, unpleasant and neutral scenes. FaceReader (FR) valence and arousal were compared with facial EMG (valence) and skin conductance (arousal).
hofling_2020_read.conclusion: FaceReader has yet to surpass established psychophysiological measures in sensitivity, though it is promising for non-contact assessment.

skiendziel_2019_assessing.cit: Skiendziel, T., Rösch, A. G., & Schultheiss, O. C. (2019). Assessing the convergent validity between the automated emotion recognition software Noldus FaceReader 7 and Facial Action Coding System Scoring. PLOS ONE, 14(10), e0223905.
skiendziel_2019_assessing.design: SMoFEE stimulus set: 80 Caucasian adults instructed to mimic JACFEE prototypes of six emotions plus neutral. 640 stills manually FACS-coded for intensity by two certified coders (agreement index .83 on 50 double-coded stills). FaceReader 7 run on 480 video sequences; Spearman correlations and F1 for 20 AUs.
skiendziel_2019_assessing.numbers: Emotion classification 79% (no calibration) and 80% (calibration). AU convergence (Spearman): good for AU1 and AU2; insufficient for 10 AUs including AU6 and AU12. AU 4, 6 and 12 within-emotion r = .08-.53. Manual FACS agreement index .83.
skiendziel_2019_assessing.conclusion: FaceReader 7 classifies posed basic emotions well, but AU-level validity is only moderate. Accuracy will likely be lower for non-optimal, more naturalistic video.
skiendziel_2019_assessing.caveats: Posed, mimicked expressions of young Caucasian adults; optimal recording conditions.

stockli_2018_facial.cit: Stöckli, S., Schulte-Mecklenbeck, M., Borer, S., & Samson, A. C. (2018). Facial expression analysis with AFFDEX and FACET: A validation study. Behavior Research Methods, 50(4), 1446-1460.
stockli_2018_facial.design: Study 1: 600 standardized posed pictures (WSEFEP, ADFES, RaFD) classified by AFFDEX and FACET (iMotions); accuracy = 'matching scores' against intended emotion. Study 2: 110 participants (63 female; mean age 21.2) (a) viewed IAPS/GAPED pictures for 6 s each and responded spontaneously, with responses scored for correct valence; (b) imitated RaFD expressions, scored for the correct emotion.
stockli_2018_facial.numbers: Study 1: AFFDEX 73% overall (ADFES 73%, WSEFEP 66%, RaFD 77%); FACET 97% (ADFES 99%, WSEFEP 92%, RaFD 99%); human judges about 85% on WSEFEP and ADFES. Study 2, spontaneous valence: AFFDEX 57% (positive pictures 17%, negative 97%), FACET 67% (63%, 71%). Imitation of RaFD: AFFDEX 55%, FACET 63% correct emotion; happiness 91% and 98%; fear 1% and 10%.
stockli_2018_facial.conclusion: Both modules reach acceptable accuracy for standardized prototypical pictures (FACET better) but perform worse for more natural expressions; accuracy varies strongly by emotion and database.
stockli_2018_facial.caveats: Ground truth for spontaneous responses was stimulus valence, which the authors call 'controversial'. Software versions have since changed (FACET is no longer commercially available, per Dupré et al., 2020).
terms: standardized pictures of prototypical (vs. natural) facial expressions

yan_2014_casme.cit: Yan, W.-J., Li, X., Wang, S.-J., Zhao, G., Liu, Y.-J., Chen, Y.-H., & Fu, X. (2014). CASME II: An improved spontaneous micro-expression database and the baseline evaluation. PLOS ONE, 9(1), e86041.

yan_2013_casme.cit: Yan, W.-J., Wu, Q., Liu, Y.-J., Wang, S.-J., & Fu, X. (2013). CASME database: A dataset of spontaneous micro-expressions collected from neutralized faces. In 2013 10th IEEE International Conference and Workshops on Automatic Face and Gesture Recognition (FG).

kollias_2019_expression.cit: Kollias, D., & Zafeiriou, S. (2019). Expression, Affect, Action Unit Recognition: Aff-Wild2, Multi-Task Learning and ArcFace. In Proceedings of the British Machine Vision Conference (BMVC).

benitezquiroz_2016_emotionet.cit: Benitez-Quiroz, C. F., Srinivasan, R., & Martinez, A. M. (2016). EmotioNet: An accurate, real-time algorithm for the automatic annotation of a million facial expressions in the wild. In Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR).

mavadati_2013_disfa.cit: Mavadati, S. M., Mahoor, M. H., Bartlett, K., Trinh, P., & Cohn, J. F. (2013). DISFA: A spontaneous facial action intensity database. IEEE Transactions on Affective Computing, 4(2), 151-160.

zhang_2014_bp4dspontaneous.cit: Zhang, X., Yin, L., Cohn, J. F., Canavan, S., Reale, M., Horowitz, A., Liu, P., & Girard, J. M. (2014). BP4D-Spontaneous: A high-resolution spontaneous 3D dynamic facial expression database. Image and Vision Computing, 32(10), 692-706.
zhang_2014_bp4dspontaneous.design: Read in the conference version: 41 participants (23 women, 18 men), aged 18–29, recruited from psychology, computer science and engineering at Binghamton; ethnicity Asian 11, African-American 6, Hispanic 4, Euro-American 20 (Table II). Production type: laboratory-elicited (eight emotion-induction tasks, about 1–4 min each, run by an experimenter; Table I). Measure: manual FACS (2002 edition), 27 AUs coded for onset/offset by two FACS-certified coders, AU 12 and AU 14 also for intensity (0–5); only a 20-s segment per task 'that had the highest density of facial expression' was coded (whole video if shorter). Emotion check: participants rated felt emotions after each task on 5-point Likert-type scales (Section III.C, Figure 4). AU statistics (Table IV) are pooled across tasks for the first 30 participants.
zhang_2014_bp4dspontaneous.numbers: Conference version. Sample: N = 41 (23 F, 18 M), 18–29 years; 328 3D+2D sequences (Table II). Mean coded segment length per task, s (Table III, first 30 participants): T1 19.60, T2 20.21, T3 12.24, T4 19.73, T5 20.04, T6 18.95, T7 19.91, T8 11.49. AU events / frames pooled over all 8 tasks (Table IV, first 30 participants): AU1 411/27610; AU2 317/20898; AU4 351/25204; AU5 176/6418; AU6 428/51498; AU7 440/62001; AU9 89/5066; AU10 518/67086; AU11 7/1153; AU12 379/67586; AU13 2/138; AU14 477/48017; AU15 542/16892; AU16 158/3420; AU17 1010/40430; AU18 30/418; AU19 50/901; AU20 86/2718; AU22 39/623; AU23 616/18405; AU24 363/16039; AU27 55/1529; AU28 94/4797; AU30 17/631; AU32 22/1365; AU38 33/1208; AU39 7/232. Overall kappa .931 (weighted average; per-AU kappa .261 for AU18 to .999 for AU11). […]
zhang_2014_bp4dspontaneous.conclusion: Read only in paraphrase for the IVC article (SUNY record): emotions were elicited with well-validated emotion inductions, frame-level ground truth was FACS-coded, and the database supports research on naturally occurring facial action. In the conference version the authors state that, except for task 7, the target emotion was the one most highly rated by the majority of participants, and that for task 7 most participants reported at least 'a little' anger/upset.
zhang_2014_bp4dspontaneous.caveats: The 2014 IVC article itself could not be retrieved (publisher site not accessible; no open copy found); everything substantive was read in the earlier conference version, which lacks Girard as author and may differ from the journal version (e.g., the journal version may add by-task AU data for all 41 participants; unverified). The PDF was read in excerpts, so quotes should be spot-checked against the PDF. […]

dupre_2020_performance.cit: Dupré, D., Krumhuber, E. G., Küster, D., & McKeown, G. J. (2020). A performance comparison of eight commercially available automatic classifiers for facial affect recognition. PLOS ONE, 15(4), e0231968.
dupre_2020_performance.design: 937 dynamic videos: 467 posed (BU-4DFE; 78 people instructed to portray the six basic emotions) and 470 spontaneous (UT-Dallas; 292 students watching a 10-min emotion-eliciting video; emotion labels assigned by the database authors without validation; uneven categories: anger 3, disgust 119, fear 13, happiness 196, sadness 38, surprise 101). 14 human observers (forced choice among six labels) vs 8 commercial classifiers (Affdex, FaceVideo, Facet, Microsoft, EmotionalTracking, EmotionRecognition, FaceReader, FaceAnalysis). Accuracy = match to database label (true positive rate); ROC/AUC compared by bootstrap.
dupre_2020_performance.numbers: Overall TPR: humans 72.48% [71.72, 73.24] vs classifiers 53.88% [52.75, 55.01]. Classifiers: Emotient/Facet 61.9%, VicarVision/FaceReader 57.31%, Neurodata Lab 56.78%, Visage 55.07%, Microsoft 52.61%, Affectiva 50.48%, MorphCast 48.56%, CrowdEmotion 48.35%. Fleiss' kappa: humans 0.58, classifiers 0.47. AUC: humans higher than every classifier for both posed and spontaneous (p < .001). Separate posed and spontaneous accuracies per system are given only in figures and supplementary tables (S5, S6), not in the text.
dupre_2020_performance.conclusion: Humans outperformed commercial classifiers. The best two approximated humans for posed expressions, but most classifiers were consistently less accurate for spontaneous expressions, probably because of training on posed, prototypical data. Classifiers based on Basic Emotion Theory 'may therefore stand on questionable theoretical and empirical grounds'.
dupre_2020_performance.caveats: Posed and spontaneous stimuli came from different databases, people, resolutions and label procedures, so stimulus type is confounded with database. Human 'accuracy' is also agreement with labels, not a measure of felt emotion. Classifier versions are from about 2019 and may have changed.

namba_2021_assessing.cit: Namba, S., Sato, W., Osumi, M., & Shimokawa, K. (2021). Assessing Automated Facial Action Unit Detection Systems for Analyzing Cross-Domain Facial Expression Databases. Sensors, 21(12), 4222.
namba_2021_assessing.design: FaceReader 7, OpenFace 2.0 and AFAR evaluated against manual frame-by-frame FACS (A-intensity threshold) on Aff-Wild2 (30 YouTube clips, 169,686 frames), DISFA+ posed (9 adults, 12,394 frames) and GFT conversations (96 participants, 133,194 valid frames). ROC-AUC per AU; co-occurrence bias.
namba_2021_assessing.numbers: Mean AUC on Aff-Wild2: OpenFace 0.72, FaceReader 0.67, AFAR 0.65. GFT: OpenFace 0.72, FaceReader 0.58, AFAR 0.72. DISFA+ posed: OpenFace 0.81, FaceReader 0.55, AFAR 0.79. All systems over-predicted AU1-AU2 co-occurrence.
namba_2021_assessing.conclusion: All systems detect AUs above chance across domains; the open-source tools beat FaceReader. Accuracy is AU- and context-dependent, and tension-related AUs (14, 23) are hard.
namba_2021_assessing.caveats: AUC only in the main text (F1 in supplements). Aff-Wild2 AU labels are partly automatic (per Kollias, 2022), although the authors describe all databases as manually coded.

krumhuber_2021_emotion.cit: Krumhuber, E. G., Küster, D., Namba, S., Shah, D., & Calvo, M. G. (2021). Emotion recognition from posed and spontaneous dynamic expressions: Human observers versus machine analysis. Emotion, 21(2), 447-451.
krumhuber_2021_emotion.design: Perception study plus automated analysis. Observers: 70 students (79% female), aged 18-24 (M = 19.61, SD = 1.57), 96% White/Caucasian; ethics approval from UCL Department of Experimental Psychology (country of recruitment not stated beyond this). Stimuli: 162 dynamic video clips (108 posed, 54 spontaneous) from 14 databases; nine databases contained posed expressions 'emerging from instructions to perform an expression/facial action' and five contained spontaneous expressions 'elicited in response to emotion-specific tasks'; two exemplars per emotion per database; six emotions (anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise). The database-by-type list is in Table S1, which could not be read; the main text footnote names BINED, DynEmo, ADFES, DISFA and GEMEP (and the text read also mentions MPI and D3DFACS). Human task: not forced choice; for each clip participants rated their confidence (0-100%) for eight categories (anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness, surprise, other emotion, neutral), summing to 100%; accuracy = confidence for the target emotion averaged over the two exemplars per category and database; chance 'set conservatively at 25%'. Machine: FACET […]
krumhuber_2021_emotion.numbers: Manuscript pp. 7-8. Overall target accuracy: humans 54.83% (SD = 27.84), FACET 61.91% (SD = 41.52); both above the 25% chance level (humans t(161) = 13.64, p < .001, d = 1.07; machine t(159) = 11.24, p < .001, d = 0.89, as extracted); machine > humans overall, Z = 2.70, p = .007 (r = .21 as extracted). Posed: humans 61.95 (SD = 25.17) vs machine 69.82 (SD = 38.12), Z = 2.67, p = .008 (r = .26 as extracted). Spontaneous: humans 39.40 (SD = 27.20) vs machine 45.49 (SD = 43.81), Z = 0.79, p = .428 (r = .11 as extracted). Posed > spontaneous within raters: humans U = 1654, p < .001; machine U = 2036, p = .004. Posed clips were more prototypical than spontaneous (U = 1980.5, p = .002, r = .24, as extracted); prototypicality predicted the machine advantage, beta = .287, t(158) = 2.78, p = .006. As extracted, per-emotion posed advantages: humans for anger (U = 9, p = .003) […]
krumhuber_2021_emotion.conclusion: Posed expressions were better recognised than spontaneous ones by both humans and machine, linked to their greater prototypicality; 'automated systems rely on expression prototypicality for emotion classification' and 'may perform just as well as humans when tested in a cross-corpora context' (published abstract); in the manuscript discussion, 'AFEA can be equally sensitive to spontaneously occurring behavior'. Limitations stated: few clips per database may not represent the full databases, and the number of response categories should be equated in future work.
krumhuber_2021_emotion.caveats: The full text read was the UCL Discovery author manuscript, not the typeset article; numbers should be checked against the published version (only its abstract was read). Human 'accuracy' is mean confidence (0-100%) assigned to the target label among eight options, not forced-choice hit rate; how FACET outputs were converted to a percentage is described only in Supplementary Materials, which were not read. Which databases were posed versus spontaneous (Table S1) was not available. 'Happiness'

krumhuber_2021_human.cit: Krumhuber, E. G., Küster, D., Namba, S., & Skora, L. (2021). Human and machine validation of 14 databases of dynamic facial expressions. Behavior Research Methods, 53(2), 686-701.

bennett_2002_facial.cit: Bennett, D. S., Bendersky, M., & Lewis, M. (2002). Facial expressivity at 4 months: A context by expression analysis. Infancy, 3(1), 97-113.
bennett_2002_facial.design: 150 four-month-old infants (mean 19.1 weeks corrected age) videotaped in five situations: tickle, sour taste, jack-in-the-box, arm restraint and masked stranger. Expressions were coded second by second with Izard's MAX, per the Method.
bennett_2002_facial.numbers: Table 1 (n = 150): number of infants showing each MAX expression by situation. Arm restraint: surprise 80, joy 37, anger 36, fear 29, sadness 28, disgust 3. Masked stranger: surprise 90, joy 56, anger 23, fear 20, sadness 19, disgust 4. Jack-in-the-box: surprise 78, joy 38. Sour taste: sadness 60, joy 28, anger 25, surprise 22, disgust 22, fear 20. Tickle: joy 83, surprise 29.
bennett_2002_facial.conclusion: Joy, and surprise to the jack-in-the-box, showed predicted specificity, but surprise was also most common in arm restraint and masked-stranger situations. Negative discrete expressions showed no predicted specificity. The results give little support to DET situational specificity and point toward a synthesis of DET and dynamic systems theory.
bennett_2002_facial.caveats: Specificity was judged from MAX formulas, so the same a priori-formula validity problem raised by Oster et al. (1992) applies. Situations were assumed to elicit specific emotions without independent validation. Counts are of infants showing an expression at least once, not durations.

camras_1998_production.cit: Camras, L. A., Oster, H., Campos, J., Campos, R., Ujiie, T., Miyake, K., Wang, L., & Meng, Z. (1998). Production of emotional facial expressions in European American, Japanese, and Chinese infants. Developmental Psychology, 34(4), 616-628.

sullivan_2003_contextual.cit: Sullivan, M. W., & Lewis, M. (2003). Contextual determinants of anger and other negative expressions in young infants. Developmental Psychology, 39(4), 693-705.

hiatt_1979_facial.cit: Hiatt, S. W., Campos, J. J., & Emde, R. N. (1979). Facial patterning and infant emotional expression: Happiness, surprise, and fear. Child Development, 50(4), 1020-1035.

rosenstein_1988_differential.cit: Rosenstein, D., & Oster, H. (1988). Differential facial responses to four basic tastes in newborns. Child Development, 59(6), 1555-1568.

soussignan_1997_facial.cit: Soussignan, R., Schaal, B., Marlier, L., & Jiang, T. (1997). Facial and autonomic responses to biological and artificial olfactory stimuli in human neonates: Re-examining early hedonic discrimination of odors. Physiology & Behavior, 62(4), 745-758.

steiner_2001_comparative.cit: Steiner, J. E., Glaser, D., Hawilo, M. E., & Berridge, K. C. (2001). Comparative expression of hedonic impact: Affective reactions to taste by human infants and other primates. Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews, 25(1), 53-74.
steiner_2001_comparative.design: Comparative observational study of taste-elicited orofacial reactions in 8 newborn human infants and 27 infant or adult non-human primates from 11 species. These comprised three great apes (chimpanzee, orangutan, gorilla), three Old World monkeys, four New World monkeys and one lemur. Stimuli included sucrose and quinine. Reaction components were scored from video, with component durations analysed allometrically.
steiner_2001_comparative.numbers: 8 human newborns and 27 non-human primates from 11 species. Human infant and great ape patterns were more similar to each other than either was to Old World or New World monkeys. Some components were shared by all primates and others were restricted to particular taxonomic groups.
steiner_2001_comparative.conclusion: Taste-elicited orofacial reactions show homologous positive (sucrose) and negative (quinine) hedonic patterns across primates, with similarity tracking phylogenetic relatedness. Positive and negative valence and intensity of affective reaction can be assessed quantitatively across species, and infant reaction patterns are systematically related to those of other primates.
steiner_2001_comparative.caveats: Only the abstract was read. Small samples per species (27 animals across 11 species). The 'hedonic' interpretation rests on the stimulus (sweet vs bitter) and on taste-reactivity theory rather than on independent measures of experience.
terms: positive hedonic patterns of facial affective reactions

matsumoto_2009_spontaneous.numbers: Sample sizes not given in the abstract.
matsumoto_2009_spontaneous.conclusion: Spontaneous expression does not depend on observational learning, though social management of expressions has a learned component.
matsumoto_2009_spontaneous.caveats: Emotion inferred from match outcome; configurations classified with EMFACS-type dictionaries.

peleg_2006_hereditary.cit: Peleg, G., Katzir, G., Peleg, O., Kamara, M., Brodsky, L., Hel-Or, H., Keren, D., & Nevo, E. (2006). Hereditary family signature of facial expression. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 103(43), 15921-15926.
peleg_2006_hereditary.design: Family study comparing facial movements of congenitally blind individuals with those of their sighted relatives and of people outside the family, during an interview designed to evoke think-concentrate, sadness, anger, disgust, joy and surprise. Two analyses: an 'in-out family test' (frequency of each movement within vs outside the family) and a 'classification test' (assigning blind subjects to families from the gestalt of movements). Per Valente et al. (2018, secondary): 21 congenitally blind individuals and 31 sighted participants (relatives or strangers), with 'documentary and computational' analyses. The coding scheme was not described in the abstract.
peleg_2006_hereditary.numbers: Classification of blind subjects to their families from movement gestalt: 80% correct over the whole interview and 75% in anger. The in-out family frequency effect was significant for think-concentrate, sadness and anger. Per Valente et al. (2018, secondary): 21 congenitally blind and 31 sighted participants. Chance level for classification, the number of families, and the coding system could not be checked.
peleg_2006_hereditary.conclusion: Facial movements of congenitally blind people resemble those of their relatives more than those of non-relatives, which the authors take as evidence for a hereditary 'family facial expression signature'. Because blind subjects could not have learned the movements by sight, the authors argue for a heritable component, and they anticipate finding genes that influence facial expression.
peleg_2006_hereditary.caveats: Only the abstract was read. Small sample (about 21 blind participants per Valente et al.). Familial similarity is attributed to heredity, but shared non-visual environment (for example, vocal or tactile learning) is not ruled out. Emotional states were assumed from interview topics rather than measured independently. The coding approach and chance levels were not verifiable here.

kohler_2008_static.cit: Kohler, C. G., Martin, E. A., Stolar, N., Barrett, F. S., Verma, R., Brensinger, C., Bilker, W., Gur, R. E., & Gur, R. C. (2008). Static posed and evoked facial expressions of emotions in schizophrenia. Schizophrenia Research, 105(1-3), 49-60.
kohler_2008_static.design: 12 outpatients with stable schizophrenia (DSM-IV) and 12 healthy controls matched on gender, ethnicity, age and parental education (7 men and 5 women; 6 Caucasian and 6 African-American per group), University of Pennsylvania. Each produced happiness, anger, fear, disgust and sadness (fixed order; surprise excluded a priori) at low, medium and high intensity, first posed (mechanical/English method; intensities cued by the instructor) then evoked (Stanislavski-based reliving of the participant's own biographical situations, summarised as vignettes and recounted to them). Static digital photographs; FACS by three certified raters blind to emotion and group, AU present if at least 2 raters agreed; AU intensity not analysed; 'frequent' AUs = present in ≥15% of control expressions for that emotion in either condition. Conditional logistic regression on matched pairs (diagnosis, condition, intensity); self-rated experience on 0–10 scales.
kohler_2008_static.numbers: Self-rated experience greater for evoked than posed (χ² = 16.73, df = 1, p < .001); the posed–evoked difference was larger for sad, anger and fear and smaller for happy (χ² = 16.48, df = 4, p = .002) and less pronounced in patients (χ² = 5.11, df = 1, p = .024) (3. Results). Happy: frequent AUs less common in schizophrenia for evoked (OR = .41, p < 0.001) but not posed expressions (OR = .87, p = .595; diagnosis × condition Wald = 4.1, p = .044) (3.1). Inter-coder κ .46–.79 for frequent and .32–.36 for infrequent AUs (2.6).
kohler_2008_static.conclusion: Facial expression patterns were similar between groups, but patients showed fewer frequent AUs (e.g., Duchenne-smile components in happy expressions; furrowed brows in all negative emotions) and more infrequent AUs; the predicted selective impairment of evoked expressions held only for happy expressions.
kohler_2008_static.caveats: AU numbers inside the Results sentences, the in-text citations and all tables (including frequent-AU lists by condition) were stripped from the PMC-derived text, and the PMC page could not be accessed, so posed vs evoked AU frequencies could not be read. Small sample (12 + 12); static photographs; fixed emotion order; posed always before evoked; patients on antipsychotics.

centorrino_2015_honest.design: Published abstract: senders were '198 participants from Lyon, France' who decided whether to send money to trustees on the basis of short video clips; trustees came from Toulouse (repository summary). [DP8374, Sec. IV, as read in excerpts]: trustees were 84 volunteers aged 18–35 from the general population of Toulouse, France (mean age 25; 46% students; 55% women), each filmed twice (168 clips, about 10–20 s, mean about 15 s) saying a memorised sentence giving their name, age and occupation; trustees were not told anything about smiling ('We said nothing to trustees about smiling', Sec. I); each trustee was filmed under a low-stakes (4 euros) and a high-stakes (8 euros) treatment, with real payouts. Smile measure: the senders themselves rated each clip on 8-point scales for how much the trustee smiled and 'how genuine were their smiles' (about 40 ratings per clip, range 38–45, fn. 17); no FACS, AU6/AU12 (Duchenne) coding or automated detection is reported in DP8374. Perceivers: 198 University of Lyon students (84 in wave 1, 114 in wave 2; gender-balanced; mean age 22; 92% students). Behaviour: binary send/not-send decision in a trust game […]
centorrino_2015_honest.numbers: Published abstract: 198 senders (Lyon); +1 SD in rated smile genuineness associated with an unconditional expected gain of 'about one dollar and thirty cents' to senders over the two trials. [DP8374 only, Table 3/Sec. IV–V, read in excerpts; may differ from the published analyses]: high-stakes treatment raised rated genuineness, coefficient 0.124 (p = .017, one-tailed; about 36% of 1 SD of clip means); smile quality -> trustworthiness rating 0.54 (p < .001); smile quality -> sending (probit) 0.219 (p < .001; text: about 21% higher probability per scale point, about 7% per SD); smile quality -> sender gains 0.911 (p = .005; about 0.9 euros per point, 0.3 euros per SD); senders sent to 37% of partners on average; high-stakes treatment did not predict sending (-0.011, p = .400); smile quality did not significantly predict 'unselfish behavior' (0.403, p = .126, Table 4) […]
centorrino_2015_honest.conclusion: Published abstract: smiles rated as more genuine 'strongly predict' trustworthiness judgments, higher-stakes trustees' smiles are rated 'significantly more genuine', those rated as smiling genuinely return more money on average, and 'Potential gains for senders could be significantly increased from taking smiles rated as genuine into account' (TSE abstract excerpt). Framed as honest signalling: smiles perceived as genuine are informative about the earning opportunities available to share. DP8374 adds that evidence that smiles signal intrinsic trustworthiness was weaker.
centorrino_2015_honest.caveats: Published full text not read (open access, but the publisher site could not be accessed); basis is the published abstract. All design details and coefficients come from the 2011 CEPR discussion-paper version, which has a different title and preliminary analyses (it reports gains in euros, while the published abstract reports about $1.30 per SD over two trials), so the published numbers may differ. DP8374 numbers were read in excerpts and only short passages were verbatim. […]

krumhuber_2007_facial.design: From the abstract only: participants played a 2-person trust game; before the game, the facial dynamics of the other player were manipulated using brief (<6 s) 'highly realistic facial animations' (synthetic/computer-animated dynamic faces). Measures named in the abstract: (a) choice of with whom to play the game, (b) decisions to cooperate, and inferences about the other player's trustworthiness, tested as a mediator. Sample size, population, country, the number of target faces, which facial actions or AUs were animated (the abstract does not use the word 'smile' and does not mention Duchenne markers), the onset/apex/offset timings, the stakes and all statistics are not reported in the abstract.
krumhuber_2007_facial.numbers: Abstract: animations were 'brief (<6 s)'. No N, percentages, test statistics, p values or effect sizes are given in the abstract.
krumhuber_2007_facial.conclusion: Facial dynamics 'significantly influenced' partner choice and decisions to cooperate in a trust game, and inferred trustworthiness of the other player mediated the effect of facial dynamics on cooperative behavior (Abstract).
krumhuber_2007_facial.caveats: Abstract only; full text was not retrievable (closed access; author copy now redirects). Therefore not verified here: that the animated displays were smiles, whether they differed in Duchenne marking (AU6) or only in timing (onset/apex/offset), the comparison conditions (e.g., neutral face), number of synthetic targets, participant N and population, whether payoffs were real, and all statistics. If the manuscript describes this study as contrasting 'genuine' and 'fake' smiles by their dynamics […]

reed_2012_facial.cit: Reed, L. I., Zeglen, K. N., & Schmidt, K. L. (2012). Facial expressions as honest signals of cooperative intent in a one-shot anonymous Prisoner's Dilemma game. Evolution and Human Behavior, 33(3), 200–209.
reed_2012_facial.design: From the abstract: strangers took part in an unrestricted face-to-face acquaintance period during which they made verbal promises of commitment; their specific positive and negative facial actions displayed immediately after these promises were measured with the Facial Action Coding System (Ekman & Friesen, 1978) (spontaneous production during a laboratory interaction; manual FACS coding). Directly afterwards, each person made an anonymous, behaviourally defined decision to cooperate or defect in a one-shot, two-person Prisoner's Dilemma. Participants also predicted their partner's decision. Not reported in the abstract: N, population, country, which AUs were coded and how they were grouped into 'enjoyment' and 'contempt' actions, the analysis model, and all statistics.
reed_2012_facial.numbers: None in the abstract (no N, AU frequencies, coefficients, accuracy rates or p values).
reed_2012_facial.conclusion: Enjoyment-related facial actions predicted cooperative decisions and contempt-related facial actions predicted non-cooperative decisions 'within dyads'; participants accurately predicted their partners' decisions; 'facial actions may function as honest signals of cooperative intent', and the findings offer 'a possible explanation for the association between subjective affective experience and facial expression' (Abstract).
reed_2012_facial.caveats: Abstract only; full text not retrieved (closed access). The specific AUs (e.g., whether 'enjoyment' meant AU6+AU12 and 'contempt' meant unilateral AU14) cannot be confirmed here and should not be filled in from other sources. 'Within dyads' is ambiguous: it may mean that a person's own displays predicted their own decision, or a dyad-level analysis. 'Enjoyment' and 'contempt' are the authors' category labels for groups of facial actions, not measures of felt emotion. […]

scharlemann_2001_value.cit: Scharlemann, J. P. W., Eckel, C. C., Kacelnik, A., & Wilson, R. K. (2001). The value of a smile: Game theory with a human face. Journal of Economic Psychology, 22(5), 617–640.
scharlemann_2001_value.design: From the abstract: 120 subjects took part in a laboratory experiment consisting of a simple two-person, one-shot 'trust' game with monetary payoffs. Before the game each subject was shown a photograph of the partner, taken from a collection with one smiling and one non-smiling image for each of 60 individuals (static photographs). A separate set of subjects rated the photographs on a semantic differential survey of affective and behavioural interpretations; factor analysis of these ratings produced a factor the authors termed 'cooperation'. Behaviour measured: trusting behaviour in the game. Not reported in the abstract: subjects' population and country, sex split, whether smiles were posed or spontaneous, whether they were FACS-coded or differed in Duchenne marking (AU6), payoff amounts, and all statistics.
scharlemann_2001_value.numbers: Abstract: 120 subjects; 60 photographed individuals, each with one smiling and one non-smiling image. No effect sizes, percentages, test statistics or p values are given in the abstract.
scharlemann_2001_value.conclusion: Results 'lend some support' to the prediction that smiles elicit cooperation among strangers in a one-shot interaction; other facial characteristics also elicit cooperation; a rated 'cooperation' factor correlated with smiling was 'somewhat more strongly predictive of behavior than a smile alone'; males were more cooperative, especially towards female images, and females least cooperative towards female images (Abstract).
scharlemann_2001_value.caveats: Abstract only; full text not retrievable (figshare copy failed to load; Sussex repository copy reportedly under permanent embargo). The size and significance of the smile effect, the participant population, whether smiles were posed and whether Duchenne marking was controlled are not verified. The abstract's own wording ('some support') is weaker than a claim that smiles reliably increase trust. Sex-of-participant by sex-of-image interactions qualify any main effect.

nota_2021_facial.numbers: Eyebrow frowns: 13% of questions vs 8% of responses; of 1,269 frowns, 895 (71%) occurred with questions (the paper prints '39% (374)' for responses, which should read 29%). Stable clusters: frowns + squints + nose wrinkles; raises + eye widenings.
nota_2021_facial.conclusion: Questions and responses carry distinct, early-timed distributions and clusters of facial signals, so facial signals may help listeners recognise social actions quickly; eyebrow frowns mark questions most confidently.
nota_2021_facial.caveats: Dutch acquaintances only; holistic (not FACS) annotation; one arithmetic misprint (39% should be 29%).

grammer_1988_patterns.conclusion: Content-level only: the brow raise has a cross-culturally constant movement pattern, co-occurs most often with smiling, and has a range of functions (agreement, acceptance of social contact, emphasis), with brow lowering as its antithesis.
grammer_1988_patterns.caveats: The abstract was available only as a garbled list of words; treat as provisional.

strack_1988_inhibiting.cit: Strack, F., Martin, L. L., & Stepper, S. (1988). Inhibiting and facilitating conditions of the human smile: A nonobtrusive test of the facial feedback hypothesis. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 54(5), 768–777.

wagenmakers_2016_registered.cit: Wagenmakers, E.-J., Beek, T., Dijkhoff, L., Gronau, Q. F., Acosta, A., Adams, R. B., Jr., ... Zwaan, R. A. (2016). Registered Replication Report: Strack, Martin, & Stepper (1988). Perspectives on Psychological Science, 11(6), 917–928.
wagenmakers_2016_registered.design: 17 independent direct replications of Strack, Martin & Stepper (1988) Study 1 following one vetted, preregistered protocol. Participants held a pen in the teeth ('smile') or lips ('pout') and rated four moderately funny Far Side cartoons (0-9). A video camera recorded participants to check pen holding. Exclusions: hypothesis guessers, misunderstanding cartoons, incorrect pen holding on 2+ cartoons, outliers beyond 2.5 SD. Combined N = 1,894 analysed.
wagenmakers_2016_registered.numbers: 17 labs; N = 1,894 analysed. Original difference = 0.82 units; meta-analytic difference = 0.03 [-0.11, 0.16]. 9/17 lab effects in the predicted direction; 0/17 as large as 0.82. 33 of 34 Bayes factors favoured the null.
wagenmakers_2016_registered.conclusion: The pen-in-mouth effect on cartoon funniness ratings did not replicate, in a statistically compelling way, but this does not invalidate the more general facial feedback hypothesis.
wagenmakers_2016_registered.caveats: The outcome was funniness judgments, not reports of felt emotion. Unlike the original, participants were filmed; Noah et al. (2018) argued this matters. Facial movement was not measured (pen position was checked on video).
terms: the more general facial feedback hypothesis

noah_2018_both.cit: Noah, T., Schul, Y., & Mayo, R. (2018). When both the original study and its failed replication are correct: Feeling observed eliminates the facial-feedback effect. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 114(5), 657–664.
noah_2018_both.design: Replication of the Strack et al. (1988) pen-in-mouth cartoon paradigm with vs without a video camera present.
noah_2018_both.numbers: Not available from the abstract (N and effect sizes not given).
noah_2018_both.conclusion: Minute protocol differences (being recorded) can produce theoretically meaningful changes, which reconciles the original and the failed replication.
noah_2018_both.caveats: Abstract only. The Many Smiles study (2022) also found no pen-in-mouth effect; whether cameras were used there was not checked.

coles_2019_metaanalysis.cit: Coles, N. A., Larsen, J. T., & Lench, H. C. (2019). A meta-analysis of the facial feedback literature: Effects of facial feedback on emotional experience are small and variable. Psychological Bulletin, 145(6), 610–651.
coles_2019_metaanalysis.design: Meta-analysis of studies that manipulated facial feedback and collected emotion self-reports; random-effects meta-regression with robust variance estimation; 12 moderators; three publication-bias detection methods.
coles_2019_metaanalysis.numbers: Published version: 286 effect sizes from 138 studies; 12 moderators tested, 3 significant: (a) type of outcome (emotional experience < affective judgments of stimuli), (b) presence of emotionally evocative stimuli (larger effects on experience when stimuli absent), (c) type of stimuli (e.g., emotional sentences > pictures). No publication bias detected for emotional-experience outcomes by 3 methods; bias detected for affective-judgment outcomes by all 3. The 2017 thesis version (286 effects, 136 studies) reported d = .20 and ~70% of variation due to heterogeneity. The Many Smiles paper (2022) describes the same meta-analysis as '286 effect sizes from 137 studies'. The final published overall estimate and CI were not visible in the sources read.
coles_2019_metaanalysis.conclusion: Facial feedback influences emotional experience, as the hypothesis claims, but the effects are small and heterogeneous; they are stronger for affective judgments of stimuli (where publication bias is evident) and when no emotionally evocative stimulus is present.
coles_2019_metaanalysis.caveats: Published full text not reachable; the effect size and heterogeneity values are from the thesis version. Study counts differ across sources (136 in the thesis, 137 in Many Smiles' description, 138 in the published abstract). The meta-analysis pools very different manipulations (pen-in-mouth, posing, mimicry, etc.) and self-report outcomes, so demand characteristics remain a live concern (see Coles et al., 2023).
terms: affective judgments of a stimulus (e.g., the objective funniness of a cartoon)

coles_2022_multilab.cit: Coles, N. A., March, D. S., Marmolejo-Ramos, F., Larsen, J. T., Arinze, N. C., Ndukaihe, I. L. G., ... Liuzza, M. T. (2022). A multi-lab test of the facial feedback hypothesis by the Many Smiles Collaboration. Nature Human Behaviour, 6(12), 1731–1742.
coles_2022_multilab.design: Preregistered, multicentre adversarial collaboration. 2 (Pose: happy vs neutral, within participants) x 3 (Facial Movement Task: facial mimicry, voluntary facial action, pen-in-mouth; between) x 2 (Stimuli Presence: positive images present vs absent; between). n = 3,878 participants, 26 groups, 19 countries. Primary analyses: 1,504 participants after exclusions (attention-check failures 17%, mobile device 3%, pose deviation 1%, pose mismatch 3%, distraction 3%, any awareness of hypothesis 46%). Outcome: Discrete Emotions Questionnaire 4-item happiness subscale (1-7). Facial measure: none (posed-expression manipulation; self-report outcome).
coles_2022_multilab.numbers: Overall Pose effect: Mdiff = 0.31 [0.21, 0.40], 5.17% of scale range, BF10 = 61.06-102.63. Facial mimicry: Mdiff = 0.49 [0.36, 0.61], 8.17%, BF10 > 100. Voluntary facial action: Mdiff = 0.40 [0.23, 0.56], 6.67%, BF10 = 25.20-39.26. Pen-in-mouth: Mdiff = 0.04 [-0.07, 0.15], 0.67%, P = 0.46, BF10 = 0.11-0.17. Pose x Task: F(2, 32.95) = 17.11, P < 0.001. Pose x Stimuli Presence: F(1, 29.50) = 1.33, P = 0.26, BF10 = 0.06-0.13. Positive images alone: Mdiff = 0.30. Anger: Mdiff = -0.02 (n.s.). Awareness moderation: beta = 0.08 [0.06, 0.10].
coles_2022_multilab.conclusion: Strong evidence of facial feedback effects: mimicking or voluntarily posing smiles both initiated (no stimulus) and amplified (with positive images) self-reported happiness, but the effects were small; the pen-in-mouth task gave no unequivocal evidence. Facial feedback is best seen as 'one of many components' of emotional experience.
coles_2022_multilab.caveats: The outcome is self-report only, and the overt posing tasks are obtrusive (demand cannot be excluded, although effects remained among unaware participants). Mimicry and voluntary poses were of happy versus neutral expressions only, so the study says nothing about other emotions' feedback. The authors themselves doubt practical well-being applications.
terms: happy versus neutral facial expression poses

kleck_1976_effects.design: Two laboratory experiments; participants received electric shocks (painful stimuli) either alone or while observed by another person; measures: pain-related nonverbal expressivity (rated from video; method unverified), skin conductance, and self-reported pain/arousal. Experiment 2 replicated Experiment 1 and varied sex of observer. PubMed MeSH terms list 'Male' (participants apparently male; unverified). N not available from the abstract.
kleck_1976_effects.conclusion: Being observed attenuated expressive responses to painful shocks, and this was accompanied by decreased (not increased) subjective pain and skin conductance responses; replicated in Experiment 2 with no sex-of-observer effect on arousal measures. Authors discuss an interpretation linking expression to subjective and autonomic responses (consistent with the Lanzetta/Kleck facial-feedback programme).
kleck_1976_effects.caveats: Abstract-level only; observer manipulation, expressivity coding (likely observer ratings, not FACS), shock levels and N unverified. Direction of causality (does inhibited expression reduce pain, or does observation reduce pain?) not established.

vervoort_2011_social.cit: Vervoort, T., Caes, L., Trost, Z., Sullivan, M., Vangronsveld, K., & Goubert, L. (2011). Social modulation of facial pain display in high-catastrophizing children: An observational study in schoolchildren and their parents. Pain, 152(7), 1591–1599.
vervoort_2011_social.design: 38 schoolchildren (22 boys, 16 girls; 10–18 years, M = 14.5) and one parent each (28 mothers, 10 fathers). Two cold pressor tasks: first told no-one was observing (alone), then told the parent was observing (parent present). In reality the parent observed both immersions, and the child could not see the parent. A 3-minute parent–child interaction between immersions was coded for parental pain-attending vs non-pain talk. Facial display was coded with the Child Facial Coding System (CFCS; 13 actions) and self-report with a 100-mm VAS. Child pain catastrophizing was assessed by questionnaire (the instrument name was not captured in the text read).
vervoort_2011_social.numbers: N = 38 child–parent dyads. Catastrophizing × parental presence on CFCS: F(1,34) = 4.38, p < .05. Low catastrophizers increased expression with the parent: F(1,36) = 15.90, p < .0001. High catastrophizers showed no change: F(1,36) = 0.24, n.s. Catastrophizing × parental non-pain talk on facial expression: t = 2.12, β = .35, ΔR² = .10. For high catastrophizers, non-pain talk was associated with more expression: β = .51, p < .05. Same interaction for self-report: t = 2.17, β = .37, ΔR² = .11.
vervoort_2011_social.conclusion: High-catastrophizing children's facial pain display is not increased by parental presence, so it 'may not always or solely be driven by communication goals'. It is, however, related to parental non-pain-attending talk. This challenges the direct extension of adult communal-coping and operant accounts to children.
vervoort_2011_social.caveats: The condition order was fixed (alone first, then parent), so parental presence is confounded with a second immersion. The parent watched both times. The sample is small, and 74% of parents were mothers. The text read was the submitted version; check numbers against the published version before quoting statistics. CFCS is an observational facial coding system for children, not full FACS.

marsh_2005_effects.cit: Marsh, A. A., Ambady, N., & Kleck, R. E. (2005). The effects of fear and anger facial expressions on approach- and avoidance-related behaviors. Emotion, 5(1), 119-124.
marsh_2005_effects.design: From the abstract only: perceivers responded to facial expressions of fear and anger, and the outcome was 'approach- and avoidance-related behaviors'. The abstract does not report the sample (N, population, country), the stimulus set (posed photographs? which face set? which facial actions or AUs), the comparison expressions, the motor response used, the dependent measure (e.g., reaction time) or any statistics. PubMed MeSH indexing lists 'Reaction Time', 'Psychomotor Performance', 'Pattern Recognition, Visual' and 'Sex Factors', but these are indexing terms, not reported design details.
marsh_2005_effects.numbers: None in the abstract (no N, means, reaction times, test statistics or effect sizes).
marsh_2005_effects.conclusion: The anger expression facilitates avoidance-related behaviour, consistent with its being a threatening stimulus; the fear expression facilitates approach behaviour, which 'contradicts the notion of the fear expression as predominantly threatening or aversive' and suggests it 'may represent an affiliative stimulus' (Abstract).
marsh_2005_effects.caveats: Abstract only; full text not retrievable (closed access). Not verified: the stimuli and which facial actions they contained, the sample, the response measure (likely a motor task, but the abstract only says 'approach- and avoidance-related behaviors'), and all numbers. Whatever the measure, it is a motor approach/avoidance tendency, not a social or economic decision such as trust or cooperation. A later study found the opposite for anger (see below) […]

vick_2007_crossspecies.cit: Vick, S.-J., Waller, B. M., Parr, L. A., Smith Pasqualini, M. C., & Bard, K. A. (2007). A cross-species comparison of facial morphology and movement in humans and chimpanzees using the Facial Action Coding System (FACS). Journal of Nonverbal Behavior, 31(1), 1-20.
vick_2007_crossspecies.design: Methodological development of ChimpFACS. Human FACS was adapted using new dissections of chimpanzee facial musculature (Burrows et al., 2006) and observation of static and video images of about 150 chimpanzees. This included an existing database of over 200 short video clips and about 40 h of focal footage of the face. Each human AU was checked for a muscular basis and observable appearance change in chimpanzees.
vick_2007_crossspecies.numbers: Development sample: about 150 chimpanzees, over 200 short video clips and about 40 h of focal footage. Human AUs not retained or not identified in chimpanzees per the full text include AU4 (brow lowerer), AU5 (upper lid raiser) and AU7 (lid tightener), owing to heavier brows and low scleral contrast. AU1 and AU2 are merged as AU1+2 because medial and lateral frontalis do not act independently. A novel AD160 (lower lip relax) was added. Exact AU counts could not be checked from the tables.
vick_2007_crossspecies.conclusion: FACS can be adapted to chimpanzees when modifications rest on both anatomy and observation. Facial musculature differs little between the species, but morphology (prognathism, heavy brows, low scleral contrast, no chin boss) changes how the same muscle actions appear, which affects detection and comparison. Systematic comparison with a common tool is needed to identify what is uniquely human. The article is about measurement and structure, not emotional meaning.
vick_2007_crossspecies.caveats: The full text was read in excerpts on the Springer site, and table contents were not visible. The AU inventory is inferred from text statements, not tables. Quotes from this source were read in excerpts; check them against the source before quoting.

parr_2007_classifying.cit: Parr, L. A., Waller, B. M., Vick, S.-J., & Bard, K. A. (2007). Classifying chimpanzee facial expressions using muscle action. Emotion, 7(1), 172-181.
parr_2007_classifying.design: 259 chimpanzee facial displays from about 100 individuals (87 identified by name), drawn mainly from L. A. Parr's database at Yerkes National Primate Research Center and from Chester Zoo and other colonies. Displays were categorized a priori by Parr using published ethogram categories, then coded with ChimpFACS by certified coders (mean agreement 0.78 on 76 displays). A discriminant function analysis (DFA) tested whether AU combinations reproduced the a priori categories. Prototypical configurations were derived from displays with over 90% probability of correct DFA assignment. Comparison with human expressions (Table 3) used FACS-coded human expressions that were posed.
parr_2007_classifying.numbers: N = 259 displays from about 100 chimpanzees. Category ns: bared-teeth 41, relaxed open-mouth/play face 31, pant-hoot 56, ambiguous 24, neutral 15, scream 34, alert 18, pout 29, whimper 11. DFA correct assignment: 71.0% overall (67.6% cross-validated); by category, scream 97.1%, pant-hoot 94.6%, relaxed open-mouth 87.1%, bared-teeth 70.7%, whimper 63.6%, alert 50.0%, neutral 40.0%, pout 24.1% (over 72% of pouts classed as pant-hoots), ambiguous 16.7%. Prototypes reported for six categories: bared-teeth (AU10+12+25, AU10+12+16+25), play face (AU12+25+26, AU12+25+27), pant-hoot (AU22+25+26, AU22+25), scream (AU10+12+16+25+27), whimper (AU12+22+25), pout (AU17+22+25). Table 3 shared AUs with humans: silent bared-teeth/smile AU12, AU25; scream/scream AU10, 12, 16, 25, 27; relaxed open mouth/laughter AU12, 25, 26.
parr_2007_classifying.conclusion: ChimpFACS can reproduce most observer-defined chimpanzee expression categories from muscle-based codes, and each category has a characteristic AU combination. The authors suggest structural homologies with human expressions (silent bared-teeth with smile, relaxed open mouth with laughter, scream with scream) and frame this as contributing to the evolution of 'emotional communication'. They explicitly limit the comparison to structure, not meaning or emotional function, and argue that homology needs several levels of analysis (appearance, muscle basis, signal function).
parr_2007_classifying.caveats: The a priori categories were assigned by one expert, so the DFA tests agreement between ChimpFACS codes and an observer's categories, not emotion. Several categories had small ns (whimper 11, neutral 15). The human comparison expressions were posed. The abstract's framing ('evolution of emotional communication') is stronger than the Discussion caveat. Quotes from this source were read in excerpts; check them against the source before quoting.

demorree_2010_face.numbers: N = 20 men (fatigue group n = 10). Correlation coefficients not verified.
demorree_2010_face.conclusion: Frowning (corrugator) muscle activity increases with task difficulty and muscle fatigue and covaries with perceived effort, so it reflects effort during physical tasks.
demorree_2010_face.caveats: Abstract only. Effort and physical load are confounded by design; facial EMG might partly reflect discomfort or general muscle co-activation rather than effort per se.

demorree_2012_frowning.numbers: N = 20; heavy 63 ± 3% vs severe 80 ± 5% peak power; facial EMG rose over time only in the severe group.
demorree_2012_frowning.conclusion: Facial EMG differentiates exercise intensities, but its tracking of perceived effort over time is inconsistent at lower intensities.

topolinski_2015_corrugator.cit: Topolinski, S., & Strack, F. (2015). Corrugator activity confirms immediate negative affect in surprise. Frontiers in Psychology, 6, 134.
topolinski_2015_corrugator.design: Within-subject lab experiment. N = 28 adult volunteers from Würzburg, Germany (21 female, 7 male; M age 26). Participants passively read 22 high-surprise and 22 low-surprise neutral trivia statements (pre-normed surprise ratings) for 6 s each during a supposed 'recreation phase'; cover story that electrodes measured skin conductance. Facial EMG over zygomaticus major, corrugator supercilii and frontalis (left side), baseline-corrected and averaged over 6 s. No self-report affect measure was taken.
topolinski_2015_corrugator.numbers: Corrugator: high > low surprise, t(27) = 2.61, p = .014, d = 0.48, 95% CI [0.06, 0.53]. Zygomaticus and frontalis: no effect (ts < 1.4, ps > .19). Muscle x trivia interaction only marginal, F(1,26) = 3.15, p = .060. Fewer than 8% of trials excluded.
topolinski_2015_corrugator.conclusion: Surprising (schema-discrepant) information elicits immediate, brief negative affect, indexed by corrugator activity, which they propose switches processing to a more systematic mode; they explicitly acknowledge the alternative that the corrugator reflects mental effort and that negative affect may be a by-product.
topolinski_2015_corrugator.caveats: Small sample, marginal omnibus interaction, a single planned test carrying the effect; no manipulation check of felt affect; stimuli may also have elicited confusion or annoyance (authors' own caveat). The absence of a frontalis response is itself relevant evidence that the brow raise is not a reliable marker of surprise.
