v3_mortillaro_et_al_2011.cit: Mortillaro, M., Mehu, M., & Scherer, K. R. (2011). Subtly different positive emotions can be distinguished by their facial expressions. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 2(3), 262–271. https://doi.org/10.1177/1948550610389080
v3_mortillaro_et_al_2011.design: Portrayed (acted) expressions: 40 audio-video portrayals from the Geneva Multimodal Emotion Portrayals (GEMEP) corpus, 10 professional actors x 4 emotions, selected for high recognition rates; actors were given short descriptions and scenarios. Full FACS microcoding of 21 AUs by two certified coders (mean agreement .86), apex rate and duration analysed.
v3_mortillaro_et_al_2011.numbers: Proportion of portrayals with AU12: pride 1.00, interest .80, joy 1.00, pleasure 1.00; with AU6: pride .70, interest .20, joy .90, pleasure .80 (Table 4). Pride: more frequent but shorter AU12 than interest (p = .031) and pleasure (p = .035), and high AU17. Joy: more frequent and longer AU6 than interest; more AU1/AU2 than pleasure. Interest: longer AU7 than joy. Pleasure: fewer AU1/AU2 than joy and pride. Main-effect F(3, 27) values about 4.6-10.6; Bonferroni-corrected pairwise tests. Definitions given to actors: joy 'Feeling of great happiness caused by an unexpected event'; pleasure 'Experiencing an extraordinary feeling of well-being or sensual delight'; pride 'Feeling of triumph following a success or a personal achievement'; interest 'Being attracted, being fascinated, or having one's attention captured'.
v3_mortillaro_et_al_2011.conclusion: Actors did not use the same expression pattern for the four positive emotions; an appraisal perspective can describe the differences; subtle differences 'may be more clearly conveyed by the dynamics of the expressions than by the presence of different AU combinations'. AU12 did not differ on the intrinsic-pleasantness appraisal contrast, which the authors take to agree with AU12 as 'the common signal for all positive emotions' (p. 268).
v3_mortillaro_et_al_2011.caveats: Portrayed, pre-selected stimuli; small N (10 portrayals per emotion); differences partly in dynamics; the authors call for tests on spontaneous expressions and note their descriptions may have shaped the portrayals. 'Joy' here is elated joy, not happiness or amusement as separate categories.

v3_gosselin_et_al_1995.cit: Gosselin, P., Kirouac, G., & Doré, F. Y. (1995). Components and recognition of facial expression in the communication of emotion by actors. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 68(1), 83–96. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.68.1.83
v3_gosselin_et_al_1995.design: Study 1: facial behaviour of 6 actors portraying six emotions in two encoding conditions ('felt' vs 'unfelt'), coded with FACS and compared with the expression of genuine emotion as described in the literature. Study 2: decoders judged emotion category and encoding condition. According to Sato et al. (2019, secondary), the actors were six Canadian drama students working from scenarios.
v3_gosselin_et_al_1995.numbers: 6 actors (drama students per Sato et al., 2019), 6 emotions, 2 encoding conditions; felt portrayals closer to genuine expression for 3 of 6 emotions. AU frequencies not obtained.
v3_gosselin_et_al_1995.conclusion: Portrayals of felt emotions were closer to genuine expression than unfelt portrayals for half of the emotions; decoders recognised the emotion category very accurately but not whether the portrayal was felt or unfelt.
v3_gosselin_et_al_1995.caveats: Full text not reached (closed access). Small sample (6 encoders).
terms: portraying emotions as felt or unfelt

v3_ekman_et_al_1990.cit: Ekman, P., Davidson, R. J., & Friesen, W. V. (1990). The Duchenne smile: Emotional expression and brain physiology: II. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 58(2), 342–353. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.58.2.342
v3_ekman_et_al_1990.design: Spontaneous lab-elicited expressions. 37 right-handed women aged 17-41 watched two pleasant films (puppy playing with flowers; monkeys playing and gorillas bathing at a zoo) and two unpleasant films (leg amputation; third-degree burn victim) alone. Full FACS coding of all observable facial activity by two trained coders (reliability established). D-smile = zygomatic major (AU12) plus orbicularis oculi pars lateralis (AU6); O-smile = AU12 without AU6. Self-report scales after films; EEG at F3/F4, C3/C4, T3/T4, P3/P4 (alpha 8-13 Hz and beta power). 34 completed all self-report ratings; 31 had some usable EEG; only 13 had both a D-smile and an O-smile during the positive films coinciding with artifact-free EEG (the N for the EEG smile comparison).
v3_ekman_et_al_1990.numbers: Frequency: more D-smiles in positive than negative films, t = 2.48, p = .005 one-tailed; O-smiles did not differ, t = 1.06, p = .15; ratio positive:negative 10:1 for D-smiles vs about 2.45:1 for O-smiles (PDF renders it '2:45 to 1'). Table 1 (N = 34; correlations of total D-smile or O-smile duration with self-report): D-smile with amusement r = .70, happy r = .59 (p < .001 one-tailed), interest r = .40, excitement r = .39 (p < .05 two-tailed), contentment r = .20 (ns); D-smile with sadness r = -.44 and anger r = -.38 (p < .01). O-smile with amusement .14, happy .18, interest .19 (ns); O-smile with disgust r = .34 is starred in the table (the star was not clearly legible in the copy read). EEG (N = 13): D- vs O-smile difference in asymmetry significant at anterior temporal (T3/T4, p < .05) and parietal (P3/P4, p < .01) sites; NOT significant at frontal (F3/F4), F(1,12) = 2.06 […]
v3_ekman_et_al_1990.conclusion: The Duchenne smile, but not other smiling, is related to 'enjoyment' (when it occurs, how it relates to subjective experience, and distinctive physiological changes). Ekman and Friesen (1982) are cited as predicting that the Duchenne smile signals any positive emotion (amusement, relief, contentment, satisfaction with achievement, sensory pleasure, or general 'enjoyment' or 'happiness'); the authors note that correlations with emotions other than amusement 'remains to be demonstrated'.
v3_ekman_et_al_1990.caveats: 'More reported positive emotion' is a between-subject correlation of smile duration with post-film ratings, not a within-person comparison of feelings during D- vs O-smiles. The positive-emotion association is mainly with amusement and happiness ratings; contentment was not associated. 'Left anterior EEG asymmetry' is accurate only for anterior temporal sites; the frontal difference was not significant, and the parietal difference (a non-anterior site) was also significant. EEG N = 13. […]

v3_girard_et_al_2019.cit: Girard, J. M., Shandar, G., Liu, Z., Cohn, J. F., Yin, L., & Morency, L.-P. (2019). Reconsidering the Duchenne smile: Indicator of positive emotion or artifact of smile intensity? In Proceedings of the 8th International Conference on Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction (ACII) (pp. 594–599). IEEE. https://doi.org/10.1109/ACII.2019.8925535
v3_girard_et_al_2019.design: Spontaneous smiles of 136 participants during elicitation of amusement, embarrassment, fear and pain (BP4D+ dataset); Bayesian multilevel models relating AU6 to self-reported amusement, controlling for smile intensity.
v3_girard_et_al_2019.conclusion: The Duchenne marker is likely an artefact of smile intensity rather than a unique indicator of genuine positive emotion.
v3_girard_et_al_2019.caveats: Conference paper; smiles only; listed here as the one BP4D-family coherence analysis found.

v3_ruch_1995.cit: Ruch, W. (1995). Will the real relationship between facial expression and affective experience please stand up: The case of exhilaration. Cognition and Emotion, 9(1), 33–58. https://doi.org/10.1080/02699939508408964
v3_ruch_1995.design: Female participants were assigned to one of three alcohol conditions (no ethanol, low dose, high dose) and shown 30 slides of jokes or cartoons; rated funniness and 'overt behaviour' (smiling and laughter) were intercorrelated with five correlational designs applied to the same data set (within- and between-subjects, with and without aggregation). N not verified. Facial coding: FACS according to Reisenzein et al. (2013; 'FACS-coded smiling (AU12; Ruch, 1995)').
v3_ruch_1995.numbers: Abstract gives no coefficients. Secondary (Reisenzein et al., 2013): intraindividual r = .71 between funniness ratings and FACS-coded AU12.
v3_ruch_1995.conclusion: The size of the face–experience correlation depends on the correlational design: within-subject coefficients exceed between-subjects coefficients, aggregation raises within-subject but not between-subject coefficients, and low correlations reported elsewhere may reflect method artefacts.
v3_ruch_1995.caveats: Full text not reached, so N, exact coefficients and coding details are unverified. Positive-emotion (humour) case only.

v3_kraut_johnston_1979.cit: Kraut, R. E., & Johnston, R. E. (1979). Social and emotional messages of smiling: An ethological approach. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 37(9), 1539–1553. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.9.1539

v3_schutzwohl_reisenzein_2012.cit: Schützwohl, A., & Reisenzein, R. (2012). Facial expressions in response to a highly surprising event exceeding the field of vision: A test of Darwin's theory of surprise. Evolution and Human Behavior, 33(6), 657–664. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.evolhumbehav.2012.04.003
v3_schutzwohl_reisenzein_2012.design: Single experiment, N = 60 adults (39 women; mean age 24.3). While participants listened to a story over headphones, the adjoining room was transformed; on leaving the laboratory they unexpectedly entered a small room with bold green walls and a red office chair that 'engulfed' their field of vision. Three conditions: alone (n = 20), stranger present (n = 19), friend present (n = 21). The first 4 s were coded present/absent with FACS-based codes for brow raising (AU1/2), eye widening (AU5), mouth opening (AU25/26), plus brow knitting (AU4) and smiling (AU12); primary coder a FACS-trained student, all videos recoded by the second author (kappas .52 to .71).
v3_schutzwohl_reisenzein_2012.numbers: N = 60. Full three-component display: 3/60 (5%). At least two components: 10/60 (17%), all brow raising plus eye widening. Brow raising and eye widening: 21% to 33% across the three conditions (no significant group differences). Mouth opening: 0% (alone) to 16% (stranger); 20% to 33% if 'Oh' exclamations are counted. Brow knitting (AU4) about as frequent as brow raising (15% to 24%). Self-reported surprise M = 8.14 (1–10); 83% rated above 7; all participants found the room unexpected; all but one believed their surprise had shown on the face.
v3_schutzwohl_reisenzein_2012.conclusion: Even a highly surprising event that exceeded the field of vision, which a refined Darwinian (visual-search) account predicts should produce brow raising and eye widening, produced the full expression in only 5% and components in only a minority; this gives no support to the Darwinian account and reinforces doubts about affect program theory for surprise. Social context did not change surprise displays.
v3_schutzwohl_reisenzein_2012.caveats: Read from the accepted manuscript (dated 2011), not the typeset version; wording may differ slightly. Coding window was only the first 4 s.
terms: affect program theory of facial displays

v3_camras_et_al_2002.cit: Camras, L. A., Meng, Z., Ujiie, T., Dharamsi, S., Miyake, K., Oster, H., Wang, L., Cruz, J., Murdoch, A., & Campos, J. (2002). Observing emotion in infants: Facial expression, body behavior, and rater judgments of responses to an expectancy-violating event. Emotion, 2(2), 179–193. https://doi.org/10.1037/1528-3542.2.2.179
v3_camras_et_al_2002.design: Cross-cultural laboratory study of 11-month-old European American (n = 23), Japanese (n = 21) and Chinese (n = 15) infants (N = 59). Infants were videotaped during a baseline episode and a stimulus episode of a covert toy-switch procedure (the expectancy-violating event). Measures were looking time, surprise-related facial expressions, bodily stilling and facial sobering, plus judgments of the episodes by naive raters. The abstract does not name the facial coding system; the same group's companion papers used Baby FACS.
v3_camras_et_al_2002.numbers: N = 59 (23 European American, 21 Japanese, 15 Chinese), all 11 months old. Primary (abstract): longer looking during the stimulus episode; surprise-related facial expressions did not increase relative to baseline. Secondary only (Reisenzein et al., 2006, p. 297): 'only 7% complete surprise displays' in this study, where a complete display means brow raise (AU1+2), upper-lid raise (AU5) and jaw drop (AU26/27). The secondary source does not say whether 7% is of infants or of episodes. The primary frequencies could not be checked.
v3_camras_et_al_2002.conclusion: Expectancy violation produced longer looking and, in some groups, bodily stilling and facial sobering, but no increase in surprise-related facial expressions. Raters still identified the expectancy-violating episode and judged surprise from stilling and sobering. The authors conclude that observer judgments of infant emotion can rest on behaviours other than prototypic facial expressions.
v3_camras_et_al_2002.caveats: The full text is closed and could not be read, so the claim of rarity rests on a secondary number whose unit is not stated. The central finding is a null: no differential production relative to baseline. Infants produce MAX/Baby FACS 'surprise' configurations in many non-surprising contexts (see Bennett et al., 2002), so 'surprise faces are rare' should not be generalized beyond expectancy-violation paradigms at this age. Cultural subgroups were small (15 to 23 infants). […]

v3_ritter_et_al_2016.cit: Ritter, R. S., Preston, J. L., Salomon, E., & Relihan-Johnson, D. (2016). Imagine no religion: Heretical disgust, anger and the symbolic purity of mind. Cognition and Emotion, 30(4), 778–796. https://doi.org/10.1080/02699931.2015.1030334

v3_ritter_et_al_2016.conclusion: Heretical disgust is felt and reported, distinct from anger, but is symbolic rather than embodied in a physical disgust facial response.

v3_kunz_et_al_2013.cit: Kunz, M., Peter, J., Huster, S., & Lautenbacher, S. (2013). Pain and disgust: The facial signaling of two aversive bodily experiences. PLoS ONE, 8(12), Article e83277. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0083277
v3_kunz_et_al_2013.design: Within-subject experiment. N = 60 healthy volunteers (30 men, 30 women; mean age 22.9). Pain block: phasic contact heat, 10 painful (pain threshold +3 °C) and 10 non-painful (threshold −3 °C) 5-s stimuli. Disgust block: 5-s pictures of three kinds: 'pure' disgust (e.g., excrement, vomit), 'pain-disgust' (e.g., mutilation; IAPS plus internet) and neutral. Block order was counterbalanced. Full FACS coding of 5-s segments by two coders (reliability .90). Similar AUs were combined (AU1/2, 6/7, 9/10, 25/26/27). An AU counted as relevant if it occurred in >5% of segments and exceeded control by d ≥ .5. VAS pain and disgust ratings, plus SAM valence and arousal.
v3_kunz_et_al_2013.numbers: Table 1, % of trials and d vs control. Pain: AU4 24%, d = 0.96; AU6/7 52%, d = 1.08; AU9/10 8%, d = .68; AU12 17%, d = 0.92; AU25/26/27 24%, d = 0.73; AU1/2 14%, d = .47. 'Pure' disgust: AU4 28%, d = 1.05; AU6/7 31%, d = 1.35; AU9/10 11%, d = .55; AU1/2 15%, d = .56; AU12 21%, d = .58. Pain-disgust: AU4 38%, d = 1.39; AU6/7 36%, d = 1.32; AU9/10 14%, d = .55. Strength (MANOVA F(6,234) = 9.39): AU4 F(2,118) = 19.63, weaker in pain; AU6/7 F = 9.11, strongest in pain; AU9/10 n.s. (F = 0.95, p = .39). Combinations differed: pain vs pure disgust χ²(6) = 20.64, p = .002; pain vs pain-disgust χ²(6) = 22.75, p < .001; the two disgust kinds did not differ (χ²(6) = 5.72). AU6/7 alone or with AU4 made up 'nearly 2/3' of facial responses to pain. Pain and pure disgust had comparable SAM valence (p = .989) and arousal (p = .562).
v3_kunz_et_al_2013.conclusion: Pain and disgust recruit nearly the same single facial actions (AU4, AU6/7, AU9/10), but they differ in how strongly the actions are shown and how they are combined. Pain is marked by orbit tightening alone or with brow lowering. Disgust is marked by brow lowering, upper-lip raise and their combination. The authors infer that facial expressions encode the specific threat, not only valence and arousal, and that observers could therefore decode them without context.
v3_kunz_et_al_2013.caveats: Induction methods were not matched: physical heat for pain vs pictures for disgust. Pain was mild to moderate (threshold +3 °C). Participants were young students. Distinctness rests on group-level frequencies and combinations within 5-s windows, not on per-trial classification. Table 1 lists AU12 for pure disgust at d = .58, above the stated d ≥ .5 cut-off, yet the text lists AU12 only for pain (bold marking not visible in the PMC text). The Methods misprint the cut-off as 'd ≥ .05'. […]

v3_tsai_et_al_2002.cit: Tsai, J. L., Chentsova-Dutton, Y., Freire-Bebeau, L., & Przymus, D. E. (2002). Emotional expression and physiology in European Americans and Hmong Americans. Emotion, 2(4), 380–397. https://doi.org/10.1037/1528-3542.2.4.380
v3_tsai_et_al_2002.design: Laboratory-elicited production (relived emotion task). N = 98 undergraduates in the Twin Cities, Minnesota: 50 Hmong Americans (HA; age M = 20.12, 52.0% female) and 48 European Americans (EA; age M = 20.65, 47.9% female). Each participant recalled and described a time they felt the target emotion very strongly, then relived it for up to 2 min, for happiness, pride, love, anger, disgust and sadness in random order; 3-min resting baseline. Facial measure: FACS (Ekman & Friesen, 1978) scored by three certified coders blind to the relived emotion and coding without sound (one fifth of tapes coded by all; mean agreement ratio 0.97, range 0.70–1.0); AUs grouped into categories: Duchenne smile AU 6+12, non-Duchenne AU 12 without AU 6; anger period: AU 4 ('general negative states including anger') plus unilateral AU 10, 12, 14 ('contempt'); disgust period: AU 4, 9, 10; sadness period: AU 4 and crying. Scored as percentage of participants showing the behaviour at baseline vs during reliving (Wilcoxon). Emotion criterion: the recall instruction plus self-rated intensity (0–8) of the target emotion during reliving; physiology (skin conductance, cardiovascular) also measured.
v3_tsai_et_al_2002.numbers: Table 2 (p. 386), whole sample, % of participants showing the category at baseline -> during relived emotion (n; Wilcoxon Z; p): anger (AU 4 and/or unilateral AU 10/12/14) 18 -> 25 (n = 95; Z = 1.10; p = .27); disgust (AU 4, 9, 10) 13 -> 25 (n = 97; Z = 2.12; p < .05); sadness (AU 4, crying) 10 -> 20 (n = 96; Z = 1.88; p = .06); happiness Duchenne 0 -> 12 (n = 98; Z = 3.32; p < .01); happiness non-Duchenne 10 -> 34 (Z = 4.00; p < .01); pride non-Duchenne 10 -> 28; love non-Duchenne 10 -> 30 (both p < .01). Sadness-associated AU combination: one instance in the entire sample (footnote 3, quoted as 'AU14+15'). Self-reported intensity during reliving, 0–8 scale, M (SD) (Table 2): anger 4.52 (1.99), disgust 4.36 (1.88), sadness 4.89 (1.73), happiness 4.97 (1.58), pride 4.87 (1.86), love 5.35 (1.80); group means (SE), Table 3: anger EA 3.91 (.27), HA 4.89 (.28); sadness EA 4.56 (.25) […]
v3_tsai_et_al_2002.conclusion: For most emotions EAs and HAs showed more cultural similarities than differences in facial behaviour and physiology; the consistent exception was that fewer HAs than EAs showed non-Duchenne ('social') smiles during relived happiness, which the authors attribute to the American cultural emphasis on emotional expression rather than to EAs masking negative emotion.
v3_tsai_et_al_2002.caveats: The categories are broad (AU 4 alone counts for anger, disgust and sadness), so the percentages overstate emotion-specific configurations; full prototypes (e.g., AU 4+5+7+23 for anger, AU 1+4+15 for sadness) were not reported separately. Relived emotion is an imagery/recall task with a social audience (experimenter, camera) and speaking beforehand, which may dampen or alter faces. v3_lerner_et_al_2007.cit: Lerner, J. S., Dahl, R. E., Hariri, A. R., & Taylor, S. E. (2007). Facial expressions of emotion reveal neuroendocrine and cardiovascular stress responses. Biological Psychiatry, 61(2), 253–260. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biopsych.2006.08.016
v3_lerner_et_al_2007.design: Laboratory-elicited production. N = 92 adults (45 men, 47 women), 18–29 years (M = 20.6), UCLA university community; ethnicity 43.5% European American, 43.5% Asian American, 8% Latino, 3% African American, 2% other. Elicitor: three 'annoyingly difficult' mental arithmetic tasks (serial subtraction by 7s, WAIS arithmetic, serial subtraction by 13s) framed as intelligence tests, with a harassing experimenter who reported each error and urged speed. Facial measure: EMFACS (emotion-relevant FACS) coding of fear, anger and disgust (frequency, intensity on a 5-point scale, duration) by FACS-certified coders blind to hypotheses (one coded all, a second coded 24%; mean agreement ratio .82); 14 segments per participant (about 5.6 min). Because upper-face fear and anger action units also signal concentration, only lower-face codes were used for inferential analyses of the stress tasks; anger and disgust were averaged into an 'indignation' composite. Emotion criteria: the elicitor plus self-report (16 emotions rated 0–8 after the tasks and during recovery). Outcomes: cortisol, heart rate, blood pressure.
v3_lerner_et_al_2007.numbers: Table 1 ('Characteristics of Emotional Expressions Displayed', p. 256), participants showing expression, stress tasks / rest (N = 92): fear 56 / 17; anger 76 / 43; disgust 30 / 11 (percentages computed here for stress tasks: 60.9%, 82.6%, 32.6%). Average frequency / intensity / duration (s), stress tasks: fear 1.39 / 1.53 / 1.07; anger 2.64 / 3.19 / 1.91; disgust .95 / 1.37 / .66; rest: fear .29 / .38 / .47; anger .41 / .81 / .36; disgust .16 / .39 / .07 (Table 1; read in excerpts). Self-report vs face (footnote 2, p. 255; comparison symbols garbled): baseline self-reported anger with lower-face anger frequency r = .27, intensity r = .35, duration r = .23 (p at or below .05/.01); self-reported disgust with disgust frequency r = .19 and intensity r = .19 (p = .07); self-reported fear not significant; at peak stress only disgust: frequency r = .21, intensity r = .26, duration r = .18 […]
v3_lerner_et_al_2007.conclusion: Stress is not undifferentiated negative affect: facial expressions of specific emotions signal biological stress responses, with fear expressions signalling elevated cortisol and cardiovascular reactivity and indignation (anger plus disgust) signalling attenuated reactivity, implicating individual differences in stress appraisals.
v3_lerner_et_al_2007.caveats: The emotion labels come from EMFACS interpretation of facial codes, so 'fear' and 'anger' expressions are defined by the face itself; self-report validated them only weakly (anger at baseline, disgust at stress), not for fear. Fear and anger expressions co-occurred in the same people. Only lower-face codes were used for stress-task analyses, so classic brow components of fear (AUs 1+2+4) and anger (AU 4) were not analysed.
