v3_camras_et_al_2007.cit: Camras, L. A., Oster, H., Bakeman, R., Meng, Z., Ujiie, T., & Campos, J. J. (2007). Do infants show distinct negative facial expressions for fear and anger? Emotional expression in 11-month-old European American, Chinese, and Japanese infants. Infancy, 11(2), 131–155. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1532-7078.2007.tb00219.x
v3_camras_et_al_2007.design: Cross-cultural laboratory study of 11-month-old European American, Chinese and Japanese infants; sample sizes per culture were not available in the abstract. Infants were videotaped in two procedures: arm restraint, designed to elicit mild anger or frustration, and a disembodied growling toy gorilla head, designed to elicit fear. Facial behaviour was coded with Baby FACS, and configurations were also evaluated against MAX formulas. Nonfacial behaviour was measured through observer judgments and objective coding of instrumental behaviour. Per Camras & Shutter (2010), both intersituational and intrasituational specificity were tested.
v3_camras_et_al_2007.numbers: Age: 11 months; three cultures. Two elicitors: arm restraint and growling toy gorilla. Per Camras & Shutter (2010, p. 125): MAX anger-related patterns were more frequent than MAX fear-related patterns in both situations, and the rank orderings of a larger set of Baby FACS-coded expressions correlated r = .50 across the anger and fear situations. Per-culture Ns and frequencies could not be checked because the full text is closed.
v3_camras_et_al_2007.conclusion: Nonfacial behaviour (observer judgments and coded instrumental behaviour) showed that the target emotions were elicited differently, but no distinct fear-specific versus anger-specific facial configurations were found. Faces were largely similar across cultures, with some differences.
v3_camras_et_al_2007.caveats: Based on the abstract plus a secondary account by the first author. The finding is a null result for facial specificity and rests on the assumption that nonfacial behaviour validly indexes the target emotion. Only two negative elicitors were used, at a single age (11 months).
terms: Baby FACS, an anatomically based scoring system

v3_shuster_et_al_2020.cit: Shuster, M. M., Camras, L. A., Grabell, A., & Perlman, S. B. (2020). Faces in the wild: A naturalistic study of children's facial expressions in response to an Internet prank. Cognition and Emotion, 34(2), 359–366. https://doi.org/10.1080/02699931.2019.1611542
v3_shuster_et_al_2020.design: 60 YouTube videos of children aged 4–7 reacting to the unexpected 'scary face' in an online maze game. Untrained undergraduates rated emotion from non-facial behaviour, and faces were coded with anatomically based facial codes.
v3_shuster_et_al_2020.numbers: N = 60 videos (children aged 4–7). Prototypic expressions were produced by fewer than half the children; exact percentages are not in the abstract.
v3_shuster_et_al_2020.conclusion: The findings give partial support for the ecological validity of fear and surprise expressions under a strong naturalistic elicitor, but prototypic expressions were produced by fewer than half the children.
v3_shuster_et_al_2020.caveats: Abstract only. YouTube videos were selected by uploaders, a biased sample likely to favour dramatic reactions.

v3_zhang_et_al_2016.cit: Zhang, Z., Girard, J. M., Wu, Y., Zhang, X., Liu, P., Ciftci, U., Canavan, S., Reale, M., Horowitz, A., Yang, H., Cohn, J. F., Ji, Q., & Yin, L. (2016). Multimodal spontaneous emotion corpus for human behavior analysis. In Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (pp. 3438–3446). IEEE. https://doi.org/10.1109/CVPR.2016.374
v3_zhang_et_al_2016.design: Laboratory-elicited production database. N = 140 (58 male, 82 female), aged 18–66, Binghamton University; ethnicity White 64, Asian 46, African American 15, Latino/Hispanic 14, other 1 (Table 1). Ten experimenter-run tasks (Table 2): T1 joke/interview (amusement), T2 3D avatar of self (surprise), T3 911 emergency call video (sadness), T4 sudden burst of sound/siren (startle/surprise), T5 true-or-false interview (skeptical), T6 silly song (embarrassment), T7 physical threat in a dart game (fear/nervous), T8 cold pressor (physical pain), T9 complained at for poor performance (angry), T10 smelly odour (disgust). Emotion check: post-task tablet self-report with 5-point Likert-type intensity ratings (Figure 2). FACS: 34 AUs coded for occurrence by five expert coders in the most facially expressive 20 s of four tasks (amusement, embarrassment, fear/nervous, pain; 560 sessions); intensity coded for AUs 6, 10, 12, 14, 17 in a subset. Multimodal sensors: 3D/2D video, thermal, physiology.
v3_zhang_et_al_2016.numbers: Table 3, AU base rate (% of coded frames) pooled over the four coded tasks, all 140 participants: AU1 10%, AU2 8%, AU4 6%, AU5 1%, AU6 50%, AU7 66%, AU9 4%, AU10 65%, AU11 41%, AU12 58%, AU14 60%, AU15 11%, AU16 33%, AU17 13%, AU20 15%, AU23 17%, AU24 4%, AU28 2%, AU30 3%, AU38 1%, AU39 1%, others 0–2%. Events: e.g., AU4 374, AU5 59, AU20 808, AU15 865, AU23 1614. Occurrence reliability (94 double-coded sessions, AUs with base rate > 5%): mean S = 0.79 (0.59 for AU11 to 0.94 for AU4). Self-report results per task: shown only in Figure 2, no numbers in the text. AU occurrence by task or emotion: not reported; the sadness (T3), startle (T4), anger (T9) and disgust (T10) tasks were not FACS-coded.
v3_zhang_et_al_2016.conclusion: The corpus is a well-annotated, multimodal spontaneous emotion resource (FACS occurrence and intensity, 3D/2D/thermal video, physiology) released to support research on expression and AU detection; the authors state that the majority-vote self-reported emotion fitted each task's intended emotion.
v3_zhang_et_al_2016.caveats: Read in excerpts; the Table 2 task–emotion alignment was partly garbled (T3 'sadness' as printed), and which four tasks were coded was inferred from the text's emotion names. Coding only the most expressive 20 s inflates base rates. Self-report results are in a figure without numbers. This is a database description, not a hypothesis test of emotion–expression coherence. DOI added later from Crossref (2026-10-21).

v3_jakobs_et_al_2001.cit: Jakobs, E., Manstead, A. S. R., & Fischer, A. H. (2001). Social context effects on facial activity in a negative emotional setting. Emotion, 1(1), 51–69. https://doi.org/10.1037/1528-3542.1.1.51
v3_jakobs_et_al_2001.design: Pairs of friends or strangers watched film clips eliciting different degrees of sad affect, in the same or different rooms; control group alone. Measures: facial activity, subjective emotion, social motives.
v3_jakobs_et_al_2001.conclusion: Social context effects generalise from smiling to facial displays in a negative (sad) setting.
v3_jakobs_et_al_2001.caveats: Full text not read; facial measurement method (EMG and/or coding) not verified.

v3_keltner_1995.cit: Keltner, D. (1995). Signs of appeasement: Evidence for the distinct displays of embarrassment, amusement, and shame. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 68(3), 441–454. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.68.3.441
v3_keltner_1995.design: Study 1 (production): spontaneous expressions following trials of the Directed Facial Action (DFA) task, in which participants posed awkward facial configurations alone in a room; for each participant only the first trial after which they reported embarrassment or amusement was coded, giving 35 embarrassment displays (23 female, 12 male) and 28 amusement displays (14 female, 14 male). Embarrassment classified from self-reports of feeling 'embarrassed, silly, stupid, self-conscious, and ridiculous'. Full FACS coding plus gaze, head and hand behaviours. Studies 2-5 (perception): observers judged embarrassment, amusement and (Study 5, 12- to 13-year-old male targets) shame displays (e.g., Study 2: 81 + 71 observers; Study 4: 187; Study 5: 183).
v3_keltner_1995.numbers: Embarrassment sequence vs amusement: gaze down 81% vs 24%; gaze down then smile control 70% vs 14%; gaze down, smile control, then head movement 46% vs 7% (all p < .01). Embarrassed smiles more often accompanied (70% vs 32%) and terminated (55% vs 14%) by a smile control. Amused participants showed more non-Duchenne smiles (71% vs 39%) and tended to show more Duchenne smiles (36% vs 17%, p < .10); i.e., Duchenne smiles occurred in 17% of embarrassment displays. Timing (Table 1): embarrassment gaze-down onset about 0.71 s; smile onset 1.95 s (embarrassment) vs 2.27 s (amusement); smile-control onset 1.46 s vs 3.02 s; whole embarrassment display about 5 s. Self-reported embarrassment related to longer gazes down (r = .51), more intense smile controls (r = .40) and briefer smiles (r = -.35). Observer accuracy above chance: Study 2 .61 (chance .50); Study 4 .57 (.50); Study 5 .53 […]
v3_keltner_1995.conclusion: Embarrassment has a distinct display that resembles the temporal pattern of emotional expressions and is distinct from amusement; the findings argue 'at least partially' for distinct displays of shame and amusement; displays are interpreted as appeasement signals.
v3_keltner_1995.caveats: Single eliciting situation (awkward posing task, alone); 'amusement' was also elicited by the same task; Duchenne smiles were not exclusive to amusement (17% of embarrassment displays). Observer accuracies were modest (.53-.61). Later work failed to find the embarrassment prototype in perception of spontaneous smiles (Ambadar et al., 2009).

v3_kunz_et_al_2012.cit: Kunz, M., Lautenbacher, S., LeBlanc, N., & Rainville, P. (2012). Are both the sensory and the affective dimensions of pain encoded in the face? Pain, 153(2), 350–358. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pain.2011.10.027
v3_kunz_et_al_2012.design: Experimental within-subject study. N = 22. Tonic and phasic heat pain was given before and after hypnotic-type verbal suggestions aimed at increasing the affective or the sensory dimension of pain. Measures: FACS-coded facial expression, pain intensity and unpleasantness ratings, skin conductance responses.
v3_kunz_et_al_2012.numbers: N = 22; tonic and phasic heat; two suggestion conditions (sensory-increase, affect-increase). Effect sizes and the exact AUs are not in the abstract. Per Prkachin & Hammal (2021): eye movements relate to sensory features, brow and upper-lip movements to affective features.
v3_kunz_et_al_2012.conclusion: Facial pain expression is multidimensional. Movements around the eyes (orbit tightening) mainly track the sensory dimension, and brow lowering and upper-lip raising track the affective dimension. The authors suggest this differential encoding may have evolved so that the specific character of pain is communicated.
v3_kunz_et_al_2012.caveats: Abstract only, so AU-specific statistics are unverified. Small N. Manipulation by suggestion: demand characteristics could act on both ratings and faces. No direct replication found in this check (not exhaustively searched). The evolutionary rationale in the abstract is speculative.

v3_jancke_kaufmann_1994.cit: Jäncke, L., & Kaufmann, N. (1994). Facial EMG responses to odors in solitude and with an audience. Chemical Senses, 19(2), 99–111. https://doi.org/10.1093/chemse/19.2.99
v3_jancke_kaufmann_1994.design: Two experiments (Germany). Exp. 1: n = 20 smelled odours in private; EMG over corrugator, procerus, nasalis, levator, orbicularis oculi, zygomaticus major. Exp. 2: experimental group (n = 10) smelled odours while visually inspected by the experimenter sitting in front of them vs control group (n = 10) in private; EMG over nasalis, levator, zygomaticus, orbicularis oculi; hedonic (valence) ratings.
v3_jancke_kaufmann_1994.numbers: n = 20 (Exp. 1); n = 10 per group (Exp. 2). No statistics in abstract.
v3_jancke_kaufmann_1994.conclusion: Facial displays to odours have a social communicative function; audience presence amplified smile- and disgust-related EMG, whereas in private pleasant odours did not evoke smiles and EMG did not track valence ratings (except strong malodours evoking disgust-related activity).
v3_jancke_kaufmann_1994.caveats: Very small groups (n = 10); experimenter as a watching audience; abstract-level.

v3_nath_et_al_2019.cit: Nath, E. C., Cannon, P. R., & Philipp, M. C. (2019). An unfamiliar social presence reduces facial disgust responses to food stimuli. Food Research International, 126, Article 108662. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodres.2019.108662
v3_nath_et_al_2019.design: New Zealand; N = 70 (52 female, 18 male) viewed food images of varying acceptability alone or in the presence of the researcher; EMG over zygomaticus major, corrugator supercilii and levator labii superioris; liking ratings on a labelled affective magnitude scale; linear mixed models.
v3_nath_et_al_2019.conclusion: Both emotional stimuli and social context influence food-evoked facial expression; an unfamiliar observer inhibited disgust-related activity but not smiling/frowning, while EMG tracked liking in both contexts.
v3_nath_et_al_2019.caveats: Stranger audience only; abstract-level; static food images.

v3_jakobs_et_al_1999b.cit: Jakobs, E., Manstead, A. S. R., & Fischer, A. H. (1999b). Social motives, emotional feelings, and smiling. Cognition and Emotion, 13(4), 321–345. https://doi.org/10.1080/026999399379212
v3_jakobs_et_al_1999b.design: Participants listened to stories varying in rated funniness, told by a friend or a stranger via tape recorder, telephone, or face-to-face. DVs: facial activity, subjective feelings, social motives; mediation tested.
v3_jakobs_et_al_1999b.conclusion: Both stimulus (funniness) and social context affect smiling; the stimulus effect was not mediated by experienced affect, whereas the social context effect appeared mediated by social motives.
v3_jakobs_et_al_1999b.caveats: Abstract-level; mediation inferences rest on self-report measures of affect and motives.

v3_hess_et_al_1995.cit: Hess, U., Banse, R., & Kappas, A. (1995). The intensity of facial expression is determined by underlying affective state and social situation. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 69(2), 280–288. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.69.2.280
v3_hess_et_al_1995.design: Laboratory experiment (per abstract) varying three factors: (1) sociality of the viewing context, (2) intensity of the emotion elicitor, and (3) relationship between expressor and audience (friend vs stranger), with intensity of facial expressive displays as the dependent measure. The first author's later summary (Hess, 2001) describes the stimuli as comedy routines; the co-author's chapter (Kappas, 2003) describes an implicit condition in which a friend watches the same funny video in a different room. The facial measure (EMG vs coding), sample size, culture/sex of participants, number of intensity levels and the exact sociality conditions could NOT be verified from a primary text.
v3_hess_et_al_1995.numbers: None verifiable from a primary text (the abstract reports no numbers).
v3_hess_et_al_1995.conclusion: Neither social context nor emotional state alone predicts the intensity of expressive displays; intensity reflects an interplay of stimulus (emotion) intensity, sociality and the expressor-audience relationship (friend vs stranger). The study was framed as a test of Fridlund's (1991) proposition that displays are better predicted by social context than by emotional state.
v3_hess_et_al_1995.caveats: Full text not readable (author PDF is an image-only scan; APA paywall). Design specifics and statistics are unverified; descriptions by the authors in later chapters are secondary. Do not cite specific numbers or the direction of the stranger effect from memory or from third-party summaries.

v3_rosenberg_ekman_1994.cit: Rosenberg, E. L., & Ekman, P. (1994). Coherence between expressive and experiential systems in emotion. Cognition and Emotion, 8(3), 201–229. https://doi.org/10.1080/02699939408408938
v3_rosenberg_ekman_1994.design: Laboratory study. Participants ('subjects') watched brief films selected to elicit disgust and fear; facial expressions were measured (FACS, per the reprint volume's title; not confirmed from the paper) and participants then rated, in a 'cued-review' procedure, how much of each of several emotion categories they had felt at many points during the film. Expression and report were compared for specific moments in film time. N and number of films could not be verified (Reisenzein et al., 2013, describe self-ratings for 'two disgusting film clips').
v3_rosenberg_ekman_1994.numbers: Abstract gives no numbers. Secondary (Reisenzein et al., 2013): pooled across emotions and expressions, the probability of the matching expression given the reported emotion was about .50; the disgust-specific statistic and correlations were not reported.
v3_rosenberg_ekman_1994.conclusion: At specific moments, facial expression and self-report showed a high degree of temporal linkage and categorical agreement, as predicted, more so for intense events; first evidence of momentary linkage.
v3_rosenberg_ekman_1994.caveats: Full text unreachable (closed access; publisher page not accessible). N, films, FACS details and numerical results unverified. The analysis was restricted to moments when expressions or reports occurred, which favours finding agreement (inferred from the abstract wording 'specific moments'; not confirmed).

v3_witkower_et_al_2023.cit: Witkower, Z., Rule, N. O., & Tracy, J. L. (2023). Emotions do reliably co-occur with predicted facial signals: Comment on Durán and Fernández-Dols (2021). Emotion, 23(3), 903–907. https://doi.org/10.1037/emo0001162
v3_witkower_et_al_2023.design: Commentary reanalysing and reinterpreting a published meta-analysis by benchmarking against meta-analytic effect sizes in personality and social psychology. Also questions inclusion/classification choices.
v3_witkower_et_al_2023.numbers: Effect 'as large as 1.5 times' the average social-psychology effect; larger than 76% of meta-analytic effects in personality/social psychology.
v3_witkower_et_al_2023.conclusion: The meta-analytic associations are large by field benchmarks and would be larger with more inclusive study selection (e.g., intraindividual designs; amusement studies for happiness).
v3_witkower_et_al_2023.caveats: Abstract only. The disagreement centres on what counts as 'reliable', which bears directly on the reverse-inference/specificity framing of Barrett et al. (2019).

v3_fang_et_al_2022.cit: Fang, X., Sauter, D. A., Heerdink, M. W., & van Kleef, G. A. (2022). Culture shapes the distinctiveness of posed and spontaneous facial expressions of anger and disgust. Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology, 53(5), 471–487. https://doi.org/10.1177/00220221221095208
v3_fang_et_al_2022.design: Production. Dutch and Chinese participants (164 university students per Gallant et al. 2026) posed anger and disgust or recounted autobiographical events eliciting spontaneous anger/disgust; activated facial action units classified with supervised machine learning.
v3_fang_et_al_2022.conclusion: Culture shapes how distinct anger and disgust expressions are, for both posed and spontaneous production.
v3_fang_et_al_2022.caveats: Abstract-level; AU coding method (manual FACS vs automated) not verified.

v3_park_et_al_2020.cit: Park, S., Lee, K., Lim, J.-A., Ko, H., Kim, T., Lee, J.-I., Kim, H., Han, S.-J., Kim, J.-S., Park, S., Lee, J.-Y., & Lee, E. C. (2020). Differences in facial expressions between spontaneous and posed smiles: Automated method by action units and three-dimensional facial landmarks. Sensors, 20(4), Article 1199. https://doi.org/10.3390/s20041199
v3_park_et_al_2020.design: 115 adults aged 18–40 enrolled in Seoul, Korea; 58 wearing glasses excluded; 57 analysed (19 men, 38 women). Within participants, fixed order: posed then spontaneous. Posed: saw a photograph of a smiling face, identified the emotion, and were asked to “make a happy face for 15 s towards the camera”. Spontaneous: watched a ~120-s film clip to elicit positive emotion ('About Time', per Figure 1 caption; a wedding scene), recorded for 60 s. Measure: OpenFace 2.0 automated AU detection and intensity (AU06, AU12) with person-specific normalisation against a neutral recording, plus 68-point 3D landmarks (CE-CLM) aligned to neutral; smiles detected by OpenFace and manually cross-checked. Analysis: repeated-measures ANOVA (posed vs spontaneous) for AU intensity; expression × side repeated-measures ANOVA for landmarks with Bonferroni-corrected pairwise tests.
v3_park_et_al_2020.numbers: N = 57 (19 men, 38 women) of 115 enrolled; 58 excluded for glasses (2.3). Smile moments: 317 spontaneous, 185 posed (2.3). AU06 intensity spontaneous > posed; AU12 and AU06+AU12 intensity posed > spontaneous (3. Results; Figure 5 caption marks the comparisons '*** P < 0.001'; means, F values and effect sizes are in Table 3, not read). Landmarks (3. Results): eyebrows left > right (P < 0.001) and spontaneous > posed (P < 0.001); eyes spontaneous > posed (P < 0.001); outline and upper face spontaneous > posed (P < 0.001; P < 0.001); mouth posed > spontaneous (P < 0.001); no significant expression × side interaction (4.2).
v3_park_et_al_2020.conclusion: The eye region was more involved in genuine (spontaneous) smiles and the mouth region in posed smiles, which the authors relate to different neural control of upper and lower face; upper-face intensity and left-eyebrow movement are proposed as indicators of a genuine smile (4.1, 4.4).
v3_park_et_al_2020.caveats: One emotion only (happiness/smiles); fixed order (posed always first); one film clip, and no check of felt emotion was reported in the text read; automated AU intensity from OpenFace 2.0, which the authors note was trained on other populations; Table 3 numbers not read; half the enrolled sample excluded (glasses); analysis used smile 'moments', and how these were aggregated per participant is not clear from the text read.

v3_schmidt_et_al_2009.cit: Schmidt, K. L., Bhattacharya, S., & Denlinger, R. (2009). Comparison of deliberate and spontaneous facial movement in smiles and eyebrow raises. Journal of Nonverbal Behavior, 33(1), 35–45. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10919-008-0058-6
v3_schmidt_et_al_2009.design: 57 adults (16 men, 41 women) from the University of Pittsburgh community; videotaped interview including a facial movement assessment. Deliberate: first smile and eyebrow raise produced on request ('raise your brows'; 'smile with your usual smile'). Spontaneous: first smile and eyebrow raise occurring elsewhere in the interview, sampled without regard to social or emotional context; emotion not assessed. Measures: certified FACS coder recorded AU6, dampening AUs (14, 15, 17, 23, 24), AU12 and speech (AU50) (inter-rater agreement .87); automated facial image analysis tracked lip corners and inner eyebrow corners for maximum speed, amplitude and duration of onset and their asymmetry. Analysis: repeated mixed MANOVA (deliberateness within, gender between), Bonferroni; smiles n = 57, eyebrow raises n = 42.
v3_schmidt_et_al_2009.numbers: Smiles (n = 57): deliberateness main effect F(3,53) = 4.89, p < .01; deliberate onsets faster, F(1,55) = 12.95, p < .01 (maximum speed); amplitude and duration n.s. (F < 2.7, p > .10). Eyebrow raises (n = 42): F(3,38) = 12.11, p < .01; deliberate faster F(1,40) = 6.65, p < .05, higher amplitude F(1,40) = 25.61, p < .01, shorter F(1,40) = 12.71, p < .01. Asymmetry: no effect of deliberateness (F < 2.00, p > .10). AU6 in deliberate smiles .56 (n = 32) vs spontaneous .97 (n = 55); dampening in deliberate .26 (n = 15) vs spontaneous .19 (n = 11). AU12 during deliberate eyebrow raises 9% (of 57 coded) vs spontaneous .29 (n = 14 of 48; the Discussion gives .25); speech during spontaneous eyebrow raises .58 (n = 28); 9 participants (16%) showed no spontaneous eyebrow raise. (Analysis and Results; Discussion.)
v3_schmidt_et_al_2009.conclusion: Deliberate smiles and eyebrow raises have faster (for eyebrows also larger and shorter) onsets than spontaneous ones, with similar symmetry, suggesting a common control mechanism for spontaneous facial signalling; the Duchenne marker can be produced voluntarily by some individuals.
v3_schmidt_et_al_2009.caveats: Not emotion-specific: spontaneous displays were sampled from an interview regardless of context and emotion was not measured, so this is a deliberate-vs-spontaneous display comparison, not a comparison of the same emotion. Only onsets analysed. Automated tracking measured point displacement after manual initialisation, not AU detection; AU6 and other AUs were FACS-coded descriptively without tests. Descriptive tables were not available in the text read. The paper gives .29 (Results) and .25 […]

v3_cohn_schmidt_2004.cit: Cohn, J. F., & Schmidt, K. L. (2004). The timing of facial motion in posed and spontaneous smiles. International Journal of Wavelets, Multiresolution and Information Processing, 2(2), 121–132. https://doi.org/10.1142/S021969130400041X
v3_cohn_schmidt_2004.design: Between-subjects comparison of smiles from two independent studies: spontaneous smiles from a film-clip (comedy) emotion-induction study (N = 48, participants alone in the lab) vs deliberate smiles from a directed facial action task (n = 33, recorded for a facial-expression image database). 81 young Euro- and African-American adults; one smile per participant (first analysable sequence). Automated feature tracking of the lip corner over the smile onset (the longest continuous increase in lip-corner displacement); AU 12 confirmed by FACS; tracked onset correlated r = 0.95 with EMG onset where both were available. Linear discriminant analysis with leave-one-out cross-validation.
v3_cohn_schmidt_2004.numbers: Spontaneous n = 48, deliberate n = 33. Onset duration about 0.52 vs 0.54 s (n.s.). Amplitude 0.051 vs 0.142 (p < .001). Amplitude-duration relation explained 69% of variance in spontaneous and 9% (n.s.) in deliberate smiles. LDA leave-one-out: 93% (timing + amplitude), 89% (timing only).
v3_cohn_schmidt_2004.conclusion: Dynamic as well as morphological features let automatic analysis 'begin to discriminate among the message values of morphologically similar expressions'.
v3_cohn_schmidt_2004.caveats: Confound between smile type and source study or setting is not discussed as a limitation in the text read. Small samples; the classifier was evaluated by leave-one-out within the same 81 smiles, not on an independent sample. Out-of-plane head motion was restricted and such smiles were omitted.

v3_hess_kleck_1990.cit: Hess, U., & Kleck, R. E. (1990). Differentiating emotion elicited and deliberate emotional facial expressions. European Journal of Social Psychology, 20(5), 369–385. https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.2420200502
v3_hess_kleck_1990.design: Two experiments with undergraduates. Exp. 1: 40 recruited (20 male, 20 female), 35 analysed (17 female, 18 male); spontaneous expressions elicited by video and imagery vs posed expressions (pose without feeling). Exp. 2: 48 (23 male, 25 female); spontaneous expressions while watching videos vs 'masking deceptions' (showing an incongruent emotion to deceive an observer); 95 expressions analysed. Emotions: happiness and disgust. Measure: FACS-identified episodes timed for onset, apex and offset; irregularity = number of onset, offset and apex phases (pauses and stepwise intensity changes). Second rater on 20 episodes; reliability for number of phases r = 0.88.
v3_hess_kleck_1990.numbers: Exp. 1: n = 35 analysed; no onset/offset/apex-time differences between posed and spontaneous expressions; posed expressions had more phases. Exp. 2: n = 48, 95 expressions; deliberate (masking) expressions had shorter offsets (significant) and onsets (marginal) and more phases for happiness, but fewer for disgust. Inter-rater reliability for phase counts r = 0.88 (20 episodes).
v3_hess_kleck_1990.conclusion: Dynamic aspects differentiate elicitation conditions. Irregularity distinguished spontaneous from deliberate happy expressions more consistently than onset or offset speed. The differences between experiments show that 'deliberate expression' has different realisations (poses vs masking deceptions).
v3_hess_kleck_1990.caveats: Small samples; only happiness and disgust. Group-level differences, with no test of classifying individual expressions. Deliberate expressions came either from posing or from masking, which behaved differently. The author PDF text has OCR errors.
terms: emotion elicited vs deliberate facial expressions
spontaneous versus deliberate emotional facial expressions

v3_namba_et_al_2021.cit: Namba, S., Matsui, H., & Zloteanu, M. (2021). Distinct temporal features of genuine and deliberate facial expressions of surprise. Scientific Reports, 11, Article 3362. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-83077-4
v3_namba_et_al_2021.design: 126 analysed videos (mostly women, UK students): Genuine (jack-in-the-box, n = 32), Improvised, External (mimicking a genuine video) and Rehearsed deliberate conditions; landmark tracking with DeepLabCut; ICA, speed and cross-correlation analyses. No self-report of surprise.
v3_namba_et_al_2021.numbers: Genuine displays had the weakest eyebrow–eyelid coupling (left side mean r about .20 vs .58 improvised); mouth opening smaller in Genuine than Improvised.
v3_namba_et_al_2021.conclusion: Genuine and deliberate surprise displays differ in temporal features; production method matters.
v3_namba_et_al_2021.caveats: Tracking of landmarks rather than FACS; 2-D video.

v3_gallant_et_al_2026.cit: Gallant, A., Mazerolle, M.-P., Pelot, A., & Roy-Charland, A. (2026). Cultural differences in the production of emotional facial expressions: A review. Frontiers in Psychology, 17, Article 1699374. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1699374
v3_gallant_et_al_2026.design: Systematic review (PRISMA; PsycINFO, PubMed, Scopus; 1972-2024; searched May 2024); 21 studies: 15 spontaneous, 4 posed, 1 both, 2 'in the wild' (classification as given).
v3_gallant_et_al_2026.conclusion: Universality is clearest for spontaneous production; cultural variation is larger for posed expressions; methods (posed vs spontaneous) drive apparent contradictions.
v3_gallant_et_al_2026.caveats: Search ended May 2024; studies such as Cowen et al. (2024) and Brooks et al. (2024) are not included.

v3_saumure_et_al_2023.cit: Saumure, C., Plouffe-Demers, M.-P., Fiset, D., Cormier, S., Zhang, Y., Sun, D., Feng, M., Luo, F., Kunz, M., & Blais, C. (2023). Differences between East Asians and Westerners in the mental representations and visual information extraction involved in the decoding of pain facial expression intensity. Affective Science, 4(2), 332–349. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42761-023-00186-1
v3_saumure_et_al_2023.design: Three experiments with Canadian (Western) and Chinese (East Asian) participants. Exps 1–2 (N = 60, N = 74): reverse-correlation mental representations of pain intensity on avatar base faces with AU4, AU6/7 and AU9/10 partially activated. Exp 3 (N = 60): Bubbles task discriminating pain intensities.
v3_saumure_et_al_2023.numbers: Exp 1 N = 60; Exp 2 N = 74; Exp 3 N = 60. East Asians needed significantly more bubbles in all intensity conditions.
v3_saumure_et_al_2023.conclusion: Cultural norms about acceptable pain behaviour shape expectations about pain faces and decoding strategies. Similar facial features may carry different intensity expectations across cultures.
v3_saumure_et_al_2023.caveats: Decoding and mental-representation study (Canadian vs Chinese observers) with synthetic avatar faces. It does not measure pain production.

v3_miller_et_al_2022.cit: Miller, E. J., Krumhuber, E. G., & Dawel, A. (2022). Observers perceive the Duchenne marker as signaling only intensity for sad expressions, not genuine emotion. Emotion, 22(5), 907–919. https://doi.org/10.1037/emo0000772
v3_miller_et_al_2022.design: Perception experiments (four experiments on sad expressions plus smile analyses) comparing ratings of Duchenne vs non-Duchenne smiles and sad expressions for genuineness, sincerity and emotional intensity. N and stimulus details not verified.
v3_miller_et_al_2022.conclusion: The Duchenne marker makes a unique contribution to perceived genuineness of smiles beyond perceived happiness intensity, but in sad expressions it only increases perceived sadness/negativity, not genuineness.
v3_miller_et_al_2022.caveats: Says nothing about whether the smiler felt anything; abstract only.

v3_etcoff_et_al_2021.cit: Etcoff, N., Stock, S., Krumhuber, E. G., & Reed, L. I. (2021). A novel test of the Duchenne marker: Smiles after botulinum toxin treatment for crow's feet wrinkles. Frontiers in Psychology, 11, Article 612654. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.612654
v3_etcoff_et_al_2021.design: Perception study with deliberately posed smiles. Stimuli: photographs of 32 clinical-trial patients (27 women, 5 men) asked to show their 'biggest natural smile' before and about 1 month after botulinum toxin injection into the lateral orbicularis oculi. FACS-certified coder (blind) scored AU6 and AU12 (kappa AU6 .875, AU12 1.00): AU12 intensity matched pre vs post (3.19 vs 3.22); AU6 present in 97% pre vs 19% post. Raters: 393 US MTurk adults (mean age 54) rated perceived emotions (happiness, sadness, anger, disgust, fear, surprise, embarrassment; 0-8), how felt, spontaneous and intense the expression was (0-10), attractiveness and age. Funded by Allergan.
v3_etcoff_et_al_2021.numbers: Post-treatment (AU6 largely absent) vs pre-treatment: happiness -0.11 (0-8 scale, p = .01), embarrassment -0.07 (p = .03), felt -0.30, spontaneity -0.25, intensity -0.24 (0-10 scales, all p < .001); no effect on attractiveness; looked about 0.9 years younger. About 3,090 observations per time point.
v3_etcoff_et_al_2021.conclusion: Duchenne smiles communicate 'genuine and more intense happiness', but removing AU6 produced only 'subtle' decreases; the strongest version of the Duchenne hypothesis was not supported.
v3_etcoff_et_al_2021.caveats: Static photographs; posed maximal smiles only; US raters; industry funding; small effects on rating scales.

v3_krumhuber_kappas_2005.cit: Krumhuber, E., & Kappas, A. (2005). Moving smiles: The role of dynamic components for the perception of the genuineness of smiles. Journal of Nonverbal Behavior, 29(1), 3–24. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10919-004-0887-x
v3_krumhuber_kappas_2005.design: Three perception experiments using realistic computer-generated (Poser 4) Duchenne smiles: onset and offset durations varied (Exp. 1), offset duration only (Exp. 2), onset and apex durations (Exp. 3). Observers rated perceived genuineness. Sample sizes not given in the abstract. Facial measure: none (synthetic stimuli; observer judgments).
v3_krumhuber_kappas_2005.numbers: Not available from the abstract (no N, no durations, no effect sizes). The direction of each effect (e.g., longer onset = more genuine, longer apex = less genuine) is not stated in the abstract.
v3_krumhuber_kappas_2005.conclusion: The timing of onset, apex and offset in Duchenne smiles affects how genuine they look to observers, consistent with Ekman and Friesen's (1982) observations about the duration of enjoyment smiles.
v3_krumhuber_kappas_2005.caveats: Abstract only (closed access). Synthetic avatar faces. Observer judgments of 'genuineness' are the outcome, not the expresser's state.

v3_nelson_russell_2013.cit: Nelson, N. L., & Russell, J. A. (2013). Universality revisited. Emotion Review, 5(1), 8–15. https://doi.org/10.1177/1754073912457227
v3_nelson_russell_2013.design: Review of cross-cultural judgment (matching) studies of posed facial expressions published 1992-2010, tabulated in an appendix; perception only; no facial measurement of expressers.
v3_nelson_russell_2013.numbers: Appendix table: 39 samples in three sections: 'Literate, Western cultures (20 samples)', 'Literate, non-Western cultures (18 samples)', 'Illiterate cultures (1 sample)'. Printed overall mean row: happiness 89.6, sadness 70.2, anger 67.3, fear 58.5, surprise 82.5, disgust 57.3, overall 70.9 (%). Group means computed here from the rows as extracted (this computation reproduced the printed overall means exactly): Western H 88.6, Sa 74.2, A 75.2, F 68.9, Su 81.3, D 64.7 (mean of row means about 76); non-Western H 91.1, Sa 66.7, A 60.3, F 48.6, Su 86.0, D 51.6 (about 67); the single illiterate sample (Burkinabe, N = 39, Dioula) H 84, Sa 51, A 33, F 30, Su 58, D 44 (about 50). No numerical breakdown by method (forced choice vs free labeling, within vs between subjects) was found in the accessible portions. […]
v3_nelson_russell_2013.conclusion: Basic emotions are not universally recognized from the face; matching scores vary with culture and language and are inflated by standard methods; without those aids scores are 'modest and subject to various explanations'.
v3_nelson_russell_2013.caveats: Main text not read (paywall); interpretive statements beyond the abstract could not be checked. Matching scores here are 'percentage of observers who matched the face with the predicted emotion'. The table mixes response formats and stimulus sets.
terms: posed, exaggerated facial expressions (devoid of context)
multiple examples of each type of expression
response format that funnels a variety of interpretations into one word specified by the experimenter

v3_crivelli_et_al_2017.cit: Crivelli, C., Russell, J. A., Jarillo, S., & Fernández-Dols, J.-M. (2017). Recognizing spontaneous facial expressions of emotion in a small-scale society of Papua New Guinea. Emotion, 17(2), 337–347. https://doi.org/10.1037/emo0000236
v3_crivelli_et_al_2017.design: Perception. Stimuli: 5 photographs of facial expressions 'spontaneously produced' by Fore individuals (Eastern Highlands Province, PNG) that Ekman photographed, labeled and published in The Face of Man (1980) as happiness, sadness, anger, surprise and disgust. Study 1: Trobrianders (Milne Bay Province; N = 32, 14-17 years) free labeling plus valence and arousal ratings. Study 2: other Trobrianders (N = 24, 12-14 years) chose from a short list.
v3_crivelli_et_al_2017.numbers: Agreement with Ekman's labels: free labeling 0-16% of observers; short-list choice 13-38%. N = 32 and N = 24 adolescents.
v3_crivelli_et_al_2017.conclusion: Trobrianders' interpretations of Fore spontaneous expressions showed low agreement with Ekman's predicted emotion labels.
v3_crivelli_et_al_2017.caveats: Abstract-level only; valence/arousal results and per-photo values not checked. Very small stimulus set; adolescent samples; between-society (not Western) comparison.
terms: choose their response from a short list

v3_lecker_et_al_2025.cit: Lecker, M., Hallock, S., Danielson, A., Van Aertrickc, M., Kindt, M., & Aviezer, H. (2025). Real-life intense fear is communicated through context, not facial expressions. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America, 122(11), Article e2414677122. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2414677122
v3_lecker_et_al_2025.design: Perception; 12 preregistered experiments (N = 4,180) with authentic videos of intense fear situations; face alone vs context without face vs full video; forced choice, open-ended, multiple emotion scales, valence-arousal.
v3_lecker_et_al_2025.conclusion: Isolated real-life fear faces have minimal diagnostic value; context is critical.
v3_lecker_et_al_2025.caveats: Abstract-level only; selection of 'fear-inducing situations' defines the criterion, not expressers' reports.

v3_nakamura_et_al_1990.cit: Nakamura, M., Buck, R., & Kenny, D. A. (1990). Relative contributions of expressive behavior and contextual information to the judgment of the emotional state of another. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 59(5), 1032–1039. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.59.5.1032
v3_nakamura_et_al_1990.design: Perception; spontaneous facial-gestural expressions (videotaped while viewing slides) paired with eliciting slides matched in 'source clarity'; 72 undergraduate receivers.
v3_nakamura_et_al_1990.numbers: Study 1: 28 raters; 18 expressions and 9 slides selected; Study 2: 72 receivers.
v3_nakamura_et_al_1990.conclusion: With clarity equated, faces dominated context in judgments of another's emotion.

v3_dawel_et_al_2026.cit: Dawel, A., Krumhuber, E. G., & Palermo, R. (2026). Faking it isn't making it: Research needs spontaneous and naturalistic facial expressions. Affective Science, 7(1), 88–103. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42761-025-00320-1
v3_dawel_et_al_2026.design: Review plus new data on perceived genuineness and naturalness of standard posed stimulus sets.
v3_dawel_et_al_2026.conclusion: Posed prototypical stimuli can answer only perceiver-response questions. Naturalistic or spontaneous stimuli, now available, are needed for questions about production and accuracy.
terms: direct readouts of internal emotional experience

v3_van_boxtel_jessurun_1993.cit: Van Boxtel, A., & Jessurun, M. (1993). Amplitude and bilateral coherency of facial and jaw-elevator EMG activity as an index of effort during a two-choice serial reaction task. Psychophysiology, 30(6), 589–604. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-8986.1993.tb02085.x
v3_van_boxtel_jessurun_1993.design: Tonic bilateral EMG of six facial and jaw-elevator muscles during a paced two-choice serial reaction task: Exp 1 constant maximal load for 20 min; Exp 2 load increased stepwise over six 2-min periods from sub- to supramaximal.
v3_van_boxtel_jessurun_1993.numbers: Not verified beyond design (20-min task; six 2-min load steps).
v3_van_boxtel_jessurun_1993.conclusion: Frontalis, corrugator and orbicularis oris EMG amplitude is a sensitive index of mental effort.
v3_van_boxtel_jessurun_1993.caveats: Abstract-level; effort inferred from load manipulation, no subjective measure mentioned.

v3_dix_gro_2023.cit: Dix, C., & Groß, A. (2023). Surprise about news or just receiving information? Moving and holding both eyebrows in co-present interaction. Social Interaction. Video-Based Studies of Human Sociality, 6(3). https://doi.org/10.7146/si.v6i3.142906
v3_dix_gro_2023.design: Conversation-analytic study of video-recorded co-present interaction (German data likely; corpus details not verified).
v3_dix_gro_2023.conclusion: Two eyebrow-raise practices (move vs hold) do different interactional work in receiving information.

v3_reilly_bellugi_1996.cit: Reilly, J. S., & Bellugi, U. (1996). Competition on the face: Affect and language in ASL motherese. Journal of Child Language, 23(1), 219–239. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305000900010163
v3_reilly_bellugi_1996.design: Cross-sectional and longitudinal video analysis of 15 deaf mothers signing to their deaf toddlers (0;9-2;8); maternal wh-questions coded with FACS (Ekman & Friesen, 1978).
v3_reilly_bellugi_1996.numbers: 15 deaf mothers; children aged 0;9-2;8. Proportions not verified.
v3_reilly_bellugi_1996.conclusion: Because the same brow action serves affect and grammar, deaf mothers initially favour affective facial expression with toddlers and switch to grammatical (furrowed-brow) marking of wh-questions at about age 2.

v3_de_vos_et_al_2009.cit: de Vos, C., van der Kooij, E., & Crasborn, O. (2009). Mixed signals: Combining linguistic and affective functions of eyebrows in questions in Sign Language of the Netherlands. Language and Speech, 52(2–3), 315–339. https://doi.org/10.1177/0023830909103177
v3_de_vos_et_al_2009.design: Elicited polar and content questions in NGT produced with neutral affect and with various affective states; FACS coding of brow AUs and intensity (Ekman, Friesen & Hager, 2002). N of signers not verified.
v3_de_vos_et_al_2009.conclusion: Linguistic and affective brow functions influence each other in NGT; conflicts are resolved by blending or sequencing, with brow lowering (AU 4) apparently dominating brow raising.
terms: linguistic and affective functions of eyebrows

v3_mussel_et_al_2013.cit: Mussel, P., Göritz, A. S., & Hewig, J. (2013). The value of a smile: Facial expression affects ultimatum-game responses. Judgment and Decision Making, 8(3), 381–385. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1930297500006045
v3_mussel_et_al_2013.design: Online study; 1,326 of 7,319 contacted members of a web-based respondent pool ('people from all walks of life'; not students) took part; mean age 39 (SD = 12.9); 61% female; country not stated (authors at German universities); no exclusions reported; preregistration not mentioned. Perception task: behaviour in an economic game. Participants acted as responders in 42 one-shot ultimatum games (pie 12 cents; offers 1–7 cents, 6 cents described as fair; real payment according to decisions, maximum EUR 1.68). Each offer was shown with a photograph of the proposer; 42 proposer identities (half female) from two validated posed sets, Lundqvist et al. (1998) and Tottenham et al. (2002), each available with smiling, neutral and angry expressions; each participant saw each proposer with only one expression (three counterbalanced lists), and a proposer's offer did not vary with expression. Static photographs posed by amateur actors; Duchenne marking and AUs not specified. Measure: acceptance rate. Analysis: 7 (offer) x 3 (expression) repeated-measures ANOVA; effects explaining under 1% of variance not interpreted.
v3_mussel_et_al_2013.numbers: Results section (read in excerpts): N = 1,326 (of 7,319 contacted). Offer fairness F(6,7950) = 848.1, p < .01, partial eta squared = .39 (acceptance 93% at 6 cents, 92% at 7 cents, about 50% at 2 cents, 44% at 1 cent). Facial expression F(2,2650) = 139.9, p < .01, partial eta squared = .10; post hoc, all three expressions differed at p < .01, smiling > neutral > angry. Offer x expression F(12,15900) = 4.4, p < .01, partial eta squared < .01 (small); expression effects strongest at 1, 2, 4 and 7 cents; smiling and neutral did not differ at 3, 5 and 6 cents. Stimulus set had no main effect or interaction. Acceptance percentages by expression are given only in Figure 2 (not read). Missing responses (<1%) were replaced with the participant's mean for that offer.
v3_mussel_et_al_2013.conclusion: A proposer's facial expression affects a respondent's willingness to accept an offer: smiles increase acceptance and thus successful bargaining and payoffs for both sides, and angry expressions decrease it; bargaining behaviour is 'not purely rationally driven'. The authors attribute the effect to perceived social intentions but did not test mediators (e.g., perceived trustworthiness) and leave mechanisms to future research.
v3_mussel_et_al_2013.caveats: Not preregistered; not a meta-analysis. Posed static photographs from standard databases (amateur actors); no Duchenne or AU specification, so this cannot speak to smile type. Stakes were very small (cents). Ultimatum-game acceptance by responders differs from trust or Prisoner's Dilemma cooperation. Acceptance rates per expression were only in a figure that was not read. Numbers were read in excerpts and should be checked against the PDF before quoting. […]

v3_wilkowski_meier_2010.cit: Wilkowski, B. M., & Meier, B. P. (2010). Bring it on: Angry facial expressions potentiate approach-motivated motor behavior. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 98(2), 201–210. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0017992

v3_krumhuber_kappas_2022.cit: Krumhuber, E. G., & Kappas, A. (2022). More what Duchenne smiles do, less what they express. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 17(6), 1566–1575. https://doi.org/10.1177/17456916211071083
v3_krumhuber_kappas_2022.design: Commentary/review re-examining the literature cited by Sheldon et al. (2021).
v3_krumhuber_kappas_2022.conclusion: The literature cited for Duchenne smiles signalling the presence, intensity, or chronic level of positive emotion is mostly inconclusive, irrelevant, incomplete or misread; the authors propose a functional view focusing on what Duchenne smiles do (e.g., favourable interpersonal perceptions) rather than what they express.
v3_krumhuber_kappas_2022.caveats: A commentary by authors with a stated position in the debate (Krumhuber co-authored M4); abstract only.

v3_waller_dunbar_2005.cit: Waller, B. M., & Dunbar, R. I. M. (2005). Differential behavioural effects of silent bared teeth display and relaxed open mouth display in chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes). Ethology, 111(2), 129–142. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1439-0310.2004.01045.x
v3_waller_dunbar_2005.design: Observational study of chimpanzees comparing rates of behaviour after the silent bared teeth display (SBT) and the relaxed open mouth display (ROM) with baseline rates, and comparing durations of dyadic play bouts with unidirectional versus bidirectional ROM. Study population, group size and observation hours were not available in the abstract.
v3_waller_dunbar_2005.numbers: Abstract only: affinitive behaviour rose above baseline after both SBT and ROM. Dyadic play bouts were significantly longer with bidirectional ROM. Sample size, observation time and effect sizes were not verifiable.
v3_waller_dunbar_2005.conclusion: In chimpanzees, SBT functions as a signal of affinity and ROM as a signal of play. Both are followed by increased affinitive behaviour, so both may share an ultimate function of social bonding, which could explain the convergence of smiling and laughter in humans. The analysis is functional, based on the behavioural consequences of displays, not on the producer's emotional state.
v3_waller_dunbar_2005.caveats: Only the abstract was read. 'Affinitive behaviour' categories and baseline definitions could not be checked. Correlational sequence analysis does not establish that the display causes the following behaviour.
terms: convergence of the two displays in humans

v3_van_kleef_2009.cit: Van Kleef, G. A. (2009). How emotions regulate social life: The emotions as social information (EASI) model. Current Directions in Psychological Science, 18(3), 184–188. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8721.2009.01633.x
v3_van_kleef_2009.design: Brief theoretical review (Current Directions). Proposes the EASI model from research on interpersonal effects of emotions in close relationships, parent–child interaction, conflict, negotiation and leadership, much of it the author's own experimental work.
v3_van_kleef_2009.conclusion: Emotional expressions regulate social life by providing information to observers. Their effect on observers' behaviour runs through inferences (about the expresser's feelings, appraisals and intentions) and through affective reactions (e.g., contagion, liking). Which route predicts behaviour depends on observers' information-processing depth and on social-relational factors such as power, display rules and appropriateness.
v3_van_kleef_2009.caveats: Scope: interpersonal effects, i.e., observer responses to manipulated, often explicit emotion signals. The model treats display rules and appropriateness as moderators of effects, not of production. The repository copy is the submitted version, so check wording against the published article.

v3_ekman_1992.cit: Ekman, P. (1992). An argument for basic emotions. Cognition and Emotion, 6(3–4), 169–200. https://doi.org/10.1080/02699939208411068
v3_ekman_1992.design: Theoretical argument/review. Proposes nine characteristics that distinguish basic emotions from one another and from other affective phenomena (Table 1) and reviews evidence for each: cross-cultural studies of judgements of posed facial expressions and some spontaneous-expression studies, primate comparisons, emotion-specific autonomic activity (Ekman, Levenson & Friesen and later work), antecedent events, coherence among response systems.
v3_ekman_1992.numbers: Nine characteristics (Table 1). 'More than 60 anger expressions' specified. Five emotions with 'robust, consistent evidence' of a distinctive universal facial expression (anger, fear, enjoyment, sadness, disgust); evidence 'not as firm' for surprise and contempt. He also raises contempt, shame, guilt, embarrassment and awe as possible further basic emotions (p. 170), and expects embarrassment's signal may be the blush (p. 191).
v3_ekman_1992.conclusion: A basic emotions framework, in which each emotion is a family of related states with a common theme and variations, organises the nine characteristics that distinguish emotions from other affective phenomena. Facial expression is the strongest line of evidence for distinguishing emotions. He states the claim as evidence of a 'distinctive, universal facial expression' for five emotions, not as a claim that every episode of an emotion produces that expression.
v3_ekman_1992.caveats: Scope: the 'evidence' Ekman cites is mostly recognition (judgement) studies of posed expressions plus some spontaneous-expression and ANS studies. Ekman's own concessions: signals need not occur ('can occur without any evident signal'); a family has many variants; positive emotions share one signal (the Duchenne smile), so not every emotion has a distinct facial signal; coherence evidence is contradictory. Quotes were read in excerpts from the PDF. […]

v3_barrett_2017.cit: Barrett, L. F. (2017). The theory of constructed emotion: An active inference account of interoception and categorization. Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience, 12(1), 1–23. https://doi.org/10.1093/scan/nsw154
v3_barrett_2017.design: Theoretical article (neuroscience-based). Derives a constructionist account of emotion from brain structure and function (allostasis, interoception, predictive processing / active inference, concepts as embodied whole-brain predictions). Reviews selected neuroanatomical, lesion (S.M., Urbach-Wiethe), meta-analytic and pattern-classification findings. Facial movements are discussed only briefly, as one class of 'core features' that instances of a category are unlikely to share.
v3_barrett_2017.conclusion: Instances of an emotion category are constructed by the brain's predictive categorisation of interoceptive and exteroceptive sensations using emotion concepts. Categories are populations of variable instances (population thinking). Degeneracy makes a shared core (including a single facial expression) unlikely. Facial muscle movements alone can never measure an emotion. Variability is the norm, and essentialism should be abandoned.
v3_barrett_2017.caveats: Theoretical and hypothesis-generating. Barrett presents the core claims as hypotheses ('My hypothesis...'; 'I hypothesize...'). The paper does not review facial production data. 'Degeneracy' is used in the biological sense (many-to-one structure–function mapping), not as a statistical concept.
terms: theory of constructed emotion (formerly conceptual act theory)

v3_crivelli_fridlund_2018.cit: Crivelli, C., & Fridlund, A. J. (2018). Facial displays are tools for social influence. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 22(5), 388–399. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tics.2018.02.006
v3_crivelli_fridlund_2018.design: Opinion/review article. Contrasts the behavioral ecology view of facial displays (BECV) with basic emotions theory (BET). Draws on signal-evolution theory and animal communication; audience effects and implicit sociality (solitary faces); field studies in small-scale societies (e.g., Trobriand Islanders' reading of the gasping face as a threat display); studies of spontaneous displays (e.g., in athletes); work on context dependence.
v3_crivelli_fridlund_2018.conclusion: BECV, an externalist, functionalist and non-mentalistic account, should replace essentialist BET. Facial displays are flexible tools that influence the behaviour of interactants (real, imagined or virtual) and act as lead signs of the displayer's contingent next actions. They are not read-outs of emotions or intentions. BECV accommodates cultural diversity, audience/context dependence and solitary faces (implicit sociality), and suits AI and social robotics. The authors predict it 'will always be a tough sell'.
v3_crivelli_fridlund_2018.caveats: The paper is a theoretical synthesis. The supporting evidence (audience effects, small-scale-society fieldwork, solitary-face sociality) is reviewed, not newly reported. The authors treat display rules as an ad hoc auxiliary of BET. They concede that some 'as yet uncertain brain processes' intermediate displays. A recurring later characterisation (e.g., Keltner et al., 2019: displays evolved to signal 'social intentions or motives instead') fits Fridlund (1994) better than this paper […]
terms: behavioral ecology view of facial displays (BECV)

v3_scherer_et_al_2013.cit: Scherer, K. R., Mortillaro, M., & Mehu, M. (2013). Understanding the mechanisms underlying the production of facial expression of emotion: A componential perspective. Emotion Review, 5(1), 47–53. https://doi.org/10.1177/1754073912451504
v3_scherer_et_al_2013.design: Short theoretical review in the Emotion Review special section on facial expression. Sets out the Component Process Model (CPM) account of facial production, with Table 1 predicting AUs for appraisal-check outcomes and modal emotions. Reviews facial EMG and FACS studies from several labs on appraisal–muscle links and on the timing and sequence of facial actions (e.g., Aue et al., 2007; Aue & Scherer, 2008; Delplanque et al., 2009; Lanctôt & Hess, 2007; Scherer & Ellgring, 2007; Mortillaro et al., 2011; Krumhuber & Scherer, 2011).
v3_scherer_et_al_2013.numbers: Table 1 (adapted from Scherer & Ellgring, 2007; values as extracted, so verify against the PDF): novelty/sudden → AUs 1+2, 5; unfamiliar/unpredictable → 4+7; intrinsically pleasant → 12+25(+38); unpleasant → 9, 10, 15, 39; discrepant from expectation → 4+7; goal conducive → 6+12+25; goal obstructive → 17+23, 17+24; low power/control → 20, 26, 27; high power → 23+25, 17+23, 6+17+24; external standards violated → 10; internal standards violated → 14. EMG timing: novelty effects at c. 100 ms and pleasantness at c. 500 ms (Delplanque et al., 2009).
v3_scherer_et_al_2013.conclusion: Facial expressions are best explained as cumulative, sequential efferent effects of appraisal-check outcomes (push effects), interacting with socially shared signal codes (pull effects). Individual facial actions are probabilistic symptoms of appraisal outcomes, not parts of fixed emotion programs. Full prototypical basic-emotion configurations are 'the exception rather than the rule'. Evidence from several labs is 'extremely promising', and the predictions are detailed enough to be falsified.
v3_scherer_et_al_2013.caveats: Predictions for coping potential and normative significance had not been tested at the time. The authors stress expression control, masking and strategic manipulation as complications and call for understanding of shared signal codes. Much of the supporting EMG evidence concerns valence/goal-conduciveness (corrugator, zygomatic) and novelty (frontalis), not the full appraisal set. Table values were read in excerpts, so check them before reproducing.
terms: sequentially accrued and cumulated appraisal results
prototypical facial configurations (of discrete/basic emotion theory)
TEEP (Tripartite Emotion Expression and Perception) model

v3_clark_et_al_2020.cit: Clark, E. A., Kessinger, J., Duncan, S. E., Bell, M. A., Lahne, J., Gallagher, D. L., & O'Keefe, S. F. (2020). The Facial Action Coding System for characterization of human affective response to consumer product-based stimuli: A systematic review. Frontiers in Psychology, 11, Article 920. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.00920
v3_clark_et_al_2020.design: Systematic review: 1,935 records screened, 55 studies included that used FACS or its AUs to assess affect elicited by consumer-product stimuli; Cochrane risk-of-bias assessment.
v3_clark_et_al_2020.numbers: 55 studies; 73% manual FACS. 53% did not validate FACS-determined affect. 11 studies (20%) at high risk of bias in at least one category; 6 with selective outcome reporting. 4 studies defined AUs divergently from FACS and 2 were unclear. 15 of 44 manual-coding studies did not report coder certification.
v3_clark_et_al_2020.conclusion: There are inconsistencies in how FACS is carried out and how emotion is inferred from AUs. Researchers should validate FACS-based affect with additional measures and follow the Investigator's Guide rules when inferring basic emotions.
v3_clark_et_al_2020.caveats: Domain-specific sample of studies. Risk-of-bias judgments were made by two reviewers.

syn.summary: People in sadness conditions showed the actions proposed for sadness (AU1 + AU4 + AU15) whole or in part in 28% (meta-analysis, 5 effect sizes), and a sad film moved no faces among 31 Japanese students. Posers use brow lowering and chin raising (AU4, AU17); observers gave lip-corner depression (AU15) alone the highest sadness ratings.
syn.posed: 28 Japanese students posing sadness showed chin raising (AU17) in 36%, brow lowering (AU4) in 21% and lip-corner depression (AU15) in 4%.
syn.spontaneous: Reliving sadness, 20% of 96 young adults showed brow lowering (AU4) or crying, vs 10% at rest (p = .06).
syn.perception: On avatars, lip-corner depression (AU15) alone drew the highest sadness rating (28.7, -100 to 100); observers only tended to use the brows.
syn.agreement: Posers use AU4 and AU17, observers AU15; felt sadness often shows nothing.

best.why: Proposed set; its parts recur, but whole or partial versions appear in only 28%.

proposed.say: Inner brows raised and drawn together, lip corners pulled down

posed.cap: of 28 Japanese students asked to pose sadness

felt.say: Mostly nothing; brows lowered in 1 of 5 people
felt.cap: 96 students; brow lowering or crying; difference p = .06

seen.say: Lip corners pulled down: the single movement observers rated saddest
seen.cap: mean sadness rating of each movement alone on animated faces

syn.summary: Cheek raising with lip-corner pulling (AU6 + AU12) appeared whole in 12% of people in happiness conditions (meta-analysis, 4 effect sizes), in judo winners almost only during interaction, and in 53% and 27% of Quebec and Gabon posers. Observers rely on AU12, and on average 89.6% matched posed smiles to happiness across 39 samples.
syn.posed: AU6 + AU12 in 53% of 30 Quebec and 27% of 30 Gabon posers; 90% of Gabonese smiled with the mouth open (AU25/26).
syn.spontaneous: Whole AU6 + AU12 in 12% of people in happiness conditions (4 effect sizes); 23 of 25 judo winners showing it were interacting.
syn.perception: Observers rely on lip-corner pulling (AU12): removing cheek raising from posed smiles lowered rated happiness by only 0.11 (0-8 scale).
syn.agreement: AU12 agrees across posed, felt and perceived; AU6 less consistently.

best.why: The pair recurs in all three types of study, but whole in only 12% when felt.

syn.summary: Posers lowered the brows (AU4 in 90% of 60), with lid tightening forming the five-country core (AU4 + AU7), but angry people showed the actions proposed for anger (AU4 + AU5 + AU7 + AU23) whole or in part in only 35% (meta-analysis, 5 effect sizes). On avatars, observers read AU4 alone as anger.
syn.posed: Brow lowering (AU4) appeared in 90% of 60 Quebec and Gabon posers, with AU5 or AU7; Gabonese most often combined AU4 + AU5.
syn.spontaneous: Young adults reliving anger showed brow lowering (AU4) or one-sided lip actions in 25% vs 18% resting (95 people, p = .27).
syn.perception: Brow lowering (AU4) alone conveyed anger on avatars; observers used lid tightening (AU7) and expected AU9 early, as for disgust.
syn.agreement: AU4 links posed and perceived anger; felt anger rarely shows it.

best.why: Core of posed anger in five countries; observers read AU4 as anger and use AU7.

syn.summary: Five-country posers lowered the brows and tightened a lip corner, lips parted (AU4 + AU14 + AU25). In film viewers, lid tightening and upper-lip raising (AU7, AU10) went with higher contempt ratings. Observers matched a one-sided lip curl (AU12 + AU14) to contempt in forced choice, not in free labelling.
syn.posed: Five-country posers: AU4 + AU14 + AU25; Gabonese used AU10 with AU15 or AU17, Quebecois mostly AU4 and AU10 among other actions.
syn.spontaneous: In 29 film-viewing students, AU7 and AU10 predicted higher contempt ratings and AU12 lower ones; contempt ratings correlated .83 with disgust ratings.
syn.perception: Observers in 10 cultures matched a one-sided lip curl (AU12 + AU14) to contempt in forced choice; free labelling elsewhere did not.
syn.agreement: Posed and perceived share AU14; AU7 and AU10 predicted reported contempt.

best.why: Lip-corner tightening (AU14), often one-sided, links posed contempt and forced-choice judgments.

syn.summary: In disgust conditions, 42% of people showed the actions proposed for disgust (AU9 + AU15 + AU16) whole or in part, the most of six emotions (9 effect sizes); upper-lip raising (AU10) ranged from 50% of 28 viewers to 0 of 22. Posers add brow lowering (AU4); observers read AU9 or AU10 alone as disgust.
syn.posed: Posing, 28 Japanese students used brow lowering (AU4, 69%) and chin raising (AU17, 25%) but rarely upper-lip raising (AU10, 4%).
syn.spontaneous: Upper-lip raising (AU10) in 50% of 28 students; of 22 horror viewers reporting disgust, nose wrinkling (AU9) in 8, AU10 in none.
syn.perception: On avatars, upper-lip raising (AU10) or nose wrinkling (AU9) alone conveyed disgust; observers uncovering faces used the mouth region.
syn.agreement: AU9 and AU10 recur in all three, but also in pain.

best.why: Linked to reported disgust and read alone as disgust; frequency varies widely across studies.

syn.summary: People in surprise conditions rarely show brow raising, upper-lid raising and jaw drop together (AU1 + AU2 + AU5 + AU26): 6% in a meta-analysis and none of 220 adults meeting surprising events in eight experiments; 57% to 75% of 28 posers produced each brow and lid action. Observers infer surprise from upper-lid raising (AU5) or mouth stretching (AU27) alone.
syn.posed: 28 Japanese students posing surprise showed AU5 in 75% and AU1 in 57%, versus 36% and 23% when surprised by a film.
syn.spontaneous: Of 220 adults meeting surprising events in eight experiments, 11% showed brow, eye or mouth components (AU1 + AU2, AU5, AU26, AU27), never all three.
syn.perception: On avatars, mouth stretching (AU27) or upper-lid raising (AU5) alone drew the top surprise ratings (67.1, 37.8 on -100 to 100).
syn.agreement: Posed and perceived actions agree; felt surprise rarely shows them.

best.why: Brow raising with eye widening: commonest combination when surprised (10 of 60), core when posed.

syn.summary: Fear portrayals by 120 posers in five countries raised the brows and upper lids (AU1 + AU2 + AU5), but only 25% of frightened people showed the actions proposed for fear (AU1, AU2, AU4, AU5, AU7, AU20, AU26) whole or in part (meta-analysis, 4 effect sizes). Observers rely on upper-lid raising (AU5), which surprise shares.
syn.posed: Five-country posers: AU1, AU2, AU5, AU7 and AU25 above chance; among 604 actor photos, one cluster resembling fear was AU1 + AU2 + AU25.
syn.spontaneous: Of 60 children (about 4-7) filmed reacting to a scary prank, 28 showed a FACS-manual fear face, e.g. AU1 + AU2 + AU5 + AU26.
syn.perception: Observers rely on upper-lid raising (AU5) and need the whole face; published models predicted fear choices at AUC .57 (chance .50).
syn.agreement: AU5 links posed and perceived fear; felt fear shows it inconsistently.

best.why: Core of posed fear and an actor cluster (AU1 + AU2 + AU25); AU5 guides observers.

syn.summary: In amusement conditions, 60% of people smiled or laughed (meta-analysis), and cheek raising with lip-corner pulling (AU6 + AU12) ranged from 15% to 100% across studies; posers added parted lips and head up (AU25 + AU53). Smiles observers judged amused more often had AU6 and an open mouth and lasted about 4 s (19 of 53).
syn.posed: Five-country posers (120) smiled with cheek raising and lid tightening (AU6 + AU7 + AU12), lips parted and head up (AU25 + AU53).
syn.spontaneous: Smile or laughter in 60% (meta-analysis); AU6 + AU12 in 15% of people being tickled to 100% of people watching a clowning experimenter.
syn.perception: The 19 of 53 smiles judged amused had AU6 and an open mouth (AU25 or AU26) more often than polite ones.
syn.agreement: AU12 in all three; posed and felt differed only in order.

best.why: AU12 appears most often; AU6 and parted lips mark posed amusement and smiles judged amused.

syn.summary: In Keltner's (1995) study, 81% of 35 embarrassment displays began with gaze down (AU64), against 24% of 28 amusement displays; 70% (vs 14%) went on to a smile held back by lip actions, and 46% (vs 7%) then moved the head. Five-country posers smiled with head down (AU6 + AU12 + AU54).
syn.posed: 120 posers in five countries smiled (AU6, AU7, AU12, AU25) with head down (AU54) and a second action dampening the smile.
syn.spontaneous: Embarrassed (35) vs amused (28): 83% vs 48% checked smiles with lip actions (AU14, AU15, AU17, AU24), 51% vs 17% lowered heads.
syn.perception: Smiles judged embarrassed or nervous (11 of 53) had more downward head pitch than amused or polite ones (101 judges).
syn.agreement: Head down links posed, spontaneous and perceived; gaze down only spontaneous.

best.why: Gaze down, a lip-checked smile, then head down separated 35 embarrassed from 28 amused people.

syn.summary: In 37 FACS studies of adults, brow lowering, orbit tightening and nose wrinkling or upper-lip raising (AU4, AU6/AU7, AU9/AU10) were pain-related in over 70%, mouth opening in about 60%; posers added stretched lips and closed eyes (AU20, AU43). Observers' pain models in two cultures share AU4, AU6, AU9, AU10 and AU20.
syn.posed: Five-country posers: brows lowered, eyes tightly closed, lips stretched and parted (AU4, AU6, AU7, AU20, AU25, AU43), head up or down.
syn.spontaneous: Heat pain drew orbit tightening (AU6/AU7) in 52% of 5-s segments in 60 adults; disgust pictures drew it in 31%.
syn.perception: Pain models from 40 Western and 40 East Asian observers shared brow, cheek, nose and lip actions (AU4, AU6, AU9, AU10, AU20).
syn.agreement: AU4 and AU6 in all three; AU9/AU10 felt and perceived only.

best.why: Pain-related in over 70% of 37 FACS studies; observers' pain models share AU4, AU6, AU9, AU10.

syn.summary: Among 87 sighted and 53 blind Olympic and Paralympic judo athletes, winners tilted the head back (AU53; d = 0.84, 1.11), smiled and expanded the chest more than losers; pride was not measured. All 10 actors portraying pride smiled (AU12), and observers in three countries read smile, head back and expanded posture as pride.
syn.posed: All 10 actors portraying pride smiled (AU12), 7 with cheek raising (AU6); other posers added head back and expanded posture.
syn.spontaneous: Judo winners tilted the head back more than losers (87 sighted athletes, d = 0.84; 53 blind, d = 1.11); pride was not measured.
syn.perception: US, Italian and Burkinabe observers recognized pride from a small smile (AU12), head tilted back (AU53) and expanded posture (abstracts only).
syn.agreement: Smile and head back recur in posed, post-victory and perceived pride.

best.why: Small smile with head back recurs after wins, in portrayals and in recognized pride displays.

syn.summary: Posers in five countries showed brow lowering, chin raising and head down (AU4 + AU17 + AU54) for shame, and reviews describe head and gaze down (AU54 + AU64) as recognized across cultures. Yet losing Olympic judo athletes slumped the shoulders (d = 0.82, 87 sighted) without lowering the head more than winners.
syn.posed: 120 posers in five countries: brow lowering, chin raising, head down (AU4 + AU17 + AU54); Gabonese posers lowered head and gaze.
syn.spontaneous: In 87 sighted judo athletes, losing predicted slumped shoulders (d = 0.82) and a narrowed chest, not head tilt down or face hiding.
syn.perception: Shame ratings of 39 airport videos (98 students) tracked brow, lid and lip actions (AU2, AU5, AU7, AU20, AU25) in exploratory models.
syn.agreement: Posed head down lacks spontaneous support; perceived actions differ from posed.

best.why: Head and gaze down recur in posed shame and reviews; losers' heads did not drop.

felt.say: No facial action: losing predicted slumped shoulders and a narrowed chest
