display.label: solicit affiliation or play (social motive)
display.gloss: Fridlund's behavioural ecology view (1994) reads the face usually called happy as a bid for affiliation or play, not felt happiness.

display.label: recruit succor or help (social motive)
display.gloss: Fridlund's behavioural ecology view (1994) reads the face usually called sad as recruiting comfort or help from others, not felt sadness.

display.label: threaten or deter (social motive)
display.gloss: Fridlund's behavioural ecology view (1994) reads the face usually called angry as a threat display meant to deter, not felt anger.

display.label: signal submission or withdrawal (social motive)
display.gloss: Fridlund's behavioural ecology view (1994) reads the face usually called fearful as signalling likely submission or retreat, not felt fear.

social motive: indicate rejection/intent.label: social motive: indicate rejection/intent to expel

display.label: rejection, intent to expel (social motive)
display.gloss: Fridlund's behavioural ecology view (1994) reads the face usually called disgusted as signalling rejection or intent to expel, not felt disgust.

display.label: sudden or unpredictable event (appraisal)
display.gloss: An appraisal result in Scherer's component process model: the event seems sudden or unpredictable. Its facial actions are theoretical predictions.

display.label: intrinsically unpleasant event (appraisal)
display.gloss: An appraisal result in Scherer's component process model: the stimulus itself is unpleasant. For fear, the model leaves this check open.

display.label: goal obstructiveness (appraisal)
display.gloss: An appraisal result in Scherer's component process model: the event obstructs the person's goals or needs. Its facial actions are theoretical predictions.

display.label: low coping potential (appraisal)
display.gloss: An appraisal result in Scherer's component process model: little power or control to cope. Its facial actions are theoretical predictions.

display.label: suppressing or masking expressions
display.gloss: Group used here: studies of hiding, inhibiting or masking expressions, such as instructed suppression during films (Gross & Levenson, 1993, 1997).

display.label: facial feedback on own feelings
display.gloss: Group used here: studies testing whether producing or blocking facial actions changes one's own feelings, e.g., pen-in-mouth tasks (Strack et al., 1988).

display.label: trust and cooperation
display.gloss: Group used here: studies of whether facial displays, mostly smiles, raise trust or cooperation, often in economic games such as the trust game.

display.label: rapport and reciprocity
display.gloss: Group used here: studies of how smiles, mimicry and responsive listener faces build rapport or are returned in interaction.

display.label: perceived strength, formidability
display.gloss: Sell et al. (2014): students picked which computer face looked physically stronger after single anger-face actions were added.

display.label: competitive intent (baseball pitchers)
display.gloss: Faces read as signalling a competitor's next move: students rated professional baseball pitchers' anger and predicted pitches (Cheshin et al., 2016).

display.label: vigilance, risk assessment (anxiety)
display.gloss: Perkins et al. (2012) argue a posed anxiety expression with darting eyes and head swivels serves risk assessment, by analogy to rodents.

display.label: positive emotion (type unspecified)
display.gloss: Positive emotion in general, no specific emotion named: EMFACS-coded faces of bereaved spouses in interviews (Bonanno & Keltner, 1997).

display.label: signalling distress or need (tears)
display.gloss: Provine et al. (2009): observers rated faces with visible tears and the same faces with tears digitally removed.

display.label: eliciting help or support
display.gloss: Group used here: studies linking faces to helping, mainly whether tears, sadness or pain displays draw help (e.g., Balsters et al., 2013).

display.label: mixed emotional expressions
display.gloss: Two emotional expressions at once, EMFACS-coded during a social-exclusion game; more frequent in borderline personality disorder (Staebler et al., 2011).

display.label: engagement, flow (while learning)
display.gloss: A learning-centred affective state judged during a 32-minute session with the AutoTutor computer tutor (D'Mello & Graesser, 2010).

display.label: several emotions pooled
display.gloss: Category used here for results pooled across several emotions, such as overall recognition accuracy, rather than for one emotion.

display.label: emotion not specified
display.gloss: Category used here for results whose emotion the source did not specify, such as overall facial expressiveness in a patient group.

display.label: loss in a gamble (appraisal)
display.gloss: Losing feedback in a computer gambling task, treated by Gentsch et al. (2015) as a goal-obstructive appraisal in Scherer's model.

power appraisal (low vs. high control ov.label: power appraisal (low vs. high control over outcome)

display.label: power appraisal (choice over outcome)
display.gloss: Gentsch et al. (2015) let gamblers choose the outcome (high power) or not (low power), following Scherer's appraisal model.

display.label: control appraisal (gambling task)
display.gloss: Perceived control over gambling outcomes, varied across blocks in Gentsch et al.'s (2015) second experiment; an appraisal in Scherer's model.

display.label: goal obstacle (appraisal)
display.gloss: Smith's (1989) 'perceived goal obstacles': judging that something blocks one's goals, varied in imagined scenarios while recording brow-frown activity.

display.label: caused by someone else (appraisal)
display.gloss: Smith's (1989) 'other-agency' appraisal, judging that someone else caused the event; imagined scenarios showed no link with brow frowning.

display.label: viewer's emotion-recognition ability
display.gloss: The viewer's own emotion-perception skill, related to their corrugator responses to emotion videos by Künecke et al. (2014).

positive vs negative valence (peak-inten.label: positive vs negative valence (peak-intensity spontaneous reactions)

display.label: valence of peak-intensity reactions
display.gloss: Whether isolated faces at peak intensity, such as winners' and losers', looked positive or negative to observers (Aviezer et al., 2012).

positive vs negative valence (compound f.label: positive vs negative valence (compound face+body manipulation)

display.label: valence (face on mismatched body)
display.gloss: How positive or negative observers rated winners' or losers' faces placed on bodies from the opposite outcome (Aviezer et al., 2012).

display.label: emotional intensity (eye movement)
display.gloss: How East Asian observers' mental representations of expressions signalled emotional intensity: with distinctive dynamic eye activity (Jack et al., 2012).

display.label: happy, delighted (data pattern)
display.gloss: One of four patterns underlying 62 expression models built from observers' judgments (Jack et al., 2016): AU6 + AU12.

display.label: shame, anguish (data pattern)
display.gloss: One of four patterns underlying 62 expression models built from observers' judgments (Jack et al., 2016): AU4 + AU20 + AU43.

display.label: surprise, excited, ecstatic (data pattern)
display.gloss: One of four patterns underlying 62 expression models built from observers' judgments (Jack et al., 2016): AU5 + AU26.

display.label: rage, fury (data pattern)
display.gloss: One of four patterns underlying 62 expression models built from observers' judgments (Jack et al., 2016): AU9 + AU10.

display.label: low power (inferred appraisal)
display.gloss: Low end of the power appraisal that observers rated from avatar faces (Scherer et al., 2018), read as submissiveness.

display.label: high power, confrontation (inferred appraisal)
display.gloss: High power and readiness to confront, an appraisal observers could attribute to avatar faces in Scherer et al. (2018).

display.label: threat (face picked as most threatening)
display.gloss: Crivelli et al. (2016): Trobrianders picked the gasping face (wide eyes, open mouth) as most threatening; Spanish adolescents picked the scowl.

display.label: valence (pleasant vs unpleasant)
display.gloss: Pleasant versus unpleasant feeling while viewing scenes; Höfling et al. (2020) compared FaceReader's valence score with EMG and self-report.

display.label: valence (positive vs negative pictures)
display.gloss: Whether software (AFFDEX, FACET) classified reactions to positive or negative pictures correctly as positive or negative (Stöckli et al., 2018).

display.label: sweet taste (liked)
display.gloss: Facial reactions to sweet solutions in newborns (Rosenstein & Oster, 1988) and other primates (Steiner et al., 2001), read as liking.

display.label: sour taste (disliked)
display.gloss: Newborns' facial reactions to a sour citric-acid solution two hours after birth: negative upper-face actions with lip pursing (Rosenstein & Oster, 1988).

display.label: bitter taste (disliked)
display.gloss: Facial reactions to bitter quinine in newborns (Rosenstein & Oster, 1988) and other primates (Steiner et al., 2001), read as aversive.

display.label: odour reaction (disgust-like)
display.gloss: Newborns' nose wrinkling and upper-lip raising (AU9, AU10), which distinguished vanillin from butyric acid odour (Soussignan et al., 1997).

display.label: odour reaction (general)
display.gloss: Newborns' overall facial and breathing changes to odours; Soussignan et al. (1997) found no convincing sign they judged odours as adults do.

display.label: leniency toward a wrongdoer
display.gloss: How lenient observers were toward a person accused of academic misconduct, shown smiling or neutral (LaFrance & Hecht, 1995).

display.label: warmth and competence impressions
display.gloss: How warm and competent a marketer seemed with a broad versus slight smile, in photos and videos (Wang et al., 2017).

display.label: listener feedback (backchannel)
display.gloss: Group used here: signals listeners give while someone else talks, such as nods, blinks and brow raises, showing attention or understanding.

display.label: emphasis on words (prominence)
display.gloss: Group used here: facial actions, mostly brow raises, that accent words in speech or make them more prominent (e.g., Krahmer & Swerts, 2007).

display.label: turn-taking and stance shifts
display.gloss: Group used here: facial signals that open a turn or shift stance, e.g., a smile before speaking (Kaukomaa et al., 2013).

display.label: word search, thinking
display.gloss: Group used here for signs of thinking or searching for words; here, gaze shifts away during self-directed questions (Nota et al., 2023).

display.label: grammar marking in sign language
display.gloss: Facial actions that are part of sign-language grammar, e.g., Israeli Sign Language conditionals (Dachkovsky, cited by Pfau & Quer, 2010).

display.label: play face (relaxed open mouth)
display.gloss: A chimpanzee play display; its typical actions in chimpanzee FACS are AU12 + AU25 + AU26 (Parr et al., 2007).

display.label: acute sickness (endotoxin injection)
display.gloss: Short-term sickness induced by injecting endotoxin (LPS); naive observers rated these faces against placebo faces (Axelsson et al., 2018).

display.label: physical exertion, effort
display.gloss: Effort during physical work, such as leg extensions or cycling; de Morree and Marcora (2010, 2012) recorded corrugator (brow-lowering) muscle activity.

display.label: stress from performance demands
display.gloss: Stress induced by demanding performance tasks; Dinges et al. (2005) tracked brow and mouth movements with 3-D face-tracking software.

display.label: taste reactions (sweet, bitter, bitter-sweet)
display.gloss: FACS-coded facial reactions to sweet, bitter and bitter-sweet tastes, before and after inducing joy or sadness (Greimel et al., 2006).

display.label: visual attention (fewer blinks)
display.gloss: Attention while watching a video story, indexed by blinking (AU45) less often than at rest (Nakano et al., 2009).

expectation violation (schema-discrepant.label: expectation violation (schema-discrepant information; authors frame as a negative-affect account of surprise)

display.label: expectation violation (surprising trivia)
display.gloss: Reading surprising trivia statements; Topolinski and Strack (2015) found more corrugator (brow-lowering) activity and read surprise as immediately negative.

display.label: muscle fatigue during exercise
display.gloss: Arm-curl sets taken to muscle failure; Uchida et al. (2018) tracked lip-corner pulling (AU12) and forehead muscle activity as fatigue grew.

display.label: reaction to unpleasant taste, odour
display.gloss: Adults' FACS-coded facial reactions to unpleasant tastes and odours, reported together in the abstract of Weiland et al. (2010).

display.label: wh-questions in ASL
display.gloss: Questions such as who, what and where in American Sign Language, which its grammar marks with furrowed brows (Reilly & Bellugi, 1996).

display.label: questions in Dutch sign language
display.gloss: Yes/no and content questions in Sign Language of the Netherlands, marked by brow actions (de Vos et al., 2009).

display.label: smiling photo of a partner
display.gloss: Players saw a photo of their game partner smiling or not (Scharlemann et al., 2001; Mussel et al., 2013).

display.label: smile genuineness (as rated)
display.gloss: How genuine senders judged a trust-game partner's smile in a short video, on an 8-point scale (Centorrino et al., 2015).

display.label: posed angry face
display.gloss: An actor's posed angry face, shown in a 6-second clip to ultimatum-game proposers (Reed et al., 2014).

display.label: affiliation in chimpanzees
display.gloss: Affinitive (friendly) behaviour between chimpanzees after silent bared-teeth and relaxed open-mouth displays (Waller & Dunbar, 2005).

display.label: social motives (behavioural ecology view)
display.gloss: In the behavioural ecology view, facial displays are social tools signalling contingent next actions, not emotion readouts (Crivelli & Fridlund, 2018).

display.label: appraisals (component process model)
display.gloss: Evaluations of events, such as novelty or goal obstruction, that componential theory links probabilistically to facial actions (Scherer et al., 2013).

relspec.notes: ORIGIN OF THE 'ABOUT 35%' FIGURE. A random-effects weighted mean, across k = 5 effect sizes, of the proportion of PARTICIPANTS in anger-eliciting samples who showed the whole or any part of the predicted anger expression. It is not a proportion of time or of episodes, and it is not specific to a full scowl: a study reporting only one component (e.g., brow lowering) counts. The CI is wide (.14-.64). Anger contributed no data to the whole-expression-only meta-analysis (MA1). The MA3 correlation for anger was r = .18 [.07, .28] (k = 10). Per-study N, coding systems and countries for the 5 anger effect sizes are only in the supplementary database (not read). Barrett (2022) glosses this as 'study participants partially scowl about 35% of the time'; Barrett (WSJ, 2024) as 'in Western cultures, they scowl about 35% of the time'. Effect size defined as 'the proportion prp of participants in the experimental sample who displayed the predicted expression' (manuscript p. 10). Whole expression = 'a facial display that included all the facial movements predicted by Ekman and Friesen'; partial = 'a part of the predicted facial pattern' (p. 6). Page/table numbers refer to the author manuscript in the UDIMA repository (read only as a summary with short quoted excerpts), not to the typeset Emotion 21(7):1550-1569. No non-target (other-emotion or neutral) conditions were pooled, so specificity / P(emotion | expression) cannot be derived; the authors note 'the absence of systematic information about unpredicted facial movements observed in the experiments' (p. 32). Totals for all analyses: 55 articles, 69 studies, 110 effect sizes, 3847 participants (p. 8); N per analysis/subgroup not reported. Amusement was analysed separately, not as part of happiness.

debate.title: Emotions do reliably co-occur with predicted facial signals
debate.quote: The data that they report indicate an association of substantial magnitude—as large as 1.5 times the size of the average effect in social psychology and larger than 76% of meta-analytic effects previously reported throughout personality and social psychology

debate.title: Basic emotions do not reliably co-occur with predicted facial expressions
debate.quote: They claimed that similar degrees of correlation are found in other areas of psychology, but they confuse co-occurrence of two intrinsic manifestations of the same event (expression and experience of emotion) with the correlation between one potential causal antecedent and an observed event
